Whether explained horizontally or vertically, they are all contained within the sphere of *Complete Enlightenment*.

Yet, some insist on scrutinizing every single character without seeking the essential point, merely following in the footsteps of their predecessors; they have already fallen into a secondary meaning. This is to be "complete" all day long [without ever realizing it].
Although one has awakened, it has not been long since that awakening was perfected; how much less so for those who speak of awakening based upon illusion?
Qi has long been devoted to this sutra and has perused all its commentaries. Incidentally, through the dregs [of these works], he suddenly realized the essence of the rich wine.

He respectfully takes the Imperial Commentary by Emperor Xiaozong, along with the lectures, exegeses, hymns, and verses of various great masters of the Dharma, and classifies them for inclusion here, carving them into printing blocks. May it be that—
He shared this with those of high virtue. Like the waters of the great ocean, they were drawn at will for refreshment;

Truly, there are those whose faculties are sudden. To say that one discards the trap to obtain the fish is still like a phantom cataract falsely perceiving emptiness.
Flowers! If you insist on marking the boat to seek the sword, then both illumination and awareness will be called obstacles. Today, I shall speak through to you face-to-face:

it is because of revolving in birth and death that it is called ignorance (*avidyā*). If there were no revolving, only then would it be awakening. Do not attempt to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow;

The Mañjuśrī Chapter: One suddenly awakens to the originally present, perfect, and wondrous mind of *bodhi*; realizing that ignorance and the cycle of birth and death have never existed from the beginning is what is called "faith and understanding," which constitutes the cause for the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment.

The Samantabhadra Chapter: Because the principle of awakening through cultivation is difficult to clarify, it is necessary to provide an inquiry and explanation to enable one to understand the application of the mind.

The Universal Eye Chapter: It reveals that the body and mind lack inherent nature; thus, the principle of the two kinds of emptiness (*dharma-śūnyatā* and *pudgala-śūnyatā*) becomes manifest, as do the sense organs, their objects, and all phenomena.

Universally pure and all-pervading, one perceives the objective realm as identical to that of the Buddha. In the "Vajragarbha" chapter, one is led to a profound realization of saṃsāra and to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox;

thus, the text provides both inquiry and explanation. In the "Maitreya" chapter, one exhaustively investigates the root source of the revolving cycle and examines the various lineages of spiritual capacity, leading one to sever craving and attachment.

In the "Viśuddhamati" chapter, having already understood that there is no distinction between defilement and purity within Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodhi*), one discerns the stages of practice and realization in accordance with this truth. In the "Vīra" [chapter]...

The Chapter on the Sovereignty of Virtue: Since the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ and the thickness of their afflictions is unequal, three gates of contemplation are established so that they may enter according to their faculties.

The Chapter on Discerning Sounds: Based upon the aforementioned three contemplations, it demonstrates the interlacing web of these observations, so that each may accord with the Dharma according to what is appropriate for them.

The Chapter on Purifying Karmic Obstructions: Calculating the depth and shallowness [of practice], one distinguishes the four marks of the self (*ātman*). If one eliminates attachment to the self, this is precisely Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

The Chapter on Universal Enlightenment: Following the previous removal of obstructions, one applies the intention for cultivation and relies upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to avoid drowning in the four maladies.
As well as all subtle afflictions. In the "Chapter on Perfect Enlightenment," one sets a fixed period for the practice hall and applies effort and cultivation to seek realization and entry.

Those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities all universally return to Perfect Enlightenment. In the "Chapter on the Foremost of the Virtuous and Good," the Dharma of the True Teaching has already been fully explained regarding its principles and meanings.

*A Collected Commentary on the Verses of the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhichitta-sūtra-nītārtha-sūtra*.
Lecture Notes.
The Imperial Commentary states: "Mahāvaipulya" (Great Vaipulya) refers to an expanse that is immeasurable and boundless.

This is because the essence of the Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) pervades the entire Dharma-realm, much like the vastness of a great square. "Perfect" (*pari*) signifies complete and perfect illumination;

"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) signifies empty, luminous, and numinous awareness. Regarding "Sūtra," according to various commentaries and sub-commentaries, it is a term that encompasses all scriptures. It is "complete" (*liao*).
Regarding the *Yijing* (The Scripture on the Meaning): it praises this single scripture as the meaning of ultimate and thorough realization.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xichuan’s *Classified Explanation of the Lecture Notes* states: "The title of the scripture consists of eleven characters, which are explained through eight meanings:
first, in terms of essence and function; second, in terms of phenomena and principle; third, in terms of subject and object; fourth, in terms of name and meaning; fifth, in terms of establishment..."

[The text consists of] eight sections: first, the essence and function; second, the title; third, the meaning of the title; fourth, the purpose; fifth, the outline; sixth, the selection and rejection; seventh, the interrogation; eighth, the summary. Regarding the first, the essence and function:

within this, there is both the arising of function from essence and the subsuming of function into essence. Specifically, the two characters "Da" (Great) and "Zi" (Letter) belong to the essence, while the two characters "Fangguang" (Vast and Broad) belong to the function.
This is the arising of function from essence. Next, the two characters "Yuanjue" (Perfect Enlightenment) belong to the essence, followed by the character "Shang" (Supreme).
The three characters "Vaipulya" (fangguǎng) pertain to function; this is to subsume function back into essence. Second, regarding the meaning of the Dharma (*dharmārtha*):
in order to explain various sutras and treatises, one must clearly elucidate the meaning of the Dharma. By interpreting the meaning in reliance upon the Dharma, the meaning becomes distinct;

by illuminating the Dharma through the meaning, the Dharma becomes manifest. Within the title of the present sutra, the two characters "Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuanjue*) pertain to its Dharma, while "Great" (*dà*) and "Square" (*fāng*)...

The three characters "vast" (*guǎng*) pertain to its meaning; that is, upon the Dharma of original enlightenment—which is, in its very essence, void and luminous, vast, and eternally abiding—there exist these meanings of greatness, direction, and expansiveness.
Next, the single character "sutra" (*jīng*) pertains to its teaching.
The five characters "Śūtra-artha-nītārtha" (脩多羅了義) signify the excellence of the capacity of the teaching. Regarding the third point, the "subject and object":

the six characters "Sūtra-artha-nītārtha-sūtra" (脩多羅了義經) belong to the expressive text (*vyañjana*), while the five characters "Mahāvaipulya-pariniṣpanna-bodhi" (大方廣圓覺) belong to the expressed meaning (*artha*).
Furthermore, there is a distinction between the general and the specific; the three characters "Śūtra" (脩多囉) [represent the general].

"Belonging to the whole" (*zong*) refers to the entirety of the teachings given during the Buddha’s lifetime. "The three characters of the definitive sūtras" (*liao-yi jing*) belong to the specific (*bie*).

This means they specifically praise this *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), stating that among all the various sections of the teachings given during the Buddha’s lifetime, this sūtra proclaims the supreme truth—the definitive, ultimate meaning—and does not proclaim the provisional meanings of worldly cause and effect.
It is said: "Sūtra" (脩多羅) is a general term referring to all sections [of the canon], whereas "Definitive Meaning" (了義) is a specific praise for this particular text.
Regarding the fourth [part], the name and meaning, it is further divided into two: first the Chinese (唐), and subsequently the Sanskrit (梵).

This refers to the eight characters of the *Mahāvaipulya-bodhimaṇḍala-samyak-artha-sūtra*, which are the Chinese (唐) terms for this land. The three characters "Sūtra" (脩多羅) are the Sanskrit words from the Western Regions.

Furthermore, "Great" (Mahā) is named according to its essential nature; "Eternal" (Nitya) and "Pervasive" (Vyāpin) are its meanings. The enlightened nature of this essential body is boundless, and thus it is conventionally termed "Great.

"Eternal" means vertically penetrating the three periods of time; "Pervasive" means horizontally encompassing the ten directions. "Direction" (Dik) is named in relation to phenomena; its meaning is "guidance" and "sustenance.
As for "guidance," it provides a standard that gives rise to understanding in sentient beings, enabling them to awaken to and enter the Buddha's wisdom.
"Seeing" refers to this. "Holding" means maintaining its own nature; within the ocean of birth and death, this nature has never arisen or ceased.
"Extensive" is named from its function; its meaning is encompassing and broad. "Encompassing" means having no exterior; "broad" means universal.
"Perfect" is named from its lack of partiality; its meaning is complete and all-sufficient. "Awakened" is named from its lack of obscurity; it is empty and luminous.
"Numinous illumination" (*lingzhao*) constitutes its meaning. These [explanations] all interpret the names and meanings according to the Chinese language.

Next, *sūtra* is translated as "Sutra of Accordance" (*qijing*). "Accordance" (*qi*) means to accord with reality, to harmonize with the capacities [of sentient beings], and to conform to principle. "Sutra" (*jing*) carries the sense of "stringing together" and the sense of "upholding.
This refers to stringing together the teachings spoken by all Buddhas and upholding all sentient beings.
Therefore, it is titled the *Mahāvaipulya-bodhimaṇḍala-pariniṣpanna-sūtra-nītārtha*. Fifth, regarding the establishment of the title:
generally, the titles of various sūtras are established either by the Buddha himself, by the compilers, or by both.
As for the title of this present sūtra, according to the five names found in the "Chapter of Worthy Leader" (*Bhadrapāla*) below, the first is "Mahā... [The text continues with the remaining names].
It is called the Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment Dhāraṇī; second, the Sūtra of Definitive Meaning; third, the King of Secret Samādhis;
fourth, the Tathāgata’s Decisive Realm; and fifth, the Distinctions of the Self-Nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Inferring from this, we know that the title of this sūtra was established by the Buddha himself. Regarding the sixth point, "Inclusion and Exclusion":
although there are five names within the sūtra, only two are adopted for the primary title.

This is because the fundamental principle and its functional manifestation constitute the grand framework of the dharma’s meaning, while the explanatory indications and their capacities serve as the clear mirror for words and images; thus, these matters are exhaustive.
The meaning is exhausted. One must establish five names to provide a concise title, yet only two designations are retained;
thus, the first two are preserved while the latter three are omitted. This is the skillful intent of the translator. Regarding the seventh section on objections, it is further divided into two parts:

first, an objection to the main title, and second, an objection to the specific title. The objection to the main title states: "Sūtra" and "Jing" (scripture) are merely the Chinese and Sanskrit [terms for the same thing].

The phrasing of these two titles differs. Now, that both titles are placed side by side—is this not redundant? Answer: The former refers collectively to all the various sections (or divisions), whereas this one specifically names only the present sutra.
Since it praises the specific in contrast to the general, there is no redundancy. Next, within the critique of the specific title, it is further divided into two parts:
first, the critique of the meaning of "Dharma" (the teaching), and second, the critique of the "Three Greats. Regarding the critique of the meaning of "Dharma," it says: "Furthermore..."

Regarding the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: in that scripture, the three characters "Great, Vast, and Extensive" (Dafangguang) constitute the Dharma, while the three characters "Buddha, Flower, and Adornment" (Fohuayan) constitute the person.
Why, then, does this present scripture instead take the three characters "Great, Vast, and Extensive" as the meaning?
Answer: In that scripture, it is called "Dharma" because it is addressed to persons; in this scripture, it is called "meaning" because it is addressed to the Dharma. [Objection: ...

Regarding the Three Greatnesses (*trimahānta*): Are the three greatnesses taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, those taught in the *Awakening of Faith*, and those taught in the present sūtra the same or different?

Answer: In terms of their correspondence to the three greatnesses, they are the same regarding the phenomena (*dharma*). However, in terms of the interpretation of their meaning according to their respective schools (*nikāya*), they are different.
The *Awakening of Faith* establishes the three greatnesses upon the basis of ordinary beings as its primary tenet, whereas the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*... [proceeds from the perspective of the Buddhas].

In the *Xuanshang* and the *Shishang*, the three great elements (*trisvabhāva*) are established upon the phenomenal aspect as their primary tenet (every single character therein possesses ten meanings).
In the present sutra, however, the three great elements are established upon the essence of original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣaṇajñāna*), and thus it differs from them.

Therefore, the *Qixin lun* takes the ordinary person as its basis for "mind," while the *Yuanjue jing* designates its name based on the Buddha. The *Huayan jing* does not follow after the capacities of sentient beings, but directly reveals the One.

It is the true *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, the *Awakening of Faith* primarily explains from the perspective of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), whereas the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* primarily explain from the perspective of the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*).

Regarding the eighth point, which summarizes all [the preceding], the intention is that these twenty-eight pages of explanatory text were specifically composed by our Buddha, the Great Sage, among all the various sections of the teachings throughout his entire life.
For those of sudden capacity, it proclaims the definitive, ultimate, true, and eternally abiding meaning.
It is intended so that those in future generations who follow the Buddha-dharma in their practice may recite these expressive words and understand the principles they express;
by practicing as taught, they shall, in all circumstances, cut away excrescences, burst open abscesses, extract ailments, remove poisons, and dispel hindrances.
Having eliminated all doubts, one realizes the essence of one's own vast, luminous, true, and eternally abiding *bodhi* (perfect enlightenment).
Upon this essence, one gives rise to such great significance, such profound meaning, and such expansive significance. From this point, one transcends the mundane and enters the sacred;
once attained, it is forever constant. Reaching to the end of the future, one benefits oneself and others with inexhaustible enjoyment.

Furthermore, Master Cong of Siming’s *Xinjing* (Mirror of the Mind) states: "The *Mahāvaipulya-bodhimaṇḍala-parivarta-sūtra* (The Great Vaipulya Perfect Enlightenment Sutra) is a work that exhausts principle and perfects nature;
it is a teaching that is pure, refined, and subtle. Although its category belongs to the Vaipulya teachings, its flavor is exclusively..."
Returning to the One Perfect [Vehicle], Gautama revealed the excellent model of the stage of practice, and Samantabhadra opened the correct path of cultivation;
therefore, it is praised as "Mahāvaipulya" (Great and Vast) and substantiated as "Sūtra. Herein, "Perfect" (*yuan*) signifies the "Great" (*mahā*), while "Model" (*gui*) refers to the circle;
"Awakening" (*jue*) signifies the "Square" (*fang*), while "Ruler" (*ju*) refers to the square. Indeed, the Sage employs these as patterns so that sentient beings may achieve perfection.

The standard practice of all Buddhas of the ten directions is called the "Practice of Wholesome Dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma-caryā*). Furthermore, "round" (*yuan*) signifies perfect fusion; "awakening" (*jue*) signifies the nature of awakening.
This nature of true awakening is the Way of perfect fusion, like the waters of the great ocean—tranquil, limpid, and perfectly fused.

As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The nature of the ocean of awakening is tranquil and round; this round and tranquil awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous. Moreover, "round" implies stillness, while "awakening" implies illumination.
Furthermore, because it is luminous yet eternally quiescent, it is called "perfect" (yuan); because it is quiescent yet eternally luminous, it is called "enlightened" (jue).

"Enlightened" takes the sense of luminosity, while "perfect" takes the sense of quiescence. Luminous yet quiescent, and quiescent yet luminous—quiescence and luminosity share the same source; therefore, it is said that "perfect clarity is the primordial wondrous enlightenment.
This does not mean that "perfect enlightenment" (yuanjue) is taken solely in the sense of being vast and boundless; one must know that for sentient beings...

Wandering through the three realms, one is bound by the roots of birth and death; the karmic consciousness of ignorance cannot be eliminated by the power of the perfect enlightenment of quiescent illumination alone—how else could the illusory cataracts and flowers in the sky be dissolved?
Thus, the meaning of Perfect Enlightenment (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) is fully exhausted herein.

Regarding *sūtra*, this is translated as "Sutra of Accordance" (*qijing*); it accords with principle and accords with the capacities of beings, hence it is called a "Sutra of Accordance. Regarding "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*), it refers to the *Lotus Sūtra*.
In the past, everything outside of Perfect Enlightenment (Yuánjué) was considered provisional in meaning (*neyārtha*), for the provisional and the ultimate had not yet been integrated.
Now that the revelation has been heard, it is identical to the perfection of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and is thus entirely definitive in meaning (*nītārtha*).

Consequently, phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused, and cause and effect are instantaneously complete. How could the subtlety of the Buddha-dharma ever surpass this? "Sūtra" means a path; one proceeds by way of it.
The minds and mouths of the sages are such that they may be followed alike for ten thousand ages and remain unchanged for a hundred generations.

Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xichu said: "At the beginning of a sutra, there must be the sixfold accomplishment.
If these six conditions are not fulfilled, the teaching cannot flourish. These are: first, the accomplishment of faith; second, the accomplishment of hearing; third, the accomplishment of time."
Fourth is the accomplishment of the masters; fifth is the accomplishment of the locations; sixth is the accomplishment of the assembly. This present passage possesses the first four of these.
"In this way" refers to the accomplishment of faith. The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma can be entered through faith alone.
If one has faith, one says, "This matter is thus"; if one lacks faith, one says, "This matter is not thus. Furthermore, as for faith...
When the principle of speech is harmonious, the way of teacher and disciple is perfected. Thus we know that the single character "faith" (*śraddhā*) is a term for faithful compliance.
It is like a person with hands who, upon taking up an object, succeeds in obtaining it. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit;
it nurtures all roots of goodness, cuts through the net of doubt, and enables one to emerge from the river of craving. It reveals...
"The path to Nirvana for humans and devas. As for my statement "I have heard," this refers to the accomplishment of hearing. There are four kinds of "I": first, the real self of ordinary worldlings;
second, the divine self of non-Buddhists; third, the provisional self of Bodhisattvas; and fourth, the true self of the Buddhas. Here, it refers to the provisional self.
Hearing arises from the faculty of the ear; since it is heard by the ear, why now refer to it as "I"? This is because the ear is set aside [in favor of the subject].

This distinguishes it from the general "I" (the self). Therefore, it is called "I. Furthermore, the Vijñānavādins interpret the two characters *evam* ("thus") as words of specification, meaning they specify the teachings to be explained hereafter.
Ānanda served as the Buddha’s attendant for twenty years and personally heard them from the Buddha; therefore, it says: "Thus, I have personally [heard] this profound meaning."
It is heard that the Bodhisattva Bandhuprabha took these six types of accomplishment and designated them as the five preliminary matters preceding the sūtra.
Faith is distributed throughout the time of hearing, the teacher, the place, and the assembly. "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the accomplishment of time;
this means that the time is not fixed, but rather the occasion when the teacher and disciples have assembled to listen and speak. "Bhagavān" refers to the master.
Accomplishment. This possesses six meanings: first, mastery; second, brilliance; third, majesty; fourth, renown;
fifth, auspiciousness; sixth, nobility. These six distinct meanings should collectively be designated as *bhagavat*.
Generally, there are five reasons for not translating certain terms in the scriptural traditions: first, non-translation due to secrecy, such as divine mantras (*dhāraṇī*) and the like. Second...

such as the *Jambū* tree, *bhikṣu*, and so forth. 3. Not translated out of deference to antiquity: such as *Anuttara* and so forth. 4.

Because [the term] "thin" (*bō*) does not give rise to wholesome qualities. Now, regarding the Blessed One (*Bhagavān*), among the five reasons for not translating [Sanskrit terms], it is not translated because it contains multiple meanings (*bahvartha*).
Nevertheless, the Blessed One is none other than the Buddha; if one were to express his essential nature, it is Perfect Enlightenment (*Pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
The lecturer Cōng of Siming said: "In this way," means that there is no principle that does not accord [with reality];

when Ānanda refers to himself as "I," it is not the "I" of the human ego; rather, it is the "I" in which the myriad dharmas are all complete. This is the fundamental...
"This is heard by the ear. This is because "I" am the sovereign of the ear. Regarding "at one time": "one" (一) refers to that which is the primary source of the many;
furthermore, "time" (時) refers to the arising of that one. The durations of time differ between the heavens and the human realm.

In the land of India, the four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—are not distinguished; they speak only of the three periods (trikāla). [The first period begins on] the sixteenth day of the first month.
From the [first day of the fifth month] until the fifteenth day of the fifth month, it is called the hot season (*uṣṇa*).

From the sixteenth day of the fifth month until the fifteenth day of the ninth month, it is named the rainy season (*varṣā*). From the sixteenth day of the ninth month until the fifteenth day of the first month, it is named the cold season (*śīta*).
The phrase "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) here already encompasses all four seasons. *Bhagavān* refers to the Teacher who expounded this sutra;
that is, the Buddha. He is also called *Bhagavān* and *Bhagavat*. As stated in the *Buddhoṣṇīṣa-sūtra*:

"The Bhagavats of the ten directions [enter] the single path to the gate of Nirvāṇa. He is endowed with six meanings: sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), brilliance (*tejas*), majesty (*yaśas*), and renown (*śrī*).
Auspiciousness, nobility, and so forth—these six qualities of meaning being perfectly complete, one should collectively designate [the Buddha] as Bhagavat.
Although he is frequently referred to as "Buddha" in various sutras, this is merely due to differences in the translators' choices and nothing else. Now, we shall definitively discuss the sutras:
by which body was it definitively spoken? The Buddha possesses the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. Of these, the Dharma-body is twofold.
There are two kinds of Dharma-body: the Dharma-body as the essence of principle (*li-ti-fa-shen*) and the Dharma-body within its functioning (*yong-zhong-fa-shen*).
The Reward-body (*pao-shen*) also has two kinds: the self-reward and the other-reward. The Response-body (*ying-shen*) likewise has two kinds: the superior response and the inferior response.

Now, it is definitively established that the Dharma-body within its functioning is also called the "other-reward" and the "superior response. These three bodies are one essence. They are also said to be identical with the birth-body (*sheng-shen*).
The Buddha of the Sublime Universal Body is indeed Śākyamuni.

He has come to this Jambudvīpa eighty times to personally attend to his parents and take birth from their physical bodies, preaching the Dharma for fifty years and discussing the sutras in three hundred assemblies. Yet he remains merely with these sixteen-foot form and forty-eight marks.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "My father’s name is Śuddhodana, my mother’s name is Māyā, and my name is Siddhārtha. This refers only to the Great [Form].
The perspectives of those with the capacities of the Hīnayāna differ. Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages of the Mahāyāna perceive this with their *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*);
thus, this sixteen-foot form is itself the *Sambhogakāya* (the Body of Exalted Marks), which is in turn the *Dharmakāya* within the midst [of phenomena].

This is the "subtle, pure Dharmakāya endowed with the thirty-two marks" praised by the Dragon Girl. Śrāvakas and ordinary worldlings perceive it only with their six consciousnesses; this is the [form of the] father and mother.
The birth-body (*janma-kāya*) possesses the thirty-two marks and teaches the Dharma of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). While they share the same seat, their two perspectives differ.
However, this *viśeṣa-kāya* (exalted special body) is of two kinds. The first is the manifested *viśeṣa-kāya*, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
its halo extends one fathom and can illuminate the immeasurable; when one exhaustively examines a single mark, it is ultimately ungraspable. This is like [the case of] Upadhāna.

Reaching to the very crown of his head, Maudgalyāyana could not fathom the extent of its sound. When a non-Buddhist wished to measure the Buddha’s body, he cut bamboo from the Southern Mountains that was sixteen feet long to measure it;
yet the Buddha’s head remained above the sixteen-foot bamboo. An ancient saying has it: "Though all the bamboo of the Southern Mountains were exhausted, he would still remain sixteen feet tall.
Second is the manifestation of the *vairocana* (exalted) form, such as the marks resembling the dust motes within the ocean of the Ten Lotus Treasuries.

Excellent. Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations) states that the body of the True Dharma is six million billion *yojanas* in height; his eyes are like the waters of the four great oceans;
and the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows is like five Mount Sumerus. These are all manifestations of the sublime and extraordinary marks (*vyañjana-lakṣaṇa*).
How could such inconceivable virtues ever be measured by the conceptualizing minds of ordinary beings?
He entered the Great Treasury of Luminous Supernatural Powers.
When the Buddha enters the Great Samādhi, his supernatural powers and radiance are inexhaustible; therefore, it is called a "Treasury.
This is the state of right reception within samādhi.
Samādhi is the wondrous state spontaneously attained within right reception (*samyaksamāpatti*). Right reception means not receiving any sensations; hence it is called right reception.
Master Huì of Fù-ān in Xīshǔ said: "This refers to the accomplishment of the dwelling, meaning that the Buddha enters the source of the Dharma-nature and manifests [it]."
The boundless and unobstructed buddha-fields do not have fixed distinctions between self and other regarding their enjoyment; therefore, it is said that they "rely on the Truth.

Thus, the Great Commentary states: "Since the core tenet of this sutra elucidates the reality of the objective realm, the teaching lord must be understood as the True Body (dharmakāya) abiding in the Land of Enjoyment, preaching the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* for the sake of all great bodhisattvas. Now, concerning the location where this sutra was preached and the master who taught it:

This differs from other sutras. In the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the location is the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park at Śrāvastī, and the teacher is the sixteen-foot transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This present sutra, however, is not so.
The place of teaching is within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), relying upon the realm of ultimate reality. The teacher is the Dharmakāya and Saṃbhogakāya inseparable; this is the True [Body].
This refers to the body [of the teaching]. The spirit (*śen*), however, has a wondrous function that is difficult to fathom; its penetration is sovereign and unobstructed.

Because the Great Luminous Treasury (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*) possesses three meanings, there are: first, the elimination of confusion; second, the breaking of names; and third, the manifestation of principle. What is meant by "eliminating confusion"?
It means that within the teachings of the various periods throughout the one lifetime of the Buddha, there are what are called the *tathāgatagarbha*, the *prakṛti-viśuddhagarbha*, and...

Regarding the "Dharmakāya-treasury" and the "Dharma-realm-treasury," fearing that these might be confused with other concepts, it is now said that this refers to the treasury of the great radiance of the true nature of spiritual powers (*abhijñā*). What is meant by "breaking through names"?

The Buddha feared that future generations would not know that the essence of the Dharma is fundamentally equal, and would thus forcibly generate distinctions within that equality, claiming that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are [distinct].

The Great Luminous Treasury (Mahā-ābhāsagarbha) encompasses heaven and earth; its radiance is brilliant and blazing, such that there is nothing it does not illuminate, nothing it does not encompass, nothing it does not gather, and nothing it does not contain.
If one possesses such a name and appearance, and forms such a conceptual understanding, one consequently creates duality.
Therefore, to shatter the mind that clings to existence, [one realizes] that while there are appearances, they are without marks (lakṣaṇa). Thus, the character "Great" (Mahā-) is absent.
Names and signs. There are no names or signs of luminosity; there are no names or signs of ignorance; there are no names or signs of concealment.
What is meant by "revealing the principle"? This refers to the exhaustion of delusion regarding this single meaning, wherein awakened clarity is fully opened.
In all places, it is perfectly round, pure and naked, vividly clear, and present in every head and whole in every thing. Throughout the entire world of the ten directions, there is none...
It is not a matter of intellectual synthesis. It is like the great sun rising in the sky, illuminating the world with penetrating clarity;
this is what is called "revealing the principle. Nevertheless, one must still personally take that final step before the discourse can be perfected.

Thus, the Treatise says: "When the nature of mind does not arise, this is the universal illumination of great wisdom. *Samādhi* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "right reception" (*zhèngshòu*).

This is an instance where both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are presented together. "Entering meditative absorption" (*samāpatti*) refers to "right reception" (*samyak-saṃprajanya*). It is called "right reception" because one does not undergo any [defiled] sensations.
"Right" (*samyak*) serves to distinguish it from the false; "reception" (*saṃprajanya*) has the sense of experiencing or receiving.

This includes the eye experiencing forms, the ear experiencing sounds, the nose experiencing odors, the tongue experiencing tastes, the body experiencing tangibles, and the mind experiencing mental phenomena (*dharma*), as well as experiencing at all times with craving, joy, and pleasure.

Regarding "equanimity" (*upekṣā*) and so forth: this is termed "wrong reception. It occurs only at the time of entering meditative absorption, when one correctly and precisely reflects upon and examines the object of focus, such that the eye no longer perceives forms, and so on up to the body, mind, and mental objects (*dharmas*).

Even throughout all times, while the factors of love, joy, bliss, and equanimity are present, it does not hinder the eye from seeing forms with intense clarity, nor the ear from hearing sounds with intense clarity. Thus...
This extends from the nose, tongue, body, and mind up to their being ablaze with radiance. Thus, Master Xianshou said:

"Though emptiness is so void that all traces are severed, it does not prevent the constellations of the Dharma-heaven from shining brilliantly. Though the profound depths are beyond words, how could they obstruct the vast and surging waves of the ocean of teachings?
Indeed, from the Buddhas of the ten directions above down to the sentient beings of the six realms below, all possess this [nature]."
Regarding the samādhi of the Great Radiant Treasury (*mahā-āvabhāsa-garbha-samādhi-samāpatti*), how does one enter it?
Simply, throughout the twelve periods of the day, cease all deluded thoughts,攀缘 (*pán-yuán*—clinging to objects), inverted views, and discriminative minds.
When wisdom merges with principle and the objective realm unites with the spirit, one immediately enters this samādhi of the Great Radiant Treasury. If it is not otherwise, you will know only...
They run outside the gate; how could they know that [the Buddha] is within it?
As all Tathāgatas say in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "A Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called a Tathāgata."
"Radiant Adornment and Abiding.
"Radiant Adornment" means adornment by light. "Abiding" means dwelling eternally without ceasing. "Maintaining" means upholding without loss.
Chan Master Fu’an Huī of Xishu said: "The term 'all' (sarva) is a word that universally encompasses.

As for the meaning of 'Tathāgata,' there are four aspects. First, regarding the Dharma-body (dharmakāya): it means that there is nowhere from which he comes, nor anywhere to which he goes. Second, regarding the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya):
it means that having cultivated causes in the past, he has now attained the fruit of Buddhahood. Third, regarding the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya)..."
This means that by riding upon the path of reality as it is, one comes to achieve perfect enlightenment. Fourth, in terms of the principle of wisdom (*jñāna*):

"As" (*tathā*) refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), and "come" (*āgata*) refers to initial awakening (*ādi-awakening*). Because non-awakening exists due to original enlightenment, and because initial awakening exists due to non-awakening, the original and the initial are non-dual;
therefore, one is called a Tathāgata. Furthermore, because the Buddhas of the ten directions have realized this principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they are so named.

The Tathāgata—because the beings of the six realms and four modes of birth are deluded regarding this principle of True Suchness (Tathatā), he is called "Thus Gone" (Tathā-gata) and cannot be called "Come.

The term "Tathāgata" here refers specifically to the Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Body). Regarding "Radiant Adornment" (Prabhāśobhana): it is the mutual interpenetration of light, shining with brilliant clarity;
it abides in and sustains the wondrous marks, forever severing all攀緣 (pān-yuan, objective clinging), never being lost or abandoned.
The preface states that it "fully possesses the abiding and maintaining of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). Perfect Enlightenment is the Tathāgata;
it is the ground of pure awakening of all sentient beings.
Since Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally of one and the same nature, the place where the Buddhas abide and maintain their majestic radiance is precisely that of sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "The Ground of Pure Awakening" (*jingjue xindi*), Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xichu said: "The former passage [describes] the sameness of sages; this passage [describes] the sameness of ordinary beings.
These characters are terms used for specific designation, carrying the sense of various, non-uniform categories. As for "sentient beings" (*zhòngshēng*): by means of form, sensation, perception...
The five aggregates of consciousness arise through the harmonious conjunction of various conditions; therefore, they are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*).

Furthermore, because there are many cycles of birth and death, they are called "sentient beings. As for "purity": it means being free from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and free from the obstacle to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
thus, defilements cannot stain it and delusions cannot transform it—hence, it is called "pure. "Awakening" refers to the dharma, while "ground" is a metaphor; this is what is meant by "dharma."

This is an analogy presented by way of a dual illustration. It means that all sentient beings, deluded regarding the Truth and having lost their profound stillness, pursue appearances and cling to names, thereby falsely perceiving themselves as sentient beings.
Yet the substance of this delusion is fundamentally empty; it is entirely identical to original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Upon the substance of this original enlightenment, one can give rise to all the virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, just as the great earth can produce all things. Question: Sentient beings...
Question: Why is it not called "abiding and maintaining" (*zhùchí*)? Answer: Because the Buddhas have realized this realm, they may be called "abiding and maintaining.
Sentient beings have not realized this realm; they merely possess Buddha-nature. Therefore, they cannot be called by the two characters "abiding and maintaining.

It simply indicates that within their own portion there exists this ground of pure original enlightenment (*prabhāsvara-ādi-bodhi*). Thus, the Preface says: "Throughout the day, it is perfectly round..."
One who is aware yet has never attained perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says:

"Though one acts all day long, if one is not self-aware, one will pointlessly enter the various realms of existence. In the Chan school, this is called "burning incense all day long without knowing that one's own body is the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
In the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*), it is called "the common people using [it] daily without knowing it. In Mencius, it is called...
Throughout their lives, many follow this path without knowing its Way. In the *Laozi*, it is called "not being good at preserving the person";
the meaning is the same. Furthermore, Master Faden said: "Without roots, one can still live."
Leaving the ground yet not falling—though used daily, one does not even know it. Where else could one seek it?
Body and mind are quiescent and extinguished; this is the fundamental limit of equality.
Having realized this extinction, the essence of the sage and the ordinary person is identical. Only then does one see the original true limit, where there is absolutely no distinction or hierarchy.
It is perfected throughout the ten directions;
the nature of awakening is perfect because it pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
It accords with non-duality.
Although it accords with all conditions, the nature of awakening is eternally one.
Master Huì of Fù’ān in Xīshǔ said: "The body and mind are quiescent and extinguished at the fundamental limit of equality, which is perfectly complete throughout the ten directions.
Here, "body" refers to the deluded body that is grasped; "mind" refers to the deluded mind that is grasped. Quiescence and extinction are...
Regarding the meaning of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*): "perfect" (*yuan*) means it is not partial, and "full" (*man*) means it is complete.

This refers to the preceding passage which cites the light-adornment and sustaining power of all Tathāgatas, as well as the pure ground of awakening of these sentient beings; this constitutes the establishment of the thesis (*siddhānta*).
This sutra takes the emptiness and stillness of mind and object, and the equality of ordinary beings and sages, as its primary tenet;
it takes the forgetting of emotions and becoming equal to the Buddhas through contemplative practice as its goal.

Fearing that practitioners might not realize that the nature of awakening is fundamentally equal, they give rise to a discriminating mind, asserting that "the ordinary are ordinary" and "the sages are sages. If one interprets it in such a way, when will one ever attain realization? Therefore...
It is said that all mental discrimination is erroneous; when the mind no longer grasps at objects, the myriad paths are naturally rectified.
It is further said that when the mind differs, a thousand divergences arise in competition; yet when the mind is as it truly is, the Dharma-realm is vast and level.
This very grasping mind can create the Buddhas, can become sentient beings, can create celestial palaces, and can become the hells. Thus one knows that by clinging to it—
If one observes through [phenomenal] characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is a vast difference between the ordinary and the sage; therefore, they are not equal.

However, if one observes through the nature (*prakṛti*), then the characteristics of the ordinary and the sage, as well as defilement and purity, are such that all phenomena are, in their very essence, entirely empty and quiescent.

Thus, one perceives the nature of the primordial limit of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*): it is fundamentally equal, fundamentally lacking nothing, and not merely devoid of the four types of noble beings.
It is high, yet there is nothing below it among the six classes of ordinary beings. Every person is fully endowed with it; each and every one is perfectly realized.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. Therefore it is said: "As when a vessel is already full, no more can be added.
The Way of all Buddhas is equal; all dharmas are impartial. This awakened nature, in the east, is entirely eastern; in the south, west, and north, it is likewise so.

It is likewise thus: it envelops heaven and earth, fills the six voids, and pervades the entire Dharma-realm. With its six powers penetrating in all four directions, there is nothing—whether great or small, refined or coarse—in which it is not present.
This is what is called the Great Immortal of the land of Chu (India) transmitting his mind secretly from east to west.
As the "Equanimity of Things" chapter of the *Zhuangzi* also says: "His form is like withered wood; his mind is like dead ashes. He has forgotten [all things].
When things avoid the intellect, then all phenomena are a single treasury and life and death share the same state. It is also said:
"Viewed from their differences, the liver and gallbladder are as far apart as Chu and Yue; viewed from their sameness, all phenomena are one. As for "non-duality and compliance":
to follow is to not conflict, and to comply is to be in resonance. Furthermore, there are two ways of explaining this: "two" refers to two distinct entities.
Non-duality is one thing. Duality refers to ordinary beings who follow the cycle of birth and death, and the followers of the Two Vehicles who head toward nirvana.

Ordinary beings are deluded regarding the essence of perfect enlightenment and lose the function of perfect enlightenment; they give rise to afflictions and create karma, revolving within the great ocean of suffering.
They die only to be born again, and are born only to die again; emerging and submerging like heads in water, they possess no liberation. This...
At that time, being defiled and attached by false dharmas, they are unable to proceed toward nirvāṇa. For immeasurable kalpas, they remain only on this shore of birth and death.
Therefore, regarding the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles, they view the other shore as being dualistic.
Those of the two vehicles see that the three realms offer no peace, being like a burning house; they long for liberation, as if saving their heads from fire.
However, it is like a wild deer leaping alone, paying no heed to the herd behind.

Although such a one may succeed in escaping birth and death and liberating themselves from the three realms, they nonetheless extinguish their physical form and annihilate their wisdom, sinking into emptiness and stagnating in quiescence; they fall into the pit of liberation and lie within the city of nirvana.
There are three meanings [to this]: first, a narrow and inferior mind; second, fear of the triple world; and third, a deficiency in great compassion.
They understand only how to go thus, but do not understand how to come thus. Furthermore, they are detained by emptiness and remain stagnant within it.
Compared to the birth and death of ordinary beings, these two types of people—though distinct—are both greatly deficient and fail to reach the mark. Neither of them...
Abiding in the Middle Way, only our Buddha, the Great Sage, has realized the Great Nirvana of Non-abiding.

Because of his great compassion, he is ever-present within the cycle of birth and death yet does not abide in nirvana; because of his great wisdom, he does not abide in birth and death yet is ever-present in nirvana.
Thus, while being on this shore, he is not hindered from being ever on the other shore; while being on the other shore, he is not hindered [from being here].
One always remains on this shore; this is the sphere of activity of the Buddha, which is called "non-dual conformity.

When a practitioner speaks of this, throughout the twelve periods of the day, they are caught in the攀缘 (pān-yuan) of deluded thoughts, with every moment being ignorance—the very root of birth and death.
They are either grasping at the mundane or grasping at the sacred; they are either grasping at the real or grasping at the false. It is not...
To cling to existence is itself to cling to non-existence; this is no different from ordinary people or those of the Two Vehicles.

Only when, at all places and at all times, one does not adhere to the categories of ordinary and sage, true and false, or existence and non-existence, can one then be fully true while in the true and fully false while in the false, merging them into a single whole.
Only then does one accord with the non-duality of following along.
Within the realm of non-duality, he manifests all pure lands.
That which is within the single nature of the Buddha is called the realm of non-duality; by means of dharmas that are unattached and unstained, he receives and transforms sentient beings.
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "The character *yu* (於) means 'to rely upon. In the teachings, it is referred to as the sound of the 'object' (*jing*).

This sound of the character *yu* is derived from the perspective of the object. As for 'the non-dual object,' this refers to the non-dual object of accord with the Middle Way mentioned in the preceding text.
As for 'all' (*zhu*), it means responding universally according to the various types [of beings]. As for 'Pure Land' (*jingtu*), it is contrasted with the 'defiled land.'"
Regarding the designation of "land" (*kṣetra*): there are four such lands. First is the *dharmatā-kṣetra*, the dwelling place of the *dharmakāya*.
Second is the *saṃbhoga-kṣetra*, which is further divided into two: first, the *svasaṃbhoga-kṣetra*, which is perceived only by the Buddha himself;

second, the *parasaṃbhoga-kṣetra*, which is perceived only by Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), and not by those prior to the stages or by followers of the Hīnayāna. Third is the *nirmāṇa-kṣetra*, [measuring] one *zhang*...

The abodes of the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are sixfold; however, this sutra generally categorizes them into only two types: pure lands (*śuddhakṣetra*) and defiled lands (*saṃkliṣṭakṣetra*).

When the Buddha preached this sutra, the great assembly of those below the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*) saw the Buddha’s transformation body dwelling within a defiled land of the Sahā world—amidst rubble, thorns, pits, hollows, and mounds—preaching the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*圆觉经*). As for the great assembly of those on the grounds...

They see the Buddha’s *parabhogika-sambhogakāya* dwelling within a pure land of jade forests, jeweled trees, precious palaces, and golden terraces, where he preaches the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* for them.
While the Dharma heard is one and the same, those who see it differ from one another.
Is this not our Buddha responding universally in accordance with beings within the non-dual realm of the Middle Way? The commentary states:
The great assembly prior to the stages [of the Bodhisattvas] perceives the *saṃbhogakāya* only when they receive the Buddha’s empowerment; if they do not receive such empowerment, they do not see it.
Furthermore, as previously stated, the identity of ordinary beings and sages refers to entering the *dharmatā-dhātu* from the *svasaṃbhoga-kṣetra*.
Now, this manifestation of various pure lands for the sake of the bodhisattvas refers to manifesting from the *dharmatā-dhātu*.
This refers to the land of enjoyment for others (*para-sambhoga-kṣetra*). Therefore, the subsequent text states, "together with the great Bodhisattvas," and so forth.
Master Cong of Siming said: "Entering the Great Treasury of Supernatural Powers and Radiance" up to "manifesting all pure lands":

"Supernatural" (*shen*) is named the Heavenly Mind; "Powers" (*tong*) is named the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*); "Great" (*da*) is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); and "Radiance" (*guang*)...

The "wisdom" (prajñā) refers to the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*). "Clarity" (*míng*) refers to the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*). These three virtues synthesize the infinite dharmas of the three truths and return to the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*).
It is called a "treasury" (*garbha*) because it encompasses all wholesome dharmas. *Samādhi* is translated as "harmonious and direct concentration";

"right reception" (*samyag-vedana*) refers to the sphere of right mental activity. *Samādhi* is the Sanskrit term; "right reception" is the Chinese translation. Here, both the Sanskrit and the Chinese are provided.
Taken together: in reality, all sages and worthies take the correct reception of samādhi as the gateway for entering and exiting.
Because they employ non-discriminative wisdom to take the markless principle as their object, it is called "the sphere of practice for the correct mind.
"Radiant Adornment" refers to the wisdom of the *li-yin* (revealing cause); "Abiding and Sustaining" refers to the merit of the *yuan-yin* (conditioning cause). All Tathāgatas...
By employing the two causes—the conditional (*pratyaya*) and the contributory (*hetu*)—one adorns the originally existent true cause (*tathāgata-garbha*) and thereby attains Buddhahood.

Regarding the phrase "all these sentient beings" (*sarvasattvāḥ*), the word "all" (*sarva*) is a term for multiplicity; it encompasses the single Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), all of whom are called "sentient beings.

The Buddha also refers to them as "unsurpassed sentient beings," because the principle of the purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is what is termed the "ground of awakening" (*bodhibhūmi*). In the context of the Buddha, this is called the "fruit" (*phala*); in [the context of sentient beings], it is...

Sentient beings are called the cause. Now, comparing the Buddha-fruit with the causal ground of sentient beings, both are fully endowed with the nature of wondrously bright perfect enlightenment and lack the characteristics of body and mind;
therefore, they are called "quiescent extinction. Furthermore, they lack any characteristic of differentiation; therefore, they are called "equal."

In the sutras, whenever the "ten directions" are mentioned, they refer to the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). Now, it is said that these ten realms are mutually interpenetrating and harmonious, entering into wondrous, perfect *bodhi*.
Therefore, it is called "perfectly complete. It is simply the single true suchness of Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), which follows conditions of either defilement or purity;
thus, it is called "non-dual accordance. Within this non-dual realm, the manifestation of lands is clearly revealed: transforming the impure into...

Purity: that is, transforming the defilement of the Sahā world into the purity of the Land of Peaceful Light (*śānta-prabhāsvara*). Regarding the *Dharmameghā-sūtra*: Śākyamuni is named Vairocana, pervading all places.
The dwelling place of that Buddha is called the Constant Peaceful Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsvara*). It is a place established by being encompassed by the perfection of permanence (*nitya-pāramitā*);
it is a place founded upon the perfection of self (*ātma-pāramitā*); it is a place where the perception and sensation are extinguished through the perfection of bliss (*sukha-pāramitā*).
The *Pāramitā of Purity* does not abide in the characteristics of body or mind, nor does it perceive the characteristics of phenomena as being either existent or non-existent.
Furthermore, in the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations*, the Buddha manifested various pure lands for Lady Vaidehī:
some lands consist entirely of lotus flowers; some lands are like crystal mirrors; and some lands are like those of the Lord of Sovereignty (*Īśvara*).
The celestial palace—could this not be none other than this very Vulture Peak? This is precisely the unsurpassed act of repaying the nation.
There is no need to destroy this Vulture Peak to manifest a separate realm of quiescent illumination; fearing that people might harbor doubts, I cannot help but explain this at length.
(The names and ranks of the various bodhisattvas are listed below, with detailed annotations and explanations.)
He was accompanied by one hundred thousand great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. Their names were as follows:
*Bodhisattva* (菩提薩埵) in the language of India; the people of the Qin state preferred brevity, thus omitting the two characters *ti* and *duo*, referring to them simply as *Pusa* (菩薩).
It is translated as "one who achieves sentient beings through the mind of the Great Way. Alternatively, *bodhi* may be translated as "Way" (*dao*) or "Awakening" (*jue*).

These one hundred thousand followers are all those dwelling on the stages adjacent to the Truth or nearly equal to the Sages—saints and worthies who are either provisional or real, manifest or hidden—all of whom have entered the Light of Stillness (*śāntaprabhā*) to proclaim and exalt Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

This sutra does not fall into the hands of those of the Two Vehicles, nor is it listed among the assemblies of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; yet, for the sake of its final circulation, it instead lists the assembly of ordinary beings. [Mount] Sumeru...

Mañjuśrī attained perfect enlightenment long ago; he is the Buddha Uṣṇīṣa-śikhi-rāja (Dragon-Species Supreme Honored King). He condescended from his exalted status to a humble one to assist Śākyamuni.

This son was then the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; at that time, Śākyamuni was the youth Megha, who purchased five stalks of lotuses to offer to Dīpaṃkara and spread his hair to cover the mud.

The Bodhisattva Universal Eye takes "universal observation" as its meaning; he universally observes that all sentient beings within the dharma-realm are fully endowed with the nature of perfect enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha...

Maitreya Bodhisattva is a translation of his clan name, Maitrī; "Ajita" is his personal name. In the past, when he was a king, he was riding a white elephant as he traveled outside the city walls.

The elephant trainer replied, "That elephant was originally quite manageable, but because it saw wild elephants, a lustful mind arose within it.
Otherwise, please have the King command the trainer to bring the elephant before the King. Then, [the trainer] heated glowing iron pellets and said:
"You have offended the King; he has ordered you to swallow iron balls and to open your mouth for an elephant to swallow them, so that the balls emerge from behind.

When the elephant knelt and prostrated itself in submission, the King witnessed this act and gave rise to a heart of compassion; therefore, he was named by the clan title Maitreya (The Compassionate One).
The king said, "Since you are able to tame it, how could you allow it to go astray? He replied, "Your Majesty, I am able to tame the elephant's body, but I cannot tame its mind.
That elephant’s mind is not something I can tame. The king asked, "Who in this world is skilled at taming the mind?
He replied, "Only the Buddha is truly skilled at taming the mind. The king went to question the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
In the world, there are various methods for training the mind. Whether it be elephants, oxen, horses, or various other species, if one wishes to train them, one does not suppress their desires;
rather, one trains them gradually according to what they enjoy. Even birds, beasts, crows, ravens, and ants can all be trained.
As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says: "First, lead them with the hook of desire, and afterwards, cause them to enter the Buddha-way."
Wisdom. That which is most difficult to tame is nothing other than the human mind. As it was said of old: "The high may be shot at; the deep may be fished from;
yet within the span of a few inches lies the human heart—this heart of a mere foot or so is difficult to fathom. For this reason, Subhūti first asked about the pure mind.
This sutra reveals twenty-five wheels of meditative concentration and three kinds of sublime contemplation; these are precisely for the purpose of taming the mind.

When it is obscured, one immediately employs contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to observe it; that obscuration then becomes clarity. Cessation and contemplation are the methods of luminous stillness.
Luminous stillness is quiescent illumination. Distraction is the cessation of quiescence; obscuration is the illumination of contemplation. Using these as medicine for ignorance—
Illness does not remain far before it returns.

Now, the eleven chapters of questions and answers from the *zhengzongfen* (Section on the Correct Teaching) are condensed into two parts; that is, the first question and answer is intended to inspire faith and understanding.

therein, Mañjuśrī represents understanding (*prajñā*), while Samantabhadra represents practice (*caryā*). Indeed, those who wish to direct their minds toward cultivation must first attain such understanding.
First, one must have correct faith and understanding. If the understanding is not correct, then all that is cultivated will be erroneous;

even if one exerts oneself with diligence, it will be in vain and merely a source of toil. Furthermore, in the teachings of the *Śrāvaka*, the *Pratye-ka-buddha*, the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), and the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), one generally first practices and only later attains sudden awakening.
However, the ritual procedure of the *Avataṃsaka* and this present sutra is not like that; first, there is sudden [awakening].
One practices only after attaining the same understanding as the Buddha. This requires first realizing one's own mind. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* says:
"If one does not realize one's own mind, how can one know the right path? Due to that inverted wisdom, all evils increase.
From this we know that where there is faith, there must be understanding; where there is understanding, there must be faith. How do we know this? The *Avataṃsaka* [states]:

Only when faith and understanding are perfectly integrated do they become the foundation of practice. Nowadays, there are certain people who, though they possess faith,"

In the end, one is only stained by the views and knowledge of heterodox paths, thereby increasing all the seeds of ignorance.
Furthermore, there is another class of people who possess perverted understanding and realization, such that they understand everything.
Yet they lack faith and, consistently denying cause and effect, increase their wrong views.
Thus one knows that the two characters "faith" (śraddhā) and "understanding" (adhimukti) are like the two wheels of a cart or the two wings of a bird; these must not be lacking.

Now, this first chapter on Mañjuśrī provides a comprehensive explanation for those of the three capacities—superior, middling, and inferior. The second chapter on Samantabhadra likewise provides a comprehensive [explanation] for...

Relying upon Mañjuśrī’s understanding and Samantabhadra’s conduct, it instructs those of superior capacity to direct their minds toward the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness, while also modeling themselves after the cultivation of the Dharmadhātu-contemplation.
Since practitioners may harbor doubts when first entering this contemplation, there follows the fourth chapter, "Vajragarbha."
The chapter begins with doubt. Since there is doubt, one must necessarily investigate the root of saṃsāra; hence there is the fifth chapter on Maitreya.
Once the root of saṃsāra is known, it must be severed. Having severed the root of saṃsāra, [one attains liberation].
Only upon realizing and entering Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) does there naturally arise the arrangement of stages and levels.
Therefore, there is the sixth chapter, "Pure Wisdom" (*Vimalamati*), which arranges these stages from the mundane to the sacred.
Within these six chapters of the sutra, the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā*) is intended solely for those of superior faculties. Beyond that, there is furthermore another...

For this reason, there are majestic and virtuous bodhisattvas who act for the sake of those of middle capacity.

thus, the Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇaghoṣa makes this inquiry. Having received the Buddha’s revelation of the twenty-five wheels for twenty-five kinds of capacities, once the practitioner has entered the various wheels of the three contemplations, they may then fall into the four marks; therefore, [the following section] exists.

The Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions asks a question concerning the severance of the four marks (*catur-nimitta*). Once the four marks have been eliminated, yet the four illnesses (*catur-roga*) have not yet been extinguished;

therefore, the Bodhisattva Universal Awakening asks a question so that [the practitioner] may rely upon the teacher and depart from the four illnesses of effort, cessation, spontaneity, and extinction.
Once the four characteristics have been eliminated and the four ailments have departed, such individuals of middling capacity awaken to the Way all at once.
Furthermore, there is another class of individuals with inferior capacity, whose faculties are weak and whose obstructions are heavy; regarding the various cycles of the three contemplations:

hence it is called "dwelling together in the assembly of the equal Dharma."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right,
knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, we pray that for the sake of all the members of this Dharma assembly who have gathered here,
you will expound upon the Tathāgata’s original arising and pure practice of the causal ground."
"Fundamental arising" refers to the first thought that arose when the Buddha was still an ordinary person. "Ground" refers to the Buddha's initial stage.
"Dharma-practice" refers to the Buddha’s sublime conduct.
Master Xifu Fu’an Huī said: "This is an expression of a request. 'Thereupon' refers to the site of the assembly of the Dharma of equality;
it is a phrase used to initiate what follows from what precedes. 'Mañjuśrī' in Sanskrit means 'Wondrous Auspiciousness.

The three circuits symbolize taking refuge in the Triple Gem and severing the three poisons, among other things. Kneeling on the long legs symbolizes stability.

"Perilous yet not changed. "Joining the palms" signifies the intermingling of the human realm and the sacred realm. Furthermore, rising from one's seat and circumambulating three times signifies the purification of the karma of the body.

This also expresses the karma of speech. This entire section of text was compiled and edited by the redactors.

"The World-Honored One of Great Compassion" is where Mañjuśrī praises the Buddha. "Great" (Mahā) has the meaning of distinguishing the superior from the inferior; "compassion" (maitrī) is that which can bestow happiness.
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to save from suffering. Question: Why does [the text] not say "Great Wisdom and Great Compassion"? Answer:
This is because the intent behind Mañjuśrī’s inquiry is for sentient beings of the final age to practice the path of benefiting others rather than seeking self-benefit;
therefore, it praises [him] as "Great Compassion. Furthermore, those of the Hīnayāna possess wisdom but lack compassion, whereas those of the Mahāyāna possess both compassion and wisdom.
Fortune! Only the Buddha’s complete practice of altruism can be called "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*).

For example, if someone falls into water, a person of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) would see them and refuse to rescue them, because such a person already knows that for immeasurable eons they have been transmigrating within the ocean of birth and death, undergoing great suffering and affliction, and has themselves already escaped from the triple world (*tridhātu*).
Afterwards, he did not dare to enter again, and for that reason did not rescue them. If a Bodhisattva were to see this, they would first set foot [in the water] themselves and then rescue them;
this is both self-benefit and benefiting others. If a Buddha sees this, they immediately enter the water to cause [the beings] to quickly emerge and reach a place of safety;
therefore, they are called "Great Wisdom" (Mahāprajñā). As for the World-Honored One (Bhagavān), he is fully...

This is the fundamental, original, and pure practice of the causal ground. Generally speaking, in the ritual procedures for cultivation according to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, one must first give rise to the threefold causal ground.
What are these threefold causal grounds? First, the thorough awakening to the nature of enlightenment;
second, the arousal of the bodhicitta; and third, the cultivation of the bodhisattva practices. This means that one first attains sudden awakening regarding one's own portion [of reality].
One possesses by nature the luminous, vast, true, and perfect nature of *bodhi*.

To suddenly believe that ignorance is fundamentally non-existent, and to suddenly believe that birth and death are fundamentally non-existent—this is called the great awakening to the nature of *bodhi*. Only after this does one give rise to the *bodhicitta*.

In Sanskrit, *bodhi* means "awakening" (*jue*). Having already realized the nature of awakening, one should maintain this mind of awakening at all times and in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
whether moving, turning, bending, or looking up; whether rising, attending to daily needs, or inquiring after others; and whether in every gesture, smile, or word.
This awakened mind must, in every thought-moment, remain identical with the original, fundamental awakening first realized.
This is consistent with the Master Ben-sheng’s words: "In this very movement and activity, do you still accord with the original master?
If you do accord, then throughout the twelve hours of the day, there is no principle of empty waste."
If you cannot achieve resonance through union, you may often engage in conversation while drinking tea, holding what is called a "tea-discourse assembly.
If you do achieve such resonance, this is called the arousal of the bodhicitta. This mind is itself the mind of great wisdom. Only after that does one cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva;
that is, in all places and at every moment, to maintain thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion, benefiting and bringing joy to sentient beings.
Benefiting all classes of beings, he teaches and brings them to maturity, never abandoning or failing to embrace any sentient being as he cultivates the bodhisattva practices.

He is like Sudhana, the youth in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, who first attained realization of the nature of awakening through Mañjuśrī and subsequently traveled south to visit one hundred and ten cities, meeting fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Throughout immeasurable kalpas, before he had yet attained equal and perfect enlightenment, at the very beginning of his fundamental stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*), how did he first give rise to a single thought to cultivate the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground?

How did he practice pure, signless conduct that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*)? For what reason did Mañjuśrī, at the very outset of his inquiry, ask precisely about this matter? It is because it is the most... [supreme].

If you still fail to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, you may suddenly be led astray by companions and become permeated with the seeds of false views and ignorance. No sooner...

This section of text is precisely the instruction for the practitioner to realize the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*). This passage concerning "the resolve free from illness" corresponds to the second stage, the generation of the bodhicitta;

Its intent is to enable those in the final age who seek the Mahāyāna to attain awakening by relying upon this. Relying on...

If the mind is free from discursive thought, even the iron bed is not suffering, for there is no change or transition.
Thus, the perfectly luminous essence of our Buddha is the inherent nature and virtue possessed by all ordinary sentient beings.

Therefore, it is said that the body and land of Vairocana do not transcend the single thought-moment of the lowest commoner, and the environment and inhabitants of Avīci hell are coextensive with the self-mind of the most sublime sage.
It is like a person in a dream: while dreaming, it is not that the dream-objects do not exist; yet upon waking, nothing is found.
This illustrates how sentient beings, when deluded, deeply regard ignorance as real; only after awakening do they realize that ignorance is an illusion.
It is like various empty flowers vanishing into space; one cannot say there is a fixed place where they are extinguished.
Why? Because there is no place of birth.
The extinction of ignorance is like the extinction of empty flowers; it cannot be pointed out as a place of extinction. This is because ignorance itself has no locus.
This is because there is fundamentally no place of birth.
Master Fuaan Hui of Xichu said: "This is an explanation by way of analogy.

Since it was previously stated that all various afflictions ultimately return to ignorance, it is now further said that their lack of substance makes their principle difficult to perceive, as the path of language is cut off. This...
To explain this by means of analogies, the school of pedagogy classifies dreams into four types: first, the permeation of ignorance; second, the wandering of habitual consciousness;
third, the imbalance of the four great elements; and fourth, omens of good or evil. Furthermore, as the *Liezi* states:
"The spirit encountering [objects] constitutes a dream; the physical form contacting [objects] constitutes an event. It is just like when yin energy is predominant at night, one then dreams.
Crossing water: when yang energy is predominant, one dreams of crossing fire; when both yin and yang energies are robust, one dreams of killing or being killed;
with a disease of deficiency, one dreams of flying through the air; with a disease of repletion, one dreams of drowning. When full, one dreams of giving; when hungry, one dreams of taking.
Amidst various kinds of fear and terror, at such a time, it is as if they truly exist—nothing can be denied—and yet upon waking...
At that time, everything is utterly non-existent. Thus Longya said: "While dreaming, how could one know the dream is false? Only upon waking does one realize there was nothing in the dream.
When deluded, it is just like the events within a dream; after awakening, it is the same as rising from sleep. Furthermore, Yongjia said:
"Within the dream, the six realms of existence are vividly clear; upon awakening, all is empty, and not even a 'great chiliocosm' remains. Yet, this one...
All sentient beings, while in a state of delusion, perceive the illusory body of the four great elements and the reflected images of the six sense-objects;
yet upon awakening, these illusory bodies of the four great elements and the reflected images of the six sense-objects no longer exist.

Although this is precisely so, when one is in a state of delusion, it is likewise impossible to tell others that they do not exist. Question: As previously stated, since ignorance has no substantial reality, it is like a dream.
Regarding the matter of the middle state: upon waking, it is utterly unobtainable. I do not know from where it has ceased. He replied: "It is like the cessation of various empty flowers;
when they vanish into space, one cannot say there is a fixed place of cessation. He asked again: "If there is no place of cessation, then it must return [to existence].
By what cause and for what reason, then, can one say that at one time it was empty and non-existent? He replied:
He said: "This flower originally has no place of birth.
Master Cong of Siming said: "It is like a person in a dream; while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon waking, nothing is to be found.
One must understand that 'non-cognition' (wuzhi) has two meanings: first, the meaning of the emptiness of essence (tǐkōng); second, the meaning of the accomplishment of phenomena (chéngshì)."

The phrase "the dream was not non-existent at the time" refers to the principle of the formation of phenomena. Because of the mind of ignorance, the events of good and evil arise and are accomplished;
yet upon awakening, one realizes there is nothing to be attained. This is the meaning of the emptiness of essence. Even when awake, one still remembers the deeds performed within the dream;
thus, every phenomenon lacks any substantial reality that can be perceived. Although it is called "ignorance," that which is empty in essence remains so.
It has no substance. Yet every person cannot avoid taking a complete dream for waking, or taking being awake as a dream;
thus it is said that everyone says, "This body is like a dream. How could one ever know the body within a dream? It is like a multitude of empty flowers vanishing into space.
One cannot say that there is a fixed place of extinction. Why? Because there is no place of origination.
This statement—that truth and falsehood share the same source—is like these various empty flowers, which are false, yet they "extinguish" within empty space, which is true.
Empty space originally never gave rise to flowers; why, then, discuss their extinction now? To speak of extinction is already to know them as false. Since one knows them to be false...

The place of non-arising is extinguished; when deluded movement arises, there is deluded extinction, yet that very extinction is itself extinguished. In the fundamentally perfect nature of awakening, who gives rise and who extinguishes?
Sentient beings have not yet extinguished [delusion], so they falsely perceive arising and extinction. The Buddhas have already extinguished [delusion]; for them, quiescent extinction is bliss.
All sentient beings, within the state of non-arising, falsely perceive arising and ceasing; for this reason, it is called "revolving in birth and death.
Because sentient beings falsely perceive their illusory bodies as having the characteristics of arising and ceasing, the Buddha speaks of them as "revolving in birth and death.
To say they are so-called is to indicate that they do not truly exist.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "This is the severing of doubt. Previously, because one was engaged in biased views, it was said that [birth and death] exist;

here, because we are discussing the reality, it is said that they are fundamentally non-existent. One must not falsely conceptualize within the true nature where there is neither birth nor death, thereby viewing through biased perspectives that there is birth and there is death.
For this reason, the preceding text points to what is called 'birth and death. Therefore..."
Master Shou said: "In the realm of non-transmigration, one vainly undergoes saṃsāra; within the dharma of non-binding, one spontaneously creates bondage.
The preceding passages all concern the sudden conviction that fundamentally there is no birth-and-death, and the sudden conviction that fundamentally there is no ignorance.
Furthermore, the meaning of the passage concerning Mañjuśrī does not, for the most part, go beyond these four sections. As for those four sections:
This consists of: first, indicating the True Doctrine; second, investigating the deluded ruler; third, explaining the stage of the ground;
