Therein lies partiality. This present passage is likewise so: the initial statement, "This body of mine is a combination of the four great elements," is a general summary.
What follows thereafter is all a detailed enumeration. This is indicated by the phrase "so-called" (suǒwèi).
This is a term for analytical evaluation. To evaluate the present body:
the hair, fur, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, brain, and impurities are all material, obstructive things that must naturally return to the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
Furthermore, "hair, fur, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, marrow, and brain" are the specific items, while the two characters "impurities" (*dūṣika*) serve as the general category.
That is to say, these hairs of the head and body and so forth are all impurities and are all matter (*rūpa*).
Nasal mucus, saliva, pus, blood, spittle, lymph, froth, phlegm, tears, semen, vital energy, and the excretions of feces and urine are all moist substances;
they shall naturally return to the water element (*āpas-dhātu*). All the warmth present upon the body shall naturally return to the fire element (*tejas-dhātu*). Regarding the twelve...

In the midst of these activities—turning and revolving, moving up and down, bending and turning, bowing and looking up, rising and sitting, and exchanging greetings—one naturally returns to the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).
Yet, these four great elements are a provisional combination; the absence of even one is impossible.

If there were only the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and no water element (*ab-dhātu*), it would be like grasping dry ashes; it could never form into a ball. If there were only the water element and no earth element...

It is like oil or water, which possess no solidity or substance. If there were only the earth element and the water element, but no fire element, it would be like a mass of flesh in the shade during the summer months; without the light of the sun, it would immediately rot and decay.
If there were only the earth, water, and fire elements, but no wind element, then growth could not be achieved. Why is this so? It is because of the wind.

It is able to grow all things. Since this is so, when each of the four great elements belongs to its own respective domain, you who are now all sentient beings are merely the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
When you hold such a view, the earth returns to earth, the water returns to water, the fire returns to fire, and the wind [returns to wind].
Returning to the winds, the four great elements each depart; "departing" is the meaning of emptiness. Thus, one no longer knows where that previously falsely grasped body might be.
This is the capturing and defeating of the illusory, hollow shell of the four elements, and one is no longer deceived by it.
This is precisely right mindfulness, right understanding, and right practice.
One then knows that this body ultimately has no substance; it appears as a composite phenomenon, truly identical to a magical illusion.

Only after the four great elements have dispersed and ceased does one realize that this illusory body is fundamentally empty; it is a form provisionally formed through combination, truly identical to a magical illusion.

As Liezi says: "The puppet created by Yan Shi was skilled in singing and dancing, yet when it was dismembered, it was found to be made of nothing but leather and wood. This is precisely what is meant.

Chan Master Furan Hui of Xichu said: "This is because, through the preceding practice of the contemplation of investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*), one contemplates the four great elements and the delusory body until all delusions are exhausted;
only then does one perceive the true principle of *tathatā*.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that during the Buddha’s lifetime, there was a man traveling far from home who stayed alone overnight in an empty house. In the middle of the night, a ghost suddenly snatched away—"
A corpse arrived and was placed before them. Then another ghost came chasing after them, shouting in anger and abuse:
"This corpse is my property! Why have you brought it here? The first ghost said: "It is my property; I brought it myself.
The two ghosts each seized a hand and a foot, contending with one another without ceasing. The first ghost said: "There is someone here; we may ask him together."
Later, the latter ghost asked, "Who brought this dead person here? The man thought to himself, "These two ghosts possess great power.
Whether I tell the truth or lie, neither will spare me from death. It is better not to speak the truth. He then said, "The former ghost brought him here.
The latter ghost was greatly enraged; he seized the man's hand, pulled it out, and placed it on the ground. The former ghost—
Feeling pity for them, he hurriedly took an arm from a corpse; as soon as he attached it, it adhered.

In this manner, he replaced both arms, both legs, both hands, the head, the flanks, and his entire body. Thereupon, the two ghosts took the human bodies they had exchanged and sat facing each other to eat them together.
Having wiped their lips, they departed. By inferring from this, one knows that the bodies of all sentient beings are likewise [illusory].
Ultimately, it has no substantial reality; it is merely the corpse of a dead person temporarily attached there.
Is this not, indeed, an illusory, deceptive, and unreal thing? As Zhuangzi said: "It entrusts itself to other things to form its body. Is it not so?

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Constantly maintaining this thought—that [the body] is a manifestation of harmony and is truly identical to illusion—clarifies the realm of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the emptiness of persons, one constantly maintains this thought: that one observes this body with the wisdom of emptiness as arising from falsehood;
its original single nature is of the same substance as fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), yet it has suddenly become obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*)."
Impregnated by karma, it does not maintain its own nature but receives retribution according to that karma. Sustained by wind and fire, this consciousness-nature enters the mother’s womb.
Mistaking the discarded [embryo] for its own dwelling, it gives rise to a heart of love and delight, taking it to be its own body and generating the notion of "mine.
It gathers this impure mass into a single lump, forming what is called the physical body; this is termed the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).

To experience this body and give rise to perceptions of suffering and pleasure is called the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). To conceive of suffering and pleasure is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
To designate these formations is called the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Consciousness abiding therein is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).

Just as the five fingers together form the appearance of a fist, this is called the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), also called the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*), and also called the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*).
Because these four great elements and five aggregates are grasped to form this physical body, it is called the "object of the emptiness of beings.

When its root is investigated, it is produced from the provisional four great elements through the karma-consciousness of ignorance. The two great elements of wind and fire cause the consciousness to coalesce and enter the mother’s womb.
The two drops of red and white are called the water element (*abdhātu*). Just as bubbles arise from water and coalesce to form a body, this is called the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*).

These four great elements (*mahābhūta*) possess no real nature; they are mistakenly perceived as a body, and are thus termed the "five aggregates as substantial dharmas" (*pañcaskandha-dravyadharma*).

Although these four great elements lack a substantial essence, they arise through provisional conditions and exist through the conjunction of causes and conditions; therefore, they are called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Birth: This condition is the causal condition (*nidāna*). Due to some slight causal connection with one's parents, one comes to be born into my family.

When consciousness departs, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows it, and warmth (*uṣman*) likewise follows. Once the two great elements of earth and water are no longer sustained by fire and wind, [the body perishes].
Therefore, earth and water naturally disperse and perish. Because past virtuous karma serves as the cause, it is called "birth. "Birth" means "formation.
When the karma is exhausted, this physical body—the fruit thereof—perishes. Because the four great elements disperse, it is called "death.
"Death" means "exhaustion. The soul-consciousness is scattered; once the sovereign master has departed, the cause is thereby brought to its end.
Thus it is. Hair and body hair are the sprouts of the blood. Nails and teeth are the sprouts of the marrow.
The sites upon which skin, flesh, hair, and body hair depend grow when moistened by the blood. Tendons and bones are the sites upon which nails and teeth depend;
they grow when moistened by the marrow. There are, in total, three hundred and sixty joints and bones. Nine...
The nineteen thousand pores and the eighty-four thousand families of worms are all subsumed within the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*).
Saliva, mucus, pus, blood, excrement, and urine are the water element (*ab-dhātu*). Warmth is the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*). Movement and transformation are the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).

From the union of the vital energies of the father and mother that forms the body, through birth, growth, and until old age and death, all are termed "defiled form" (*saṃkleśa-rūpa*). These consist of earth, water, fire, and wind.
Each returns to its source; thus it is said that they "each depart. Once the four elements have dispersed, the illusory body immediately ceases.
Having died and been cremated, the ashes fly away and the smoke vanishes. Therefore, it is asked: "Where now is this illusory body? This concludes the preceding passage.

One then knows that this body is ultimately without substance; it exists as a manifestation of combination, truly identical to an illusion or a transformation, a mere empty state produced by the linking of births.
Through the false conjunction of the four conditions, the six sense organs falsely come to exist.

The four conditions are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). After the four great elements have combined in a provisional manner, there subsequently arise the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
These six organs and the four great elements are synthesized from within and without.
Within there are the four great elements; without there are the six sense organs. Through the provisional conjunction of the internal and external, this illusory body is formed.
Delusively, the energy of conditions accumulates therein.
"Conditioned qi" refers to illusory form and mind that manifest from conditions.
"Accumulated therein" means that within this illusory body, they gather and do not disperse.
There appears to be a characteristic of an object; it is conventionally designated as "mind.
The energy of conditions accumulates within, and the characteristics of conditions take shape without. That which "appears to exist" does not truly possess these characteristics;
that which is a "conventional designation" does not truly possess this mind.
Chan Master Fuyan Hui of Xishu said: "The former was observing that the body has no self; this is observing that the mind has no self.
The four conditions are earth, water, fire, and wind. The six sense organs are the 'external,' and the four great elements are the 'internal.
As for 'conditioning by air' (or 'vital energy'), this refers to the arising of a mind capable of攀缘 (*pányuán*, grasping/conditioning) upon the six sense objects. This mind is the true mind."
The qi of the aforementioned one part is in accord with the qi of the true mind.

This means that this body is merely a provisional combination of the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind; since these four elements are falsely present within it, [it is not the true self].
Thus, externally there are the delusory six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Since there are the six sense organs, there must be the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).

Since there are the six sense objects, they entice and provoke the deluded mind—the energy of conditional discrimination—within the interval between them. Amidst the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the six sense organs, this [deluded mind] accumulates as if it possessed a semblance of form and characteristics.
Consequently, [the text] refutes this by stating: "It is merely a provisional conjunction that constitutes the mind; it does not [truly exist]."
This is the true mind. It is that which thoroughly penetrates and shatters the deluded, discursive, and攀缘 (pān-yuan) mind of inverted thoughts accumulated over immeasurable kalpas.
Thus, at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, Ānanda clung to this mind but found no basis for it; he was bewildered in all seven locations.
The World-Honored One said to Ānanda: "Alas! This is not your mind. This is the discrimination of external objects."
"Deluded thoughts and inversions are not your true mind"—this accords with that meaning.
Master Cong of Siming said: "The four conditions are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). These four are a provisional combination, like bubbles arising from water;
this is what is called the 'body. This body possesses the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind as the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*). As for the eye..."

Regarding the category of objective forms (*rūpa-viṣaya*), each of the five sense organs likewise has its own respective object. As stated in the "Chapter on Emptiness": "Each [organ] individually perceives its own sphere of objects.
When these are combined internally and externally, the accumulation of the six internal consciousnesses within appears to have the semblance of an object-perceiving aspect;
this is conventionally designated as 'mind. One erroneously mistakes the perceived reflection for the characteristic of one's own mind. It further states: "The empty, false, and floating mind."
There are many such skillful illustrations. The "Chapter on the Virtuous King of Nirvāṇa" states:

For example, there was a king who placed four venomous snakes in a single basket and ordered a man to raise them. He commanded that if even one snake were to become angry, the man should be executed according to the law in the marketplace.
Terrified, the man abandoned the basket and fled. The king then dispatched five *caṇḍālas* with drawn swords.
He followed him. One man hid a knife and feigned being a close friend; the other did not trust him and, wishing to hide himself, entered a village.
Once inside the village, he saw no people and heard a voice from the air saying, "Tonight six great bandits will come.
The man was terrified and fled again. On the road he encountered a river, its waters—
The current was swift and turbulent. He immediately took bamboo and wood to construct a raft, cut across the stream, and upon reaching the other shore, was safe and free from affliction.

The Bodhisattva is likewise: hearing the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he contemplates the body as a chest, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as snakes, and the five *caṇḍālas* as the five aggregates (*skandha*).
These falsely appear as friends; one thus craves the empty village of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which are like external... [great thieves].

The six sense objects are the river, and the afflictions are the current. By means of the raft of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), one reaches the other shore of eternal bliss, nirvana.

The subsequent passage concludes the preceding discussion on the mind that conditions the sense objects through the faculties; it likewise concludes the preceding discussion on the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

This is identical to the explanation given in the "Chapter on Emptiness" regarding the two types of emptiness—of dharmas and of birth—which previous sages were unaware of and thus failed to explain in this way.
Good son, this deluded mind cannot exist if the six sense objects are absent.
If all deluded minds were not externally enticed by the six kinds of illusory objects— form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch,
and mental phenomena— from what would this mind arise?
When the four great elements are analyzed and decomposed, not a single atom of dust can be found.
When the four great elements perish, among all the various atoms by which one is defiled, not a single atom exists that can be apprehended.
Within this, the objects of perception each return to their dissolution; ultimately, no perceiving mind can be seen to exist.
After the four conditions and the six sense objects have dispersed and ceased, that which is called the "conditioned mind" (pratyaya-citta) can no longer be perceived.
Master Hui of Xichu said: "This deluded mind is the mind that registers the residual energy of prior conditions; it is this deluded mind capable of discrimination.
If externally there are no six sense objects—form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas—then internally there will be no such [discriminating] capacity."
This is because of the discriminating mind. Thus, Master Fu said: "There has never been a mind without an object, nor has there ever been a mind without an object.
When one observes correctly, the four great elements are analyzed and each is found to be empty; not even the six sense-objects can be apprehended.
Once the four great elements and the six sense-objects have each dispersed and returned to emptiness, ultimately and finally, there is also no subject that performs the act of cognition."
A distinct mind can be perceived. The previous chapter stated, "One falsely identifies the four great elements as the characteristics of one's own body.

Upon reaching this section of the sutra on the contemplation of self-emptiness, from the passage "constantly forming this thought" up to "in reality identical to illusions," [the practitioner] simultaneously shatters [this misconception].

Furthermore, regarding the false identification of the reflected images of the six sense objects as the characteristics of one's own mind, upon reaching this section of the sutra, from the "four conditions" [it proceeds].
It is a provisional combination. Upon reaching the state where no object-conditioned mind can be perceived, one further breaks through it at that moment;
thus, the delusory body and delusory mind are both found to be identical with the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Master Cong of Siming said: "One must know that when one is still in the mother’s womb and not yet born, the four great elements form the body."

Regarding the realm of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*): after emerging from the womb, the sense organs grasp external forms; these conditions of the shadows of the six objects are called the "six sense organs" (*ṣaḍindriya*).

The six objects are then termed the "realm of the emptiness of phenomena. Because the six organs, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses together constitute the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), they are referred to as "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*).
Therefore, it is called the realm of the emptiness of phenomena. The present text specifically concludes this section on the realm of the emptiness of phenomena, beginning with the organs.
One takes the reflections of objects as the mind; therefore it is said that this deluded mind cannot exist without the six sense-objects.
This concludes the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā); hence it is said that there is no mind with conditions to be perceived.
Good son, because that sentient being’s illusory body ceases, the illusory mind also ceases. Because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease.
Since the illusory body has ceased, the illusory mind has no basis upon which to rely, and thus it disperses and perishes. Once the illusory mind has ceased...
Thus, since illusory objects are free from defilement and attachment, they too are dispersed and extinguished.
Because illusory objects are extinguished, the extinction of the illusion is also extinguished.
Once illusory objects have been extinguished, all illusions are entirely empty; even the trace of the extinction of the illusion no longer exists.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "The former was the contemplation of the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); this is the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

That [previous section] pointed to the preceding stage of developing understanding and initiating practice. When sentient beings reach this point, after entering the contemplation of the emptiness of the self, they realize that the illusory body of the four elements is entirely empty.
Not only is the body empty, but the illusory mind—the intermediate conditions and vital energies—is also empty."

Regarding the phrase "because the mind ceases": this single clause summarizes what precedes and introduces what follows. It is not only that the illusory mind is empty; the illusory objects are likewise empty.
These six sense-objects and the myriad dharmas are not only empty of dharma-nature; when the illusion ceases, they also cease, and this wisdom is likewise empty.
Therefore, the Heart Sūtra says: "No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object...
even no wisdom and no attainment. Panshan said: "The moon of the mind is solitary and perfect; its light swallows the myriad phenomena.
The light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist. When both light and objects have vanished, what is it?"
Because illusions are extinguished through extinction, that which is not an illusion does not undergo extinction.
When all illusions are completely extinguished, the extinction of illusion itself is also extinguished. The nature of awakening is not an illusion; it never ceases or perishes.
Master Cixu Fuan Hui said: "The preceding sections all served to shatter attachments; this section now reveals the principle of the True Suchness of the two-fold emptiness.

There are also two parts to the text; this [first part] cites the Dharma. Since the practitioner has previously cultivated the contemplation of the two-fold emptiness to shatter the two attachments to self and phenomena, once these attachments are exhausted and views are eliminated, they realize the true principle of the threefold emptiness.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "This clarifies the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Contemplation must have an object; therefore, it is called the 'object of the emptiness of persons.

"Because the extinction of illusion is itself extinguished. It is like a fire-drill: it burns itself, and as the shavings emerge from the shavings, the shavings are suddenly exhausted.

It is said: "That which is not illusion does not perish; only the wisdom of True Suchness (tathatā) remains alone.
This wisdom also knows that images in a mirror appear when there is an image, and are void when there is no image. Cultivation is entirely this nature; nature fully constitutes cultivation.
Nature does not shift, yet cultivation is ever manifest.
It is like polishing a mirror: when the grime is exhausted, its brilliance appears.
The mirror is a metaphor for the fundamental nature; the grime is a metaphor for all illusions. When the grime is exhausted, the brilliance appears;

when illusions are exhausted, the nature is luminous. Chan Master Fu’an Hui of Xichu said: "This is an illustration offered to support the preceding Dharma-exposition, lest people [misunderstand it]."
It is difficult to clarify. Thus, he employs objects perceivable in the world as metaphors: "dirt" represents the dual attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*);

Polishing a mirror is fundamentally for the purpose of removing dust; now, following the sequence of the text, it means that by previously destroying the two attachments to a self and to dharmas, when these attachments are exhausted and views are eliminated, the true reality manifests.
This is like a worldly person using medicinal paste to wipe away dust:

once the grime on the mirror is entirely gone, the brilliance within the mirror is revealed. Generally speaking, the two characters "polishing dust" (*mò chén*) also have many interpretations, namely:
Whether it be approaching virtuous friends to hear the Mahāyāna and repenting of karmic obstructions, or applying remedies against afflictions,

or sitting in the full lotus posture in meditative absorption, or unifying the mind on a single object, or censuring desire and abandoning the hindrances— all of these are methods for polishing away the dust.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) are non-dual. This can be understood through the analogy of ice and water.
Good son, you should know that both body and mind are entirely illusory defilements.
This illusory body and illusory mind obstruct my enlightened nature, just as filth and impurities stain a pure object.
The characteristics of defilement are eternally extinguished, and the ten directions are pure.
Since the characteristics of defilement in body and mind have already been eternally extinguished, one is pure and unstained throughout the ten directions.

"All are illusory defilements; this refers to what precedes [the seal]. 'The characteristics of defilement are eternally extinguished, and the ten directions are pure';

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Eye, saying: "You all must realize and know that these four great elements constitute the deluded body, as well as the capacity..."

By means of the five roots of attachment, one grasps the five objects of desire; these five sensory realms are like dew upon a flower, which dries up when it encounters the sun.
If one does not contemplate according to the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*), how can the marks of defilement be eternally extinguished?

One should know that Perfect Enlightenment’s quiescent illumination is like a single snowflake on a red-hot furnace—it cannot endure for even a moment. The ten directions are the ten realms; when hell is transformed, it becomes heaven.
The hall [is transformed]; the defiled land is instantly turned into a pure land. The environment and its inhabitants do not obstruct one another; form and mind are without hindrance.
Good son, it is like a pure mani-jewel which reflects the five colors, appearing in each according to the direction.
The *Commentary on Perfect Enlightenment* states: "In Sanskrit, 'maṇi' refers to a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).

The substance of the jewel is luminous and pure, reflecting the colors of the five directions; likewise, the mind of Perfect Enlightenment is tranquil and pure, manifesting its response throughout the ten directions."
All those who are deluded see that mani jewel as actually possessing five colors.

These fools do not know that the essence of the jewel is luminous and pure, and that the five colors are merely reflected therein; they instead claim that the five colors truly exist within the jewel.
This is just like sentient beings who claim that the Buddha truly possesses physical form and characteristics.
Chan Master Fuyan Hui of Xishu said: "This is a metaphor. *Maṇi* here means 'rain of jewels.
It refers to the *maṇi* jewel of the world, which is perfectly luminous and pure within, originally devoid of form or color, yet manifesting according to the direction.
If this jewel is placed suddenly in the east, a blue color will appear within that jewel. If it is placed..."
When it is positioned in the center, a yellow color appears within that jewel.
If it is suddenly placed in the west, a white color appears within that jewel. If it is suddenly placed in the south, a red color appears within that jewel.
If it is suddenly placed in the north, a black color immediately appears within that jewel. Yet the substance of that jewel is perfectly luminous, clear, and pure;
fundamentally, it possesses no such characteristics of color as blue, yellow, red, white, or black, but merely manifests according to its location.
However, there are foolish people in the world who cannot distinguish east from west or south from north, yet they truly claim that this is a mani-jewel.
Within [the mirror], there truly exist these five colors; this is explained by way of analogy. If explained according to the Dharma, the five colors represent the five destinies (*gati*):

blue represents the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*), yellow represents the human realm, white represents the celestial realm, red represents the animal realm, and black represents the hell realm. Question: Are the mirror and the jewel the same or different?

"Yes. He replied, "They are different. For the previous mention of polishing a mirror was merely a metaphor for cultivating the contemplation of the two emptinesses, destroying the two attachments, and revealing the principle of the two emptinesses.
Now, this mention of the mani-jewel is intended to serve as the fundamental principle for the three successive layers of the Dharma-realm below;
therefore, they are not the same. How do we know this? Furthermore, the substance of the jewel is originally perfectly luminous."
It is luminously pure, utterly free from even a hair’s breadth of defilement; this is called the contemplation of true emptiness beyond all signs (*śūnyatā-vipākṣa-darśana*).

Furthermore, the various images manifested within the pearl do not obstruct the pearl, nor does the pearl obstruct the images; this is called the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*dharmatā-dharma-asaṃbaddha-darśana*).
The various images do not depart from the image; the image is entirely the jewel. This is called the contemplation of the non-obstruction of phenomena (dharmadharmāpratigha).

If one correlates this with the three natures (trisvabhāva): the mani-jewel is a metaphor for the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), which is the principle of the two kinds of emptiness that is revealed.

The individual manifestations of color are metaphors for the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), which refers to the various illusions described [in scripture] that fools grasp as being substantially real.
The five colors are a metaphor for the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is the aforementioned dust and grime.

However, one day the World-Honored One held up a jewel and asked the celestial kings of the five directions, "What color is this jewel? At that time, the celestial kings of the five directions each described it as a different color.
The World-Honored One then hid the jewel in his sleeve and raised his hand, asking, "What color is this jewel?"
"Color," the Heavenly Kings said. "The Buddha’s hand has no jewels; where is there any color? The World-Honored One sighed and said, "How can you be so utterly deluded?
When I show you worldly jewels, you each insist on describing them as blue, yellow, red, or white.
But when I show you the true pearl, you know nothing at all. At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the Heavenly Kings of the Five Directions all [attained realization].
"Awakening to the Way. Yet, have we ever seen our own mind-jewel? Master Cong of Siming said:

"This passage is precisely an analogy for the five sense faculties grasping the objects of the five desires. The jewel is a metaphor for the single nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Perfect Enlightenment does not abide in its own nature; it follows the five desire-faculties to grasp the realms of the five sensory objects, just as..."

A jewel reflects colors, manifesting them according to the direction. When the ignorant see these colors, ordinary beings are naturally deluded, while those of the Two Vehicles remain detached from them—like ghosts, tigers, dragons, or snakes.
A Bodhisattva sees all forms as perfect enlightenment; form is itself the Dharma-realm.
The Buddha sees form as neither identical to nor different from [the mind]. Yongjia said: "The mind is the root and dharmas are the dust; these two are like a mirror and its reflection."
The upper traces are gone; when the stains and impurities are entirely removed, the radiant goodness manifests. When both mind and dharmas are extinguished, the nature is itself the Truth.
The sages laboriously employ provisional teachings as skillful means, like gathering flowers to produce honey.
Good son, the pure nature of perfect enlightenment manifests within body and mind, responding to each according to its kind.
The pure nature of perfect enlightenment transforms and manifests as body and mind, appearing in response to each and every class of sentient beings;
this is just like the thirty-two manifestations of Avalokiteśvara.
That deluded person claims that pure, perfect enlightenment truly possesses such physical and mental self-characteristics; it is exactly like this.

When a fool sees the Buddha manifest various bodies and minds, they then say that within pure, perfect enlightenment there truly exist such forms and appearances, and that their own physical characteristics are likewise so. This may be called true delusion.
Master Chuanfeng Huì of Xishu said: "The previous [passage] concerning the mani-jewel was explained by means of a metaphor;

this [passage] is explained directly in terms of the Dharma itself. To harmonize it with the preceding metaphorical text: it means that all sentient beings, if they take this perfectly enlightened, pure nature..."
When one suddenly finds oneself in the realm of hungry ghosts, this very nature of perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-gotra) immediately manifests in the form of a hungry ghost.
One’s eyes flash like lightning, and the openings of the throat are like needles; one hears not the name of water or broth, nor does one see the face of food or drink.
Flames break out all at once in the limbs and joints, and every movement produces the sound of five hundred carts. If one were to take this perfect enlightenment...
When one suddenly enters the human realm, this perfectly awakened nature (*pariniṣpanna-gotra*) immediately manifests as the physical appearance of a person.
Each individual has brows that arch and a nose that is straight; the head is round like heaven, and the feet are square like earth.

Among them, those who are most supreme and noble may have food spread out over ten cubits and hundreds of concubines in attendance; when they call out once from above the hall, a hundred voices respond from below.
If one is extremely poor or lowly— dwelling in a humble alley or upon the road, with clothing that does not cover the body and food that does not fill the mouth—
and if this nature of perfect enlightenment were suddenly placed within the realm of animals, then within this nature of perfect enlightenment,
the forms of animals would immediately appear: perhaps with wings on the back, or horns upon the head, or tusks protruding, or fur spread across the body.

Claws. Some fly upward; others crawl prone. If this nature of perfect enlightenment is suddenly manifested in the heavenly realms, then within this nature of perfect enlightenment, the forms of celestial immortals appear:
some are five hundred *zhang* in height, and some have a lifespan of eight thousand years.
They take the awakening and slumber of dragons as their spring and autumn, and the opening and closing of lotuses as their [seasonal markers].
Day and night, surrounded by celestial men and women, celestial fragrances, and celestial music, they forget the west while looking east, and forget the north while looking south;

their bliss is inexhaustible. Yet, if this nature of perfect enlightenment is suddenly cast into the realm of hell, then within this very nature of perfect enlightenment, the manifestations of hell appear: forests of blades rise before one's eyes.
Swords and halberds pierce the heavens; boiling cauldrons surge with waves; red furnaces flare with flames;
iron cities are closed by day; bronze pillars blaze at night. Souls are boiled and spirits are stewed; heads are pounded and feet are crushed, undergoing immeasurable suffering.
Yet this nature of Perfect Enlightenment thus manifests in response to each type of being within the five realms of existence; and as for the fundamental substance of this Perfect Enlightenment—
Above all this, there is fundamentally no appearance of devas, humans, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.
It is only those ignorant people who have never clearly awakened to the mind-ground that forgetfully cling to these various differentiated appearances as being real.
It is just like a fool who clings to the idea that there are five colors within a pearl; therefore it is said, "it is also thus. An ancient said: "Within the pearl..."
There are no colors of the five directions; they arise because of being reflected by light. Within its nature, there is no body of the five destinies; it appears according to karma.
Those who are deluded regarding the pearl grasp at the notion that there is actual color within the pearl; those who are ignorant of its nature grasp at the notion of a void body within the nature.
The dharma and the analogy are perfectly clear, and the true manifestation may be verified. However, these five paths are not to be sought exclusively in the external. If...
Within a single body, there are likewise present the ten dharma-realms. How is this known? The Sixth Patriarch said:
"If you contemplate unwholesome dharmas, this mind immediately transforms into the hells; if you contemplate wholesome dharmas, it transforms into heaven.
Cruelty and harm transform into the realm of animals; greed and anger transform into hungry ghosts and asuras. Compassion, joy, and equanimity transform into the various [heavenly realms]."
O Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one thus knows that the myriad practices arise from the mind, and that this single mind resides within oneself. Internally empty, the external can never be substantial;
externally subtle, the internal can never be coarse. A virtuous cause will ultimately encounter favorable conditions, while evil conduct makes it difficult to escape an evil environment.
To incur disaster and provoke enmity is certainly not something produced by Heaven, nor is it something born from the Earth. Contemplate this teaching.
For a practitioner, if within the twelve periods of the day you settle the *maṇi* jewel within your own being, you should place it in a favorable position;
do not allow yourself to have cause for regret on another day, like one who tries to bite his own navel.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "This concludes the contemplation on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). The Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) accords with conditions to manifest as all phenomena.
When residing in the body, the entire nature of enlightenment constitutes the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.
When residing in the mind, the eyes are congealed as form, the ears as sound, the nose as fragrance, the tongue as flavor, and the body as touch."

Is it not that each should respond according to their own kind? Those who are deluded are ignorant; they claim that the nature of pure, perfect enlightenment actually possesses the characteristics of body and mind.
Recognizing this as the self, they give rise to the four views; clinging to it as the self, they falsely perceive birth and death.
Therefore it is said, "it is likewise so.
Because of this, one cannot remain far removed from illusion and transformation.
Due to this deluded attachment, sentient beings are unable to distance themselves from all illusions.
Therefore, I speak of the illusory defilements of body and mind.
Because they are deludedly attached to body and mind, the Buddha speaks of them as "illusory defilements.
In contrast to those who have abandoned these illusory defilements, one is called a bodhisattva.
For one who faces the defilement of illusion, they eliminate the illusion through awakening; this is what is meant by "administering medicine to a patient.
Now, for one who faces illusion with awakening and is thus able to leave behind the defilement of illusion—the Buddha calls such a person a bodhisattva.
Defilements are exhausted:
the illusory defilements of body and mind are all forever extinguished and eliminated.
The perception of illusion likewise does not exist; thus,
there is no opposition to defilement,
and for one who has no opposition to illusion, there is also no illusion-defilement.

As for what is called a "name," it is designated as a "bodhisattva," yet this too is an illusory name. Now, in light of the two kinds of emptiness regarding both defilement and purity, how could there be such a characteristic of a bodhisattva?
Master Cifeng Huì of Xishu said: "This [passage] 'sweeping away traces to enter the profound' uses illusory transformations to point to body and mind.
This section involves a person and a dharma; there is the agent and the object. The 'person' refers to the three agents, and the 'dharma' refers to the three objects.
Regarding the three agents of the person: first, the sentient being is the grasper, and defilement is the grasped; second, the bodhisattva..."
This refers to that which is able to abandon; "defilement" refers to that which is to be abandoned. The three Buddhas are those who are able to teach.
Such things as the attachment to defilement, the abandonment of defilement, persons, and dharmas are all that is taught. The meaning is this:

because sentient beings falsely cling to the thought that within the pure and perfect nature of *bodhi* there truly exist such illusory shadows of the four elements and the six sense-objects, they are unable to distance themselves from these empty, unreal phenomena.

Because of these circumstances, the World-Honored One was compelled to descend and be born in a royal palace, practice austerities on the Snowy Mountains, realize the Way beneath the Vajra Seat, and subdue the Māras under the Bodhi tree.
He remained in the world for forty-nine years, delivering more than three hundred assemblies of teachings. As for those teachings, they spoke only of all sentient beings.
One does not realize that this body and this mind are both illusory transformations, defiled and impure.
To counteract the grasping at these illusory defilements, the Dharma teacher causes [the practitioner] to cultivate according to the teaching so as to sever hindrances and leave behind defilement.

Furthermore, as long as sentient beings have not left behind defilement, they are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); once they have left behind defilement, they are Bodhisattvas. Although they may thus transcend the state of being an ordinary worldling, [the process continues].
Yet the Bodhisattva still remains. The ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is like a disease; the Bodhisattva is like medicine. Although the disease has been removed, the medicine still remains.

It is necessary that after the defilements of the ordinary person have been exhausted, the Bodhisattva who stands in opposition to that ordinary person must also be removed—just as when the disease departs, the medicine is also discarded.
When both the ordinary and the sage are exhausted, there is neither opposition nor defilement. This is not only...

There are neither ordinary beings nor bodhisattvas; furthermore, even the characteristics of the World-Honored One who is free from defilement, as taught according to the capacities of sentient beings, do not exist.
This is the clearing away of traces to return to the truth. Guifeng said: "The meaning of the Dharma-body preaching the Dharma lies herein.
According to the *Dajiao*, when the sutra text reaches this point, there are two kinds of skillful means: first, the proximate skillful means; second, the remote [skillful means].

The "expedient means" refers to the two preceding types of emptiness contemplation (*śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) and the mani-jewel; these are the remote expedients for the three subsequent layers of the Dharma-realm contemplation (*dharmadhātu-bhāvanā*).
This passage from the *Foji ru xuan jing* (Sutra on Erasing Traces and Entering the Mysterious) constitutes the proximate expedient for the Dharma-realm contemplation.

Within the gate of the Sudden Teaching (*dun jiao*), these two skillful means (*upāya*) are employed to guide practitioners directly into the contemplation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*) within the inconceivable gate of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Therefore, it is said: "This sutra properly belongs to the Sudden Teaching, while partially belonging to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan jiao*)."
Furthermore, if those of sudden capacity realize the contemplation of the two emptinesses, they will naturally and spontaneously proceed directly to the realm of the Avataṃsaka;
such individuals are those of perfect capacity. To explain this by means of a metaphor: the Sudden Teaching is like a gate; if one is able to open the gate, [one enters].

One naturally and spontaneously arrives at entry [into the state]. Furthermore, this present sutra’s sudden teaching takes the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) as its primary path.
As for the existence of the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*), it is a practice modeled after that [sudden teaching].

It is intended to cause practitioners to emulate the perfect capacity (*paripūrṇa-yogya*) of the *Avataṃsaka* for their cultivation. How is this known? Because the subsequent "Contemplation of Universal Interpenetration" is explained in the sutra.
It should be known that the Bodhisattva is neither bound by dharmas nor seeks liberation from dharmas; they do not loathe birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor crave nirvāṇa;
they do not revere those who uphold the precepts nor despise those who violate them; they do not value long-standing practice nor slight beginners. Why is this?
[Because] for one who practices the contemplation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it should properly be said that all phenomena are mutually unimpeded (*shishi wuai*). Now...

Since it does not speak of the non-obstruction between phenomena (*shishi wuai*), but rather declares "because of universal awakening," this is the fundamental tenet of the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*).
Those who study Buddhist texts ought to understand both its fundamental tenets and its path.
Furthermore, regarding the two characters for *dharmadhātu*: as for its essence, it neither increases nor decreases; as for its function, it pervades all that exists.
Once attained, it is eternally constant throughout the limits of the future. All Buddhas take this as their teacher; sentient beings take this as their essence;
the myriad phenomena take this as their source. It cannot be sought through form, nor can it be recognized by appearance.
It is simply the one mind. Question: Since it is the one mind, for what reason is it also called the *dharmadhātu* (Dharma-realm)?
Answer: Because within the one mind there are two meanings. First, the meaning of "guiding and sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*); therefore, it is called "Dharma. Second, the meaning of "nature and divisions";
therefore, it is called "realm" (*dhātu*). Nature refers to the *dharmadhātu* of principle; divisions refer to the *dharmadhātu* of phenomena. Indeed, nature has no limits or boundaries.
While phenomena differ in a thousand ways, the single term "Dharma" carries the meaning of "following conditions. If it pertains to principle, it is the Dharma-realm of Principle;

if it pertains to phenomena, it is the Dharma-realm of Phenomena; and if it pertains to both principle and phenomena, it is the Dharma-realm of the Unobstructed Interpenetration of Principle and Phenomena.

If it pertains to phenomena (dharma), it constitutes the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharmāpratītyasamutpāda-dharmadhātu*). This Dharma-realm should be distinguished according to its doctrinal meaning.

First, the Single True Dharma-realm belongs to the category of "Dharma" (*dharma*). Guifeng said: "When principle and phenomena are not yet clearly understood, one does not speak of existence or emptiness;
rather, one points directly to the numinous source of original enlightenment. Therefore, it is called the 'Single True Dharma-realm. Subsequently, based upon this Single True [Dharma-realm]...

Within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there are distinguished fourfold divisions: the Dharma-realm of Principle, the Dharma-realm of Phenomena, the Dharma-realm of the Non-obstruction of Principle and Phenomena, and the Dharma-realm of the Non-obstruction of Phenomenon and Phenomenon.
These fourfold Dharma-realms all pertain to the meaning [of the teaching].
Formerly, during the early Tang dynasty, there was the Venerable Dixin, who was an emanation of Mañjuśrī. Employing his own inexhaustible wisdom, he beheld the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
The principles and meanings explained therein are, without exception, each of these fourfold Dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

Within this, the meanings expressed are condensed into three levels of contemplative gates (*vipaśyanā-mukha*): first, the contemplation of true emptiness transcending all marks; second, the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena;
and third, the contemplation of universal interpenetration and containment. Within the first, the contemplation of true emptiness, there are four propositions.

There are ten gates. Their sole essential purpose is to eliminate the attachments of ordinary people and non-Buddhists to nihilistic emptiness or substantial form, thereby revealing the principle of the Single True Dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu*).
Although this reveals the principle of original oneness within the Single True Dharma-realm, one has merely attained its substance;
it has not yet clarified whether the mountains, rivers, and great earth are distinct from or identical to oneself.
First, he then employs the second contemplation, the Contemplation of the Non-obstruction between Principle and Phenomena, to give rise to wondrous function.
He suddenly perceives that principle is identical to phenomena and phenomena are identical to principle, just as a thousand waves are identical to water, or ten thousand vessels are the same gold.

Within this contemplation, while it is said from the perspective of principle that there is the meaning of "changing according to conditions yet remaining unchanging," it is also said from the perspective of phenomena that there is the meaning of "the substance of phenomena being empty. Yet, [this] is still not...
One creates the vast and inconceivable realm of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, within the third contemplation of universal inclusion and containment, it is clarified that a single dharma pervades all dharmas, and all dharmas are entirely subsumed within a single dharma.
Regarding all phenomena and all objects, it is taught that there is the non-obstruction of thing and thing (*dharmadharmāpratighāta*).
For example, when the youth Sudhana arrived before the Great Tower Adorned by Vairocana, he addressed Maitreya, saying: "I pray only that the Great Sage..."
"Open the door of the pavilion so that I may enter. Thereupon Maitreya snapped his fingers, and the door opened immediately.
He bade Sudhana enter; once he had entered, the door closed again. Sudhana then beheld the pavilion as vast and boundless as space itself.
Furthermore, he saw within them countless hundreds of thousands of exquisite pavilions, each containing a Maitreya.
Before each Maitreya stood a Sudhana, and every single Sudhana had his palms joined in reverence.
He saw the body of one Sudhana enter the bodies of all the other Sudhanas, and all the Sudhanas were subsumed within the body of one Sudhana.
Internally, one pavilion is the principal, with all other pavilions as its companions. All phenomena are thus layered and inexhaustible. As Qingliang said:
"The Buddhas and sentient beings penetrate one another; the pure lands and the defiled lands are interfused.
Every phenomenon encompasses every other, and every atom contains entire worlds. They are mutually identical and mutually inclusive, without obstruction."
Perfectly interfused, it possesses the ten gates of mystery, layer upon layer without end. Question:

Is the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness that shatters attachments the same as, or different from, the first "contemplation of true emptiness transcending all signs" within the Contemplation of the Dharma Realm? If you say they are the same:
World-Honored One, for what reason do you teach the contemplation of the absolute emptiness beyond all marks (*śūnyatā-viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) after the two contemplations of emptiness?

If these are distinct, how could one who has already realized and entered [the truth] through the two contemplations of emptiness proceed to practice the contemplation of absolute emptiness only then to eliminate the emotional attachment to "annihilating emptiness" (*uccheda-śūnyatā*) and "substantial form" (*dravya-rūpa*)?
Such a principle is certainly impossible. Answer: Within the two contemplations of emptiness, the attachments are destroyed; that is—

This contemplation of true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*) distinguishes [the mind] from emotional attachments (*qing*). In that [preceding] section, it distinguishes from emotional attachments; here, it refutes dogmatic clinging (*zhi*). This refutation of clinging has its own specific tenets in both cases.
Thus, the words are not presented together, the text is not written all at once, and the principle is not revealed all at once.

However, at the beginning, following the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), the text reveals the principle, stating: "Because illusion is extinguished through extinction, that which is not illusion is not extinguished. This single phrase is taught.
Regarding that which has not yet been exhausted: here, once again, the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*);
the external and internal four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*); all mundane and supramundane phenomena;

as well as the primary and secondary retributions of self and others—these seven sections of scripture all discuss purity, extensively revealing the principle of the true emptiness devoid of marks within the *dharmadhātu*. Furthermore, the preceding two types of emptiness [have already] refuted...

Grasping [the object] and the mani-jewel are the distant expedient means (*dūraprayoga*); together with "sweeping away traces to enter the profound" (*fují rùxuán*), these constitute the proximate expedient means (*āsannaprayoga*).

These two expedient means must not be conflated. The section on "form and characteristics being empty and pure" corresponds precisely to the third phrase within the contemplation of true emptiness (*zhēn kōng guān*), namely:
"the non-obstruction of emptiness and form. This represents the culmination of understanding leading toward practice. Next:

The section on "Emptiness and Form Being Identical" corresponds to one phrase within the fourth contemplation, "The Contemplation of Utter Extinction and Non-Reliance," among those [contemplations] within the True Emptiness of that [Dharmadhātu].
This constitutes the very essence of the practice; it corresponds to the two phrases within the True Emptiness of that Dharmadhātu:
"Bringing form back to emptiness" and "Clarifying that emptiness is identical to form. This serves to eliminate emotional attachment and reveal true understanding.

Master Cong of Siming said: "The meaning of this section of the sutra is precisely to summarize the two kinds of emptiness—of phenomena and of self—with respect to both the objective realm and contemplative observation.
When sentient beings first come to receive a womb in their intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is solely because they are deluded by ignorance."

Beginning with ignorance as the condition for volitional formations and ending with old age and death within the twelve links of dependent origination: first, one recognizes that ignorance is the beginning of erroneous application.

The four great elements and five aggregates constitute the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); the shadows conditioned by the six sense objects constitute the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

These two types of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—are the objects of the deluded attachments of sentient beings. Now, one employs the perfect enlightenment of *śamatha*, which is quiescent and illuminating; this is termed the second [emptiness].
The Contemplation of Emptiness: One contemplates that these four great elements, five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen realms are all devoid of any fundamental source.

Realizing that the characteristics of the sense organs and objects are like empty flowers and illusory transformations, they are transformed into awakened clarity. This nature of perfect enlightenment is itself fundamentally empty.
When the defilement of ignorance is exhausted, there is no longer the defilement of opposition. Once the defilements are exhausted, the practice of the six perfections is perfected;
thus, one is conventionally designated as a "Bodhisattva. Within the state of equality, even the names "sentient being" and "Buddha" do not exist. Therefore it is said:

"As for what is called 'name,' it is the mark of the emptiness of all dharmas—neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, and likewise without old age and death, nor the exhaustion of old age and death."
There is no suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path; there are no Four Noble Truths. There is neither wisdom nor attainment—only then can one be called a Bodhisattva.
Good son, because this Bodhisattva and the sentient beings of the final age have realized all illusions and extinguished their reflected images, they are thus.
At that time, one immediately attains directionless purity.
All illusory images are extinguished, and one thus attains directionless purity. "Directionless" means not being restricted by spatial location.
Boundless space is manifested by awakening;
once the purity that is free from directionality is attained, then boundless space is revealed through awakening.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "The scriptural text clearly shows that it leads the practitioner to enter the inconceivable realm of the Huayan Dharma-realm.
This is achieved by virtue of the functional effort applied within the preceding realm of the two-fold emptiness;
it is because of this functional effort that one attains realization and entry, as expressed in the subsequent passage. The meaning is as the World-Honored One declared:"

The Universal Eye Cloud states: How do Bodhisattvas who have entered the contemplation of the two empties (dvaya-śūnyatā), as well as sentient beings of the末代 (final age), attain realization and enter the contemplation of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) to perceive the purity of the ten directions?

It is precisely because they have perfected the practice of the contemplation of the two empties that they awaken to their own mind as being illusory and unreal, and further extinguish the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), the twelve bases (dvādaśāyatana), and the eighteen realms (aṣṭādaśa-dhātu).
Regarding the dharmas that are images dependent on others: if one clings to body and mind, there are then directions of east, west, south, and north.

Now, at this time when one no longer clings to body and mind, one perceives that throughout the worlds of the ten directions, the immeasurable and boundless void is entirely the nature of vast, numinous, and perfect enlightenment;
there is nothing that is not fully revealed. "Manifest" (xian) refers to emptiness.
The awakening manifests and arises; "arising" means that delusion is exhausted and the mind opens. This is what is meant by "the entire earth is the single eye of the śramaṇa.
When one has not yet awakened, upon seeing that empty space, one understands it as being merely empty space. However, after awakening, [one perceives it differently].
That very emptiness is the original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); one no longer perceives the characteristics of emptiness.
This is called taking the entirety of emptiness as the essential nature (*dharmatā*). One enwraps and pervades all through the practice of vows; thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"If there is a person who awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions will all be dissolved. Is this not what is meant by "boundless"?
"Is empty space manifested by awakening?

Master Cong of Siming said: "This clarifies that for the assembly of those who are responsive to the teaching, as well as for sentient beings of the末代 (final age), extending even to the five hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa—those who thus cultivate Perfect Awakening—once their contemplative practice has reached completion, the multitude..."

Birth occurs within delusion, like an ancient mirror that has not yet been polished; thus, the nature of awakening is not manifest. Now, by employing perfect contemplation to illuminate the aspect of awakening, the object and the contemplation function in tandem.
It is like the mirror becoming bright when the grime is removed: the three thousand realms of the ten dharma-realms manifest all at once.

Furthermore, one must know that the mirror of the mind is fundamentally luminous and that the three thousand virtues of the inherent nature are primordially complete; it is simply that perfect awakening has not yet been revealed. This is because the three...
Enveloped by the defilements of delusion, the images have now vanished along with the dust being removed. Thus, the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi) manifests before one;
this is entirely due to the inherent nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*). Reaching this state, all phenomena (*dharma*) are pure in every respect, possessing no location whatsoever.
Therefore, it is called "pure without direction. As the *Buddhapiṭaka* states: "The empty space of the ten directions arises within my mind. Hence, it is called "without [direction]."

The periphery is empty space; object and wisdom are fused as one. Thus it is said, "that which is manifested by awakening. "Awakening" refers to contemplation (*guan*); "that which is" refers to the object (*jing*).

"Manifested" means the mutual resonance of the path of response and stimulus. The *Zhiyao chao* states: "The three thousand worlds of the ordinary ground are not separated [from those of the Buddha]; they are all perfectly complete with every single thought.
Since the three thousand worlds of the Buddha-ground are already fused, they are fully present with every single response. How much more so for sentient beings!"

The Buddha is moved by the Buddha within the mind; the Buddha responds to the sentient being within the mind. Since the essence of this resonance and response is identical, how could there be any distinction in the benefits of the provisional and the ultimate?
Therefore, it is said that he transforms only bodhisattvas and does not act for the sake of those of the two vehicles. As for those who hear the Dharma:
There is not one who does not attain Buddhahood. Thus far, the principle has been revealed through upward contemplation.

As for the subsequent scriptural text, it further takes the three thousand wonderful dharmas thus revealed and applies them one by one to matter and mind, the environment and its inhabitants, sentient beings and Buddhas, and the hundreds of thousands of samādhis and immeasurable gates of practice;
each and every one is none other than the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment. In this way, all sentient beings...
All that is born is the essence of Vairocana; all lands are eternally the Dharma-realm of Constant Tranquility and Light. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the purity of the mind is revealed.
Once the awakening that has been realized is perfectly luminous, the original purity of one's own mind is revealed.

Because the mind is pure, the objects of perception are pure; because the objects of perception are pure, the faculty of sight is pure; and because the faculty of sight is pure, the visual consciousness is pure.
Whatever one desires to see consists entirely of defiled thoughts; therefore, it is called "seeing dust. The eye is the fundamental source of seeing;
therefore, it is called the "eye-faculty" (*cakṣur-indriya*). The eye is able to differentiate various forms; therefore, it is called "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣur-vijñāna*).
Because consciousness is pure, the objects of hearing are pure. Because hearing is pure, the faculty of the ear is pure. Because the faculty is pure, the auditory consciousness is pure.
Whatever one desires to hear consists entirely of the objects of thought; therefore, they are called "objects of hearing. Since the ear is the fundamental source of hearing, [it is pure].
It is said: "The ear-faculty. Because the ear can discriminate various sounds, it is called ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*).
Because consciousness is pure, the objects of perception are pure. This applies likewise, even unto the nose, tongue, body, and mind."

When the mind perceives something, it is likewise a defiled thought; therefore, it is called "perceiving objects. The nose, tongue, body, and mind each have their own objects, faculties, and consciousnesses;
yet because the self-mind is fundamentally pure, they all attain purity.
Good son, because the sense faculties are pure, the objects of form are pure; because form is pure, the objects of sound are pure.
It is likewise for the objects of odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
Once the six sense faculties have become pure, the six kinds of illusory objects—form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—are likewise all purified.
Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "To realize the purity of the six faculties, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses is precisely form."
Within the emptiness and purity of marks (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā-viśuddhi*), there are two aspects: first, the internal body consisting of the sense organs and consciousness;

second, from the section on the "purity of the six sense organs" (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) downward, the external objects consisting of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). The sense organs have the meaning of generating consciousness; the sense fields have the meaning of defiling or dusting; and consciousness has the meaning of discernment.

Furthermore, within the six sense fields, the single character "form" (*rūpa*) carries three meanings: first, it is visible and possesses resistance (*sanidarśana-sapratigha*); second, [it is... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated after the second definition.)
There are those that are invisible but resistant, and three that are both invisible and non-resistant. Now, regarding those that are visible and resistant: these are the forms perceived by the eye.
Those that are invisible but resistant are sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects (*dharmas*). Although these cannot be seen, they are nonetheless resistant.

However, there is that which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*). That which is invisible and non-resistant (*anidarśana-apratigha*) is exclusively matter (*rūpa*) subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

Furthermore, within the coarse matter perceived by the eye, there are three types: first, manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), namely blue, yellow, red, white, light, shadow, brightness, darkness, and so forth;
second, shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), namely large, small, square, round, coarse, fine, long, short, high, low, regular, irregular, and so forth.

The three types of informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) consist of: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up; taking, discarding, and discerning; as well as sounds such as pleasant and unpleasant.
Regarding the sense of being appropriated (*upātta*) or non-appropriated (*anupātta*), there is the sense of being both appropriated and non-appropriated.

Odors include the pleasant, the unpleasant, and their combinations. Tastes include the transformed, the raw, the cooked, the agreeable, and so forth. Tangibles include the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), heat, cold, and roughness.

Regarding "smoothness, satiety, hunger, and so forth": among phenomena (*dharma*), there is an object known by the mind; with the exception of the five sensory objects, all else is *dharma*. Master Mingcong of Siming said:
"Because awakening is perfectly luminous, it extends to the nose, tongue, body, and mind, which are likewise so.
The wisdom of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is termed "perfectly luminous awakening. This awakened wisdom merges with original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Upon merging—

The arising of the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment is called Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Perfect Enlightenment is itself the Buddha. Having already attained Buddhahood, Vairocana pervades all places.
Taking this Vairocana and traversing through all phenomena (*dharma*), one thereby subsumes all phenomena back into one's own cognitive mind (*vijñāna-citta*).
One reflects back that all phenomena are created solely by the mind. This present traversal of phenomena is essential...
The manifestations of the mind possess nothing separate from them; all are dependently originated. Arising possesses nothing separate from it;

all are manifestations of the mind. The mind gives rise to its manifestations, and every phenomenon is pure. Therefore, it is said that the mind is pure when manifested. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"In the triple world there are no phenomena apart from this; it is solely the creation of the one mind. When the mind is pure, one perceives the purity of objects. As many sūtras frequently state:

Regarding "the mind seeing": this simply means that the mind and the eye are first clarified [in their distinction]. In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the mind is investigated through the "seven locations" and the seeing is analyzed through the "eight returns.
This sutra also states: "The false and floating mind possesses many clever perceptions. These perceived objects belong to the category of form (*rūpa*).
Form is the Dharma-realm because the sense objects are pure; thus, the eye-faculty is pure. This "floating dust" faculty is precisely the eye itself. As the *Yuxing fayu* states:
"The eye gradually perceives external objects beyond obstructions—is this not purity? Since the faculty is already pure, how could consciousness not also be pure?
Therefore, it is said that consciousness is pure. This consciousness is the seventh consciousness, also called the "transmitter."
"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is like the common expression "sending a message. This refers to the pair of mind and vision; therefore, it is explained first.

The "object of hearing" (*śabda-viṣaya*) is the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*); these three—faculty, object, and consciousness—are all pure. The "object of sensation" (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*) is the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*);
these three—object, faculty, and consciousness—are likewise pure. The nose, tongue, body, and mind are also entirely pure; hence it is said, "it is also thus. [Sūtra]

In the middle [section], "mind" (*citta*) is mentioned first, followed by "intellect" (*manas*). Mind and intellect are one and the same. "Perceiving touch" refers to the body. These two [sections] both emerge from the Buddha’s compassionate gravity.
Thus, having finished examining the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) in sequence, it says: "Good son, because the faculties are pure... up to 'it is likewise so.
These six objects are also called the six bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), as they belong to that which consciousness traverses and engages. They are also—
These are called the six *viṣayas* (dusts). "Dust" (*rajas*) has the meaning of defilement; because they can defile the conscious faculties (*citta-vijñāna*), they are collectively termed "dusts.
That which resides in the eye is called form (*rūpa*); that in the ear is called sound (*śabda*); that in the nose is called fragrance (*gandha*);

that in the tongue is called taste (*rasa*); that in the body is called touch (*spraṣṭavya*); and that in the mind is called phenomena (*dharma*). "Phenomena" refers to all dharmas that are objects of mental conceptualization. These six—

The realm of sensory objects is greatly capable of leading people into the evil paths. Whether they be practitioners of the Way or laypeople, those who cultivate extensively must guard against them with as much vigilance as one would against a domestic thief.
As for those whose greed and desire are raging, one should for the time being allow them their way, like using a spinning wheel to catch fish.
The fish is strong and the line is weak; it cannot be pulled by force. Rather, once the bait has entered its mouth, it will be caught before long, regardless of how near or far it may be.
Cultivating contemplation amidst the dust of the world is also like this. For example, when the Buddha was in the world, even laypeople all attained the fruits of the Path.
Aṅgulimāla became increasingly compassionate as he killed more people, and Queen Mallikā took only the abstention from alcohol as her precept.
Vasumitra engaged in sexual conduct yet maintained the holy life; Devadatta held wrong views yet they were immediately rectified.
One should know that evil does not obstruct the Path, provided it is employed with the proper method. The Patriarch said: "Those who revile the five desires do so because they hinder the Path."
Now, as this sutra examines each of these six sensory realms one by one, they are all Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa).
Brothels, taverns, willow alleys, and flower-lined streets are all the nature of awakening. Form itself is not deluded; it is people who are deluded by it.

Wine has no intention to intoxicate people; it is people who intoxicate themselves with it. The sages view such things as venomous snakes; thus Xu You washed his ears, and Chao Fu drank from the stream.
Ox! Even the sages of antiquity still feared sound and form; how could I alone not fear them? Thus, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"One who does not cling to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. How excellent those words are!
Good son, because the six sense objects are pure, the earth element is pure; because the earth element is pure, the water element is pure;
and the fire and wind elements are likewise so.
Once the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) have become pure, then the false conditions of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—earth, water, fire, and wind—are likewise all purified.
Master Huì of Fù-ān in Western Shu said: "The three internal [elements] and the four external great elements.
Indeed, a human body is composed entirely of the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind; while in life, it follows conditions and harmonizes with them.
[They] merge. After death, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), both internal and external, all become empty; therefore, it is said that "all are completely pure.
Master Cong of Siming said: "This refers to the four great elements of a single person pervading all places, as in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*..."

In the midst of the solemnity, there was a family in Western India. Whenever they needed fire, they had no means of producing it by friction; instead, they used a *yangsui* (a sun-stone or fire-mirror) to obtain fire.
First, they would hold the mirror in their hands and place tinder before it, then face the sun;
in a mere moment, fire would naturally emerge. Now, investigating the nature of the four great elements is also like this: fire descends from heaven.
If it were produced by the service of mowing grass, or emerged from a mirror, or descended from the heavens, there would necessarily have been a trail of fire in the air as it came.
If it were produced from tinder, tinder is a thing found on wild paths; yet we do not see fire being produced in the wilderness.
If fire were to emerge from the mirror, one would not see fire produced while the mirror is on its stand before the fire has been taken up.
It is through the combination of such causes and conditions that the three—the mirror, the tinder, and the sun—exist; when each resides separately and is not in combination, fire is not produced.
"Conditioning" refers to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Within dependent origination, the three factors of fire-nature, the mirror, and the sun are fully present.
Even when they are differentiated, although each possesses its own inherent nature, fire will not arise if the conditions do not coincide.

By analogy with this, if there is no power of the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) will never be eliminated. To employ the illumination of Perfect Enlightenment is what constitutes dependent origination; it is the cause.
Through the harmony of conditions, sensory objects dissolve and awareness becomes perfect; the delusions of birth and death are exhausted.

Good son, because the four great elements are pure, the twelve bases—the six sense organs and the six sense objects—combine to form the twelve bases. As for the six sense organs: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The six...
"Dust" refers to form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena—
the eighteen realms.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that these consist of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six types of discerning consciousness.
The purity of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). (Imperial Commentary states: Regarding the purity of the twenty-five states of existence, the *Zhuāngchūn lù* says:

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are twenty-five kinds of existence. Those termed the four continents are: Pūrvavideha (Eastern Victory Body Continent), Aparagodānīya (Western... [text truncated])... [and so forth].
The continent of Godānīya, the continent of Jambudvīpa in the south, and the continent of Uttarakuru in the north. The six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are:
the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*), the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven.
The four miserable destinies (*apāya*) are: hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras. The heavens of the four dhyānas are: the heavens of the first dhyāna.
The heavens of the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna;
