the four formless heavens—namely, the heaven of the sphere of infinite space, the heaven of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the heaven of the sphere of nothingness, and the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
furthermore, there is one Brahmakāyika heaven, one Asaṃjñisattva heaven, and one Śuddhāvāsa heaven. Altogether, these constitute twenty-five types.
That which exists is collectively termed "existence" because it all pertains to the outflows (*āsrava*).
Now, by virtue of the purity of one's own mind, all things attain purity.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "The four [realms] are worldly dharmas. The twelve *āyatanas* consist of the six sense organs (*indriya*) and the six sense objects (*viṣaya*);

these are the places where the mind-consciousness arises. The eighteen *dhātus* consist of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses, which together constitute eighteen.
'Realm' (*dhātu*) takes the meaning of 'nature' (*prakṛti*) and 'division. The eye-organ and its consciousness form a realm; consciousness and form [form another]."

Regarding the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth: A question is raised that since the twelve bases (*āyatana*) are mentioned, and then again the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are spoken of, is this not redundant?
The answer is: These three categories of phenomena are as follows. When first the five aggregates (*skandha*) are presented, they already correspond to the six sense faculties (*indriya*).

Next, when the six objects (*viṣaya*) are explicitly presented, the six faculties are implicitly included; this is called the twelve bases. Finally, when the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are presented, the six faculties and the six objects are implicitly included; this is called... [the eighteen elements].

Because there are eighteen *dhātus*, they are not redundant. The verse says: "They are called aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) because they are accumulations, gateways for the arising [of consciousness], and lineages.
The five aggregates have the meaning of an accumulation (*caya*) of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The twelve bases are so called because they are the gateways through which the mind and consciousness arise and enter; they are also called the six entrances (*ṣadāyatana*). As for "lineage," it refers to the eye and its corresponding forms...
Regarding "lineage" (*gotra*): the ear and sound constitute a lineage, and so forth. As for the "twenty-five existences" (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*):

they consist of the four continents, the four miserable destinies, the four dhyāna heavens, the four formless abodes, the heaven of non-conception, the pure abode heavens, and the six heavens of desire—these constitute the twenty-five existences.
This means that each is a distinct substantial retribution; because they are not subsumed under correct wisdom, they are called "existence."

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "This sequence of sentient beings, the four great elements, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, and the twenty-five states of existence—namely, the four continents, the four evil destinies, the six heavens of the desire realm, the Brahma heavens, the four dhyāna heavens, the four formless heavens, the heaven of non-conception, and the heaven of the non-returners (anāgāmin)—each possesses its own realms, bases, faculties, and objects. [End of] the "Chapter on Emptiness."
It is said: His mind was constantly dwelling upon the various sense-faculties, like a bird caught in a net.

Once, there was a bhikṣu in the world of the Buddha who sat in meditation beneath a tree for twelve years; yet his mind remained attached to the six sense-objects, and he was unable to attain awakening.
The Buddha manifested a monk and stayed with him under the tree that evening. Suddenly, a tortoise emerged from the river and gradually approached.
By the roadside, there was a wild dog that pounced upon a tortoise. The tortoise withdrew its six limbs and remained hidden; the dog, finding no opening, departed. The tortoise entered the water.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu, "Did you see that? He replied, "I saw it. "What did you see? "I saw the tortoise withdraw its six limbs to preserve its life and maintain its vitality.
The Buddha said, "For twelve years, you have been greedy for odors, flavors, and tactile sensations, clinging to sensory objects as conditions."

He was unable to enter the Path; on the contrary, he was not even as capable as a tortoise in its ability to hide. His realization of nature led him to act contrary to the norm. Upon hearing this, a bhikṣu realized the fruit of Arhatship.
Because he was pure, he possessed the ten powers.

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: First is the power of the reality of what is possible and what is impossible; second is the power of knowing the retribution of karma throughout the three periods of time;
third is the power of knowing all dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis; fourth is the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties of beings;

fifth is the power of knowing the various inclinations of sentient beings; sixth is the power of knowing the various natures of the world; seventh is the power of knowing all paths leading to [their respective goals].
The powers: eighth, the power of knowing past lives; ninth, the power of possessing the divine eye to perceive all things; tenth, the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows.
The four fearlessnesses.

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; third, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of obstacles to the path;
and fourth, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of the path to the exhaustion of suffering.

The four unhindered knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*): first, the unhindered knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); second, the unhindered knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); third, the unhindered knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*);

and fourth, the unhindered knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* states: "The unhindered knowledge of meaning refers to the attainment of the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*). Regarding phenomena...
The unimpeded [knowledge] refers to knowing all phenomena as they truly are. The unimpeded knowledge of language refers to making various distinctions through skillful words.
The unimpeded knowledge of eloquence refers to preaching according to the capacities of beings without forming dualistic marks.
The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of a Buddha.
The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: first, no error; second, no abrupt or harsh voice; third, no loss of mindfulness; fourth, no unconcentrated mind;
fifth, no perception of diversity; sixth, no equanimity lacking discernment; seventh, no regression in aspiration.
Eight, non-retrogression in diligence; nine, non-retrogression in mindfulness; ten, non-retrogression in *prajñā*;
eleven, non-retrogression in liberation; twelve, non-retrogression in knowledge and vision; thirteen, his knowledge and vision are unattached and unimpeded regarding the past;
fourteen, his knowledge and vision are unattached and unimpeded regarding the present; fifteen.
Whether it be knowledge or vision, they are unattached and unimpeded regarding the future.
(16) All bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. (17) All verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.
(18) All mental actions are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom. This is the Buddha.
These are the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). As for "unique qualities," they are attained by the Buddha alone and are not shared with the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*) are pure.

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) constitute, in total, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣadharmāḥ*). Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness:
one contemplates the body as impure, feelings as suffering, the mind as impermanent, and phenomena as selfless. Regarding the four right efforts: [one applies] diligence...

The faculty of energy, the awakening factor of energy, the power of energy, and right effort; the four bases of psychic power consist of the faculty of concentration, the awakening factor of concentration, the power of concentration, and right concentration.
The five faculties are: the faculty of faith, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of energy, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

The five powers are: the power of faith, the power of mindfulness, the power of energy, the power of wisdom, and the power of concentration. The seven factors of awakening are: mindfulness awakening, investigation of phenomena...
The awakening factors of dharma, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity; and the eight branches of the noble path:
right speech, right action, right livelihood, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, and right view.
In this way, it extends even to the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates, all of which are utterly pure.
The *Zangjing* (Treasury of Scriptures) states: "The *dhāraṇī* gates are the gates of total retention (*saṃgraha*).

Because sentient beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), there are eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates. Now, as one's own mind is pure, one is completely liberated from these afflictions."
Because of this exertion, all these dharma-gates are entirely pure.
Master Cixu Furan Hui said: "The five are the supramundane dharmas. As for what are called the 'ten powers,' they are able to crush enemies and cannot be subdued;
thus, they are categorized according to their function. The ten types are: first, the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñāna*)."

1. The power of knowledge regarding one’s own faculties; 2. the power of knowledge regarding the karma of the three periods of time; 3. the power of knowledge regarding the dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis; 4.

the power of knowledge regarding the superior, middling, and inferior degrees of the five faculties; 5. the power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations and pleasures; 6. the power of knowledge regarding all aspects; 7. the power of knowledge regarding all paths;
8. the power of knowledge regarding past abodes; 9. the power of knowledge regarding the divine eye; 10. the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).

The powers (*bala*). The four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are: first, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*); third, fearlessness regarding teaching the Dharma;
and fourth, fearlessness regarding teaching the path that leads to the end of suffering. The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) are:

first, unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma*); second, unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*artha*); third, unimpeded knowledge of language (*nirukti*); [and fourth, unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna*)].
Fourth is the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). Regarding the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*):
first, no failure in physical action; second, no failure in verbal expression; third, no failure in mindfulness; fourth, no divergent thoughts; fifth, no lack of concentration;
sixth, no relinquishing without full awareness; seventh, aspiration; eighth, diligence; ninth, mindfulness; tenth, wisdom; eleventh, liberation; twelfth, the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Knowledge and vision (jñāna-darśana). [Verses] 13, 14, and 15: that is, all three karmas of body, speech, and mind proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Verses 16, 17, and 18: by means of wisdom, one knows the three periods of past, future, and present, penetrating them without obstruction.
Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas): "assistance" (pakṣa) means to provide support; they assist the right path. As for the "path" (mārga)...

This is precisely the cause, namely *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. "Category" (*pakṣa*) refers to the class; because they belong to the same class as the true cause, they are also called the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
"Factor" (*pakṣa*) also carries the meaning of "cause. As for the "thirty-seven," these refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of power.

The five faculties (*pañcendriya*), the five powers (*pañcabala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). However, these thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*saptatriṃśadbodhipākṣikadharma*) belong to the cause;
all others are the dharmas realized by the Tathāgata and thus belong to the fruit.

As for the eighty-four thousand gateways of *dhāraṇī*, for one who has not yet awakened to and clarified the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*), they are the eighty-four thousand afflictions and deluded thoughts; once awakened, they are reversed.
It transforms defilement into purity; it is the possessor of eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates of total retention (*saṃgraha*).

The Dharma Master Chongming said: Regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*): first, the power of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*); second, the power of karma (*karma-bala*); third, the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*);

fourth, the power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*); fifth, the power of aspiration (*ruci-bala*); sixth, the power of disposition (*gotra-bala*); seventh, the power of the path leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-bala*); eighth, the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-bala*).

The nine powers of the divine eye; the tenth power is the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): first, fearlessness regarding knowledge; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows;
third, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of obstacles to the path; and fourth, fearlessness regarding the proclamation of the path leading to the exhaustion of suffering.
The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*) are: first, unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*); second, unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*);

third, unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*); and fourth, unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*). The eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharmāḥ*) are: first, no failure of physical action;

second, no failure of verbal action; third, no failure of mindfulness; fourth, absence of divergent thoughts; fifth, absence of an unconcentrated mind; sixth, absence of non-retention [of what has been taught].
1. He has already abandoned [the defilements]. 2. His desire does not diminish. 3. His diligence does not diminish. 4. His mindfulness does not diminish.
5. His wisdom does not diminish. 6. His liberation does not diminish. 7. His knowledge and vision of liberation does not diminish. 8.
All his bodily actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom. 9. All his verbal actions are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom. 10. All...
Mental karma proceeds in accordance with wisdom. (16) Wisdom knows the past without obstruction;
(17) wisdom knows the future without obstruction; (18) wisdom knows the present without obstruction.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) are the categories according to the depth of one’s entry into the Path. The four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): (1) the foundation of mindfulness on the body; (2) the foundation of mindfulness on feelings.

The three foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness (the mindfulness of phenomena); the four right efforts: (1) the diligent exertion to abandon evil states that have already arisen; (2) the diligent exertion to prevent unarisen evil states from arising; (3) the diligent exertion to give rise to unarisen wholesome states;

(4) the diligent exertion to increase wholesome states that have already arisen; the four bases of power: (1) the base of power of desire; (2) the base of power of energy; (3) the base of power of mind;

(4) the base of power of investigation; the five faculties: (1) the faculty of faith; (2) the faculty of energy; (3) the faculty of mindfulness; (4) the faculty of concentration; (5) the faculty of wisdom; the five powers (which are the same as the aforementioned).

The five faculties increase; because they can destroy wrong faith and afflictions, destroy indolence, destroy wrong mindfulness, destroy distracted thoughts, and obstruct the delusions of views and thought, they are called "powers" (*bala*).

The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*): (1) the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of dharmas; (2) the factor of enlightenment of vigor; (3) the factor of enlightenment of joy; (4) the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; (5) the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; (6) the factor of enlightenment of concentration; (7) the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness. The eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*):

(1) right view; (2) right intention; (3) right speech; (4) right action; (5) right livelihood; (6) right effort; (7) right mindfulness; (8) right concentration. The gateways of *dhāraṇī* are extensively eighty-four thousand in number.

One thousand. (Guifeng said: "Since afflictions (*kleśa*) number eighty-four thousand, each has a corresponding counterpart that is a pure dharma (*viśuddha-dharma*); thus, the numbers of the defiled and the pure neither increase nor decrease.
It is spoken of as five hundred in the intermediate [classification], and briefly as three kinds:

the *āvartanī-dhāraṇī*, the *koṭī-nayuta-śata-sahasrāvartanī-dhāraṇī*, and the *dharmaruta-upāyāvartanī-dhāraṇī*. All these carry the meaning of "obstructing and maintaining": obstructing evil and maintaining goodness.
Just as water does not leak from a complete vessel, so too this Dharma-gate, upon entering into Perfect Enlightenment, becomes pure all at once.
Good son, because the nature of all true marks is pure, the single body is pure.

The nature of the faculties, objects, and the four great elements previously mentioned, as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and so forth, is called "the nature of true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) because it possesses the characteristic of existing as it truly is.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "That which is true reality is itself non-reality;
therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'true reality. Because these natures are pure and untainted, they are the One True [Reality].
The Dharma-body is entirely pure.
Because one body is pure, many bodies are pure.
Since the one true Dharma-body is already pure, all transformation bodies are likewise pure, as stated in the Lotus Sutra.
The Sūtra states that the Buddha’s transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) pervade as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and that all of these are the Buddha’s body.
Is this not to say that when one body is pure, then many bodies are also pure?
Because the bodies of many are pure, and so on up to the fact that the sentient beings of the ten directions possess the purity of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
Because the bodies of many are pure, one universally contemplates the nature of the sentient beings of the ten directions and finds them all to be thus pure in perfect enlightenment.
The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué shū*) also states: "This is when one person awakens to their own nature and knows that all sentient beings [are likewise enlightened]."
The fundamental nature is pure. This does not mean that one person practices the Way while many others attain Buddhahood.
Chan Master Fu-an Hui of Xi-chu said: "That which is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the markless. The dharma-nature is fundamentally void;

it is only by way of convention that we speak of a 'true mark. Regarding 'one body' and so forth: this refers to the sixth [category], the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*), namely the physical form of a human being."
The "substance" (zhì) refers to that which is either fat or thin, where the blood and qi gather, and which the mind-consciousness perceives and knows.
Master Cóng of Sīmíng said: "The first [stage] is the Bodhisattva who has ascended to the first abode (prathamābhūmi) of the Perfect Teaching (yuan), having shattered one grade of ignorance."

He realizes one portion of the three virtues (*triguṇa*). These three virtues are the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Having realized the true mark, this Bodhisattva manifests as a Buddha throughout a hundred worlds;

how could it stop at merely one body or many bodies? Even all sentient beings throughout the ten directions enter into perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), which is perfectly bright and pure.
How much more so for those from the forty-second stage up to the wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*); their manifestations of bodies are beyond measure.
Contemplate this with the mind: this is the Buddha’s true retribution (*vipāka*). This "true retribution" refers to the body of true retribution.
It is by means of this body that one experiences all phenomena. Son of good family, because one world is pure, many worlds are pure.
Once a single world-system has been purified, there is no multitude of worlds that is not purified. As stated in the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra:
"The Buddha-fields are as pure as the palaces of the sovereign gods (Īśvara)," and as when the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe.
As for the statement that the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system is entirely adorned and purified:
is this not the case that when one world is pure, many worlds are pure?
Because many worlds are pure, it extends in this manner until it exhausts all of space, encompassing the entirety of the three periods of time. All...
It is equal, pure, and immovable.
Because many worlds are pure, all immeasurable and boundless worlds are entirely of one and the same purity and immovability.
"Encompassing the three periods of time" refers to the entirety of the empty space of worlds, extending vertically, horizontally, and in every direction.
It is contained therein; it does not refer to the three periods of past, present, and future.
Master Furan Hui of Xichu said: "This is the seventh, the dependent retribution (*pariṇāmanā-vipāka*).
It refers to the dwellings, beds, platforms, pavilions, gardens, groves, and all objects of enjoyment that belong to dependent retribution. When perfected, it is perfectly pervasive."

Space: when it envelops, it contains and wraps the three periods of time. These seven sections of the sutra constitute, in general, the category of the emptiness and purity of phenomenal forms (*rūpa*).

This corresponds to the third contemplation within the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), namely, the Contemplation of the Non-obstruction of Space and Form. The *Commentary* states: "The preceding seven sections of the text concern the emptiness and purity of all phenomena;
because these phenomena do not need to be further removed [to realize emptiness], they correspond to the third phrase. The Dharma-realm..."
The Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Although the two characters 'form' (rūpa) and 'emptiness' (śūnyatā) appear, the fundamental intent returns solely to emptiness.
This is because form is a false name and a false appearance, possessing not even a hair’s breadth of substantial essence to be found; it serves merely to reveal the principle of true emptiness.
Nevertheless, the states of delusion and awakening always follow one another."
The lecturer Cōng of Sìmíng said: "A Bodhisattva in the first stage manifests as a Buddha in a hundred worlds; how could it stop at merely encompassing the three periods of time?
Such is the power and function of this sage: even if a fire were to break out across a trichiliocosm, he could extinguish it with a single spittle."
The three thousandfold world-system is swept away into emptiness; with a single breath it is formed.

One casts the great chiliocosm beyond the four quarters and swallows the myriad phenomena within the breast. One may swallow the waters of the great ocean with a single hair without disturbing the dragons and fish;
one may hide Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed without harming the trees. Therefore, it is called "pure."
"Good son, just as space is thus equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable.

Because the four great elements are immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable. In this way, up to the eighty-four thousand dharani-doors being equal and immovable, you should know that the nature of awakening is equal and immovable."
Space, the four great elements, and all dharma-gates are merged into a single equality, utterly devoid of any sign of movement.
One should know that the nature of awakening is likewise so.
Master Fuan Hui of Xichu said: "Space, the four great elements, and the *dhāraṇī*-gates all belong to..."

"Illusory form" and "awakened nature"—these two terms are precisely true emptiness (*zhēnkōng*). This unity of emptiness and form constitutes one section, which corresponds to the fourth contemplation within the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm and the Contemplation of True Emptiness:
the "Contemplation of Utter Extinction and Non-Reliance. The preceding text generally corresponds to the "Contemplation of True Emptiness Beyond All Characteristics.
Its intent is to reveal that all phenomena are, in their very essence, fundamentally quiescent, equal, and immovable.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "The ultimate consummation of the Perfect and Sudden (yuanton) has no original stages or positions; rather, its gradations are established based on the depth of what is realized.

Now, following the initial stage of the Perfect [Teaching], the forty-one intermediate positions are established through the completion of contemplation (*guan*) and the sequential engagement with phenomena (*li fa*).
These encompass all dharmas without exception, for they do not arise apart from the mind. This is because the nature of empty space and..."
Regarding the immovability of the equality of the awakened nature, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The empty space of the ten directions arises within your mind, like a single cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the great sky.

Since the Buddha-lands and worlds of the ten directions exist within that empty space, and even empty space itself resides within my mind, how could the Buddha-lands and worlds not likewise reside within my mind? My mind is immovable."
The nature of empty space is also unmoving; as empty space is unmoving, so too are the Buddha-lands of the ten directions unmoving.

The body is unmoving, the mind is unmoving, and both the primary and secondary retributions are unmoving. This non-movement is eternal abiding, unchanging and immutable. All phenomena are suchness (tathatā);
this is called the mark of the quiescence of all dharmas, which cannot be expressed in words. This is not...
As for the nature of movement: it is not that one must exert effort to make it motionless; rather, the nature of awareness is inherently unmoving.
Within its own fundamental emptiness, it naturally lacks the characteristic of movement. The four great elements do not move, nor do they emerge as the environment supported by them.

One should know that this nature of awareness is precisely the nature of Perfect Enlightenment—it is neither moving nor unmoving. This movement within immovability is what constitutes "movement. This nature of immovability encompasses all.
The eighty-four thousand dharani-gates all return to the immovable nature; neither expansive nor narrow, they abide eternally in profound stillness.
This nature is inherently pure; it is the emptiness of the Tathagatagarbha, the ultimate truth.
Good son, the nature of awakening is all-pervasive, pure, and immovable; because it is perfect and boundless, you should know that the six sense organs pervade the dharma-realm.
Because the sense organs pervade, you should know that the six sense objects pervade the dharma-realm.
Because the sense objects pervade, you should know that the four great elements pervade the dharma-realm. In this way, even up to the gates of dhāraṇī, they pervade the dharma-realm.
"Perfectly boundless" means that the nature of awakening is complete and vast, without limit.
Since this nature pervades the entire dharma-realm, it is likewise so for the sense faculties, their objects, and the four great elements.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "This is the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena.

The awakened nature is the true reality of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the four great elements are all categorized as phenomenal phenomena (*dharma*).

Thus, principle does not obstruct phenomena, and phenomena do not obstruct principle; they mutually interpenetrate and integrate, giving rise to wondrous function. Therefore, principle is itself phenomena."
Therefore, there is no suchness outside of wisdom that could be entered by wisdom, because phenomena are themselves the principle (*dharmatā*).
Likewise, there is no wisdom outside of suchness that could be realized by wisdom. Regarding the "six sense organs pervading the Dharma-realm":

this refers to the gates of the six sense organs, each of which individually shakes the earth and emits great radiance, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions. Master Fuguo said: "If one uses the eye..."
When seeing Mañjuśrī, his body lies across; when hearing with the ears, Avalokiteśvara manifests his function; when knowing with the mind, Samantabhadra presides in the hall.
Furthermore, Gaocheng said: "When the eye functions, it is like a thousand suns; the myriad phenomena cannot escape their shadows and forms."

Ordinary people simply have not yet practiced contemplation; why should they disparage themselves and become disheartened? One’s ears should be like a deep valley, where sounds great and small are all received without deficiency;
even when drums are struck in the ten directions, they are heard simultaneously, as the numinous light shines forth clearly and continues perpetually.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When one faculty returns to its source, the six faculties are liberated," and so on, up to "separating from both [existence and non-existence]."
It is not that there is no "is" or "is-not"; rather, the true and the provisional are mutually fused, and the primary and the secondary are equal.

Within the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm, there are ten gates in the Contemplation of the Non-obstruction between Principle and Phenomena; this present sutra corresponds precisely to the second gate, wherein phenomena pervade principle, while also encompassing the other gates.
In the preceding Contemplation of True Emptiness, one merely subsumes phenomena back into principle; now, however, movement and stillness are each fully interfused.

Regarding the "pervasive arising of function," the Lecturer Mingcong said: This refers to the ultimate world of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), wherein the fruition-enlightenment traverses all phenomena;
therefore, it is called "pervasive. Furthermore, because the forty-one intermediate stages are not yet perfected, they are not described as "full. As for "wondrous enlightenment":

It is like the moon on the fifteenth night: its orb is full and free from any aberrant light. That which all Buddhas realize is the realization of the faculties and objects of all sentient beings—seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
The Buddha is identical to sentient beings, and sentient beings are identical to the Buddha; how much more so, then, is the gateway of *dhāraṇī* not all-pervasive?
One must know that the eighty-four thousand afflictions are themselves the eighty-four [thousand gates of liberation].
The four thousand treasuries of Dharma, as well as the eighty-four thousand marks and embellishments, manifest the fundamental within the phenomenal and the phenomenal within the fundamental.
Upon the tip of a single hair-pore, the Jewel-King Buddha-land appears; within a single mote of dust, the Great Dharma-Wheel is turned.
Is this not the Great Sage traversing all phenomena? If some should say otherwise, the subsequent text states: "That wondrous enlightened nature..."

Since it refers to that [state], it is precisely the aforementioned scriptural passage concerning the fruit-enlightenment (*phala-bodhi*) traversing through all phenomena. Beyond this, there are no further characters;

at the final moment of the Vajra-like Samādhi, one enters the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*). Since what is realized is ultimate, all is pure. The Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) encompasses all, being fundamentally devoid of form or image.
How could there be any further existence of coming or going? Therefore, the subsequent text explicitly speaks of "Sublime Enlightenment."
Good son, because that wondrous nature of enlightenment is all-pervasive, the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled.
Because the faculties and objects are neither destroyed nor intermingled, this extends even to the gates of dhāraṇī, which are likewise neither destroyed nor intermingled.
The wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment pervades the entire dharma-realm; thus, the nature of all phenomena—the sense organs and their objects—is like empty space, neither defiled nor attached.
Therefore, it undergoes no transformation or decay, nor does it become intermingled or confused.
It is like the light of a hundred thousand lamps illuminating a single room; that light pervades everywhere, neither destroyed nor mixed.
The light of the lamps is a metaphor for the nature of the sense faculties, objects, and so forth; the single room is a metaphor for the boundless *dharmadhātu*.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "This is the Contemplation of Universal Interpenetration.

The two characters 'Sublime Enlightenment' (Miaojue) serve as the causal basis for the subsequent 'Phenomenon within Phenomenon. The following six sense organs and six sense objects all take phenomena as their primary focus.
This is like the third contemplation of the *Dharmadhātu-āloka*, which consists of ten gates; while the first three gates discuss principle and phenomenon, the latter seven gates all..."
It does not discuss principle; it speaks only of non-obstruction. The two characters "wondrous enlightenment" (*miaojue*) in this sutra likewise convey the meaning of the first three gates therein.
Upon reaching this state of total non-obstruction, one says: "Seeing the mountain, it remains as before a mountain."
Seeing water, it is still water as before; seeing a staff, it is still a staff as before.
Not even a single hair’s breadth of alteration is permitted. Xuedou said: "Do not touch it. To touch it, you will receive thirty blows. Doushuai Yue said:

"When the real is sought, it belongs entirely to the real; when the provisional is established, it returns entirely to the provisional. It is like rowing a boat on level ground or walking within empty space."
"Running horses. Now, the room is a metaphor for the Dharma-realm; the lamp is a metaphor for true emptiness; and the light is a metaphor for phenomenal phenomena.

Just as each person within themselves possesses a bowl of lamp-light—such radiance, such universal illumination—they mutually manifest and illumine one another, never obstructing one another and never becoming confused or destroyed. Try to investigate this thoroughly: if you can recognize this, [you will understand].
In principle, you are permitted to enter the Great Pavilion of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, where you may personally behold Sudhana and Maitreya. The *Yanyi* states:

"The ordinary and the sagely do not obstruct one another; it is like many mirrors reflecting various forms, where this and that do not hinder each other, as if a thousand lamps were together in a single room.
It further states: "Principle accords with the transformations of phenomena; through the dependent origination of the one and the many, [it is] boundless..."
Phenomena attain the fusion of principle; though a thousand differences interpenetrate, they do so without obstruction. Question:
Within the *dharmadhātu*, by what meaning do all phenomena attain such mutual integration? Answer: The Great Commentary (*Dàshù*) states there are ten meanings.

First, because all is manifested solely by the mind. Second, because phenomena have no fixed characteristics. Third, because the marks of dependent origination are mutually contingent. Fourth, because all phenomena... [text continues]
Because they are interfused; fifth, because they are like illusions and dreams; sixth, because they are like reflections; seventh, because their causes are limitless;
eighth, because the Buddhas have realized them to the ultimate; ninth, because of the function of profound meditative concentration; and tenth, because of supernatural powers and liberation.
If one mentions any one of these ten, one immediately perceives that all phenomena are interfused and unimpeded.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Good son, from that wondrous enlightenment up to 'neither destroyed nor mixed'—the term 'wondrous enlightenment' refers to original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*).
Original enlightenment is precisely the nature-virtue of a single thought-moment of sentient beings as seen before us. This nature is the nature of original enlightenment;
it is like ice and water, which are not two. This nature is perfectly interfused and pervades within the faculties and objects of all sentient beings, neither destroyed nor..."
It is a mixture. How could one who is indestructible be destroyed? One cannot discard one faculty and separately grasp another.

It is simply because the minds of people today give rise to intellectual contrivances that they fail to see the seamless integration and perceive the existence of arising and ceasing. For a Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths, the six faculties are pure;
their unchanging birth-body is itself the Dharma-body. As the Lotus Sutra says: "The eyes born of one's parents see all three thousandfold worlds."
The realm [of the ear]—the ears born of one's parents—hear the sounds of the trichiliocosm.

The Dragon Girl, with this very body born of her parents, immediately went on to attain Buddhahood. When the Great Master Zhiyi realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he saw Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as remaining solemnly without dispersing;
these were all his physical eyes, which can thus be considered indestructible. As for being "unmixed," it is, for instance, like a person...
The eyes and ears do not exceed one or two inches in size; each maintains its own distinct domain. The eye can only see and cannot hear; the ear can only hear and cannot see.
It is the same for the nose, tongue, body, and mind. Although they are interconnected within, they each remain distinct.

Externally, they are always separated; this may be called non-intermixture. A pine tree is straight and a thorn bush is crooked; a crow is black and a crane is white; likewise, they do not intermingle.
Although there is neither destruction nor intermixture, one must further understand that there is both destruction and intermixture.

For in the Buddha-dharma, that which is without characteristics is taken as a characteristic; therefore, all things that possess characteristics are entirely illusory and false. One should know that this is *dhāraṇī*.
The gates of the nuns [are] precisely the cessation of thought and the maintenance of goodness. Now, this treatise discusses good and evil as being neither corrupted nor mixed.
Evil is not corrupted; it is inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*). Inherent evil is like water; inherent good is like ice.

If inherent evil were removed, from what would the various Buddhas’ manifestation of form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) arise? If one removes the water, there is no ice. By this, one knows that inherent evil exists.
It is not severed. Although it is said that *dhāraṇī* wards off evil, evil is itself good; what evil could there be?
Though evil is not severed, good and evil are naturally distinct, neither corrupted nor intermingled.

Just as the spring breeze knows no high or low, yet the flower branches are naturally short or long, if even worldly illusions can manifest both non-existence and existence, how much more so for that which belongs to the Great Sage?
He realized the arts of the real and the illusory. When illusion exists, it constitutes all phenomena; when illusion is absent, it is empty.

That all marks are empty yet not empty is called emptiness; that they exist yet are not existent is called existence. One should know that with the arising of the mind, phenomena arise; with the cessation of the mind, phenomena cease.
Even Lord Lü could take a pinch of soil and turn it into incense, let alone the Buddha’s ability to dissolve the Five Sacred Peaks.
To exhaustively investigate the four seas and the events of immeasurable kalpas—how could these be fathomed by an ordinary mind?

It is like hundreds of thousands of lamps reaching a state where they are neither destroyed nor confused. As described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, when an altar is established and ten mirrors are arranged in a circle with a single lamp lit in the center, the forms of the lamps interpenetrate so that their orientations cannot be distinguished.
How much more so when the light of hundreds of thousands of lamps illuminates a single room!
Although the light of a hundred thousand lamps returns to oneness, so too does the light from the ten mirrors return to oneness.

The wondrous awakening that realizes the nature universally enters the faculties and their objects; the nature of the faculties and the nature of the objects are both the nature of awakening. Because the nature of awakening is all-pervasive, the natures of the faculties and objects are likewise pervasive.
Since the gates of *dhāraṇī* are neither destroyed nor mixed, it is said: "It is also thus," as in the ancient [scripture].
It is said: "The mirror and the lamp, the lamp and the mirror—fundamentally there is no difference between them. The great earth, mountains, and rivers are but flowers in the eye.
Yellow leaves flutter, filling the courtyard; one knows not whose house the pounding stones belong to.

People only know that Buddha-nature is all-pervasive, yet they do not realize that self-nature is all-pervasive. Do you wish to know that self-nature is all-pervasive? When hungry, eat; when weary, sleep.
Do not seek to distinguish right from wrong within the human world.
Son of good family, because awakening is fully accomplished, you should know that a bodhisattva is neither bound by phenomena nor seeks liberation from phenomena.
The perfect clarity and luminosity of the awakened nature is called accomplishment. Regarding all phenomena, it is neither bound nor liberated;
it neither loathes birth-and-death nor craves nirvana.
Once awakening is accomplished, one knows that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are like flowers in the sky; therefore, there is nothing to loathe and nothing to cherish.
One does not revere those who uphold the precepts, nor does one detest those who violate them.
Once awakening is accomplished, then regarding all prohibitions and precepts, because there is neither upholding nor violating, there is nothing to revere and nothing to loathe;
one does not value long-standing practice, nor does one slight initial realization.
Once awakening is accomplished, one views all awakened beings as equal and non-dual;
therefore, one does not treat them with excessive weight based on long-standing practice, nor does one treat them with neglect based on recent study.
This is like Confucius, who suppressed yet respected Zilu when he had ascended to the hall, while encouraging and advancing the young boy Chik-i.
Why is this? Because it is the awakening of all things. The eight [aspects] are all devoid of hatred and attachment; this is because everything is awakening.
Master Cifeng Huì of Fù'ān in Western Shu said: "This is the mind employing itself to perceive objects, each one corresponding to reality in sudden realization."
It is the realm perceived by all Buddhas. "Bondage by phenomena" refers to the six classes of ordinary beings, for these six classes are bound by greed, anger, and delusion.
"Liberation from phenomena" refers to the Dharma of the four types of noble ones. "Birth and death" refers to defiled phenomena.
Nirvana is the pure dharma. Upholding the precepts means faithfully maintaining the monastic discipline.
When facing the eight sensory objects, if one does not give rise to thoughts of superiority or inferiority, one’s mind is identical to that of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
there is no longer any duality. Therefore, Huìtáng said: "Do not crave the holy, for 'holy' is an empty name. Do not loathe the mundane, for the mundane..."
This is a false establishment. One merely attains the exhaustion of the sentiments of both sages and ordinary people, whereby the natural body reveals its true permanence.
Furthermore, a monk asked National Teacher Nanyang, "What is the Buddha? He replied, "Buddha and sentient beings are simultaneously cast aside;
liberation occurs right where one stands. The monk further inquired, "By what principle do the four pairs and eight classes of practitioners achieve such accomplishment?"
This is precisely why it is so stated: because at all places and at all times, every thought-moment is constantly in accord with original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
In Sanskrit, this is called *buddhatā*, which here means "enlightenment" (*bodhi*). Guifeng said: "My mind is fundamentally equal to the Buddha-mind;
for kalpas on end I have been submerged only because of delusion. In Sanskrit, this is called *bodhi*, which here means "awakening. It is the awakening of the mind.
Quiescent illumination is bodhi; its reality is identical to that of the Buddha, differing only in being awakened or unawakened.
Yongjia said: "Since attaining sudden awakening to the non-arising of phenomena, what cause for sorrow or joy could there be amidst all honors and insults?"
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Enlightenment" refers to the person of fruition, the Sublime Enlightenment.

Since what has been realized is ultimate, one observes that all worldly phenomena are without subject or object, without bondage and without liberation. One should know that "Bodhisattva" refers to the person on the causal stage;
although a Bodhisattva dwells in the ground of causes, they also understand that the mind is empty and pervasive, and they also perceive all dharmas.
The fundamental source is neither defiled nor pure; it is neither bound nor liberated. Such a bodhisattva neither loathes birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor craves nirvāṇa.
Indeed, although this bodhisattva has not yet attained liberation for themselves, they first desire to liberate others. As the *Buddhottamasikhara-sūtra* states:
"To desire to liberate others before one has liberated oneself—this is the resolve of a bodhisattva. Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday. Thus it is said:
Because it is like a dream from yesterday, whether one upholds the precepts or violates them, upon initial awakening, long-standing habits do not give rise to hatred or attachment.
The *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The pure practitioner does not enter nirvāṇa; the bhikṣu who has committed a grave offense does not enter hell.
Why? Because all is awakened. This means that for the person on the path and the person who has attained the fruit, all dharmas are equal—there is neither cultivation nor realization.
For example, when the light of the eye clearly perceives objects before it, that light is perfect and complete, such that it is free from both aversion and attachment.
The nature of awareness is likewise perfectly luminous, illuminating all objects just as the light of the eye clearly perceives what lies before it.
Because its radiance is perfect and fully endowed, one attains a sudden, comprehensive vision, remaining free from all aversion and attachment.
Why is this? Because the essence of light is non-dual, being free from both aversion and attachment.
The light of the eye and the light of awakening are of one and the same empty essence, and likewise lack both aversion and attachment; therefore, they may be used as a metaphor for one another.
Master Cixu Fuan Hui said: "The preceding passage cited the Dharma; this one cites a metaphor. The eye is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It is just like using the eye to penetrate and clearly perceive all objects before one—whether pure or defiled, high or low."

Furthermore, how could the light of the eye harbor aversion toward the foul or attachment to the pure? How could it feel aversion for what is low or attachment to what is high? For what reason is this so?
It is because the essential substance of the eye’s light is fundamentally non-dual; therefore, there is neither aversion nor attachment.
The light of the eye serves as a metaphor for the equality of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), which is devoid of the marks of self and other.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "This refers, for the time being, to when the light of the eyes illuminates an object before one. At that moment, the light merely gazes directly at the thing;

it does not yet distinguish between aversion and affection. For aversion and affection arise from the human mind. Now, we take the illumination of the object by the light as a time when aversion and affection are not yet distinguished.
If they were distinguished, then one would illuminate those whom one loves and [avoid] those whom one hates."
Thus, light is obscured by them. Since light involves both aversion and attraction, objects are likewise divided into two. Now, using light as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s mind of equality:
toward all phenomena, it is perfectly complete, neither deficient nor redundant; it neither values nor despises, neither disparages nor praises. As Maitreya said:
"A single bowl of food from a thousand homes, a solitary body wandering ten thousand miles; no one casts either a favorable or a hostile gaze."
"Ask the way at the head of the white clouds.
Good son, when these Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age cultivate this mind and attain accomplishment,
there is herein neither cultivation nor accomplishment."
Once the cultivation of Perfect Enlightenment has been perfected, one then realizes that originally there was nothing to cultivate, nor is there anything to be attained.
Perfect Enlightenment shines universally;
the radiance of Perfect Enlightenment pervasively illuminates the Dharma-realm.
Quiescent and non-dual:
quiescence is the absence of thought; cessation is the absence of marks. This is the pure source, profound and eternally one.
Within it, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya [aeons].
The *Tripiṭaka* states: "A" means "none"; "saṃkhyeya" means "number. Taken together, this signifies "innumerable.
It refers to unspeakably many Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"Ganges sands" refers to all the sand within the Ganges River. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Ganges itself is already countless; how much more so its sands?
This serves as a metaphor for the fact that within the nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), there are such countless Buddha-lands.
It is like flowers in the sky that arise and perish in confusion;
the worlds of the Buddhas originally have no place of abiding. Like flowers in the sky that arise and perish as they go, they are neither identical to nor separate from it.
Regarding the arising and ceasing, the impermanence, of the manifested worlds: from the outset, they are neither identical to nor separate from Perfect Enlightenment;
they all exist within Great Perfect Enlightenment, and thus cannot be discussed in terms of separation or identity.
There is neither bondage nor liberation.
Since there was originally nothing to bind, what could there be to release?
Only then does one know that sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning.
Having cultivated and realized this point, one has already attained the fruit of Buddhahood. Only then does one know that the primordial nature of sentient beings is manifest as the Buddha;
birth and death, as well as nirvana, are like a dream from yesterday.

Once one knows that one's own fundamental nature is already manifest as the Buddha, one then realizes that the birth-and-death of delusion and the nirvana after awakening are both merely like events in a dream.
Chan Master Fuyan Hui of Xishu said: "The former 'mind' refers to using the mind as identical to the Buddha;
the latter 'mind' refers to seeing objects as identical to the Buddha. This 'using the mind' is precisely the wisdom capable of observing non-discrimination.

It is not only that this wisdom is identical to the Buddha's, but the objects being observed are likewise cultivated as identical to those of the Buddha. This 'mind' points back to the preceding contemplative practice."
And as for the eight objects: "neither cultivation nor realization" is said because one fears that [the practitioner] would further place a head upon a head, or build a house upon a house.

If there were truly cultivation and realization, then there would be two *pariṇirvāṇa* (perfect enlightenments). This refers generally to the fact that quiescence (*śānti*) is the essence of *pariṇirvāṇa*, while universal illumination (*samantaprabhāsa*) is its function.
Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) is illumination within quiescence; Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyakṣabodhi*) is quiescence within illumination. Upon reaching this point—
Function is the essence; the essence is function. They are neither two nor divided; they are without distinction and without interruption.
It is like space merging with space, or water poured into water, leaving no trace at all. Question: Why does this passage not first speak of "quiescent extinction" (śānti)?
Why, then, was it said earlier that [the light] "universally illumines"? The answer is: This was intended to show that the practitioner, while within contemplation, suddenly questioned the Buddha;

thus, the state of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is identical to that of the Buddha. If one were in the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyekabuddha*), that would be the rank of a Buddha—how could there be any question of identity?
Therefore, the preceding statement "universally illuminating within" refers to the state of universal illumination within the quiescence of *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti*.

Whether it be hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, or billions—these are all small numbers and large numbers according to this region. *Asaṃkhyeya* (translated here as "incalculable") refers to kalpas;
*anabhilāpya-gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (unspeakably many sands of the Ganges) is a numerical system of the Western Regions. The Ganges River there is forty *li* in width.
The sand is as fine as flour. Take a single grain of sand and count it as one Buddha-world;
even as many worlds as these, within Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), are like flowers in the sky, arising and ceasing chaotically in mid-air.
Yet they do not constitute Perfect Enlightenment, nor do they exist apart from Perfect Enlightenment. Why?
Therefore, it is thus. Because they are not separate, the nature of awakening seizes them and transforms them into empty flowers.
Because they are not identical, the world is nonetheless subject to arising and ceasing. Since this is neither bound nor liberated, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:

"The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is illusory, like empty flowers. Only upon reaching this state does one truly know.
The three realms, the four modes of birth, and the nine classes of beings are fundamentally Buddhas; it is only upon reaching this realization that one comes to know it.
All Buddhas and sentient beings are like reflections; nirvana and birth-and-death are both merely provisional names.

Therefore, the Chan school says: "Every person grasps the pearl of the divine serpent; every individual embraces the raw jade of Mount Jing. There is neither lack nor excess, and nothing further remains."

Having provisionally practiced and realized [the path], one then returns to observe that the phenomena of birth and death of ordinary beings and the phenomena of nirvana of the supramundane sages are one and the same. It is like seeing events in a dream last night;
were they ever truly real? Regarding this word "dream," according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, five meanings are explained. First, fever...
Dreams caused by *vāyu* (wind-energy). Second, dreams caused by cold energy. Third, dreams caused by an abundance of wind-energy. Fourth, dreams caused by frequent seeing and hearing.

Fifth, dreams bestowed by celestial deities (*devatā*). This present dream is one caused by frequent seeing and hearing. Furthermore, this section of text corresponds to the three types of worlds (*triloka*) and the three kinds of awakening.
"World" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*); "sentient beings" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*).
The Buddha is itself wisdom and the perfectly awakened world. When this contemplative practice is accomplished, one is able to harmonize the three kinds of worlds into a single-flavored Dharma.
Furthermore, that which is "initially known" is initial awakening (shijue), which is fundamentally identical to original awakening (benjue). Becoming a Buddha is ultimate awakening (jiujing jue).
In terms of the teachings, initial knowledge corresponds to the Sudden Teaching (dun jiao), while being originally a Buddha corresponds to the Perfect Teaching (yuan jiao). If...
Each of the five teachings speaks of the attainment of Buddhahood. Specifically, the Teaching for the Ignorant (Yujiao) states that Prince Siddhārtha attained Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

The Initial Teaching (Shijiao) states that one attains Buddhahood through cultivation over three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. The Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) states that one attains Buddhahood through the manifestation of nature upon the exhaustion of marks.

The Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao) states that one attains Buddhahood in a single thought-moment. The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) states that one is originally enlightened from the very beginning; this refers to the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
At that time, one is indeed a Buddha. Regarding the phrase "inexpressible," Guifeng’s commentary states: "This refers to the great numbers of the *Avataṃsaka*.
A later passage in the sutra says: "The cultivation of bodhisattva practices is incalculable, immeasurable, boundless, incomparable, and uncountable."
It is ineffable, inconceivable, immeasurable, and unspeakable; it now constitutes the ninth number.
The Dharma Master Mingcong said: "This clarifies the dharma realized by the Bodhisattva when his merit is perfected and his Way is discerned, as well as the dharma he has accomplished.
It is free from intrinsic nature and transcends non-existence; it perceives that the fundamental source of nature is the Dharma-realm of nature itself, which does not arise from the mind."
It does not enter from without; therefore, it is neither cultivated nor realized. It is neither identical with nor separate from [phenomena]; it is neither bound nor liberated.
Although Buddhas appear in the world and pass away from it, they are like sparks from a flint or flashes of lightning.

Although they possess the sounds and languages of Brahma, these are like golden needles and jade thread. The worlds of all Buddhas arise and perish in disorder, like flowers in the sky. Birth-and-death and Nirvana...

All things are like a dream from yesterday. It can be said that the Buddha is sentient beings, and sentient beings are the Buddha. Is this not the first time you realize that you have been a Buddha from the very beginning?
Good son, because they are like a dream from yesterday, you should know that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are without arising and without cessation. They are...
Coming has no going.
Since birth-and-death and nirvana are both like a dream from yesterday, how could there be any such phenomena as arising and ceasing, or coming and departing?
That which is realized is without gain and without loss, without grasping and without abandoning.
The perfect enlightenment that is realized is, by its very nature, fundamentally such that it cannot be gained, nor can it be lost;
it cannot be grasped, nor can it be abandoned.
As for that which can realize it: there is no activity, no cessation, no indifference, and no extinction.
One who can realize perfect enlightenment possesses no mind of active function, no mind of cessation, and no mind of passive acquiescence to spontaneity.
There is no mind of ultimate quiescence. These four minds constitute the four illnesses.
Within this realization, there is neither subject nor object;
there is no wisdom that realizes, and no characteristic that is realized.
Ultimately there is no realization, nor is there one who realizes.
Fundamentally, there is no dharma to be realized, nor is there a person who realizes.
The nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.
When one cultivates and realizes Perfect Enlightenment to the point where both person and phenomena are forgotten, then the nature of all faculties, objects,
and dharmas is likewise equal and non-dual, forever immutable and indestructible.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xichu said: "This 'designation according to reality' (chengshi) is identical [to the preceding].

It means that regarding the wisdom that contemplates and the object contemplated, one designates them in accordance with the principle of true reality (*tattva*). This passage consists of four sections: first, a general presentation of designation according to reality;

second, a specific indication of the subject and object; third, the simultaneous negation of both subject and object; and fourth, a concluding summary of designation according to reality—as if it were a dream from yesterday."
Therefore, one phrase [is given]: "Tracing back to what precedes, it is just like a dream.

One should know that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are without arising and without cessation, without coming and without going; this is the general heading. To speak according to reality: when deluded regarding saṃsāra, it arises like a flower in the sky;
when awakening to nirvāṇa, it ceases like a flower in the sky. Since one knows all phenomena to be like a dream—
Afterwards, how could there be the arising of birth-and-death or the cessation of nirvana? Not only is there neither arising nor cessation, but there is also no holy dharma.
The newly arrived ordinary dharmas cease, and that which is realized is non-conceptual. Within the realm of principle, there is no gain; truly, there is no loss of the false.
Not only is there no gain of the true and no loss of the false, but the false itself is also non-existent. There is no grasping at the subtle or abandoning the coarse.

Regarding this matter: since it is so with respect to the principle realized, the non-conceptual wisdom that realizes it likewise lacks the defects of effort, cessation, indifference, or extinction. This is a specific reference to the subject and object.
Within this realization and the realized, there is neither subject nor object; ultimately, there is no realized境 (*viṣaya*) and no realizing wisdom (*jñāna*). This is...
The third pair: Sweeping away the subject and object below, the conclusion is stated as it truly is. Question:
How can one eliminate all the aforementioned ailments of the means of realization (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of realization (*prameya*)? Answer:

This is because when the practitioner enters contemplation, at all places and at all times, they suddenly become identical to all Buddhas; their mental application suddenly realizes all things—whether mundane or sagely, whether defiled or pure.
Whether it be purity, or nature, or characteristics; whether it be the beginning or the end—the nature of all such diverse phenomena is fundamentally equal, neither destroyed nor established.
Laozi said: "The Great Perfection lacks nothing. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Cessation is itself bodhi;
the holy, pure, and luminous mind is not obtained from others. An ancient said: "It is fundamentally complete, lacking nothing and having no surplus."
All of these are this same principle. If this is so, then the original nature is pure and clean;
