Within seven days, eighty thousand types of worms arise within the body. Inferring from this, among the four modes of birth and nine categories of beings, there are none who do not receive their bodies through sexual desire.
That they wander aimlessly through the five destinies and crawl about in the four modes of birth, finding no way to liberation—all of this is rooted in craving and desire.
"Root" (*mūla*) is used here as a metaphor for the fundamental basis.
This is the principle of the analogy. How is this known? If one cuts down a tree but does not exhaust its roots, the tree will grow back again and again.
If one severs craving but does not exhaust its source, suffering will arise again and again. This is a reliable proof.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: Regarding the distinctions of rebirth, let us speak briefly of the cycle of the six realms.
At the very first thought, within the nature of Great Enlightenment, one stirs up delusive ignorance and past karma; following the natures of the six realms, one undergoes birth in various places.
Driven by the two great elements of wind and fire, my consciousness rushes forth to repay its karmic debts from former lives, performing deeds that correspond to its merit.
Coming to be born into my household is entirely due to the arising of craving (*rāga*). Craving belongs to attachment (*tṛṣṇā*); desire is the cause, and the clinging to life is the fruit.

Thus, one gathers the discarded elements of the parents to form the five-aggregate physical body (*pañcaskandha-rūpakāya*). Consequently, there begins the four modes of birth: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born.

That which is born from within a shell is called egg-born (*aṇḍaja*); that which is born from a fetal sac is called womb-born (*jarāyuja*); that which is born from moisture is called moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*).

Moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*). That which suddenly comes into being where there was nothing is called transformation-born (*upapāduka*). The heavens and the hells consist entirely of transformation-birth.

Asuras possess all four modes of birth. Humans also possess all four modes of birth. Ghosts (*preta*) are born from wombs or by transformation. Animals possess all four modes of birth. Among humans, there are those born from eggs.
Formerly, in the Western Land, the mother Viśākhā gave birth to thirty-two eggs, which became her thirty-two sons.
As for those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), there was, for example, the woman from the *āmalaka* tree. A pool of water formed upon an *āmalaka* tree, and within that water a girl was born.
Having no father or mother, she took the *āmalaka* as her clan name; thus she was called the *Āmalakī*. She met the Buddha and realized the fruit [of enlightenment].
She is also called the woman *Aṇḍikā*. Later, King Bimbisāra took her as his wife and they had a son named Jīvaka, the celestial physician.
Lust (*kāma*) refers to being immersed in and attached to desire. All forms of emotional defilement are collectively termed lust.

Even for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), there is an initial reliance upon karma; such categories exist because they all result from the transmission of vital energy through mental defilement.
Since one’s nature and destiny are received [through this process], and since life and fate arise from lust, and lust in turn arises from craving, it is said that craving is the root.
Because the various desires assist in the arousal of the nature of craving, they are able to cause the continuity of birth and death.
Due to the existence of all objects of desire, they assist in the arousal of all hearts of greedy craving;
thus, there is mutual defiled attachment, and one undergoes retribution according to karma. For this reason, birth and death do not cease.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "The 'desires' (yu) are what assist in forming the cause. 'By' (you) means by means of. The 'various desires' (zhuyu) are the objects (jing).
The 'nature of craving' (aisexing) is the seed from immeasurable kalpas past. Because of external sensory objects, the seeds of the heart of craving are pulled forth.
Thus, throughout the twelve hours of the day, the ropes of craving form ten thousand knots and the nets of emotion form a thousand layers; it is because of this."
Out of affectionate craving, one creates karma; because of creating karma, one receives retribution. By this, birth and death are not severed.
Causes and conditions pull one another together, just as a magnet attracts a needle. The needle is made of iron from the north; the north belongs to yin, while the stone is a thing of the south;
the south belongs to yang. It is simply due to the mutual resonance of yin and yang. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "I love you."
"O Color, you have moved my heart with compassion. Because of this cause and condition, for hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, I have always remained bound by ropes. Zao said:
"The reason sentient beings wander in transmigration for so long is entirely due to their attachment to desire. If desire is brought to rest within the mind..."
"There will be no further birth and death. Master Cong of Siming said:
"The desirous mind of sentient beings resides within. If one has not yet encountered an object, the desirous mind does not arise.
It is because of the object that the desirous mind is drawn forth and activated. Therefore, the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* (Foding jing) says: 'You love my heart; I [love yours]...'"
I pity your physical form. Because of these causes and conditions, birth and death are not severed; it is like adding oil to a fire—how could it not burn even more fiercely?

When desire assists the heart of attachment, one creates karma and undergoes retribution. Zao said: "The reason sentient beings have wandered for so long is entirely due to their attachment to desire.
If desire ceases within the mind, then there is no birth and death. One’s spirit becomes hidden in profound stillness and..."

To have one's virtue merge with empty space—this is called nirvāṇa. The *Teaching Left Behind* (Upadeśa) says: "Because those with many desires seek much profit, their suffering and affliction are likewise many.
Therefore, although the cauldrons of boiling water are seething, they do not cook those who are free from desire.

For instance, because the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda was attached to his wife, the Buddha led him to roam through the celestial palaces; there he saw a palace where the heavenly maidens were superior [in beauty].
She was exquisite and alone without a husband. Nanda then questioned the celestial maiden, and she replied, "The Buddha’s younger brother Nanda observes the precepts;
he has been born here as my husband. Nanda, desiring to observe the precepts, sought to be reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha then led him to tour the great hells, where suddenly one hell became empty. Nanda again questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It is because of you."

He questioned the wardens of hell. The wardens replied, "The Buddha’s younger brother, Nanda, maintained the precepts for the sake of sensual desire. When his retribution was exhausted, he was reborn in this hell.
Reflecting on this, one sees that the five desires are as impermanent as dew upon a flower; they vanish at the touch of the sun.
If one knows this yet fails to observe the precepts, one is what the Bequeathed Teachings describe as 'an old elephant sinking into deep mud.'"
Desire arises from craving;
all states of mind characterized by desire originate from craving.
Life exists because of desire.
The bodies and lives of sentient beings exist because of desire.
Sentient beings cherish their lives, yet they still rely upon desire as their root.
Sentient beings cherish their lives, never relinquishing them for even a single moment; this is called relying once again upon the root of sexual desire.
Sensual desire is the cause; craving for life is the fruit.
Because one begins with sensual desire and undergoes birth, it is the cause. Because one begins with craving for life and undergoes retribution, it is the fruit.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "This clarifies that because of desire, cause and effect revolve and depend upon one another in an uninterrupted succession.
'Desire' refers to greed and lust; 'life' refers to the physical life of the body. If there were no craving and desire, this body would not be born.
One should know that the desires of all sentient beings exist upon the mind that is capable of loving. Since [this applies] to the past...
Due to past causes involving lustful desire, this body was obtained. Now, in this life, one again gives rise to a mind of attachment, cherishing, protecting, and craving this very body.
Because of this love for the body, and by depending upon it, one creates the cause for lustful desire in future lives.
Consequently, one further incurs the karmic retribution of birth and death in future existences.
In this way, they continue in succession without end; therefore, it is said that craving constitutes both cause and effect.
Master Cong of the Fourth Ming Temple said: "The *Guangming* [Sutra] states: 'This body is false and deceptive, like an empty village.

This is because sentient beings initially grasp at the aggregates (*skandhas*) to form a body. The 'aggregates' refer to the five aggregates; their harmonious combination is conventionally designated as a 'body,' just as..."
Because one grasps the five fingers together, there is the designation "fist. Ordinary people do not understand this; they cling to these conventional designations as being a self (*ātman*).

Extensively, there are sixteen such views regarding a self and a person (*pudgala*). Now, when various sutras briefly speak of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the self, it refers to the phenomena of the gathered aggregates and so forth.
Whether one considers the self to be identical with or separate from them, those who calculate a real person (*pudgala*) as "self" or "mine" likewise [regard] the five...

Those who falsely conceptualize the aggregates (*skandhas*) as a self are "practitioners. As for the "sentient being" (*sattva*), because these five [aggregates] arise together within the five aggregates, they are called "sentient beings.
The "life-span possessor" (*jīvita*) likewise falsely conceptualizes within the five aggregates that "I" receive the life-span of a single period of retribution.

The "living being" (*jīva*) likewise falsely conceptualizes within the phenomena of the aggregates that "my" life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) maintains continuity without interruption. Because they cling to these [conceptions], [they are so designated].
Because one calculates that there is a self-body, it is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Now, among these sixteen [mental states], all four views are fully presented;
they are all false imaginings and lack any real substance. When a male takes conception, he perceives his mother as the object to be grasped and his father as the object to be contended with.
He gives rise to desire for the mother and anger toward the father. Regarding the father’s emission as being his own, he relies upon this...
Due to deluded thoughts, one obtains entry into a womb; for women, it is the reverse. This is detailed in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The designations "male" and "female" originate from such deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). This physical body, being of illusory substance, is termed a "provisional name.

Since it arises from deluded conceptualization as well as from semen and blood, this body may be verified as being false and deceptive, as within the aforementioned realm of the two kinds of emptiness.
This is the objective sphere of the emptiness of the living being (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). "Desire" (*kāma*) refers to lustful craving; "life" (*jīvita*) refers to the life of the body.

If there were no craving for desire, the various conditions would not arise, and the body would not exist. One should know that desire has the attachment to the body as its cause, while the body arises because of desire.
Once this body exists, attachment to it arises in turn. Because one loves the body, it in turn becomes the cause of desire, which further brings about future birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The karmic fruition continues in this manner, revolving and succeeding one another without end.
Because of the objects of desire, various conditions of opposition and compliance arise;
due to those desirable objects, there are those that oppose me and those that comply with me. Thus, there are objects of opposition and compliance.
They arise in a chaotic jumble.
When the objects of the environment run counter to the heart of love, one gives rise to hatred and jealousy, creating all manner of karma.
Regarding the objects perceived, if they contravene one's heart of love, then the mind conceives hatred and jealousy; at its smallest, this manifests as verbal abuse and humiliation.
On a large scale, this leads to killing and other such various evil karmas.
For this reason, one is further reborn in the realms of hell and hungry ghosts.
Possessing evil karma, one immediately undergoes its evil retribution; according to one's karma, one takes birth and falls into the evil paths.
Chanshi Fuan Hui of Xichu said: "This is how evil karma invites bitter retribution. That which opposes one's desires is disagreeable, while that which accords with them is agreeable.
Because one is attached to those objects, when the objects do not accord with the mind, one immediately gives rise to feverish affliction, resentment, and jealousy."
Due to the arising of anger, one commits various evil karmas such as killing, harming, beating, reviling, or insulting.

If the objects of perception accord with the mind of attachment, one gives rise to defiled clinging, committing various evil karmas such as sexual misconduct, theft, drinking, eating meat, plundering, and frivolous or false speech.
If, throughout the twelve periods of the day, one applies the mind in this manner, one will consequently experience the retributions of the three miserable realms.
If anger arises, one experiences the retribution of the hells; if delusion arises, one experiences the retribution of animals;
if greed arises, one experiences the retribution of hungry ghosts. As for not mentioning the realm of animals [separately], there are two reasons: first, it is to complete the literary structure.
The second point indicates that by mentioning the first and the last, the middle ones are included.
Master Mingcong of the Lecture Hall said: "The objects of desire" refers to the five objects of desire: form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.

Sentient beings perceive these five objects and give rise to notions of aversion and attraction. Take the object of form (*rūpa*) as an example: if it is agreeable, it produces joy; if it is contrary, it produces anger.
Or, when it does not comply with one's wishes, it is called "object-repulsion. From this repulsion toward the beloved object, resentment and jealousy arise, and thus the mind of anger is born.
Consequently, various evil karmas such as beating, reviling, and killing originate from form. The same applies to the remaining four [objects].

The realm of desire is likewise thus. Regarding "favorable" and "adverse": if sensory forms are favorable to the mind, one then becomes addicted to lust, theft, drinking, gluttony, violence, and frivolous speech, thereby committing numerous evil karmas.
By means of these two types of karma—favorable and adverse—one attracts powerful retributions for evil:
first falling into hell, next becoming an animal, and finally becoming a hungry ghost, undergoing the retributions of the three evil realms.

In their subsequent birth as humans, they will be poor and lowly. Furthermore, they shall begin to settle their long-standing karmic debts and grievances with one another (as described at length in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*).
Although this passage from the sūtra does not explicitly mention the retribution of animals, its intent implicitly includes them.
One should know that sensual desire can produce fire that burns all worlds, just as in the case of Śukapāla of Western India, who made his living by selling fish.
Upon seeing the noble princess for the first time, he was suddenly struck by desire. Consequently, he fell ill for a long time.
When his mother asked him the reason, he recounted the matter as described above. From then on, his mother regularly provided the nobleman with fish.

When the princess asked her mother the purpose of providing the fish and what she hoped to obtain from it, the mother spoke of her son’s lustful desires. The princess then devised a plan to meet with him.
They arrived at the temple of Maheśvara on the appointed day. A fisherman had already arrived there first; the deity possessed him with the demon of sleep, causing him to fall into a deep slumber.
The nobleman’s attendants searched for him everywhere but could not find him. Suddenly, they saw him among a heap of paper money offerings.
Seeing that he was fast asleep and did not wake, she left some objects for him and departed. Upon waking, the man smelled a strange fragrance and saw the items;
realizing that a person of noble status had visited, a sudden thought arose, and the fire of lust ignited within him. He first burned the paper money.

Next, it burns the celestial temples; thus it is said that "the fire of desire burns the celestial temples. He then tied a rope around his son's throat (as recorded in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, clarifying the joyful retribution of wholesome karma).
One knows that desire is to be reviled;
one knows that desire is a cause of evil. It is deeply to be reviled and abandoned.
One feels weary of and detached from the path of karma.
To love that [path] is to feel weary of and detached from the way of evil karma. The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué shū*) also states:
"If one develops deep affection and joy for the dharma-gate of abandoning evil, forsaking evil and delighting in good, one will again manifest as a celestial or human being."
Abandoning all evil karma and delighting in the cultivation of wholesome karma, once that wholesome karma has matured, the fruits of gods and humans immediately manifest.
"Gods and humans" refers to the heavenly realm and the human realm.
Master Chuanfeng Huì of Xishu said: "This refers to the creation of goodness that invites a joyful retribution.

It means that while the preceding text stated that sentient beings do not know or perceive, giving rise to delusions and creating karma as they follow along into the evil realms, now one has already attained awareness and realization that the previously arisen mind of greed and desire was not the path of goodness, and is thus deeply loathsome and to be abandoned. Moment by moment, one only..."

This is craving. Becoming weary of the paths of evil karma in the three miserable realms, one then abandons the mind capable of creating the ten non-virtuous actions and instead gives rise to a mind that delights in the merit of the ten virtuous dharmas.
By cultivating faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, one attains the dharma of the ten virtues.
If one applies the mind in this way throughout the twelve periods of the day, one will consequently attain rebirth among humans or the six heavens of the desire realm.
Regarding the retribution of merit: although it is thus, it is still not truly good. Why? Because for humans there are the eight sufferings, and in the heavens there are the five signs of decay.
As for the eight sufferings: first, the suffering of birth; second, the suffering of old age; third, the suffering of illness; fourth, the suffering of death.
Fifth is the suffering of separation from the beloved; sixth is the suffering of encountering the hated; seventh is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;

eighth is the suffering of the intense burning of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). As for the five signs of decay: first, the clothes become soiled; second, the flower garlands wither; third, sweat flows from both armpits.
Fourth, the four limbs become foul-smelling and filthy. Fifth, one finds no pleasure in one’s own seat. These are explained in detail as the five signs of decay and the eight sufferings;
see the Chapter on Mañjuśrī. Master Mingcong of the Four Illuminations said: "Desires" refers to the five desires, of which form is the most pressing; yet people fear it. If...
Discussing the nature of desire and the fundamental nature of bodhi: it is like entering a battlefield with a sword; one not only protects oneself but also gains fame and profit.
When a Bodhisattva uses form to contemplate the dharma-realm of form, they depart from the objects of the five desires, for there is no Buddha-nature apart from them.
For now, let us discuss the loathing of sensual pleasure and the delight in goodness. As the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states: "There are Srotāpannas who dwell among humans, and there are also..."
His wife was in the process of severing the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm. As she severed these afflictions until they were exhausted, she immediately transcended the desire realm;

yet her attachment to objects of desire remained twice as intense as that of ordinary people. The wife was displeased and constantly worried about this. Suddenly, a sage arrived and spoke of this matter.
He said, "I shall instruct you; you need only say that the dharma of the fruit of *srotāpanna* should be thus.
His wife followed his words and spoke to her husband. Her husband’s lustful mind was instantly severed, like ice melting in hot water, or like ashes scattering and smoke vanishing.
The neighbors did not know the reason for this and praised them. The husband took a painted jar, adorned with five colors, which was truly exquisite.
"Affection. [The husband] said: "If you were to play with this painted vase with me," his wife, being greedy for the vase, would never let it go from her hand.

Suddenly, the husband sought out this painted vase; the wife, thinking it was for him, handed it over. The husband snatched the vase and dropped it to the ground, where it shattered and foul stench flowed out.
The husband said: "Give me back this painted vase! The wife said: "The painted vase is broken. The husband said: "By..."

I contemplate you as if you were a painted vase. Again, he spoke in verse: "When the resolute enter meditative concentration and observe the body and mind together with their objects, having seen them, they conceive revulsion, just like a painted vase. Is this not knowing that desire is to be loathed?"
Furthermore, during the time when the Buddha was in the world, there was a woman who gave birth to three or four sons, all of whom died.
Driven mad by her longing for her children, she ran about with her hair disheveled and her body naked. One day, she arrived directly at the Jetavana Monastery.
She went directly before the Buddha. By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, she was suddenly and deeply awakened to her lack of propriety and crouched on the ground.

The Buddha instructed Ānanda to fetch a *kāṣāya* robe and give it to her; after putting it on, she departed. When she came with her husband to see the Buddha, they both realized the fruit of Arhatship.
If one merely loathes evil and delights in good, at best one will be reborn among humans or devas; however, if one deeply reflects upon desire, [the result is far greater].
One may ascend the stages of the sages. Among the five precepts for humans and devas, the three refuges and the five precepts are primary.

All manner of benefits and blessings are the karmic fruits of humans and devas. Thus far, we have spoken generally of the virtues of humans and devas; now, looking downward toward the four dhyāna heavens:
the Brahmā King of the first dhyāna, the Limited Light and others of the second dhyāna, the Limited Purity of the third dhyāna, and the Cloudless, Merit-Born, and Vast [Heavens] of the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the fruits and so forth: these heavens of the four dhyānas are all attained through the cultivation of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi).
Furthermore, because one knows that all forms of craving are to be loathed, one abandons craving and delights in equanimity (upekṣā); yet, this merely nourishes the very root of craving once again.
Having realized that various forms of craving are loathsome and detestable, one abandons all cravings and devotes oneself exclusively to the dharma of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
Yet, being unaware that this very mind also gives rise to craving, it is said that one thereby nourishes the root of craving once again.
Thus, there presently manifests the superior fruit of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Since there exists the cause of abandoning craving and delighting in relinquishment, the fruits of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas immediately manifest;
these are attained through cultivation and stand above all other virtuous fruits. Therefore, they are called "superior conditioned [fruits]."
Master Chuanfeng Huì of Xishu said: "This is the retribution for karma that leads to immovability within the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Regarding their 'dependent retribution' (*niśraya-vipāka*), they are unaware that previously they both loved to create evil and loved to cultivate goodness; yet neither was able to escape the wheel of suffering.
Consequently, they simultaneously abandoned both their hearts of attachment and their hearts that delighted in practicing virtue, casting them all aside. Furthermore, they remain unaware."
This mind of equanimity is identical to that mind of attachment; it relies upon the aforementioned moisture to give rise to the root of attachment.

To employ the mind in this manner is a conditioned mind, which brings about rebirth in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). As it gradually increases, the primary and secondary retributions of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are likewise attained.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The body of the Brahmā king among the devas is ten *yojanas* in height."
The beings of the formless realm have a body height of thirty-six yojanas. Regarding "immovable karma," this refers to immovability of both cause and fruit.
As for the cause, it is not moved by the objects of the lower desire realm;
as for the fruit, it is not moved by the meditative concentration of the four dhyānas. This is just as those in the first dhyāna are not moved by the objects of the desire realm.
Furthermore, the second dhyāna is not moved by the sphere of the first dhyāna; the third dhyāna is likewise not moved by the sphere of the second dhyāna.
In this manner, one gradually ascends to the heavens of the four spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Because they are all within saṃsāra, they do not constitute the Noble Path.
That is to say, both evil fruits and good fruits, as well as the superior good fruits of conditioned phenomena, all belong to saṃsāra and do not constitute the Buddha-way.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "This is a summary. Because the aforementioned desire-mind has not been severed, one receives retribution in the three miserable realms;
because the mind of attachment has not been severed, one receives retribution in the two upper realms.
All of these are the cycle of rebirth within the triple world, and do not constitute the Way of the Buddha."
Master Cong of Siming said: "The gateway to entering the Path requires first subduing craving and desire.

As previously stated, 'abandoning evil and delighting in good' means that while among humans, one cultivates the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, provides filial support to one's parents, and practices worldly benevolence and compassion."

By repairing bridges, paving roads, copying scriptures, fashioning Buddha images, sweeping stupas, and smearing the ground with plaster—through such various meritorious deeds—one attains rebirth in the heavens.
Initially, this refers to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, then the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, up to the six heavens of the desire realm;
or one may be born among humans in a state of wealth and nobility. Therefore, it is said that "one again sees devas. Now, it is said that "one further knows that all cravings are to be loathed."

One abandons the attachment to sensual pleasure; this meditative absorption (dhyāna) is that which abandons. It abandons the coarse and forceful sensual pleasures of the prior desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This person, weary of them, abandons them and is born in the Brahma Heaven.
If they further cultivate the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) as their sovereign delight, they reach the second dhyāna heaven.

This heaven possesses the four factors of dhyāna: the factor of internal purity, the factor of joy (*prīti*), the factor of bliss (*sukha*), and the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). These already exist.
Because it is accompanied by joy and pleasure, it is called the "meditation of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-dhyāna*). "Pleasure" refers to the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna;

this dhyāna is the foremost happiness, surpassing the previous two dhyānas, and it likewise possesses the five factors of dhyāna. The state of mental serenity is termed "pleasure. "Equanimity" refers to the Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna;
this heaven possesses the four factors of dhyāna because suffering and pleasure have been abandoned, and sorrow and joy have been extinguished, resulting in neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Regarding the practitioner who cultivates equanimity and mindfulness-purity: when desiring to leave behind the first three dhyānas, they reprove various forms of pleasure.
Once pleasure has ceased and vanished, the immovable concentration arises together with equanimity; being free from pleasure, there is no regret. This state of mind is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).

As described above, having abandoned craving and pleasure through equanimity, these four [factors] conversely give rise to the savoring of dhyāna (*dhyānāsvāda*), whereby the mind becomes attached to the concentration. This is like medicine turning [into poison].
This is for the sake of illness; it merely nourishes the root of craving. These higher realms of the form and formless worlds are not easily ascended;
because of detachment from desire, one cultivates superior goodness and attains birth in these heavens. Nevertheless, this remains within saṃsāra and does not constitute the Path of the Noble Ones.
If one hopes to cultivate Perfect Enlightenment, there is a difference as vast as that between heaven and earth; therefore, it is said that the path of the sages will not be accomplished.
For this reason, if sentient beings wish to escape birth and death and avoid the various cycles of saṃsāra, they must first sever greedy desire and eliminate craving and thirst.
The cycle of birth and death has craving as its root. To escape this suffering, one must first sever craving.
"The thirsty" refers to sentient beings whose hearts of craving are like thirst.
Master Cifuan Hui of Xishu said: This is an exhortation to sever the root.
For this reason, all sentient beings who wish to escape birth and death within the triple world and exit the cycle of transmigration in the six realms must first rely upon what the Buddha has taught.
One must sever the mind of lustful desire as well as the mind that gives rise to craving; "craving" is a metaphor for thirst, meaning the seeking of water.
The *Baoying* (Retribution) says: "Matters arise necessarily from the mind; retribution follows necessarily from the matter.
Therefore, by observing matters through the lens of one's own retribution, matters can be transformed; by citing matters to hold the mind accountable, the mind can be turned back. This is like...
Just as when people in the world wish to stop the flow of a stream, they must first exhaust its source;
and when they wish to prevent boiling water from bubbling, they must first remove the fire. Thus it was said of old: "To dam the current is not as effective as blocking the source;
to fan the boiling water is not as effective as extinguishing the fire. Since the source originates from the water, as long as the source is not blocked, the water will be inexhaustible.
Fire boils the water; if the fire is not extinguished, who can still the boiling?

Therefore, the guest who blocks the source does not obstruct the current for it to dry up of its own accord, and the guest who extinguishes the fire does not stir the boiling water for it to cease of its own accord.

Discussing matters by analogy in this manner, one may understand them in detail. To weary oneself of the fruit is not as good as severing the cause; to fear the suffering is not as good as rectifying the origin.

Regarding evil: the cause nourishes the fruit; as long as the cause is not severed, the fruit will not come to an end. The root of the saṃsāra of all sentient beings is simply these three characters: greed, desire, and love (*tṛṣṇā*).
In the preceding Mañjuśrī chapter, ignorance (*avidyā*) was said to be the root of birth and death; this refers to the "arousing of karma.
Now, in this Maitreya chapter, greed and love are said to be the root of saṃsāra; this refers to the "moistening of karma. While some sutras speak only of the arousing of karma...
If this scriptural passage were concise yet complete, Master Cong of Siming said:
"Greed and craving—these two are the roots of saṃsāra and must be eliminated.
Greed is the foremost of the three poisons; craving arises because of it, marking the beginning of attachment to things. Because of craving..."

Grasping at the five aggregates as its substance is like scales gathering and facing upstream; this craving for existence exists in all beings generally, differing only in degree of lightness or heaviness.
Those whose slaughter is heavy receive retribution in hell; those whose it is light receive the retribution of ghosts or animals. Craving also has degrees of lightness and heaviness:
if superior, one is born in the heavens; if inferior, in the human realm. The substance of craving is beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikā-avidyā*). To cultivate the Perfect [Teaching]...
The Awakened One is able to contemplate that all craving and attachment are the Middle Way within Buddha-nature; thus, though one craves and attaches throughout the day, it does not obstruct Bodhi.
Mañjuśrī himself said, "I am the teacher of desire. This is like embracing a tiger or playing with a snake:
if one does not penetrate its nature, one will be harmed by the creature; but one who skillfully penetrates its nature can enter not only the Buddha's realm but also the realm of Māra.
Good son, when Bodhisattvas manifest transformations within the world, they do not take craving as their basis; rather, through compassion, they cause others to relinquish craving.
They provisionally employ various forms of desire to enter into birth and death.

When a Bodhisattva manifests birth, it is not fundamentally based on craving. Rather, it is because they give rise to a mind of compassion and mercy to gather and transform sentient beings, causing them to abandon all cravings;
thus, they provisionally employ the affairs of sexual desire to enter the sea of birth and death, employing the same activities as those beings to transform them.
It is not that they actually possess a mind of lustful desire.
Master Xifu Huishan of Western Shu said: "This is a common obstacle. [One might think that] compassion can bestow happiness and pity can extract suffering;
fearing such doubts may harm one's contemplative wisdom.
Yet, was Master Pang truly preoccupied with worldly affairs such as supporting a wife, raising sons, and nurturing daughters? Or consider the 'Pig-Headed' Chan Master and others—all were likewise."
The manifestation of a bodhisattva is merely a display of taking birth, appearing identical to ordinary beings for the purpose of benefiting,
taming, gathering, and teaching all sentient beings.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "As with Master Fu, the Bagu Monk, and the daughter of Āśvalāyana;
as with Avalokiteśvara becoming the 'Horse-Boy’s Wife,' the 'Pig-Headed One,' and the *Cūta* tree—all these used the methods of desire to transform people.
Yunmen, Nanquan, Deshan, and others all employed the methods of Māra to enter the Buddha-way. The Bodhisattvas’ compassion benefits sentient beings; if they were purely [ascetic]..."
Employ goodness. Among them, those whose wickedness and rebellion are grave cannot be transformed by goodness; they demonstrate evil and enter into evil, reaching the depths of evil through evil.
This constitutes the Dharma-gate of the nature of evil, whereby those who embrace evil are all [manifestations of] Bodhi.

Indeed, those with coarse and heavy evil find it easier to enter through evil than through goodness, for entering through goodness does not harm things—just like letting out a kite on a string; even if it has not yet succeeded...
The Buddha said: "They shall not lose their status as humans or devas.
If all sentient beings in the final age can renounce all desires, eliminate hatred and attachment, and forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra."
