This is what is meant by "the application of effort apart from the multiplicity of conditions. As for "the application of effort in the increase of conditions," it means that when one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and quiescent, one increases all conditions to manifest the practice of effort. This is what is meant by "the application of effort in the increase of conditions. As for "the application of effort apart from the increase of conditions," it means that when one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and quiescent, even the increase of conditions is ultimately unattainable. This is what is meant by "the application of effort apart from the increase of conditions. As for "the application of effort in the decrease of conditions," it means that when one realizes that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and quiescent, one decreases all conditions to manifest the practice of effort. This is what is meant by "the application of effort in the decrease of conditions. As for "the application of effort apart from the decrease of conditions," it means that
These are Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage within the ranks of the noble ones; they all cultivate the path within dreams.

It is said that only after reaching this stage do they exclusively practice the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*). Upon attaining the perfect and luminous realization, they first come to know that afflictions are fundamentally non-existent;
thus, they perceive that even the functional power of the wisdom capable of severing [afflictions] is already illusory. This is, for example, like being within a dream.
When one treats an illness with medicine and recovers, after waking up, both the illness and the medicine are gone; therefore, it is said that they exist within the sphere of false effort.
If one attains the Tathāgata’s accord with quiescence, there is in reality neither quiescence nor one who is quiescent.
Within the sphere of false effort, if one awakens to the principle of conforming to quiescence— being still and thoughtless, extinguished and signless,
and conforming to all things without clinging to the view of self— then there is truly no dharma of quiescence, nor is there any person who attains quiescence;
this may be called the mutual forgetting of both person and dharma.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "This is the stage of fruition.

If one realizes that the single mind of the Buddhas of the ten directions is quiescent and extinguished, it accords with the principle of non-contradiction. It is not merely that one does not see any dharma of quiescent extinction to be realized;
there is also no person who can realize that quiescent extinction. Reaching this state is called 'not being stuck in the two extremes. One can..."
Everything is simultaneously severed. In every place, there is a sense of carefree detachment;

in every place, there is a profound majesty. It encompasses the eight directions and towers over the great chiliocosm. There is nowhere it does not pervade, and no land where it does not appear. Thus it is said:

"Looking out beyond the heavens from atop one's head—who is this kind of person? All that precedes is a general indication. This concludes the four [categories]: ordinary beings, sages, saints, and fruits.

The stages are not different. The following text now opens up four stages: first, the stage of faith (*śraddhā*), which extinguishes the characteristic of appearance; second, the stage of the worthy (*bhadra*), which extinguishes the characteristic of difference;
third, the stage of the sage (*ārya*), which extinguishes the characteristic of abiding; and fourth, the stage of fruition (*phala*), which extinguishes the characteristic of arising.
These correspond largely to the four stages in the *Awakening of Faith*.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "As for 'sentient beings are deluded' up to 'reaching even nirvana,' those who have not yet been able to eliminate all illusory transformations refer to the two vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha teachings, as well as the Bodhisattvas of the three teachings."

It is not only the five natures that differ; there are also the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, all of whom consist of those for whom [the afflictions] have been extinguished and those for whom they have not yet been extinguished.

Now, according to the Tiantai school, we clarify the Small and the Great Vehicles. Regarding the Small Vehicle, it clarifies that the four great elements truly arise from ignorance and truly cease with the cessation of ignorance.
Regarding the Great Vehicle teachings, it clarifies that the four great elements differ according to the three teachings. Within the Shared Teaching, the four...

The great elements are fundamentally empty; therefore, they are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished. Due to ignorance, one perceives birth and extinction as being like the arising of illusions and the ceasing of illusions.
In the Separate Teaching, the essence of the four great elements is Buddha-nature; yet, due to ignorance—

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) undergo arising and ceasing; their nature (*svabhāva*) is without arising or ceasing, while their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) possess arising and ceasing. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the substance of the four great elements is also Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Yet, because they originally and fully possess the nine realms, there are nine [aspects] of the four great elements. Whether the four great elements arise or cease, they are all the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Therefore, both nature and characteristics are neither born nor extinguished; this is the inconceivable discourse on arising and ceasing. This is [the same as]... (Note: The final "與" (yǔ) appears to be a fragmentary reference to a comparison with another text or concept, such as the *Awakening of Faith*, which discusses the inconceivable arising and ceasing of the mind.)
"The world-phenomena are eternally abiding" in the *Lotus Sūtra*—its meaning is perfectly clear (as stated in the writings of Master Siming). Regarding "extinction" (*nirodha*) and "non-extinction":

for those of the Two Vehicles, the Śrāvakas, although they have severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*) and have realized the emptiness of the four great elements and five aggregates, thereby attaining non-arising and non-extinction, this refers only to the non-arising and non-extinction of their segmented bodies (*paricchinna-deha*) within the triple world. Therefore, it is said: "Regarding extinction," [referring to] the triple world.
Externally, there are the dust-like sands of ignorance and the transformations of birth and death; therefore, it is said they are "not yet extinguished.

The Buddhas at the ultimate fruit of the three intermediate teachings and the Bodhisattvas of those three teachings all rely on deluded effort; they merely halt at the "transformed city" (the *pariṇāmika-nagara*) and have not yet reached the "Precious Place" (*ratnasthāna*).
Now there is a certain class of people who do not follow the teachings of the Sages. They establish their own views and forcibly bind and constrain their body and mind.
Even if they should attain some partial knowledge or insight, it is all heterodox dharma—such as those who observe the "chicken's great precepts" and teach others to practice seated meditation.
Lacking knowledge of the proper Dharma measures, from morning until evening they sit until their bodies wither and dry, becoming increasingly dazed and delirious.

As the Lady Liang said: "It is like a clod of earth shattering and falling into a deep valley; it is like a moth flying toward a bright candle. These words are not mistaken. Thus, the Great Awakened One foresaw the customs of future ages, saying:
"Sentient beings are deluded and inverted; they have not yet been able to eliminate them. All these illusory transformations will cease only through the Perfect [Teaching]."

The Buddha’s cultivation and realization have reached the ultimate. His self-awakened noble wisdom is like a perfect mirror; it is a vast, spiritual, and penetrating true realization of the ground that is neither born nor extinguished.
Since this birth and extinction have returned to the essence of nature, there is then neither birth-and-extinction nor non-birth-and-non-extinction.
It is like a person in the world who locks his own house and loses the key.
After many years have passed, he travels far to another country and dwells there, having built another house; yet this is not ultimate.
Later, returning to his native land, he retrieves his original key and opens his own former house, whereupon all the things previously used remain exactly as they were, without moving.
Not seeking anything else even for the slightest bit, one returns to the original family business. When the Great Sage’s cultivation reaches its ultimate, he restores his original nature;
the primordial substance remains unmoving. Ignorance is itself clarity; the Four Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are fundamentally unmoving—this is called the "original face.
People themselves fail to understand this and thus take on birth and extinction; even if they were to realize the state of a Lesser Sage, it would still not be [the ultimate].
Because of their attachment to worldly affairs, they give rise to deluded efforts that emerge and perish of their own accord; our Buddha rejected these as all being non-orthodox paths.
For those who accord with true quiescence, the beginning and the source are unified, and cultivation and nature share a common origin—there is neither cultivation nor nature.
Practicing the Dharma-cloud Samādhi, one contemplates that the mind is no-mind; phenomena do not abide within phenomena; and the Truth of Cessation is quiescent.
This is the intended meaning of the aforementioned sutra. Those who are deluded regarding Perfect Enlightenment have five distinct natures.

Furthermore, among the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and various lesser bodhisattvas, there are differences in what they realize according to their respective capacities; thus, there are varying degrees of depth. If one does not clarify these coarse distinctions, how could one...?
To distinguish these subtleties: the following clarifies that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is uniquely and purely marvelous.

While the Perfect-Sudden (Yuantun) itself has no stages or ranks, it borrows the stages and ranks of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) to clarify its degrees of depth and shallowness. Now, according to the Tiantai school, we establish the six levels of "identity" (liuji) as a measure of differentiation;
otherwise, there is a fear that ordinary beings might confuse themselves with the ultimate Sage. This section of the scripture was [commented upon] solely by Cishi (Zhiyi) and Siming (Zhiyuan).

This is the true interpretation, used to clarify this meaning. However, the elucidation of the meaning therein was not yet complete. Now, relying on the sutras and the patriarchs, I divide it into six sections:
first, the Buddha as principle; second, the Buddha by name; third, the Buddha through contemplative practice; fourth, the Buddha in semblance;
fifth, the Buddha of partial truth, which refers to those from the first stage (prathama-bhūmi) Bodhisattva up to the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (samāyogi-bodhisattva). This is called...

The "partially true" is the Buddha; the "ultimately perfected" is the Buddha—this refers to the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). It is also said that these six are "is-ness" (*ju*).
This means that they are "is-ness" in principle (*li*). Because sentient beings are themselves Buddhas, it is said that these six are "is-ness."
Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed after the deluded notion of "self.
Yet the essence of this self has never existed; it is through delusion that it is taken to exist, as well as those who love this self.
"Those who love me" refers to those whose minds cling to the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).
They are unaware that their thoughts arise and perish from moment to moment.
The deluded minds of sentient beings cling to the mark of selfhood and do not realize that within each instant of thought, this mind arises and perishes in rapid succession.
It perishes; fundamentally, it lacks any mark of solidity or indestructibility. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "This body is like lightning;
it does not abide for even a single moment. This refers to that very point.
Consequently, they give rise to hatred and attachment, becoming addicted to the five desires.
The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "Because of the grasping at a self, one loves that which accords with it and hates that which opposes it;
thus, one becomes attached to the five desires. As for the five desires: first, wealth; second, form; third, food; fourth, fame; and fifth, sleep.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "Regarding these ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), there are two aspects:

first, the ordinary person fully possessed of greed, anger, and delusion; second, the ordinary person at the stage of the ten faiths. Now, this initial section of the text refers to one who has not yet entered the stage of faith.
The reason this text exists is that if one does not account for the delusion of the ordinary person, there would be no stage of faith."
First, the heading: "Sentient beings" refers to the four modes of birth and the nine categories of existence.
"Due to the deluded thought of 'self'" indicates the essence of that which is grasped; "and the attachment to 'self'" indicates the subject that grasps.
This means that all sentient beings of the nine categories, since beginningless vast eons ago, have erroneously entered [saṃsāra] due to a single moment of non-awakening and deluded thought.
Within the parents' womb, one's own singular spiritual nature is enveloped by the father’s semen and the mother’s blood;
through the conjunction of these three conditions, this body is produced. This is the "self" that is clung to.
Now, one does not know the origin from which it arose, and furthermore, upon this body of delusive thought, one gives rise to further attachment and craving.
Seeing: this refers to thinking, "This is my eye, my ear, my nose," or "This is my hand, my foot, my body, my nature, my name.
In all circumstances, one cannot move away from this "self. One contends with others and contends with the self;

yet not a single person has ever awakened to this within themselves, realizing that throughout the twelve periods of the day, the preceding thought continues into the succeeding thought. The subsequent...
Thought follows upon thought; every moment arises and perishes, like the flickering of a lamp’s flame or the trickling of a stream.

The manifestations of worldly toil and deluded thoughts take on ten thousand forms: we love what accords with us and hate what opposes us, becoming attached in every situation to the five desires of form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and mental objects.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: Tiantai stated, "If a Buddha did not appear in the world, sentient beings would not know that they inherently possess Buddha-nature;

if a Buddha did not teach it, no one would be able to know it. Regarding the phrase "the single principle is itself the Buddha," this means that perfect enlightenment (circular awakening) pervades all places and that there are no phenomena that are not clearly understood.
Thus, even the five paths of immediate retribution are all the mark of liberation. Although...
Enshrouded in darkness, blindness, inversion, and delusion, this principle nonetheless exists. This principle is manifest and eternally abiding in the world;

it cannot be benefited by the presence of a Buddha, nor can it be diminished by his absence. One does not feel elated upon attaining it, nor dejected upon losing it. Therefore, it is called "sentient beings."
Principle is itself Buddha. Siming said: "However, if one does not know that nature is defiled and nature is evil, then all defilement and evil must necessarily be severed and destroyed;
how then could one discuss the 'entire body' as being identical [to it]? Because the entire body is [Buddha], one is spared from self-abasement;
because the six [sense-objects] are distinguished, one is spared from overweening pride. The six do not depart from identity, and identity does not obstruct the six. The six...

This is precisely what constitutes the realization of meaning; the state of perfection can thus be discerned. This is truly because the sentient beings' nature is inherently endowed with defilement and evil, which cannot be altered.

That this nature is perfectly luminous is what is called "Buddha. Since the nature’s defilement and nature’s evil arise as the whole body [of reality], the cultivated defilement and cultivated evil have no separate essence.
Because the entirety of cultivation is the nature, one attains the Buddha who is non-different from principle even within deluded phenomena. Thus, by means of...
This principle gives rise to delusions and the creation of karma, causing one to cycle through birth and death; yet, one remains entirely unaware that phenomena are in fact this very principle.
For long kalpas one employs this principle, yet for long kalpas one does not know it—this is identical to the present sutra.

From beginningless time, due to the false imagination of "self" and those who "love the self," there has been moment-to-moment arising and ceasing; thus, hatred and attachment arise, and one becomes addicted to the five desires, falsely undergoing birth.
Upon death, they do not realize that they themselves possess Buddha-nature; they have lost their original wondrous clarity. This is called "Buddha as the principle" (li-ji fo).

If they encounter a virtuous friend who instructs them to awaken to the nature of pure, perfect enlightenment and clarifies the arising and ceasing [of phenomena], they will immediately know this life.
The nature itself is inherently free from toil and anxiety.

Sentient beings, however, awaken to this nature through instruction; only by clarifying the principle of the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts do they come to know that the nature originally inherent in this life is empty, and that they themselves have been laboring in vain with their discursive thinking.

Furthermore, if there is a person who has forever severed wearisome anxieties and attained the purity of the dharma-realm, such that all discursive thought is eternally stilled, then they will attain purity in all places; therefore, it is said that they have attained the purity of the dharma-realm.
That very pure understanding becomes an obstacle to itself;
taking purity as purity is what is called "pure understanding.
Because this understanding-mind has the nature of being an obstacle to itself, one does not attain mastery over Perfect Enlightenment.
Because one directs the attention toward awakening, one does not know [the nature of] this oneself;
this is called the ordinary person’s conformity with the nature of awakening.
Because sentient beings believe that the nature of awakening is originally pure, they give rise to a pure mind and practice in conformity with it, yet they do not realize it.
This mind is also an obstacle; this is the view of ordinary people, not the view of Bodhisattvas.
Chan Master Fu’an Hui of Xichu said: "Once one knows that thoughts of arising and ceasing are harmful to the Way, one consequently severs the mind of seeking and contriving from above.
By thus quelling the deluded mind, at the place where the deluded mind does not arise, one attains [realization]."
The Purity of the Dharma-realm. There are two aspects to the Dharma-realm: first, the principle Dharma-realm; second, the phenomenal Dharma-realm.
If the principle Dharma-realm is pure, then within its fundamental nature, it is from the beginning free from characteristics and transcends names;

there is nothing to be differentiated, and no mental toil regarding the objects of the six sense-fields arises at all. If the phenomenal Dharma-realm is pure, then regarding the five aggregates and the ten... [text fragment]
The two bases, the eighteen realms, and all phenomena beyond them—the mountains, rivers, great earth, grasses, trees, thickets, and forests—are empty in their very substance.
This is truly because when the mind is pure, they are pure; when the mind is defiled, they are defiled. As the ancients said: "When the mind is void, the environment is still;

when thoughts arise, phenomena are born. When the water is turbid, the waves are murky; when the pond is clear, the moon is bright. Once coarse thoughts are eliminated, one attains a measure of peace.
Regarding purity: at the time of purification, the mind gives rise to attachment and forms a conceptual view of purity, thereby being ensnared by the signs of that pure understanding.
It is as if one has pierced one's own nostrils; it is not a matter of external sensory objects coming to disturb one. Therefore, it is said to be "self-inflicted.

Consequently, within the great, perfect, unconditioned, and quiescent illumination of *bodhi*, one cannot attain sovereign mastery in either vertical or horizontal dimensions. As the ancients said: "Do not..."
Sitting toward the depths of the white clouds, one must take care not to let cold ashes burn one to death.
This refers precisely to the ordinary person at the stage of the ten faiths, who constantly accords with the nature of original enlightenment and does not turn their back upon it.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "If one encounters a virtuous friend whose innate nature naturally exerts itself in contemplation, then these names and words are themselves the Buddha.
Within the long night of ignorance and the great barrier of birth and death, there is no Buddha’s great lock;

therefore, the Buddha appears in the world to open the gate of ambrosia and illuminate the world with light, causing one to know that the Three Jewels and the Ten Epithets are the flavor of eternal constancy. This light..."
This flavor flows forth from the nature of the minds of sentient beings; it causes sentient beings to understand this light-flavor, which is none other than the Buddha of Original Nature.
Upon hearing this name, Sudatta’s body hairs stood on end; the dark night became brilliantly clear, and the great gate opened of its own accord.
The name itself is the Buddha; this is identical to the present text. If one encounters a virtuous friend, that is a teacher who instructs as a spiritual mentor (*kalyāṇamitra*).

From this, one begins cultivation, attains awakening, and achieves realization. This also occurs through the power of permeation, whereby one comes to know the originally inherent nature of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) and discerns its arising and ceasing.
However, because one has not yet cultivated it and not yet realized it, it is like an ordinary person who knows [something] exists.
The substance of jade possesses the nature of fire within wood; it does not require carving or striking to be ignited. To know this yet fail to act is for the Dharma-body to remain in delusion.
Even if one seeks a teacher, true illumination will not arise; it is merely a waste of mental effort.

It is like a worldly person standing by a river and envying the fish, devising hundreds of thousands of schemes, yet if they lack a trap or net, there is no way to catch any. This refers to the stage of "name and word" (nāma-pada).
This refers to the Buddha.

Furthermore, if there is another person who has forever severed all weariness and anxiety and attained accordance with the nature of awakening, this clarifies that the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) is itself the Buddha.

At this level, one has already cultivated the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*), contemplating the objects of the three truths (*sandiji*). As object and contemplation merge and flow together, although they still possess afflictions, [they are as if non-existent].
In nature, one is able to know the Tathāgata’s secret treasury; principle and wisdom correspond, and the mental contemplation is luminous and clear.

This is precisely the stage occupied by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe: the Five Grades of Practice in the *Lotus Sūtra*. When it is now said that "exhaustive toil and anxiety are forever severed," this means that the nature of the afflictions is forever suppressed so that they do not arise.
Because this person’s mind of understanding is empty and pervasive, it is said that they have attained the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

"Purity" refers to that very purity; it is the conceptualization of purity regarding this purity. It is like an insect gnawing through wood to form characters; one does not know whether they are characters or not.

Therefore, it is said to "act as an obstacle to oneself. Because one merely employs the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment to perfect one's own mind, yet has not perfected the ten realms, the mind has not attained universal perfection.
Therefore, it is said to be "not sovereign. Since one has not yet severed [the views of] existence...

Attachment and ignorance degrade one to the status of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Because the nature of enlightenment (*bodhisaṃvit*) never suffers retrogression upon reaching this state, it is said that one "accords with the nature of enlightenment.
Good son, for all bodhisattvas, views and understandings constitute obstacles.
Because the views of prior pure understanding act as obstacles,
even though the hindrances to understanding have been severed, one still dwells in the state of viewing and awakening.
Although pure understanding has been eliminated so that it no longer acts as an obstacle, while one is precisely in the stage of awakening, one is again hindered by that very awakening.
To perceive an obstruction as an obstruction is to be without mastery.
The Great Commentary on Perfect Enlightenment states: "Because that which is perceived is an obstruction, the perceiving subject is also an obstruction.
By retaining this trace, it in turn obstructs the awakened mind; therefore, one lacks mastery."
This is called the bodhisattva who has not yet entered the stages (bhūmi) conforming to the nature of awakening.
Such conformity to the fundamental nature is the vision of a bodhisattva who has not yet entered the Buddha-stage.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "These thirty stages—the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten transferences—belong to those of the Three Sages (Sanxian).
This is called the stage of Provisions (Ziliangwei). However, the insights of those in the Three Sages are superior to those of the ten levels of faith (Shixin);
consequently, they perceive the views and understandings of those in the ten levels of faith as being obstacles."

Regarding the object: he then eliminates the conceptualization that clings to purity. Although he has eliminated the attainment of the conceptualization of purity, there still remains the mind that is able to see and able to cognize.
Consequently, he dwells attached to this cognitive mind and does not know how to relinquish it; it is precisely this cognitive mind [that remains].
Furthermore, because of these hindrances, one cannot attain mastery within the unconditioned, quiescent illumination of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avikalpa*).

This refers to those bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva*) who have not yet entered the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), yet are in correspondence with the nature of enlightenment (*bodhi-svabhāva*).
The Dharma Master Cong of Siming said: "The fourth [stage], 'semblance,' is the Buddha. Tiantai says:

"'Semblance' means that two things resemble each other, like brass resembling gold, or a melon compared to a gourd. It is like seeing fire first as warm, or encountering the sea and initially perceiving its water as cool;
those who drink will know this for themselves. If one is thirsty and does not dig a well, what is the use of listening to explanations? This is as stated in the sixth chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*..."

The purity of the faculties is its characteristic. This stage has not yet entered the position of partial realization; it is like pure gold currently residing in the final mind of the ten stages of faith—a stage of similarity.
It is like brass compared to gold: for the time being, it is still brass, but upon taking one further step, it becomes gold.

Brass may be transformed into gold; original enlightenment (prakṛti-vijñāna) is cool and refreshing, much like cold water. When one partakes of this "enlightened water," one knows it eliminates the fever of afflictions. As for those who perceive views and understanding as obstacles:

these Bodhisattvas have already severed both views and attachments (*dṛṣṭi-rāga*). Through the first stage of faith they sever views; through the second to the seventh stages of faith they sever latent tendencies (*bhāvanā-kleśa*);

and through the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages of faith they sever the *rajas-reṇu* (dust-like) delusions. Although they employ perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) to sever views and latent tendencies, [the process continues].

One still dwells within the wisdom of understanding; therefore, it is said that "understanding and views constitute an obstruction. This understanding serves as wisdom, yet wisdom, in turn, becomes a hindrance—thus it is also called an "obstruction.

When the obstruction of understanding is severed through understanding, one still dwells in the awakening of views. As long as the obstruction of understanding is not yet severed, one continues to employ applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

Once the power of contemplation has become strong, the obstacles to liberation naturally dissolve. Although medicine is used to treat an illness, once the illness has departed, the medicine itself must also vanish;

if one continues to cling to the medicine, it will instead become a disease. Likewise, although one uses the awakening to emptiness to awaken to the dissolution of obstacles, this very awakening becomes an obstacle in turn.
Upon reaching this point, one is about to ascend to the Perfect [Stage] and dwell atop the mountain of Nirvana, abiding in the empty and profound state of awakened observation.
In the interim, they are unwilling to advance. In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations), the Buddha manifests sixty trillion bodies;
when one perceives these extraordinary marks, they quickly enter the stage of non-arising (*anutpāda*), which is called "increase.

When one dwells within the contemplative awareness of the *nien-fo samādhi*, it is called "not yet being autonomous. Therefore, the conclusion states: "This refers to Bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the [Bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*). Following...
It accords with the nature of awakening. Although one has not yet entered the stages (bhūmi), by borrowing the distinct ten stages, they are termed the "perfect ten abodes" (daśa-vihāra).
This is the perfection of the first stage within the distinct [teaching]. Because the Buddha’s state is not yet ultimate at this initial abode, it is called "accordance."
"Good son, both 'illumination' and 'awareness' are termed obstacles.
'Illumination' refers to the aforementioned mind of pure understanding; 'awareness' refers to the aforementioned mind that perceives obstacles.
Within the nature of Perfect Enlightenment, both are termed obstacles."
Master Xifu Huì of Western Shu said: "These are the ten stages of the Śrāvakas (Ten Sages).

'Those who have illumination' among the superior Bodhisattvas refers to the pure understanding of those in the preceding stage of Faith. 'Those who have awareness' refers to the capacity for insight of those in the preceding stage of Worthiness.
Both of these are objects that constitute obstacles. This refers to persons who have attained awakening prior to these two stages."
All that has been seen is incorrect. For instance, when Bodhidharma was about to return to the West, he commanded his disciples to each present their own understanding.
At that time, Dao Fu came forward and said: "As I see it, I do not cling to words and letters, nor am I separated from words and letters."
[They] then applied this as the function of the Way. Bodhidharma said, "You have obtained my skin. Nizongchi said, "What I now understand is like the joy of seeing the land of Akṣobhya Buddha once;
having seen it, one does not see it again. Bodhidharma said, "You have obtained my flesh.
Daoyu said, "The four great elements are fundamentally empty, and the five aggregates do not exist; yet in the place where I perceive, there is not a single [thing]."
"The Dharma can be attained. Dharmatrāta said, "You have attained my bones. These three Great Beings all possess illumination and awareness, yet they have not eliminated their attachment to dharmas."
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is always awakened and does not abide;
he is serenely and perpetually awakened, not abiding in signs. This is what is meant in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* when it says:
"A Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere."
The illumination and the illuminator are simultaneously quiescent;
that is to say, both the objects illuminated and the wisdom that illuminates are entirely quiescent. This is one who has already entered the stage of Buddhahood.
Master Chuanfeng Huì of Xishu said: "Constant awakening" (*changjue*)—the term "constant" (*chang*) refers to that which is eternally unchanging;
it is non-discriminative wisdom (*avikalpa-jñāna*). "Illumination" (*zhao*) is the wisdom that is capable of illuminating. "The illuminator" (*zhaozhe*) is the objective realm that is illuminated.

"Quiescent extinction" (*jimiè*) is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This refers to the non-discriminative wisdom of a Bodhisattva who has entered the [Bodhisattva] stages (*bhūmi*), which does not...
Abiding in and clinging to the wisdom that illuminates as well as the objects illuminated—both subject and object being empty, the two attachments are simultaneously abandoned.
That is to say, from the very beginning, it is free from the marks of mental conditions, free from the marks of words and letters, and free from the marks of conceptual discrimination. Free.
The characteristics of subject and object: this refers to taking an objectless realm as an object by means of objectless wisdom, and giving rise to objectless wisdom by means of an objectless realm.
It is like water poured into water, or like space merging with space; there is not the slightest trace to be found. How is this known?

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "When, regarding the object of cognition, wisdom perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in *vijñaptimātra*, because one is free from the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.
Thus, Panshan said: "Light does not illuminate objects, nor do objects exist;
when both light and objects are forgotten, what is it then? Upon reaching this state, the wind cannot enter and water cannot touch; it is pure.
Vastly empty and pure white: one is liberated from the realm of right and wrong.

Master Benren said to Qingjing, "At the summit of a high mountain, there is no one with whom to share a word or a morsel. This is like the Second Patriarch, who, having come forth and prostrated, stood in his place;
Bodhidharma then said, "You have received my marrow. Only the Second Patriarch was the illumination and the illuminator, identical as one.
"At that time, they are in tranquil extinction.
Master Cōng of Siming said: "Good son, from 'having illumination and having awareness' up to 'simultaneously entering tranquil extinction,' the five parts of reality are precisely the Buddha.
Siming relied upon the *Awakening of Faith* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to clarify the stage of the first abode (*prathamabhūmi*). This Bodhisattva..."
One breaks through a single grade of ignorance and realizes a portion of the three virtues. One manifests as a Buddha in a hundred worlds;

when the great trichiliocosm blazes with fire, one can extinguish it with a single spittle; when the great trichiliocosm becomes empty space, one can restore it with a single breath. This is sudden cultivation and sudden realization.

At the initial arousal of the mind, one arouses the mind of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhicitta*). Constantly employing quiescent illumination—because it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating—it is called "quiescent illumination" (*jizhao*).

The two are fused. By destroying one grade of delusion, one realizes the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*); by destroying ten grades, one realizes the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmayaḥ*). This treatise now discusses the function of the first stage.
Upon entering this stage, both mind and phenomena vanish; object and wisdom are simultaneously extinguished. Stillness and illumination share a single source; there is neither subject nor object.

That which has illumination is the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*); that which has awakening is the object (*ālambana*). As the preceding text states: "Pure awakening. This refers to the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
The characteristic of awakening is itself the object. If one establishes either the object or the contemplation, both become obstacles.

This person is constantly aware yet does not dwell in awareness; they are constantly illuminating yet do not dwell in illumination. Since both illumination and awareness do not abide, object and wisdom are both extinguished.
It is like the sun relying on the sky yet not dwelling in the sky: the constant object is signless, and the constant wisdom is without objective conditions. This is called simultaneous quiescence.

Although one may deliver sentient beings across the hundred realms, there are no sentient beings to be delivered. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "In truth, there are no sentient beings to be delivered;
only such a person is a true Bodhisattva. It is like a person who cuts off their own head: once the head is severed, there is no one capable of cutting it. This is because of an obstructed mind.
One extinguishes all obstructions by oneself. Once the obstructions have been severed and extinguished, there is no longer anyone who extinguishes the obstructions.
By means of the pure awakened mind, one eliminates all obstructions; once the obstructions are removed, the awakened mind itself also vanishes.
It is like a person of the world who severs his own head: once the head has been severed, there is no other person remaining who could have severed it.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "It is like a person who severs their own head. Since the head has already been severed, there is no one capable of severing it.
This is an analogy. It illustrates that when a worldly person’s head has not yet been severed, the head is the object (*karman*) and the hand is the agent (*kartṛ*).
Once they have themselves taken up the sword and severed it, the head becomes the object severed, and the hand...
It is that which performs the severing. Once one's own head has been severed, how could there still be a distinction between the hand that severs and the head that is severed?
There is certainly no such principle. Thus, Master Dongpo said: "Since the head is severed, there is no one who severs. When ice melts, how can it further know itself as ice?
Therefore, by means of the obstructing mind, all obstructions are extinguished of themselves; once the obstructions have ceased—
"Annihilation. That which is without the obstruction of annihilation is this union. 'The mind that obstructs' refers to the awareness that is capable of perceiving the obstruction;
'the various obstructions' refers to the objects of perception that constitute the obstruction.

This means that once one employs the obstructing mind of the perceiver to perceive away the awareness of the perceived obstructions, one then sweeps away the perceiving mind itself all at once; thus, there is no longer any obstructing capacity to be annihilated."

This mind is likewise one in which both subject and object are forgotten. From the scriptural passage beginning with "the constant awakening does not abide" up to this point, it clarifies that Bodhisattvas on the Grounds do not abide in or cling to either the means of realization or the object realized.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "This analogy illustrates the quiescence and illumination of object and wisdom (*ālambana* and *jñāna*).

They are non-dual yet dual; dual yet non-dual. The object belongs to that which is severed; wisdom belongs to that which severs. When object and wisdom are unified, they can no longer be divided. Who is the seer and who is the seen?
With the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*), one illuminates the object of suchness. Since object and wisdom have thus merged, form..."
The mind and its environment are of one identical body of awakening. Through the eight phases of attaining the Way, one delivers sentient beings throughout the ten realms.
Although these are like medicine and disease, because the medicine is used to treat the disease, it is said that by means of the obstructing mind, all obstructions are naturally extinguished.
When both object and wisdom have vanished, only true wisdom remains alone; therefore, it is said that there is no one who extinguishes obstruction.
The teachings of the sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon. If one sees the moon, one understands that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself.
By means of the finger one sees the moon; once the moon is seen, one forgets the finger. By means of the teachings one elucidates the mind; once the mind is realized, one forgets the teachings.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "The following clarifies non-abiding in the teachings. First, the metaphor is presented:
*Sūtra* in Sanskrit is translated here as 'Scripture of Accordance' (*Qijing*). This is a general title for the temporal teachings of a lifetime. The Commentary states:

'Now, the establishment of words and images is intended for the realization of the meaning; yet there are those who, lacking words and images, fall into delusion, or who, clinging to words and images, become lost to the Truth.'"

Therefore, the finger pointing at the moon is used as a metaphor for verbal teachings; it is said that one must rely on the tip of the finger to see the moon, and one must depend upon the Buddha’s teachings to awaken to the mind.
By means of the finger, one sees the moon; once the moon is seen, the finger is forgotten. By means of the teachings, one attains the mind; once the mind is awakened, the teachings are forgotten.
To cling to the finger is to lose the true moon; to grasp at the teachings is to lose the fundamental mind. Sengzhao said: "One who is skilled in speaking about words..."
Seeking that which words cannot express; excelling at tracking those who track tracks—seeking that which tracks cannot reach. The Patriarch said:
"The Tathāgata’s all dharmas are for removing my all-mind. Since I have no all-mind, what need is there for all dharmas?"

The Buddha said: "The teachings of the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the scriptures that I have spoken are like an empty fist used to deceive small children, or like yellow leaves used to stop their crying.
How do we know this? Master Pang said: 'While the child was crying, the mother said she would give him gold;
holding up yellow leaves was merely the sound of her stopping his tears. Zen says: 'When you see people, you must cast it away.'"

The object used for knocking at the door: having found the path, one still forgets the name of the milestone. Generally speaking, those who have not yet entered the stage must rely on the teachings to practice;
once they have entered the stage and seen the Way, ascending to the ground and realizing the principle, they no longer require the teachings.
The various verbal teachings of all Tathāgatas that reveal the bodhisattvas are likewise so:
the Buddhas’ exposition of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is just like pointing at the moon with a finger.
Chan Master Fuyan Hui of Xishu said: "This is the principle of the Dharma.

It means that the various skillful means, various verbal teachings, and various parables employed by the Buddhas of the ten directions to reveal and instruct all Bodhisattvas and all sentient beings are like a finger pointing at the moon.
This is truly because the entire body of the temporal teachings throughout the generations cannot [itself] be grasped."
Thus it is. For the sake of providing skillful means for sentient beings, he expounds and elucidates the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, one who has realized their own nature understands that all verbal expressions are ultimately not the nature itself; naturally, such a person no longer clings to written characters or spoken language.
To be mired in words and phrases, the Sūtra says: "The realization of dharmas does not reside in speech. It also says: "He has grasped his own nostrils."
He lost his mouth. Huìtáng said: "The five thousand words [of the *Diamond Sūtra*] merely point the way. One uses the finger because one observes the moon in the sky;
when the moon sets, the finger is forgotten, and there is nothing else. Whether sleeping drunk or sitting awake, simply follow conditions. As Zhuangzi said: "The purpose of the trap is for the fish;
once the fish is caught, forget the trap. The purpose of the snare is for the rabbit; once the rabbit is caught, forget the snare."
The reason words exist is for the sake of conveying meaning; once the meaning is grasped, the words are forgotten. As the Sūtra says:
"Where there are only words, there is no true meaning. Otherwise, to seek the Way by relying on empty words is to distance oneself far from the Way.
To treat the teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs as something merely marvelous is much like a fierce tiger entering a cage or a spiritual phoenix falling into a trap.
How truly joyful! Have you not seen what Dongshan said? "If one is of the superior stream, one should not take the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and paste them upon the forehead.
To paste them upon the forehead is like a tortoise carrying a map; it is a sign of bringing about its own destruction."
This is called a bodhisattva who has already entered the stages (*bhūmi*).
Such conformity to the nature of awakening—that is, conformity to the fundamental nature—is the vision of a bodhisattva who has already entered the stage of Buddhahood.
"One who has entered the stages" refers to one who has entered the stage of a Buddha.
Master Chong of Furan in Western Shu said: "This concludes the preceding discussion on non-abiding realization and non-abiding teaching;
this is how a Bodhisattva who has entered the stages corresponds with the nature of awakening."
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: Regarding the *Sūtra* up to the section on "Conforming to the Nature of Awakening," *sūtra* is translated here as "Kie-king" (Scripture of Accordance).
There is no principle for elucidating the nature that does not proceed from this. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "For one hundred and eighty kalpas, time passed in vain without a Buddha.
How could there have been a scripture capable of illuminating [the truth] had the Hero of the World not bestowed his compassion and established the teaching?

One becomes a Buddha only after serving as a model for sentient beings. For instance, although Confucius did not establish the Five Classics to govern the world, how are candidates recruited and taught in the present day?
It is like using a trap or a snare to catch fish or rabbits; one must simply not cling to the instrument itself.
The teaching itself remains an illness. Thus it is said that the finger points to the moon. When the moon is not yet recognized, one uses the finger to point toward it;

by means of the finger, one sees the moon. Once the moon is seen, the finger must be forgotten. If one were to cling to the finger as being the moon, that would already be unacceptable—how much more so when the moon is certainly not the finger?
The entire Great Canon of the Teachings is merely a provisional designation. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "As I..."

The teaching of the Dharma is like the parable of the raft: even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone that which is not the Dharma. An ancient said: "A single rabbit lies across the ancient road;
as soon as the gray falcon sees it, she swoops down to seize it. Lately, hunting dogs have lost their keen instinct;
they instead search for it at the old spot where the withered post once stood. It is just so with the Tathāgata’s various modes of speech. Having already entered...
"Ground" refers to universal conformity with the nature of enlightenment. When a sage first enters the first abode, they enter the stream and lose the object of perception.
Once that which is entered has become tranquil, the two marks of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise. How could this merely be called conforming to the nature of enlightenment?
Good son, all obstacles are themselves ultimate enlightenment.

When a Bodhisattva first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, it is called original and initial enlightenment (*mūla-ādi-bodhi*). When perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is accomplished, it is called ultimate enlightenment (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*).

That one now perceives all obstacles as ultimate enlightenment indicates that they have already entered the stage of Buddhahood (*buddha-bhūmi*), where there are no longer any distinctions whatsoever.
It is the mind.
Whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation.
Attaining mindfulness is non-mindfulness; losing mindfulness is having mindfulness. The Buddha knows that all thoughts are fundamentally empty and realizes there is nothing to be attained.
Because they have been lost, all attain liberation.
Both the establishment of dharmas and the destruction of dharmas are termed *nirvāṇa*.

To advance in practice is called "establishment"; to slander [the teachings] is called "destruction. The Buddha knows that all dharmas are fundamentally empty; he realizes that there is neither establishment nor destruction.
All are named *nirvāṇa*.
Wisdom and ignorance are both collectively termed *prajñā*.
Wisdom is the nature that has already been awakened; ignorance is the nature that has not yet been awakened. When their fundamental source is investigated, they are identical.
Because there is but one Buddha-nature, it is said that [all] universally constitute prajñā.
The dharmas accomplished by Bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists are equally bodhi.
Although the dharmas established by Bodhisattvas and non-Buddhists differ in being either heterodox or orthodox, they are all the awakening of bodhi.
The nature [of reality] is such that ignorance and true thusness are not distinct realms;
truth and falsehood are of one essence, for the nature is fundamentally liberated.
All precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as lust, anger, and ignorance, are equally the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya).
While precepts, concentration, and wisdom are pure, lust, anger, and ignorance are defiled; yet the Buddha has no mind of discrimination between the defiled and the pure.
It is said that both are the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*).
Sentient beings and their lands share the same single *dharmatā*.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "With my Buddha-eye, I universally observe all sentient and insentient beings within the triple world."
The Dharma is entirely ultimate. That which is ultimate is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Both the hells and the celestial palaces are all pure lands, for the Buddha knows that the two retributions of good and evil are both like flowers in the sky; thus, he declares that the two realms of suffering and pleasure are both pure.
Regarding those with natures and those without natures, all equally attain the Buddha-way.
Those with natures are the three vehicles; those without natures are the icchantikas. When viewed with the Buddha-eye, they are all entirely Buddhas.
"All afflictions are ultimately liberated.
The Buddha said this because afflictions are fundamentally empty; hence they are called "ultimately liberated.
Master Fu-an Hui of Xi-chu said: "This refers to the stage of the fruition of Equal Enlightenment and Sublime Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*). The preceding [stage]..."
The ten types of noble ones merely undergo a transformation of their bones and a cleansing of their entrails, becoming purely clear and devoid of a single speck of defilement.

They proceed exclusively in this manner, yet they do not know how to return in this manner. This is what is called "having emerged from the realm of Māra, yet being unable to enter the realm of Māra";
it is termed "leaving behind things and abandoning people. Beyond both good fortune and misfortune, they strike a clean ball and hold a baby who does not cry.
Child, as soon as one reaches the stage of fruition, one not only understands how to go in this way, but also understands how to come back in this way;
one not only succeeds in escaping the realm of Māra, but also succeeds in entering the realm of Māra. Reaching such places as the heavens, the hells, tiger dens, and the palaces of Māra—
Under the moon and before the wind, in brothels and taverns, on mountains of knives and trees of swords—these are all places where one may establish one’s dwelling and sustain one’s life.
Therefore, the Chan school says: "To turn one's body in the realm of demons and shift one's feet upon the path of evil. Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says:
"One attains nirvāṇa without departing from afflictions. And the celestial maiden says: "One does not exit the realm of demons in order to enter the realm of Buddhas. This...
A passage of scripture consisting of ten pairs: first, the pair of consciousness and wisdom; second, the pair of establishment and refutation; third, the pair of ignorance and wisdom;
fourth, the pair of the heterodox and the orthodox; fifth, the pair of the real and the delusive; sixth, the pair of defilement and purity;

seventh, the pair of the dependent and the primary; eighth, the pair of suffering and joy; ninth, the pair of existence and non-existence; tenth, the pair of bondage and liberation. "All obstacles are themselves ultimate enlightenment."

These two lines constitute the general heading; the following ten pairs represent the specific details. This means that upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, wisdom merges with Perfect Enlightenment (yuanjue), and there is no longer a mind that discriminates between superior and inferior.
Therefore, the dharmas of the ten subsequent pairs are all identical in their true nature (zhen-shi yixing).
Furthermore, if one perceives that there are obstacles to be severed, and considers oneself an "enlightened one" (jue) once they have been severed, this enlightenment is not ultimate.

When one reaches the ultimate, there is no longer any obstacle to be seen that could be severed; this very realization is what is called "ultimate completion" (*niṣṭhā*). To "attain mindfulness" is itself wisdom.

This means that during the twelve periods of the day, when right mindfulness manifests before one, the first five consciousnesses then become the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*);
the sixth consciousness becomes the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); and the seventh consciousness becomes the [Wisdom of Equality].
The Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). The eighth *ālayavijñāna* becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Regarding "loss of mindfulness":
if one loses right mindfulness, then the four wisdoms are successively transformed into the eight consciousnesses. Now it is clarified that mindfulness is fundamentally empty by nature;
it is not a state of non-mindfulness, and therefore all are liberated. This refers to the pair of consciousness and wisdom. "Accomplishing the Dharma" means the diligent practice of cultivation.

Furthermore, "to destroy the Dharma" means not to cultivate progress and to ruin the precepts (*vinaya*). It is also said that when the conditions (*pratyaya*) of sentient beings assemble, it is called "formation";
when the conditions disperse, it is called "destruction. Since conditions have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), formation and destruction are one and the same.
This is what is meant by the pair of formation and destruction. "Wisdom" refers to intelligence; "ignorance" refers to folly. As the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* says:
Delusion arises from conceptualization, yet conceptualization itself does not exist. The nature of delusion and the Buddha-nature are equal and without distinction;
this is called the pair of the ignorant and the wise. The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) represent the heterodox, while the Bodhisattvas represent the orthodox.
The *Suyāma-sūtra* states: "One who dwells in the right path does not discriminate between what is wrong and what is right. An ancient said:
"When the single thought-moment of mind does not arise, the six sense faculties are entirely without fault. This refers to the pair of "wrong" and "right. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the delusive dharma;
True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the true dharma. An ancient said: "In delusion, True Suchness is a false thought; in awakening..."
Thus, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is itself *tathatā*. This is what is called the dyad of the true and the false.
The three untainted trainings—precept, concentration, and wisdom—are the pure dharmas. The three delusions of lust, anger, and ignorance are the defiled dharmas.

It is said that the three poisons are fundamentally empty and are all, in themselves, pure practices. The *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Lust is itself the Way; anger and ignorance likewise [are the Way]."
It is so. Within these three matters, there are immeasurable Buddha-dharmas; this is what is called the pair of defilement and purity.
Sentient beings are the primary retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*), while the land is the secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhāna-vipāka*). The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"With my Buddha-eye, I survey all sentient beings and all persons and dharmas within the triple world, and see that they are all ultimately perfected. To be "ultimately perfected" means:
This is precisely the dharma-nature (dharmatā). This is what is meant by "integrating characteristics with nature" (*xing*), whereby all integrated characteristics are nature itself.
This refers to the identity of the environment and its inhabitants (*yi-zheng*). Hell is suffering; the celestial palaces are bliss.

However, when one who has committed the most extreme evil karma approaches [death], although their body remains in a celestial palace, it is in fact hell. Conversely, when one who has performed the most excellent wholesome karma approaches [death]...
Though the body may dwell in hell, it is in fact a celestial palace. Since the perceptions of these two karmic realms arise from the mind, how could hell or a celestial palace be real?
Thus it is said: "The mind can create all Buddhas; the mind can create sentient beings; the mind can create heaven; the mind can create hell.
When the mind differs, a thousand divergences compete to arise; when the mind is equanimous, the Dharma-realm is level and vast.
However, when the mind is ordinary, it is entangled by the three poisons; when the mind is sagely, the six supernormal powers are mastered at will. It is like an echo responding to a sound:
if the voice is bold, the resonance is fierce. It is like a mirror reflecting an image: if the form is curved, the reflection is concave.

Thus we know that the myriad practices arise from the mind; everything depends on oneself. A virtuous cause will ultimately evoke a virtuous condition, while evil conduct makes it difficult to escape the influence of an evil realm. Part one.
If the mind does not arise, there is no fault in the myriad dharmas; this refers to the pair of suffering and pleasure. "Having nature" means possessing the nature of the three vehicles.
"Lacking nature" refers to the icchantika nature, which has never heard the permeation of the teachings.

Viewed through the eye of correctness, it is not only that they will turn their minds in the future; even now they have already equally attained the Buddha-way. This is what is meant by "existence and non-existence."
This is another pair: afflictions are the phenomena of bondage, and liberation is the phenomenon of release.
However, afflictions arise merely upon the nature of consciousness; since the nature of consciousness is itself empty in its very substance, what bondage could afflictions possibly possess?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If someone says, 'I shall attain all-encompassing wisdom,' this is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

If one says, 'I shall sever all afflictions,' this is also conceptual proliferation. Furthermore, the character for "bondage" (*bó*) pertains to the six classes of ordinary beings, while the character for "liberation" (*tuō*) pertains to the four types of noble ones.
Thus, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "The sense faculties and their objects share a common source; [this is] bondage and liberation..."
There is no duality. The nature of consciousness is false and illusory, like flowers in the sky; it is with this same intent. This constitutes the pair of bondage and liberation.
Regarding these ten pairs of names and characteristics above: although their manifestations differ, their underlying meaning is not distinct. Why is this?

It is simply because the Buddha has realized the mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi-citta*); in this mind, there is no longer any superiority or inferiority, nor any grasping or rejecting. For this reason, therefore—
One attains the universal equality and perfect subtlety of all dharmas; each and every one accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), universally fusing without obstruction.
This is why the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks here of the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*śaśva-śaśva-avighnita-dharmadhātu*).
Qingliang said: "The Buddhas and sentient beings penetrate one another; pure lands and defiled lands are interfused. Every dharma encompasses and contains every other, and every atom is likewise."

It encompasses all worlds; their characteristics are identical and mutually inclusive, unimpeded and perfectly interfused, possessing the ten gates of mystery (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*), infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
Master Cong of Siming said: "Good son, that 'all obstacles are ultimate enlightenment' means..."
Ultimate awakening is precisely this. To see the ultimate Buddha, one must see him within all places of obstruction.
Obstructions are ignorance, the karmic consciousness, and the heavy barriers of affliction;

these are what must be seen. This is done by employing the Buddha-eye to see and the Buddha-wisdom to know. As stated in the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra*: "When I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light; you, for a moment..."
When the mind is stirred, the afflictions (*kleśa*) arise first. This clarifies the ultimate Buddha, also called *Myōkaku* (Wondrous Enlightenment).

Tiantai says: "The Way reaches its consummation in Wondrous Enlightenment; the rank is supreme at *Cha* (pronounced *zha*). Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Siming says:

"The path of initial enlightenment (*shijue*) reaches its end, and the principle of original enlightenment (*benjue*) attains its limit. Since the original and the initial have merged, there is no name by which to designate it."

How could one forcibly claim this to be "subtle awakening"? Once subtle clarity has reached ultimate realization, it realizes all phenomena—exhaustively encompassing the ten dharma realms, including the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind, cause and effect, good and evil, the pure and the defiled, sentient beings and Buddhas, the hells and the heavens, the realm of Māras and the realm of Buddhas—all of which enter the ocean of the nature of perfect enlightenment.
This is also called the "interpenetration of all phenomena," and it is also called "entering."

Evil entry and demonic influence are of one suchness, not two suchnesses. Whether mindfulness is attained or lost, there is nothing that is not liberation. Generally speaking, regarding worldly affairs, wherever there is thought, it constitutes an affliction. If one is without thought, one attains it at that very moment within non-thought; even now, one remains within non-thought. Since it is already attained within non-thought, what joy is there in its attainment? Since it is already... [lost] within non-thought, what sorrow is there in its loss? Thus, whether attained or lost, there is neither joy nor sorrow. This is called the Great Matter. It is said: "The mind is originally empty and silent; how could there be gain or loss? Furthermore, as for the various dharmas of the world, they are all like dreams and illusions. If one can awaken to this principle, then even if one were to lose one's life, one would have no regrets. Why? Because the body is originally empty and the mind is originally empty; both are fundamentally non-existent. How could there be anything to lose? Therefore, the sages of old have said: "The body is like a bubble on the water; the mind is like the wind in space. If one understands this, one will have no regrets even when facing death. If one does not understand this, then even if one were to live for ten thousand years, one would still be filled with regret. Therefore, one must practice diligently day and night. Do not wait until you are on your deathbed before you begin to repent. If you wait until you are on your deathbed, it will be too late. At that time, you will be unable to do anything about it. You must practice while you are still alive. If you practice while alive, you will attain peace and ease. If you do not practice while alive, you will suffer pain and distress. If one is without thought, there is loss; if there is loss, what cause for anxiety? Since one is already without thought, what joy or anxiety can there be?
Once that thought is absent, how can there be gain or loss? It is simply that the liberated one is one whose mind has severed all discursive thinking.
Since discursive thinking is severed, are not gain and loss themselves liberation? That both established phenomena and destroyed phenomena are called *nirvāṇa*—established phenomena...
Birth is the arising of phenomena; extinction is their cessation. "Nir" signifies non-arising; "vāṇa" signifies non-extinction.
All dharmas arise through causes and conditions, and they likewise cease through causes and conditions. Without conditions, they do not arise; without causes, they do not cease.
They arise because of conditions and cease because of conditions. One must reach the state of quiescent extinction as the place of bliss; then, [there is no more birth].
Birth is non-extinguishing. As for "wisdom and folly together constitute *prajñā*":
"together constitute" means that folly is turbid water, while *prajñā* is clear water. Although clarity and turbidity differ, their moist nature is fundamentally the same.
The moist nature of *prajñā* pervades the moist nature of folly. Laozi also said: "The greatest eloquence seems like stammering; the greatest skill seems like clumsiness."

The dharmas accomplished by Bodhisattvas and those of the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika) are identical. "Bodhi" is the Bodhisattva’s reversal of the "path" (mārga); the outsiders also speak of a "path.
These two instances of the word "path" differ only in being heterodox versus orthodox. The path of the Bodhisattva is orthodox, yet the orthodox is itself heterodox;
the path of the outsider is heterodox, yet the heterodox is itself orthodox. How far apart are the Buddha and Māra?
What? Between the heterodox and the orthodox, what deficiency or surplus exists? To be identical is for the heterodox and the orthodox to return to one.
When ignorance and truth are such that there is no distinct realm between them, it is like Yajñadatta (Yan’er-da-duo) in the early morning looking at his face in a mirror;

When it subsides, that is *bodhi*. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the nature of madness; True Suchness (*tathatā*) is *bodhi*. If ignorance subsides, that very subsiding is the realm of True Suchness.
This refers to the realm right before one's eyes: there is nothing that is not True Suchness, and nothing that is not ignorance. There is no distinct realm."

This is the realm (*dhātu*). All precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as lust, anger, and ignorance, are together the practice of purity (*brahmacarya*). Precepts, concentration, and wisdom are purity;

There is nothing that is not the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*). To employ one's passions in worldly affairs is a matter of such gravity that good and evil cannot be discussed on the same day.

That "sentient beings and their lands share the same *dharmatā*" refers to the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*). Sentient beings are the primary retribution—the human body. The land is what humans rely upon—the mountains, rivers, houses, dwellings, and so forth.
When one ultimately reaches the home of realization, the environment (*niśraya*) is itself the primary reality (*adhiṣṭhāna*); the primary reality is itself the environment.
This is precisely what is meant by "relying on the basis" (依), where the basis and its manifestations do not obstruct one another, and matter and mind are without hindrance.

Regarding hell: if discussed in terms of its phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), it differs from heaven as much as the sky differs from the earth; yet if one investigates it through principle (*li*), it does not transcend the creation of a single thought-moment of a human being.
As the ancients said: "The gates of heaven and hell face each other; they reside solely within a single thought-moment of the human mind.
Pure Land (*śuddha-kṣetra*) is likewise nothing but the single thought-moment of a person. When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. Jingxi said: "Avīci..."
The entirety of the environment and its inhabitants is the self-mind of the Ultimate Sage. The body and land of Vairocana do not transcend the single thought-moment of the lowest commoner.

When the son who favored the left foot emerged, the son who favored the right foot would then use a sharp blade to stab his father’s left foot;
when the son who favored the right foot emerged, the son who favored the left foot did the same. These two sons were unaware that both the left and right feet belonged to their father as one.
This is the essence. Now, it is the same for the disciples of the Buddha. They do not realize that Chan is the Buddha’s mind and the teachings are the Buddha’s words.

The primary retribution—the dharmas of the mundane and supramundane worlds, and the eighty-four thousand dharani-gates—are all utterly pure.
This white ox in the open field reaches this realm of the ten pairs, where they blend and merge into a single unity; this is precisely the final black ox.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "The ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm illuminates and comprehends all phenomena, being like empty space.

"Realization" is also called "conformity. This is stated provisionally by way of the six [perfections]. If one speaks in terms of the word "immediacy" (ji), then it is this very thing.
Since all dharmas are none other than this, how could there be anything that either conforms or does not conform?
Good son, it is only when Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age abide at all times without giving rise to deluded thoughts that they truly do not give rise to deluded thoughts;
to not give rise to deluded thoughts means to not give rise to any thoughts whatsoever.
Regarding these deluded minds, one does not seek to extinguish them;
for the deluded mind is itself the true mind, and there is no need to seek its cessation.
One dwells within the realm of false thoughts without applying further analytical cognition.

Section. It is said that at all times one does not give rise to deluded thoughts; this is the first section. One also does not suppress or extinguish the various deluded minds;

Truly so. To such an extent that whether lifting or setting down the foot, there is no difference from the path of birds; sitting, reclining, walking, or standing—none of these are not the profound Way.

O Assembly, if you hear this dharma-gate of skillful means and your minds are free from doubt and confusion, and you realize, receive, and uphold it with full understanding,

There are also those who cultivate perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi), constantly using tranquil illumination to observe these deluded thoughts.

They realize that these are merely the nature of awakening (bodhi-svabhāva) arising spontaneously; thus, they do not need to be extinguished. If they were to be extinguished, [the nature of awakening would be lost].

Then there would be no Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi). To seek water by removing the ice is of no benefit to the search. Although one dwells within this delusion, this delusion is itself Perfect Enlightenment;
it does not belong to thought, nor does it belong to creation. It does not depend on cultivation or realization, for it is inherently possessed by its own nature.
If one were to perceive it in the realm of thought, that would constitute a conscious act of knowing (*jñāna*). Now, it is said that one does not apply conscious knowing, and it does not reside—
Cultivate this; you must understand that the more deluded thoughts there are, the greater the nature of awakening becomes. This is because as the water rises, the boat rises with it.
Although, as mentioned above, the true and the deluded share the same substance, one must nevertheless refrain from discriminating between the real and the unreal within the state of non-cognition.

"Under billions of Buddhas, they planted various roots of goodness. This means that by attaining hearing, faith, and understanding in this present life, one verifies the reason why roots of goodness were planted in past kalpas.

Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "This seal is the wisdom of Buddhahood. Furthermore, this wisdom has three aspects:

Sentient beings act to resolve obstructions, yet Bodhisattvas have not yet transcended conceptualization.
