In the chapter on the Bodhisattva Majestic Virtue and Sovereignty, Chan Master Fu’an Huī of Xichu said: "The first section, the Chapter on Mañjuśrī, provides an opening for understanding for people of the three capacities—superior, middling, and inferior.
The second section, the Chapter on Samantabhadra, likewise provides an opening for understanding for people of the three capacities—superior, middling, and inferior."

This person initiates the practice. The third chapter, "The Universal Eye," relies upon Mañjuśrī’s exposition and Samantabhadra’s conduct to enter the contemplation of the two emptinesses, while also following the cultivation of the Dharmadhātu Contemplation.

Since doubt arises only once one has entered this contemplation, there is the fourth chapter, "Vajragarbha," which raises three doubts and poses questions to the Buddha; having such doubts, one must necessarily investigate them.
To investigate the root of saṃsāra, there is the fifth chapter, "Maitreya," which concerns the inquiry into severing the root of saṃsāra.

The Buddha instructs that one must sever the mind of craving and attachment. Once craving and attachment have been severed, the practitioner reaches a state where both conduct and realization are complete, and there will necessarily be realization.
Therefore, there is the sixth chapter, "Pure Wisdom. [Thus] they are arranged.
Generally, regarding the stages and gradations of the fruits of the sages and worthies, these are established to guide the practitioner from the mundane state into the state of sagehood.

Thus it is said: through understanding one gives rise to practice; through practice one enters contemplation; through contemplation one gives rise to doubt; through doubt there is severance; and through severance there is realization. Question:

When a practitioner enters the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*) within the "Universal Eye" chapter, they realize and enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) and attain Buddhahood.
"No," he replied. "He has attained Buddhahood. Again, an objection was raised:

"If he has already entered the contemplation of the two emptinesses and thus attained Buddhahood, why is there still the doubt of Vajragarbha, the craving of Maitreya, and the stages of the chapter on Viśuddhamati?"
Answer: Because they are divided into the subject and the object. Specifically, the chapter on "The Universal Eye" refers to the practitioner’s wisdom that performs the contemplation.
The two chapters concerning Vajragarbha and Maitreya both refer to the afflictions to be severed within the practitioner’s contemplation.

The chapter on "Pure Wisdom" likewise refers to the stages of realization attained within the practitioner’s contemplation. Thus, it should be understood that these three chapters of the scripture [function in this manner].
All of these are the stages of illness to be eliminated within contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Once the illnesses are exhausted, one attains Buddhahood solely within contemplation;
apart from contemplation, there are no other separate scriptural passages. Furthermore, it may be objected:

"If these are scriptures for eliminating the stages of illness within contemplation, why are they instead proclaimed after contemplation? The answer is that this refers to the fact that the words were not uttered simultaneously; such is the text.
I have not written further letters, for the underlying principle is not revealed all at once; that is why it follows later.
As for the present "Chapter on Majestic Virtue," it is because the World-Honored One extensively expounded skillful means to teach the Dharma and deliver sentient beings.

There may be a class of individuals with superior faculties who, within the preceding six chapters of the sutra, heard the Buddha’s exposition of the characteristics of the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness and the severing of craving—the root of saṃsāra.
The fundamental text and its demonstration of the stages and levels of realization and entry caused everyone to leap with joy at once;
they awakened to the ground of the mind and entered into Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), just as a fine horse from the stable moves at the mere sight of the shadow of a whip.

Within this interval, there is yet another class of individuals with middling faculties who, upon hearing the Buddha thus provide such expositions and such instructions on the gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*),
thus dispel their doubts, and thus demonstrate the stages of realization within the six-chapter sutra,

are nevertheless unable to enter the contemplations of the two kinds of emptiness and so forth due to their inferior faculties; they cling to the coarse, just as one might [cling to] a great treasure.

[They] were buried within the dust and soil. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue (Vaiśravaṇa), grieved for those lost in delusion and sought to rescue those who had gone astray, extending his grace downward to the various quarters.
For this reason, he subsequently arose to inquire: "World-Honored One, by what skillful means do you rescue those of middling faculties? Thus, there is this chapter of the sutra.
Furthermore, it is said that this separately clarifies the practitioner of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). This [section] is distinct...
The character "this" (zhi) is named in contrast to the preceding general illumination of contemplative practice (*guanxing*). This has two meanings:

first, because a certain class of individuals with superior faculties have already completed their entry by relying on the two gates of emptiness contemplation previously mentioned, they no longer require the cultivation of the various wheels of the three contemplations;
thus, it is called "distinct" (*bie*). Second, these various wheels of the three contemplations are each individually distinct.
As for the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*): either a single person may practice all three together, or they may practice only one, or two;

through these combinations—whether simple or interwoven—they form twenty-five cycles (*pañcaviṃśati-cakra*). These are designated as "distinct" because they are intended for twenty-five types of individuals.
Within this, the first two chapters of the sutra concern the practice of the three contemplations, while the latter two chapters concern two [contemplations].

The second section, "Eliminating Obstacles," is followed by the present "Chapter on Majestic Virtue," which precisely elucidates the characteristics of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
Master Cong of the Fourth Ming Temple stated: "The essence of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is quiescent; because its source is primordial stillness, it is termed *śamatha*.

Fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is an empty illumination; because it is eternally luminous, it is called *vipaśyanā*. When the winds of delusion suddenly stir, one employs the sublime *śamatha* to bring them to rest."
The jewel of the mind has long been obscured; it must be contemplated through *vipaśyanā*. Therefore, the teachings established by the Sages are not of a single form:

there is sometimes *śamatha* (calm abiding), sometimes *vipaśyanā* (insight), sometimes the "object of truth," and sometimes "calm abiding and insight. As the ailments are manifold, the remedies likewise vary accordingly.
Following his majestic virtue and conforming to the nature of awakening, he received the Buddha’s perfect voice and inaugurated the heroic regulations of the Three Contemplations.
Because it guides one along the correct path through the four gates, it possesses the meaning of [the term] "gate" (*mukha*).
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and paid homage.

"The Chan Master Huí of Fù'ān in Western Shǔ said: 'Regarding the term "majestic virtue" (wēidé), there are two meanings.

First, it is explained in terms of phenomena; second, it is explained in terms of principle. As for the explanation in terms of phenomena: it is like a person who possesses majesty, such that those below stand in awe.'"
Because he possesses virtue, those below are made to admire him. Furthermore, regarding the explanation of principle: the character "awe-inspiring" (*wei*) is like the Way and like virtue.

Indeed, awe-inspiring power is the essential virtue of Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*), and it is the function of Perfect Enlightenment. How do we know this? As the Preface to the *Huayan fajie guan* states:
"How profound is the delusion of sentient beings! Their bodies are, on the contrary, within their own minds, just as the great ocean [is within a bubble]."
It is but a single bubble. Yet one is unaware that within it lies vast majestic power (*mahā-tejas*) which remains unused.
Furthermore, as the *Daode jing* says: "If the people do not fear small terrors, then great terror will arrive. The commentary explains: "Small terrors" refer to birth and death;
"great terror" refers to the essence of the Way (*tattva*). Through this gate, the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are perfected, and their efficacy becomes fierce and sharp.
Demons cannot disturb them; delusions cannot invade them. Thus, it represents the Bodhisattva attaining great mastery within the essence and function of Perfect Enlightenment.
Therefore, it is called "majestic virtue."
The World-Honored One of Great Compassion has extensively distinguished for our sake this awakening-nature in accordance with it.
The Bodhisattva praised the Buddha, as well-spoken in the preceding chapter, regarding how ordinary beings, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas alike accord with this awakening-nature.
It causes all bodhisattvas to awaken to the luminosity of the mind. By receiving the Buddha’s perfect voice, they obtain excellent benefit without depending on cultivation;
upon hearing the Buddha’s proclamation, their minds immediately open to awakening, attaining benefit beforehand without waiting for practice.

Master Furan of Xishu said: "To explain this extensively for us:

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "It is like when I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal emits light.

It is called "perfect" because this is the Buddha’s teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun) sound. It does not depend on...

How much more so for those who practice it with diligence!
This is what is meant by bypassing the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*) and ascending directly to the "Jeweled Abode" (*ratna-sthāna*). As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says:
The madness of dharmas suddenly ceases; this cessation is itself bodhi—supreme, pure, wondrous, and luminous. It is not obtained from others;
why rely on arduous toil or laborious cultivation and realization?
World-Honored One, it is like a great city.

this is the instruction on the gate of all conditioned phenomena.

People from the east, west, south, and north each enter through their own gate; how could it be limited to but one path?
This is surely a metaphor for those who awaken to and enter Perfect Enlightenment (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra): it is not by means of but a single method.
All Bodhisattvas employ more than one expedient means to adorn Buddha-lands and realize Bodhi;
the Dharma-gates of expedient means for adorning the stage of Buddhahood and perfecting Awakened Enlightenment are not limited to a single method.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively expound for us all the expedient means and gradual stages.
We beseech the Buddha to proclaim all the gateways of practice,
as well as how many types of practitioners there are in total.
Furthermore, he requested the Buddha to speak on the various practices for cultivators,
so that the bodhisattvas in this assembly and those seeking the Great Vehicle in the final age may swiftly attain awakening and sport within the Tathāgata’s great ocean of tranquil extinction.
"The path to nirvāṇa is vast, profound, and subtle; therefore, it is likened to the ocean.

Their inclinations and desires are not the same; yet, although the entry points through the four gates differ, they are without distinction at the moment of the vision of the One True Reality.
This is like a bird-catcher who uses a net with a single opening—one cannot call a single opening a "net.

Master Cong of Siming said: "The True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is a single dharma, yet the Buddha speaks of it under various names.

To speak now of 'four' is merely to state it briefly. As for the four gates: the gate of emptiness, the gate of existence, the gate of both emptiness and existence, and the gate of neither [emptiness nor existence].
The Gate of Emptiness as Non-Existence: During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were four non-Buddhist practitioners who said, "By making offerings to the Buddha, one gains merit and is reborn in heaven;
I only wish to be reborn in heaven and do not seek to realize arhatship.

One man went first to make offerings to the Buddha and was about to depart when the Buddha said, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent. This man covered his ears and fled. The second man acted in the same manner.
The first man wished to leave. The Buddha said, "This is a phenomenon of arising and ceasing. He covered his ears and ran away. The third man did likewise.
As he was about to depart, the Buddha said, "When arising and ceasing have ceased," and he covered his ears and ran away. The fourth man did the same.

When he had finished making offerings and wished to leave, the Buddha said, "Nirvana (the cessation of all phenomena) is bliss. Again, he hurriedly covered his ears and ran away. Thus it was with the four men.
After they had departed, they gathered together in one place and asked one another, "How did you perceive the Buddha?

One person said, "The Buddha taught that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Another said, "They are subject to arising and ceasing. Another said, "When arising and ceasing have ceased," and another said, "Cessation is bliss.

Having heard this single verse together, all four attained the realization of Arhatship. That single verse was: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; This is the law of arising and ceasing. When arising and ceasing have ceased, Cessation is bliss."
Perfect Enlightenment: These four lines constitute four gates; enter through whichever one suits you.
As for what is called "expedient means" (*upāya*), it refers to the gradual methods established by the sages, which are not limited to a single form. There is a gradual sequence in realization;

since spiritual capacities (*indriya*) differ, the practices cultivated are distinct, and the levels of depth and attainment vary according to their respective stages. The great ocean of quiescent extinction is like pounding ten thousand kinds [of grain].

Incense is made into pellets; when one pellet is burned, it possesses all fragrances. Just as the myriad streams flow into the ocean and become of one salty taste, so too is the ocean-like assembly of Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue, saying: "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you..."
"Only those such as you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such skillful means for the sake of all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age.

Listen attentively now; I shall explain it for you. At that time, the Bodhisattva Sovereign of Majestic Virtue, having received these instructions, rejoiced, and together with the great assembly, listened in silence.
"Good son, the unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment pervades the ten directions and gives rise to..."
The Tathāgata’s nature of supreme, wondrous enlightenment is vast, encompassing the great void; therefore, it is said to pervade all ten directions.
When sentient beings awaken to this wondrous nature, they realize the Buddha-body; therefore, it is said that they give birth to the Tathāgata.
It is of one essence and equal with all phenomena.
Having realized the Buddha-body, there is neither defilement nor purity, neither ordinary being nor sage.
Among all practices, in reality, there is no duality.
For all practitioners, in reality there are no two dharmas.

Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "To accord with one's nature is to mark the root and the branch. The unsurpassed, wondrous enlightenment is entirely to the east when in the east, and entirely to the west when in the west;
it is the same for the south, north, above, and below. This is what is called the sixfold penetration and the fourfold opening."
Whether it be chaff, husks, tiles, or rubble; whether small or large, refined or coarse—its operation is present everywhere. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"The Dharma-nature pervades all places: all sentient beings and all lands throughout the three periods of time exist therein without exception, yet it has no form or characteristic that can be apprehended.
Furthermore, it is upon the fruition of all Buddhas that this title is attained.

As for the Tathāgatas: it is because on the causal ground they all cultivated this wondrous enlightenment together, they all realized this wondrous enlightenment together, and they all emerged from this wondrous enlightenment.

Not only do all Tathāgatas emerge from this, but even the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements, as well as the external mountains, rivers, and great earth, form and emptiness, light and darkness—all [emerge from it].
Many things—great and small, ordinary and holy, defiled and pure, mind and objects—all such various phenomena likewise emerge entirely from this wondrous enlightenment.
How do we know this? Consider, for instance, when all sentient beings open their eyes wide during the twelve periods of the day and see:
tell me, for whom is the sky high, for whom is the earth thick, and for whom are the mountains green and the waters blue?
For whose sake is there green? For whose sake is there warmth in spring, heat in summer, coolness in autumn, and cold in winter?
Zhuangzi asked: "Who presides over this? Who sustains this? Who dwells in non-action yet experiences this joy?
By inferring from this, one sees that all phenomena arise entirely from within one's own segment of radiant light.
It is manifested that one’s own nature and the nature of the Tathāgata are of one and the same true essence, equal and non-dual, without division, distinction, or interruption.
Therefore, if all bodhisattvas initiate practice and cultivation within this very context, [they shall attain realization].
There are no two paths; both are the cultivation of the aforementioned two gates of emptiness-contemplation. Within this contemplation, one inevitably shatters doubts and severs attachments;
the faculties and their objects are universally purified; compassion and wisdom are practiced together; one is detached from both objects and mind; there is neither subject nor object.
All Buddhas of the past and future cultivate in this very way—how could there be two distinct dharmas?
The skillful means that accord with these are immeasurable in number.
Through the cultivation of these means, there are many approaches;
yet, when fully encompassing their ultimate destination according to the distinctions of their respective natures, they shall be of three kinds.
The circular encompassment is gathered back into the single nature. According to the distinctions within that nature, there are *śamatha*, *samāpatti*, and *dhyāna*.
Master Huì of Fù'ān in Xīqū said: "This enumerates the practices according to the capacities of beings. If..."

According to the Buddha’s teaching, all the dharma-gates of the teachings throughout his entire lifetime were expedient means employed to treat the ailments of beings according to their specific capacities;
their number is naturally immeasurable and boundless, making them difficult to exhaustively fathom. For now, they shall be subsumed within a comprehensive synthesis.
Following the dispositions of sentient beings within this context, there are three distinct types of differences.
This is because the faculties of sentient beings vary in being sharp or dull, and their afflictions differ in being thick or thin, heavy or agitated.
Accordingly, the teachings established are manifold. If it were not so, it would be difficult for them to enter [the path]. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra*...
It is said: "What has been taught is not what is appropriate; for them, it is not a teaching.

Just as a skilled physician prescribes different remedies for various individual patients, so too, although the natures of sentient beings of middling capacity here differ in ten thousand ways, they are all simultaneously encompassed within the three gates of stillness, illusion, and quiescence.
The lecturer Mingcong of Siming said: "Supreme" refers to the Buddha, who is supreme among all sentient beings. "Wondrous Enlightenment" (Miaojue) is the ultimate of realization.

It may also be said that "enlightenment" (jue) means illumination; illumination is precisely contemplation (*guan*), which is the very threefold contemplation (*sanguan*) currently being demonstrated.

"Wondrous" means that emptiness is itself the provisional and the middle, the provisional is itself emptiness and the middle, and the middle is itself emptiness and the provisional—this is the threefold contemplation.
They are mutually integrated; therefore, they are termed "wondrous. This is how the wondrous *śamatha* in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is also explained.
Now, what follows below correctly elucidates the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*); it must necessarily be so.

That which pervades the ten directions is the awakened nature, which is also called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), also called "suchness" (*tathatā*), and also called the "empty Tathāgatagarbha. All Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions rely upon it.

These three give rise [to realization]. "Giving rise" means cultivation and realization. One cultivates and realizes them by relying on the wondrous principle of Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahā-vajra-bodhi*);

one does not cultivate them by relying on the contemplation of the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) of wondrous enlightenment. If one does not rely on this, the life-root of the karma-consciousness of ignorance, such as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), will not be severed.
As stated in the *Xingfǎ yún*: "The Buddhas of the ten directions arise from the Vaipulya; it is not merely a matter of cultivation."

One attains Buddhahood by relying on this; yet it is also by relying on this delusion that one enters into birth and death. Although there is a distinction between the sentient being and the Buddha, the wondrous principle is equal.

There is only the difference between delusion and awakening; it is not that the Buddha-nature itself possesses awakening or delusion, but rather that the sentient being and the Buddha themselves possess awakening and delusion.

Since the sentient being and the Buddha are of one suchness, they are said to be non-dual. If one is deluded regarding perfect enlightenment, one follows the distinctions of nature. How [can one attain it]?

This concludes the hundred points. Now, I shall speak of those who cultivate the three contemplations of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun). Therefore, it is said that the Perfect [Vehicle] subsumes all that is returned to its source by dividing it into three types.
"Good son, if bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment..."
Master Huì of Fù’ān in Western Shū said: "The following is the orthodox section on the three contemplations.

First, regarding the 'Contemplation of Stillness of the Spirit through the Dissolution of Phenomena,' this first part establishes the fundamental basis. This refers to what was explained in the preceding scripture:
that those who wish to enter this contemplation must first realize the inherently existing, numinous, and perfectly enlightened nature within their own being."
With a mind of pure awakening, one takes purity as one's practice.
Having realized that perfect awakening is fundamentally pure, one should then single-mindedly take stillness as the dharma-practice with this very mind.
By clarifying all thoughts, one awakens to the restless agitation of consciousness;
through this, one attains stillness. Because all mental preoccupations are clarified, the pure consciousness manifests.
Master Huì of Fù’ān in Western Shǔ said: "This precisely explains the arousal of practice. Above, one awakens to the pure *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) nature."
"Understanding" refers to liberation (*vimukti*). This taking of stillness as practice with a pure awakened mind (*bodhicitta*) refers to cultivation (*caryā*).

To have understanding without cultivation is like having eyes but no feet; to have cultivation without understanding is like having feet but no eyes. A single wheel or a solitary wing cannot fly or move.
Since one has already realized the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*), this is the root of cultivation; one must necessarily rely on understanding to practice. Thus...
This constitutes sublime practice (*sucarita*). It is like the mutual dependence of oil and light, or the complementary support of the eyes and feet.
My intention is that one takes the realization of the pure, fundamental awakening of the true mind as the basis. Throughout the twelve periods of the day, one exclusively pursues stillness;
in silence, one performs the practices to be undertaken. As Zen says: "A single thought lasts ten thousand years," "Like an incense burner in an ancient temple," "Like cold ashes and withered wood."
The wood is gone; a single length of white silk is gone. Therefore, Bodhidharma said: "Externally cease all conditions; internally let the mind be free from panting.
Let the mind be like a wall, and you may enter the Way. Furthermore, the *Pao-tsang lun* says: "As for the path to entering the Way..."
The interior is empty and the exterior is still; like water that is clear and congealed, the myriad phenomena reflect their light. The intention does not sink, the mind does not float;
there is no exiting or entering, but a profound stillness, remaining as it is. This is the swift path home and the divine remedy for curing illness.
Hitherto, throughout the twelve periods of the day, you have consistently employed a moving mind; this moving mind is consciousness (*vijñāna*). For this reason, you did not perceive consciousness.
Now, because of this clarity, various攀緣 (*pān-yuán*, objective attachments) and deluded thoughts have ceased; as soon as the mind becomes still, [consciousness is revealed].
Quiescence is itself wisdom. For this reason, one only then realizes that throughout immeasurable kalpas, the discriminative karmic consciousness has continued—
prior thought following upon subsequent thought, and subsequent thought following upon prior thought— in such restless agitation that it has never for even a moment truly abided.
Quiescent wisdom arises.
Because wisdom is born from quiescence, it is called "quiescent wisdom. That which was formerly obscured is now manifest; hence it is said to "arise.
The adventitious defilements of body and mind are forever extinguished from this point onward.
They do not possess an inherent nature; therefore, they are called "adventitious dust. Since these characteristics are forever absent, they are called "eternally extinguished.
One is then able to inwardly give rise to tranquility and pliancy.
"Inwardly arising" means it is not obtained from without. "Tranquility and pliancy" refers to the ultimate stillness and quietude, free from all burdens.
There is no affliction.
Master Huì of Fù’ān in Xīshǔ said: "This is the completion of the practice.

Previously, by means of stilling all deluded thoughts, one first realizes that the discerning consciousness (*vijñāna*) is vexed, agitated, and restless, never ceasing. From this realization, awakening arises.
Go! As soon as the conscious mind becomes still, one arrives at the state of ultimate stillness. When stillness reaches its peak, wondrous wisdom spontaneously arises.
Once this wondrous wisdom has arisen, the false dharmas of the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses are thoroughly penetrated.
Thus it is said: "When stillness reaches its peak, light penetrates through; in silent illumination, all of space is contained. Returning then to observe the world, it is as if...
Like events in a dream, these eighteen realms are not the true master. They are like travelers whose coming and going are unsettled; were they the master, there would be no such wandering.
"Dust" (rajas) takes the meaning of defilement and pollution. Now that tranquil wisdom has arisen, they are all simultaneously captured and defeated;
therefore, it is said they are "permanently extinguished. To be "extinguished" means non-existence. It is like the light of dawn.
Upon returning, one expresses gratitude in silence. When wisdom arises, delusions are forgotten, and one is able to inwardly give rise to stillness, clarity, and emptiness;

lightness and ease prevail in harmony. This is the gateway to awakening found within stillness. Like the hexagram Qian, which is firm, vigorous, central, and correct, it can ward off evil and subdue demons.
Like the perfect enlightenment of tranquil illumination and light ease, it allows one to preserve the mind and enter the Way. Truly, this is not in vain.
Because of tranquility, the minds of all Tathāgatas in the worlds of the ten directions appear therein, like reflections in a mirror.
Because of this tranquility, emptiness is limpid; the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions are all likewise.

Therefore, it is metaphorically said that they appear therein, like reflections in a mirror. This means that when the mirror is pure, the reflection appears; when the mind is pure, [the Buddhas appear].
This is because the Buddha manifests himself.
Chan Master Fu’an Huī of Xishu said: "This is a response to conditions (saṃgēn). It arises precisely because of the state of profound stillness, whereby wondrous wisdom is brought forth;

It manifests within the mind of the practitioner, clearly visible and distinct, like an image reflected in a mirror.
