Master Huì of Fù'ān in Xīshǔ replied: "This is a request for the Dharma. These 'various skillful means' refers to—"

"The first three contemplations" refers, in relation to Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), to the fundamental basis for practice—the nature of awakened awareness (*bodhicitta*)—upon which one relies for realization.

"There are several methods of cultivation" means that, as previously shown in the "Chapter on Majestic Virtue," one has received the Buddha’s instruction regarding the specific characteristics of these three contemplations.

I clearly understand all this already, yet I have not yet fully ascertained whether the practices cultivated by the various bodhisattvas are such that a single person cultivates all three contemplations together, or whether they are three distinct persons each cultivating one contemplation; furthermore, are these practiced sequentially or simultaneously?
Are they practiced simultaneously? Are they practiced non-simultaneously? Are they practiced according to a sequence? Or are they practiced by skipping over the sequence?

Thus it is asked: "How many modes of cultivation are there? The intent of the question is to inquire how the three contemplations within the "Chapter on Majestic Power" (Vīrya-paṭala) are to be cultivated.

I pray that you will, for the sake of the great assembly and sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age, skillfully provide an exposition so that they may awaken to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the empty nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*); because it is devoid of all marks, it is called the "true mark."
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again from the end after each repetition.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Viśvabhāṣin, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!

That you are able, for the sake of the great assembly and for sentient beings of the final age, to question the Tathāgata regarding such cultivation—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you."
When you said this, the Bodhisattva Vibhūṣaṇasvara, together with the great assembly, joyfully accepted the instruction and listened in silence.

Master Huì of Fù’ān in Xīshǔ said: "Because it is the mark of no-mark, it is called the 'True Mark' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Its essential substance is none other than Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*)."
"Good son, all Tathāgatas are perfectly awakened and pure; fundamentally, there is neither the practice nor the practitioner.
The original nature of all Buddhas is perfectly awakened and pure; in reality, there is no dharma to be cultivated, nor is there any person who can cultivate."
All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age rely upon the power of illusion while remaining unawakened;
because they have not yet attained awakening, they employ these various illusory powers to cultivate Perfect Enlightenment.
At that time, there were twenty-five kinds of pure wheels of samādhi.
These twenty-five wheels consist of the three contemplations of śamatha, samāpatti, and dhyāna.
They may be practiced individually, combined, sequentially, finally, in pairs, or in a complete cycle; in total, they comprise—
These are the twenty-five names. As for the term "Pure Wheel of Samādhi," it is because the nature of awakening is untainted, capable of transforming all phenomena and crushing all illusions.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "This response indicates the number according to the intention of Wenju.
'All Tathāgatas' refers to the Buddhas of the three periods of time and the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Upon the vast, luminous, perfectly enlightened, and pure essence, there is fundamentally no dharma to be cultivated, nor is there any person who can cultivate. Since this is so..."
If there is no cultivation or realization, why do the various teachings state that all bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age possess both cultivation and realization?

This is truly because, upon the basis of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*), a single thought of non-enlightenment arises, whereby one becomes deluded regarding the truth and turns one's back on the profound stillness.

The essence of the funeral rite receives the wheel of Dharma. Because that which is taught by all Buddhas relies solely upon fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), it is said that there is the power of illusion through cultivation;
thus, there is cultivation and realization. This cultivation, being adapted to the capacities of sentient beings, consists of twenty-five kinds of pure wheels of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
A "wheel" carries the meaning of crushing and grinding, signifying its ability to crush the obstacles of afflictions and bring about correctness.
Because wisdom revolves, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*). Regarding the so-called "twenty-five wheels": first, one practices the three contemplations individually;
next, one practices the twenty-one wheels (seven sets of three) in an interlaced manner; finally, one practices the last wheel by perfecting all three contemplations.

In Master Miaoxu’s commentary (*Sū*), he establishes a distinct name for each of the twenty-five contemplations based on metaphors; however, in Master Guifeng’s commentary (*Sū*), [he does not do so].
It employs the entire [text] to manage the scriptural passages, ensuring that the characteristics of their practice are clearly manifest.

Master Cong of Siming said: "In this regard, when Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva reaches the end and begins again, it is because Avalokiteśvara, having heard the meaning of the three contemplations as asked by Śrīmahādevī, explained them solely in terms of the three types of spiritual capacities (indriya). Thus did the World-Honored One open [the teaching].
This is shown; it is also spoken according to what is asked. If one discusses capacities, there are levels of depth, and faculties may be sharp or dull—how could they be limited to only three?
Therefore, when Bhadrapāla asked again about how many kinds of cultivation there are, at that time the World-Honored One spoke of "the wheel of the pure meditative concentration.
If one discusses the nature of awakening, it is fundamentally and inherently perfect and harmonious; all Tathāgatas cultivate and manifest it.
The principle of pure, ultimate perfection has no high or low; there is neither cultivation nor a cultivator, as both subject and object are transcended.
The Buddha does not "save" sentient beings. Yet, out of the profound gravity of the Great Sage’s compassion, he observes that the minds of sentient beings all possess the *tathāgatagarbha* nature;

because they have been submerged [in delusion] for a long time, he specifically opens the gate of skillful means to reveal the nature of perfect enlightenment. Thus, it is said in the *Nirgrantha Sūtra*:

It is said: There was a king named Ugratejas. A great bodhisattva prevented [the Buddha] from entering his kingdom. The king went out to welcome him from afar, whereupon the bodhisattva spoke for the king’s sake:
"Great King, you should know that one contemplates the body of the Tathāgata by relying upon the body of afflictions.
Why is this? Because this very body is the *tathāgatagarbha*. Within the treasury of all the defilements of affliction, the buddha-nature is fully present."

It is like jade within stone, fire within wood, water within the earth, curd within milk, oil within sesame seeds, grain within the husk, gold within a treasury, an image within a mold, a fetus within the womb, and the sun within the clouds.
Therefore, I say that the Tathāgatagarbha exists within afflictions.
Now, through skillful means, the Buddha desires to reveal to sentient beings their various inherent natures and extensively open them up.
They are immeasurable. Now, abiding in the middle, I shall briefly demonstrate twenty-five types of single cultivation, combined cultivation, and complete cultivation.

As for the practices themselves, they do not exceed three; they simply do not go beyond these three. These are the three [types of] cessation, the three [types of] contemplation, and the three objects.

Depending on whether the faculties are sharp or dull, and whether the contemplations are shallow or deep, there may be one, two, or three wheels that interlace with one another. If one follows the three [methods] of the Lord of Heaven...

The Eyes. Like the three dots of the Brahmi syllable *i*, I shall first set forth the similarities and differences between the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*);

subsequently, all will be easy to understand. There are two kinds of cessation: Great Cessation and Small Cessation. Regarding the three types of Small Cessation: first, cessation as quiescence, so named because it overcomes delusions;
second, cessation as stabilization, so named because it is capable of concentration; third, cessation as non-cessation, so named from the perspective of the principle of reality (*tattva*).

This is so named because it appears in the sūtras of the Hīnayāna. Regarding the "Three Great Calm-abidings" (*samatha*): these three names were established by the Tiantai master Zhiyi based on the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).
First is "Calm-abiding in the True Nature," which destroys the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) and realizes the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Second is "Calm-abiding that Follows Conditions through Expedient Means," which destroys the delusions of the sands of the Ganges (*rajas-kleśa*) and realizes the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Third is "Calm-abiding that Quells Discrimination of the Two Extremes."
Cease. To shatter the delusion of ignorance and realize the principle of the Middle Way, *śamatha* is the essential "True Cessation.
It stabilizes the mind and settles it within the principle; this is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). *Samāpatti* is the "Cessation that Adapts to Conditions through Expedient Means.

Although it is termed a state of concentration (*samādhi*), its essence belongs to the category of wisdom (*prajñā*). When Bodhisattvas emerge from the provisional to transform sentient beings, they employ the method of contemplation; this also reverses [the previous state].

"Contemplation" (*guan*) also translates the meaning of "wisdom" (*prajñā*), and it likewise returns to the principle of "calm abiding" (*śamatha*). *Dhyāna* (meditative concentration) is the cessation of the dualistic discrimination of the two extremes;

*dhyāna* translates as "tranquil reflection. "Tranquility" (*jing*) refers to the cessation within emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while "reflection" (*shu*) refers to the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*).

When emptiness and the provisional are non-dual, their cultivation is termed the "Middle Way. These three contemplations—emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—were first extensively proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Wondrous realization closely traces this to the Wisdom School (Jishi). Within a single mind, there are clearly three functions:
"Emptiness" destroys all phenomena to manifest their pervasive dissolution; "Provisionality" establishes all phenomena to manifest that they are not destroyed.

The "Middle" (Madhyamaka) is the wondrousness of all phenomena (*dharmas*), which reveals that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. Jingxi said: "A single thought-moment devoid of marks is called 'emptiness' (*śūnyatā*);
that no phenomenon is not fully contained is called 'provisionality' (*upāya*); that it is neither identical nor different is called the 'Middle'.

This is as in the *Sutra of the Jeweled Necklace*, where the Bodhisattva Jingshou asks about the three contemplations of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the path of the self-nature purity of all Buddhas.

The three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) cultivated by all Bodhisattvas are clearly elucidated in the *Mādhyamika-śāstra*, which states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions—I declare them to be emptiness;

they are also called provisional designations, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. These are all explicit textual proofs for the single mind’s threefold contemplation (*ekacitta-trividha-vipaśyanā*).
Now, these twenty-five wheels are precisely that upon which those practicing the Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) rely; they constitute the Sudden Teaching (*tongjiao*).
This is the cultivation of the Mahāyāna nature of awakening.
If bodhisattvas take only extreme tranquility as their goal, they will, by the power of that tranquility, eternally sever the afflictions and achieve ultimate perfection.
By relying solely on the single dharma of the ultimate tranquility of śamatha, one forever severs ignorance and ultimately achieves success;
without rising from one's seat, one immediately enters nirvāṇa.
Immediately upon taking his seat, he realized cessation (*nirvāṇa*), which signifies that he did not depend on the cultivation of other dharmas.
This bodhisattva is said to practice *śamatha* alone.
This is the exclusive cultivation of śamatha-vipaśyanā.
Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "If [the text were for] bodhisattvas and others, there would be headings and conclusions for each of the twenty-five wheels below;
furthermore, each one should be headed by stating: 'Awakening to pure, perfect enlightenment as the basis for initiating practice.'"

Regarding the fundamental basis [of these practices], since they have already been identified and enumerated in the preceding contemplations, I shall not record them here for fear of excessive prolixity.
Furthermore, as the characteristics of these three contemplations have already been fully explained previously, I shall now omit them;

this is merely to establish the twenty-five categories for the sake of two groups of five types of practitioners, and to clarify the distinctions between the single and the combined modes. Thus, they are omitted and not retained here.
Now, this "stilling the turbid and ceasing activity" refers to contemplation. This contemplation is like murky water that must first be settled to become clear;
once it is clear, one can then see objects within it. Cultivating this tranquil contemplation is likewise so:
it means that from immeasurable kalpas past, the practitioner has used only this ignorance and affliction.
All karmic obstructions and the deluded, inverted mind that clings to objects through conceptual discrimination have never ceased for even a moment.
Now that you have entered this contemplation, you must use the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to bring them to rest and subdue them, ensuring they do not arise again.
It is like a person holding a staff while watching an ox, preventing it from trampling the crops. "Taking only the ultimate stillness" clarifies the single flavor of tranquil mindfulness.

No longer relying on form or color, nor on earth, water, fire, or wind, nor on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, through the power of profound stillness and deep contemplation, one then realizes that both body and mind are entirely empty and quiescent.
Since even a fleeting thought does not arise, how could afflictions possibly exist? As afflictions do not arise, this is entirely the awakened mind.
Therefore, it is said that "ultimate accomplishment is achieved without rising from one's seat, and one immediately enters nirvana.
This means that without rising from the seat of the dharma-nature of emptiness itself, one immediately enters the true principle of the Tathāgata’s quiescent nirvana of all Buddhas.

Master Cong of Siming said: First is the single cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (among the three contemplations, and subsequently among the seven contemplations, the contemplation of emptiness comes first).
The *Zhi guan* states: "Because of dullness and distraction, which obscure and disturb the clarity of meditative concentration, one should neither follow them nor fear them.
To follow them leads a person toward the evil realms; to fear them hinders the cultivation of correct practice. Those who cultivate the *Yuanjue* should first attain extreme stillness."
It is used exclusively for cessation (*śamatha*). Cessation is concentration (*samādhi*). Ignorance (*avidyā*) is fundamentally the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);

because of delusion, it obscures the principle and becomes ignorance, just as cold causes water to freeze into ice, or as rheum causes the mind to give rise to dreams. Now, one employs the essence of ultimate stillness.

Ignorance is precisely the arising of the dharma-nature; this is the arising and ceasing of that nature. Once this nature has ceased, one no longer discusses the arising and ceasing of delusive inversions.
Binding the dharma-nature with the dharma-nature, and recollecting the dharma-nature through the dharma-nature, it is eternally this very nature and never a time when it is not that nature.
When the realization of its essence is perfected, one neither attains the true nor attains the false; one returns to the source and reverts to the origin.

Fundamentally, the dharma-realm is quiescent; this is "cessation. Furthermore, one contemplates that ignorance and so forth are, from the very beginning, all empty within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Thus, there is not a single phenomenon that is not itself emptiness. It is, for example, like at the end of a kalpa, when everything up to the First Dhyāna is nothing but a blazing inferno.
Moreover, that which is manifested by the Gaganagañja is entirely empty. Furthermore, as stated by Sāgaramati...
All that appears is now seen as water. At the mere stirring of a thought, whatever is thought of is immediately empty;

even this emptiness cannot be apprehended. The dharma-realm is transparently luminous and entirely vast and bright; this is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Contemplation is itself cessation (*śamatha*), and cessation is itself contemplation;
they are non-dual and without distinction. However, because the mind and spirit are obscure and swift, at times the practice of cessation only causes them to race further.

The more one attempts to dispel it, the more confused and obscure it becomes. When the enemy is powerful and one's own strength is weak, like the warbler and the clam holding each other fast, there is no way to advance or retreat.

One must employ skillful means to set it aside. If one gives rise to a resolute mind, then through the subduing of both the strong and the weak, the demon will naturally be stilled and illumination will spontaneously deepen;
thus it is said that "afflictions are forever severed and ultimate accomplishment is achieved. From this point on, one enters the stage of *bhūmi*.

Upon completing the first stage (*bhūmi*), one enters the realm of nirvana, free from arising and ceasing. To manifest as a Buddha through the division of one's body—how could this be anything less than a great contribution?
Those who practice *śamatha* alone are practicing the contemplation of emptiness alone; they are also practicing the "stopping that accords with reality" (*t'i chen chih*) alone.
Therefore, it is concluded that this is called practicing śamatha alone.
If bodhisattvas contemplate only [phenomena] as being like illusions, they can, through the power of the Buddha, manifest various functions within transformed worlds.
Fully practicing the pure and wondrous conduct of a bodhisattva,
because they contemplate all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations, they manifest transformative actions and give rise to the wondrous practice of samāpatti.
Regarding the dhāraṇī, one does not lose the tranquil mindfulness and various pure wisdoms.
Within the dhāraṇī-dharma of Perfect Enlightenment, one does not lose the tranquil mindfulness of dhyāna,
nor does one lose the still wisdom of śamatha.
This Bodhisattva practices *samāpatti* exclusively; this is the dedicated cultivation of the contemplation of illusion (*māyā-darśana*).
Master Furan Hui of Xichu said: "This is the 'Butcher Ding’s Contemplation of Wielding the Knife,' which originally derives from the *Zhuangzi*."
The Chapter on Nurturing Life (*Yangsheng pian*). That text contains a parable: There was a butcher named Ding, surnamed Bao, who prepared oxen for Lord Wenhui.
For three years, everything he saw was nothing but oxen; after three years, he no longer saw whole oxen.
His carving knife, even after nineteen years, had never suffered the slightest wear, as if it were a brand-new blade just sharpened.
It emerges from the whetstone. Now, among the hundred parts of an ox, there are separations and unions, curves and straight lines, apertures and cavities;
even down to the tips of the finest hairs, each possesses its own *dharmadhātu*.

How much more so for that which is resolved within the fine bones—could it possibly lack its own systematic order? Furthermore, where there is separation, one separates accordingly; where there is union...
He joins them where there are openings; he cuts across where there are curves; he follows through where there are straight lines.
Where there is a cavity, he moves; where there is no cavity, he stops. When the dissection of the ox reaches this stage, it is like the "Higher Dissection" (shang jie).
As soon as the movement begins, the hundred parts are already divided; what further effort could there be between them? If this is so, then the ox is already [no more than a collection of parts].
It was wounded, yet the blade remained as it was before. This is because the ox is analogous to external objects; it is analogous to life.
One who is skilled at dissecting oxen may have dissected many oxen, yet the blade has not suffered even the slightest damage.
One who encounters objects skillfully may encounter a multitude of things, yet there is nothing that does not harm life. Ten is a yin number; nine is a yang number. This—
I see that the years have already passed for a long time. When I saw the ox three years ago, this was seeing the object while failing to see the Way.
When I no longer saw the whole ox after three years, this was seeing the Way while failing to see the object.
Indeed, with my single lifetime, I dwell amidst endless changes and events.

If one does not nourish oneself by following the natural course of destiny and nature, then one will ruin one’s life and injure one’s nature, impairing virtue and shortening one’s lifespan until one stands on the very brink of death;
how then could one endure long without the spirit being exhausted and the soul being fatigued?
According to the intent of Zhuangzi, he uses the ox as a metaphor for high reputation and substantial profit in this world, as well as for glory, splendor, wealth, and honor, and wine.
Regarding physical form, wealth, and status—all such various illusory and unreal things—I liken my own body to a blade.
Using this single body to accord with the myriad things, I entrust all affairs to spontaneity (*ziran*), never transgressing the principle of one's inherent nature and lot.

In that case, one would be able to nurture the body and remain far removed from calamities, living out one's natural lifespan to the full without an untimely death, and having one’s life-span cut short by the axe only at its midpoint.
However, the intent of the present sutra is not so; it uses the ox as a metaphor for the myriad practices.
The sword is used as a metaphor for the luminous wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

It is like a Bodhisattva who, upon entering this contemplation, benefits sentient beings, extensively cultivates the myriad practices, and responds to conditions by entering the mundane world to perform various deeds.

Yet, within one's own luminous wisdom of contemplation, it remains ever-luminous and ever-clear, entirely transcendent and uniquely manifest, never lacking anything. Not for a single thought-moment...
When one is at home, it is as if one is blunting the blade of one's own wisdom; this is illustrated by the analogy of Cook Ding freely wielding his knife.
When the Sūtra speaks of the Buddha’s power, it refers to the power of awakening. To be fully engaged in the pure and wondrous practices of a Bodhisattva—
That which extensively delivers all classes of beings and fully masters the gates of the Dharma without losing silent mindfulness is *samādhi*.
That which possesses various tranquil wisdoms is *prajñā*.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Second is the single cultivation of the contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*). One contemplates only that which is like an illusion; this 'illusion' is precisely the provisional dharma (*jia-fa*).
First, one realizes the emptiness of *nirvāṇa* and penetrates the empty Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Then, one establishes the profound contemplation of sentient beings.

The nature of illusion is the myriad phenomena in their full array; one penetrates that the nature of this array all enters into the provisional of illusion, thereby manifesting transformations throughout the worlds."
By virtue of self-realized awakened nature, it is called "Buddha-power," yet this is not a result. The power of the Buddha's empowerment is what constitutes Buddha-power;
this is the nature of self-awakening. Awakening itself is the Buddha. It is the Buddha-power within oneself that manifests in its various functions.
It should pervade everywhere without end. Emerging from the conventional to transform and guide others, one does not dwell in [mere] great compassion but practices the bodhisattva path;

though emerging from the conventional to benefit beings through transformation, one does not lose the mindfulness of quiescence. Thus, by employing skillful means, one rests according to conditions, as well as those with various tranquil wisdoms.
Here, "wisdom" refers precisely to the contemplation of the conventional. When cessation and contemplation are practiced together, it is called the single cultivation of *samāpatti*.
If bodhisattvas merely extinguish all illusions and do not engage in further activity, but instead sever the afflictions alone, then upon the total exhaustion of those afflictions,
they realize the true nature of reality.
Desiring only to extinguish all illusions, one does not grasp at the functional activity of samāpatti,
but employs solely the tranquil contemplation of dhyāna to sever all ignorance, thereby realizing the markless mark of perfect enlightenment.

This bodhisattva practices *dhyāna* alone; this is the exclusive cultivation of quiescent contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). Master Fuan Hui of Xichu said: "Presenting sound as emerging from obstruction" refers to what is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: [The text continues with the verse: "The eye sees the formless; the ear hears the unobstructed. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The mind is originally empty and tranquil; the six sense objects are naturally still. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The six consciousnesses are fundamentally non-existent; the three realms are originally empty. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The ten directions are all empty space; the four elements are originally non-existent. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The five aggregates are like a dream; the twelve links of dependent origination are like an illusion. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The eighteen spheres are all empty; the eighty-four thousand dharmas are all void. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The mind-ground is originally pure; the nature of phenomena is inherently still. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The ten thousand things are all one mind; the myriad forms are but a single essence. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The ten thousand phenomena are all empty; the ten thousand sages are but one body. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The ten thousand dharmas are all empty; the ten thousand gates are but one door. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The ten thousand thoughts are all empty; the ten thousand activities are but one function. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The ten thousand teachings are but one teaching; the ten thousand doctrines are but one doctrine. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The ten thousand dharmas are but one dharma; the ten thousand principles are but one principle. This is called quiescent contemplation. As it is said: "The ten thousand causes are but one cause; the ten thousand conditions are but one condition. This is called quiescent contemplation.
