thus, all return to delusion and confusion, failing to awaken to Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) and failing to enter into Perfect Enlightenment.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Because of the aforementioned false attachments, one calculates that there is a self-body; this is called the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Once the view of a self arises, craving and attachment immediately arise. One hates that which opposes the self and loves that which accords with the self. Such are love and hate."

All arise from the grasping at a self; therefore it is said that from these two objects, namely aversion and attachment, [afflictions arise]. Aversion belongs to views, specifically the five sharp afflictive views (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*).
With a perverted mind one contemplates principles with delusion and inversion. Attachment is the mind of greedy defilement, which is termed "attachment.
If, regarding the physical bodies of men and women, one’s emotions are deluded and one follows the heart to pursue external objects, this defiling state is called entanglement.

Collectively, these are termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving belongs to the afflictions (*kleśa*); specifically, it belongs to the delusions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*), which are the five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-saṃyojana*).

Because they arise from false imagination, one mistakenly identifies and clings to the four great elements and the five aggregates (*skandha*)—along with their faculties and objects—as the self; this is already a falsehood.
Upon this, one further gives rise to aversion and craving, which constitutes a double clinging to falsehood. These two falsehoods depend upon one another, like ice and water.
One gives rise to the paths of deluded karma and transmigrates through the three realms, entering the burning house. These paths of karma are precisely the six destinies.
Due to these deluded karmas, there are those that are light and those that are heavy; thus, the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—are also divided into light and heavy.

Wholesome karma that is heavy leads to rebirth among humans and devas; if light, it results in birth as an asura. Unwholesome karma that is heavy leads to entry into hell; next, one is born as an animal.

Because of these hungry ghosts, it is said that they wander through false perceptions. Alternatively, those among the human realm who weary of such wandering cultivate the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, realizing the conditioned dharmas of the nirvana of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—the Lesser Vehicle.

These individuals have slightly awakened to the emptiness of all phenomena; they penetrate the fact that the four great elements and the five aggregates are by nature empty and quiescent, and thus do not establish the notions of self or person.

Regarding knowledge and vision: attaining the path of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and extinguishing [defilements] according to the two truths is like staying overnight in a grass hut or entering an illusory city;
it is not ultimate extinction. To call this "attaining Nirvana" is termed false vision. Because of this, one cannot enter pure awakening. This is because the Great [Vehicle] rebukes the Small:
the wisdom of the Lesser Vehicle is like a firefly; how could it be compared to the brilliance of the Great Vehicle’s wisdom?
The sun shines brightly in the sky; this is awakening as perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). For one who does not enter perfect awakening, there is still the illumination of awareness;
this is the characteristic of pure awareness. It is not that the characteristic of awareness opposes you, nor is it that perfect awakening refuses to admit you.

It is simply because your capacity to enter is the wisdom of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), which is self-secluded and self-obstructed; it is not that awareness obstructs you. Therefore, it is said that "there is."

Because all that can enter is the entrance of non-awakening, the Great Perfectly Round Wisdom shatters all darkness, extinguishing the small wisdom of fireflies and revealing the lofty brilliance of the golden grain.
A single movement of thought is the ordinary person; the cessation of thought is the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles.
Both the ordinary person and the followers of the two vehicles return to delusion and confusion. Reaching this point, incense and rotten onions are placed in the same vessel; there is no other way.
This is explained as follows.
Why is this? It is because one has been dominated by fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*) that has arisen from time immemorial;
whether in motion or stillness, one remains deluded and distressed. This is because, since beginningless kalpas, the delusive thoughts of ignorance have served as one's master.
For this reason, Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "This inquiry states: 'I further reflect that both [the movement of thought and its cessation] are contrary to awakening;

yet, the cessation of thought immediately accords with the truth. Now, for what reason are both referred to as being in a state of delusion and distress? He answered: 'It is truly because of movement...'"
Thinking, "I am moving," or thinking, "I am stilling," because the mark of self (ātman) persists, one is deluded regarding both movement and stillness;

thus, one is unable to realize entry [into the truth]. All of this is the independent ignorance (mūla-avidyā) that has arisen from the very beginning within the fundamental source throughout beginningless time.
This ignorance does not depend upon external objects; it naturally arises within the state of ordinary, non-substantiality.
It arises suddenly, like clouds appearing in the sky or dust settling upon a mirror.

By means of this ignorance (*avidyā*), one takes it as one's own sovereign master and becomes attached to the mark of self (*ātman*). "Master" (*zhu*) refers to the essence of ignorance; "sovereign" (*zai*) refers to the function of ignorance. It carries the sense of a presiding ruler who exercises judgment and control.
All sentient beings are born without the eye of wisdom;
from birth until now, they have not seen their own true nature. Therefore, it is said that they are born without the eye of wisdom.
The nature of both body and mind is entirely ignorance.
Since the eye of wisdom is absent, the four elements and five aggregates— all of which are illusory in nature— are nothing but the mind of ignorance and attachment.
It is like a person who does not take their own life.
Sentient beings delusively cling to ignorance and are unwilling to eliminate it. It is like people in the world who are unwilling to commit suicide.
Chan Master Fu’an Huī of Xishu said: "This passage, in turn, explains the preceding text.
This is truly because all sentient beings within the four modes of birth and the six realms possess a fundamental, beginningless, and independent ignorance as their own."
Because they are dominated by [deluded] sovereignty, they are unable to awaken to and enter Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

This is analogous to a certain kind of person in the world who, having lost their sight after reaching ten or twenty years of age, can still understand things through description even though their eyes do not see objects;
however, if one is born without eyes while still in the womb and remains blind from birth, then—
When dealing with those who are attached to form, one may explain it to them in various ways, yet in the end it will be of no benefit. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"It is like a blind man who does not recognize the color of milk and asks another, 'What is the color of milk like? The other replies, 'Its color is like a white shell.
The blind man asks again, 'Is this color of milk like the surface of a shell? He replies, 'No. [The blind man] asks again about the color of the shell..."
"What is it like? He replied, "It is like rice powder. He asked again, "Is the color of the milk as soft as rice powder?
And what is rice powder like? He replied, "It is like snow and rain. He spoke again, "That rice powder is cold like snow and rain.
And what is snow and rain like? He replied, "It is like a crane. This was the birth.
Among the blind, it is said that even with these four kinds of analogies, they can ultimately never perceive the true color of milk.
Thus, the poem by Hanshan says: "The causal conditions are not at all clear; the blind man asks about the color of milk.
This is the same principle as the blind man asking about milk or the lame man inquiring about the road: the nature of both body and mind is entirely ignorance (*avidyā*).
[This refers to] the previous "Mañjuśrī Chapter. When one attains the ground of the original arising, then all dharmas practiced are causes for Buddhahood.
Now, by employing the original ignorance, all dharmas practiced become the works of Māra.

Furthermore, previously, because awakening was perfectly luminous, the faculties and objects were universally purified; thus the Sūtra says that "everything is awakening. Now, by means of [ignorance]...
Since clarity (*vidyā*) is the fundamental basis, it is said that all are ignorance (*avidyā*). This is like using gold to fashion a thousand vessels;
while all thousand vessels are gold, this is like using clay to fashion vessels (where all thousand vessels are earthenware). It is, for example, like a person who does not take their own life.
This characteristic of identifying with the self is such that one is neither aware nor conscious of it, and cannot sever it by oneself;
it is like a lowly person in the world who, though perhaps humble and lacking in physical faculties, whose clothing does not cover his body and whose food does not fill his mouth.
"Have you ever been willing to sever your own life and limb? In the end, he was not willing.

This analogy can also be applied to the subsequent passages concerning the words "loving oneself" and the phrase "nourishing ignorance. Since the thematic continuity of the subsequent sections is linked like a chain, this analogy applies throughout both the preceding and following texts.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Why is this? It is because from the beginningless past, all are ignorance (*avidyā*).
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "With ignorance as the cause, the three subtle states arise; with objective realms as the condition, the six coarse states arise.

What is here called "beginningless" refers to fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodhi*), which perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness) to produce the three kinds of marks: the mark of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*).
Because they manifest through mutual transformation, it is called "fundamental arising ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*). Since this is fundamental ignorance, internal delusion serves as its cause.
The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—surround space; within this, your ignorant and deluded consciousness falsely assumes the role of a sovereign.
If one cannot subdue these [elements], one will likewise be afflicted by them. Not...
For one who is able to practice patience, these two meanings are not established, nor is a sovereign self established. Now, we discuss the mind as the confluence of the four great elements;
it is designated as the "sovereign" at the beginning of the five sense-faculties. The *Teaching Left Behind* states: "These five faculties have the mind as their sovereign.
It forms this physical body, and within it, one establishes a self, even claiming it to be one's own sovereign. If the mind were absent...

With the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), one cannot differentiate between form and mind, the four great elements, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the sense faculties, objects, and consciousness;

all are but illusory transformations, like empty flowers in the sky. Thus, the nature of body and mind and so forth are all phenomena of the arising and ceasing of ignorance (*avidyā*), not departing from falsehood.
This is likened to "a person who does not take their own life," which is a metaphor for craving and desire (*tṛṣṇā*). As for craving and desire mentioned in the preceding text:
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause, and the love of life is the fruit. Furthermore, ignorance is both the cause and the fruit [of itself].

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Old age and death have a fruit, which is ignorance; ignorance has a cause, which is pointed out as old age and death. Therefore, both arising and ceasing proceed from ignorance.
Now, it is clarified that the aforementioned ignorance acts as its own sovereign; arising and ceasing are the self-love of the "I."
Who would be willing to sever their own life-force when they cherish their physical body?

Since it is said that craving is the cause and the love of life is the effect, and since both cause and effect consist of a nature of craving that is not relinquished, one will spontaneously fail to sever one's own life-force. If one were willing to sever one's life-force, it would imply the relinquishing of craving;
yet, as long as craving is not relinquished, one does not escape the three realms.
Therefore, one should know this: toward those who love me, I accord with them;
and toward those objects that give rise to the loving heart in those who love me, I likewise accord with them.
If something is not conducive [to one's desires], one immediately gives rise to resentment and enmity;
if one develops a heart of attachment toward that which is not conducive to one's objects, one will frequently become angry when it opposes oneself, giving rise to a mind of resentment and enmity.
Because they harbor feelings of hatred and attachment and nourish ignorance, their continuous pursuit of the Way fails to achieve fruition.
As various forms of hatred and attachment increase their view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), which remains uninterrupted from moment to moment, the realization of the Way becomes ever more difficult.
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "This one passage summarizes the preceding sutra texts.
From the beginningless past until now, all of these have been the causes for obstructing the Way. Those who love me and those whom I follow and comply with [are such obstructions]."
This refers to the arising of attachment toward favorable objects, which clarifies that there is a self; it is not that one merely gives rise to hatred and resentment toward what is unfavorable.
This refers to the arising of aversion toward adverse objects, which clarifies that there is a self.

By means of these two aforementioned mental states—attachment and aversion—one nurtures the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā*), both in their latent state and in their active manifestation; that is to say, the seeds permeate the manifest.
To practice in this way—where current activity perfumes the seeds, such that one does not transcend seeing when encountering forms, nor go beyond hearing when encountering sounds;
where the mind follows as objects arise, and grasping never ceases—leading to moments of hatred and love, moments of grasping and rejecting, and moments of continuous succession:
to seek the realization of Perfect Enlightenment and achieve the Buddha-way with such a mind is impossible. Even if...

To cause them to undergo various gates of practice through diligent toil for kalpas merely serves to further increase their ignorance—what is called drilling ice to seek fire, clutching the earth to find the sky, seeking fish from a tree, or steaming sand to make rice. Their labor is misapplied, and though they cultivate, they cannot achieve success.
The preceding scriptural passage is a general summary of these faults; the following text then provides a specific explanation of the four [aspects].
This is the characteristic.
Master Cong of Siming said: "Attachment" refers precisely to the affliction of attachment through views.

It is solely because sentient beings are deluded by these afflictions—that "fan" (煩) meaning clamor and vexation, and "nǎo" (惱) meaning oppression and confusion—that they disturb and disorder the body and mind, thereby preventing true illumination from arising.
What is now called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) is precisely the mind of greedy attachment. This defiled clinging and entanglement are collectively termed "craving.
Toward that which accords with my will, I feel craving; toward that which opposes my will, I feel hatred. Both this hatred and this craving exist within my empty, deluded, and floating mind.
The essence of this deluded mind is fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodha*), the active manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Regarding the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*): before good or evil has arisen, it is fundamentally without affairs.

However, within the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the sense-bases (*āyatana*), one gives rise to feelings of aversion and attachment. One falsely conceives that "I" can nourish others;
therefore, one also conceives that since birth, "I" have been nourished by my parents. Thus, it is called "nourishing. Now, by means of this aversion and attachment, one nourishes [them].
Within the internal mind, when ignorance suddenly encounters circumstances that are either adverse or favorable, it immediately gives rise to hatred and attachment.
This is the sixth of the sixteen views of self and person, known as the "view of nurturing" (as recorded in the *Fajie Cidi*).

If one harbors hatred and attachment in the heart—hatred leading to resentment and attachment leading to delight—then resentment, hatred, views, and attachment are all merely emotional conceptions. To seek the Way by means of these is futile.
They move further and further away from the Way; therefore, it is said that none of them achieve success.
Good son, what is the mark of self? It refers to that which is realized by the minds of all sentient beings.
The minds of sentient beings do not grasp at or realize anything; thus, they do not cling to the mark of self.
As soon as there is something grasped or realized, they immediately cling to this mind and take it to be their own self; therefore, it is called the "mark of self."
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "The following text provides a separate explanation of the four phases of the bodhisattva’s delusion regarding the realm of wisdom.
For now, let us raise this inquiry: 'What constitutes a bodhisattva's transgression of the mark of self?
The answer is: the word 'deemed' (*wei*) is a term of evaluation. It refers to evaluating a bodhisattva of great resolve as soon as they enter the first [stage]."
On the stage of the Ground (*bhūmi*), one uses the seventh consciousness to realize the eighth consciousness.
Here, the seventh *manas* consciousness is the realizing subject (*pramāṇa*), while the eighth *ālayavijñāna* is the realized object (*prameya*).

Even if one cultivates the path to abandon delusion and realize the truth, so long as this realizing mind is not forgotten, it is termed the "mark of self" (*ātman-vikalpa*). Furthermore, the seventh consciousness belongs to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), whereas the eighth...
Consciousness belongs to the objective aspect (nimittabhāga). For the Sanskrit term *manas* is here translated as "defiled faculty" (*kliṣṭendriya*). As for the four delusions, they are:
self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-pride (*ātma-māna*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), and self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
The lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Guifeng’s intention was that the 'one who realizes' refers to an Arhat;

he meant that such a person still possesses the mark of self (*ātman*). However, I say this is not the case. This 'self' is the foremost among the sixteen views, namely, the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*)."

It is solely because one fails to understand name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the aggregates (skandha), and the elements (dhātu) that one falsely conceives of a self and what belongs to a self as being real.
Our Buddha, fearing that people would not recognize this view—that which lies latent within the inner mind and whose characteristics are difficult to discern—therefore said:
"That which is realized by the mind. Although it is called "realized by the mind," what is the appearance of that which is realized? Below, there is a simile to clarify this.
"Good son, it is like a person whose hundred limbs are in perfect harmony who suddenly forgets his own body;
this is a metaphor for when sentient beings have nothing to grasp or realize, they do not know that there is a mark of self."
When the strings of the four limbs are slackened due to improper methods of nourishment and care, one becomes aware of their existence only when slight moxibustion or acupuncture is applied.
This is a metaphor for how sentient beings only realize the existence of the mark of self (ātman) once they have attained some degree of realization.
Therefore, it is through realization and grasping that the essence of the self manifests.
Realization is my realization; grasping is my grasping. Thus, at the time of realization and grasping, the essence of the self appears.
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "Tightness is urgency; looseness is laxity.
These are all symptoms of the limbs being out of tune and the hands and feet losing their proper measure. Needles and moxibustion are metaphors for adverse and favorable conditions.
As the Sūtra says, 'Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables. It is like a person in the world whose hundred skeletal members..."
It is not regulated; the hands and feet lose their proper measure, and one knows nothing of the balance between tension and relaxation.
Why is this so? It is solely because the methods of regulation, care, and nourishment have been applied incorrectly.

One who prefers cold instead of heat, or who seeks heat when cold is appropriate—this is like seeking warmth by wearing clothes in the spring sun, or seeking relief from freezing by facing the winter wind. It is for this reason that one loses the proper measure.
Because they are well-maintained, one is unaware of the existence of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Suddenly, when a physician arrives and either pricks them with a needle or cauterizes them with moxa, it is only then that one cries out, "It burns me! It hurts! Those who study the Way are likewise:
whether dwelling in quiet chambers or secluding themselves in deep mountains, although things may be left behind for them, they become decrepit.
Yet, beyond matters of fortune and misfortune, the mind ceases all striving; circumstances are neither adverse nor favorable. Through habituation to tranquility, this becomes one's nature;
for a time, one forgets worldly attachments and, unaware of self or other, claims, "I have attained the Way. One thinks, "The mark of selfhood is already gone.
For such a person, even if the world’s high reputation and substantial profit, its splendor, wealth, and nobility, or its wine, women, riches, and power were all present—
One must not disturb this person; rather, one should simply praise the Dharma they have attained and the Dharma they have realized, whereupon they will immediately rejoice.
If one were to slander the Dharma they have attained, they would immediately become resentful. This very mind of joy and anger is precisely the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).
Because one considers oneself to have abandoned delusion and realized the truth, for a moment the sense of self is absent.
As soon as one is confronted by circumstances that are either adverse or favorable, my body-attachment remains as it was before.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "It is like a person who is normally healthy and free from both pain and itching; suddenly feeling slightly unwell, they are treated with needles and moxibustion.

Only when the needles and moxa touch the body do they say there is stinging and aching. Once they know this stinging and aching," [they realize their previous state was merely the absence of these sensations].

Because initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) involves the notion of a self, it is said that "that which is realized by the mind" refers, for the time being, to manifesting the selfhood of sentient beings rather than that of an Arhat.

As the Sūtra says: "Regarding all sentient beings—if they are indeed sentient beings, one must apply needles and moxibustion. Therefore, it is said that realization must first occur before [the truth] manifests.
Good son, even if that mind attains the ultimate, thorough knowledge of the pure Nirvana of the Tathāgata,
it is still the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).
As long as my mind has not been severed, even if one can enter the Nirvana of the Buddha, it is likewise entirely the mark of selfhood.
Master Xifu Fu’an Hui said: "The preceding passage collectively refers to coarse characteristics; this [passage] regarding 'binding the fingers' refers to subtle characteristics.
'That mind even attains realization' pertains to the subject (the capacity); 'the Tathāgata ultimately understands' [pertains to the object]."

This belongs to the objective realm (*grāhya*). Within that objective realm, the Tathāgata’s ultimate and thorough knowledge is the subjective agent (*grāhaka*), and pure *nirvāṇa* is the objective realm.

The intended meaning is that not only is the knowledge of the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles considered the mark of self (*ātman*), but even if one were to know the *nirvāṇa* of a Tathāgata, that too would be the mark of self.
However, the *nirvāṇa* of a Tathāgata is merely empty, non-substantial, and perfect.

Illumination is the unconditioned essence of awakening; it is not something separate that can be realized. Now, having already attained nirvana, if one does not forget the subject and object of realization, these are both merely marks of selfhood (*ātman*).
Therefore, an ancient master said: "Even if you exhaust yourself to the very bottom, you are still wading through wind and waves."
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "This example of the 'self' (ātman) is not possessed solely by ordinary sentient beings;
even the Buddha possesses it. Therefore, it says, 'his mind realizes the Tathāgata. This refers to a Buddha of partial realization, not the ultimate Buddha of wondrous enlightenment.
When the Buddha also speaks of 'I,' this is the 'I' that is without-dharma; this is the possession of the self."

This is not the "self" of the self-conceit of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Until one has realized the stage of the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), even being cut with a knife or smeared with fire is all suffering.
When a noble one (*ārya*) encounters such adversity, it is like cutting through water or blowing upon a flame; what difficulty could there be?

For ordinary beings have not yet destroyed ignorance (*avidyā*), and thus the affliction remains entirely within them. If one knows the Buddha-stage and fully realizes the realization of *nirvāṇa*, [then there is no suffering].
To realize that the mind is also the self, and to proceed until reaching wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), where the forty-two grades of ignorance are completely shattered;
where the hundred negations are clearly revealed and the myriad delusions have all vanished—like the moon on the fifteenth night.
Having reached this state, there is no you and no self, no this and no that, no ordinary person and no sage, no good and no evil, and no heaven or hell. Pure.

The defilements of the realm and the nation are forged into a single whole; therefore it is said: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally manifesting within all classes of sentient beings.
Good son, what is the mark of a person? It refers to those among all sentient beings whose minds have attained awakening and realization.
Regarding the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*): it is the realization that the self is empty, such that one is able to remain free from attachment. Regarding the realization of the mind:
it is because one realizes that the mark of a self which is taken as the object of realization is, in fact, not [a true self].
Good son, one who realizes that there is a self no longer identifies with that self. That which is realized as not-self is itself likewise realized as such.

Although one realizes that the mark of self is non-existent and no longer clings to the mark of self, since that which is realized is already not-self, then the one who realizes it must also not be the self.
This mark of "not-self" is precisely the mark of the person (pudgala).
Awakening has already transcended all those who have attained realization; they are all merely the mark of a person.
Even to cause this awakened mind to surpass all those who have realized the mark of a self is likewise nothing but the mark of a person.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "Regarding 'the mind realized through awakening,' this refers to the realization prior to awakening; it is not that the mind itself is not [realized].

The word 'this' (者) precisely denotes the mark of a person (人相). The meaning is that these sentient beings who have entered the stages, upon reaching this point, further awaken to the knowledge that the previously realized mind was the mark of a self (我相).
Since they know that the realized mind was the mark of a self, furthermore..."
They are unwilling to further realize and understand the principle that serves as the witness; hence it is said they "no longer recognize me.
As for the mind realized now, they think there is no longer any mark of self (*ātman*).

Little do they know that this very mind which realizes is itself dependent upon what preceded it—it is merely the "self" of the human mark (*pudgala-nimitta*), identical to the previous mark of self. The previously realized mind was coarse; [this one is subtle].

Consciousness. This awakened mind is a subtle form of consciousness. Even if one claims that this awakened mind transcends and surpasses all previously realized minds, it still cannot escape being categorized as a "mark of the person" (pudgala-lakṣaṇa). Why?
Because there still exists a mind capable of severing and eliminating [delusions].
The Dharma Master Cong of Siming said: The *Zhizhe fajie cidi* states:

Regarding the "mark of a person" (*pudgala-nimitta*), within the dharmas of name-and-form, the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, one falsely conceives, "I am a practitioner," distinguishing myself from those who are not practitioners;
thus it is called "person. Furthermore, one conceives, "I am born into the human realm," distinguishing myself from other realms; thus it is called "person. (Compassionate Chamber)
[The Master] said: "Furthermore, one should know that the latter three marks all depend upon the mark of self (*ātman-vikalpa*) and are established based upon it.

Jingxi said: "People take what is external to be the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Because one grasps at the characteristics (*nimitta*) within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one reckons there is the mark of a person, and thereby gives rise to the mind of 'I' (*ahaṃkāra-citta*).
Because of this mind of 'I,' the notion of 'mine' (*mama-kāra*) arises. Because the notion of 'mine' arises, there is gain..."
That which benefits me gives rise to greed; that which opposes me gives rise to anger.
These fetters do not arise from wisdom, but from delusion; this is called ignorance (*moha*). The three poisons are the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the current statement that "sentient beings awaken to and realize [the truth] through their minds," I fear people might mistakenly interpret this as the awakening to the Way (bodhi) or the realization of the Way.

Therefore, it is said that this is not so. The intended meaning is: if one compares oneself with other species, and considers oneself a human being, one may calculate based on human characteristics such as noble appearance, status, benefit, or even opposition;
thus, one thinks the human path is superior. However, in reality, this is merely self-centered...
One establishes the notion of "person" within one's own body. To "awaken" is to awaken to that other person; to "realize" is to realize one's own appearance, wealth, and nobility.
Therefore, it is said: "Having awakened, one has already transcended all who realize. The intended meaning is: I have already surpassed all people;
none are equal to me. What I can do, others cannot; what I understand, others do not. In this way, one has transcended them all.
That which is not the realization of the realm of the sages is called "transcending. Therefore, it is said that all these are human characteristics (*pudgala-nimitta*).

Good son, if the mind—even up to the perfect awakening of a Bodhisattva—is regarded as "I," and if the mind retains even a slight trace of awakening while claiming to have fully exhausted the realization of principle, all such cases are termed human characteristics.
Although one may fully awaken to the nirvana of one's own nature and exhaustively master all principles for realization,
if there remains even a hair’s breadth of a mind that seeks awakening, this too is merely the mark of a person.
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "Because one does not grasp at subject and object, it is called 'Perfectly Awakened' (Yuánwù).

Because there is nothing that is not fully exhausted, it is called 'Thoroughly Exhausted' (Bèidān). The meaning is this: these sentient beings employ the seventh consciousness, which does not grasp at the marks of subject and object;
yet the preceding marks of subject and object are all possessed of self. Even if one were to perfectly awaken to nirvana,"
Fully prepared, one attains the principle of the mind realized previously;

yet, because one still retains a slight trace of the awakening mind that does not forget, it is called the "mark of person" (*pudgala-nimitta*). Why? Because this slight wisdom of awakening is not yet a mind free from discrimination;
therefore, it is said to be "slight."
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "As for 'that mind,' this refers to the minds of all sentient beings.
The dragon girl possesses the mind of an animal; Devadatta possesses the mind of hell; King Miaozhuangyan possesses the mind of false views.
It is said that the ten dharma realms are all 'that mind. With the exception of the ultimate Buddha, who is not of the mind, since there exists a mind, the mind arises."

"Devas" (heavenly beings). [This means] having a mind that takes on the form of humans, or having a mind that takes on the form of Buddhas, even to the point of having a mind that realizes nirvana. Therefore, it is said that "both are the self":

when the mind harbors a slight degree of awakening, one awakens to the self as being human, rather than awakening to becoming a Buddha. "Exhausted" (*jin*) means to the end. To speak of it exhaustively according to its principle:
because one mistakenly identifies with one's own body and forcibly establishes a sovereign master, this is called the "mark of the person" (*pudgala-nimitta*).
Good son, what is the mark of sentient beings? It refers to that which the minds of all sentient beings cannot reach through their own self-realization;
yet each sentient being gives rise to a distinct mind, claiming for themselves the marks of a self previously realized and the marks of a person previously awakened.
One has not yet reached this point. One does not realize that this mind is precisely the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*).
Master Huì of Fù’ān in Xīshǔ said: “This is further questioned: ‘What is the mark of a sentient being?

It is said that prior awareness is the subject that awakens, while awakening is the object of that awareness. Since awakening has become the object, awareness is likewise termed the subject. Thus they revolve back and forth without end.”

Exhaustively analyzed, all things consist of subject and object. Wherever there is subject and object, there is mutual dependence. To realize that these have no fixed nature is to depart from the aforementioned errors.
To calculate that one has reached a point beyond which nothing more can be attained, thinking thereby to avoid all faults—this very calculation is itself a sentient being.
A "sentient being" refers to one who does not settle upon or cling to a single state. This means that the mind previously realized is not yet reached by this present mind; the previous awakening...
Even the mind does not reach this "mind. The single character "one" (之) is precisely the realization of the mind without forgetting it.
Good son, it is like a person who says, "I am a sentient being. One should know that when that person speaks of a "sentient being," it is neither "I" nor "another."
This is spoken by borrowing the words of others to illustrate that one's own self constitutes the mark of a sentient being; thus, it is neither the mark of a self nor the mark of another.
Why is it not the self? Because "I" am a sentient being, therefore it is not the self. Why is it not another? Because "I" am a sentient being.
It is because it is neither "that" nor "I. To say it is "not I" means that, being a sentient being, it is not the self.
To say it is "not that" means that, being oneself a sentient being, it is not another person. To say it is "neither that nor I" means it is neither the self of that other person.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: This section of text uses a metaphor to provide a comprehensive explanation;

it merely borrows the colloquial expressions of worldly people to establish its thematic force and reveal the characteristics of sentient beings. While the underlying principle is extremely simple and accessible, the phrasing is nonetheless profound and obscure.
I shall now provide a detailed analysis of this here. The World-Honored One called out to Jìngyè (Pure Deeds).
He said: "Good son, one who wishes to understand the characteristics of sentient beings should consider this:
suppose there were a person in the world who spoke these words of his own accord, asking, 'How does one speak of the Way? How does one speak of the Way? He would say:
'This body of mine is not Zhang San, nor is it Li Si. If I were Zhang San, then there would necessarily be that Li Si.'"
It exists as a counterpart. If I am Li Si, then there must be that Zhang San as my counterpart.

Now, since I am myself composed of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, produced through the harmony of various conditions, one knows that when that person speaks of "sentient beings," this is actually what the Buddha taught.
For that person has already said, "This body of mine..."

At the moment when these various conditions harmoniously combine to produce [a being], the World-Honored One immediately knows that those who speak of "sentient beings" have already realized there is no self.
Not only is there no self, but there is also no "other-self.

Since one does not grasp at it as being "I," there is then no dharma of the opposition between "self" and "other. This has already been examined and explained in the preceding text; it can be seen for oneself.

[The explanation is] complete. Furthermore, fearing that sentient beings of future generations might not understand, the World-Honored One again takes the phrase "neither self nor other" and divides it into two sections for interrogation and explanation, so that it may be easily comprehended. Now, first, he raises an inquiry regarding the two characters "not-self," asking:
"In the preceding text, it was said 'not-self. How is it 'not-self'? He answers: "That person has just arrived from..."
As for the Way: this body of mine arises from the harmony and combination of various conditions. Since it is said that I am a sentient being, then there is no self at all.
Furthermore, regarding the two characters "not that" (*fei bi*) used in the inquiry: the preceding text stated "not that."
"How is it that he is not 'that'? He replied: "That person has just come from the road.
This body of mine has arisen through the harmony of various conditions. Since he says, 'I am a sentient being,' there is immediately no distinction between 'self' and 'other.
Although one thus lacks any realization of self or other, one still ought not to harbor a mind that clings to the notion of a 'sentient being.'"
"No self" means that there is no initial realization of the mark of selflessness in the mind.
"No 'that' or 'I'" means that there is no second awakening to the mark of personhood in the mind. "Yet there are still sentient beings" means that this cognizing mind does not forget.
Generally, among Buddhist scriptures, there are those where the phrasing is easy but the meaning is difficult, and those where the phrasing is difficult but the meaning is easy.

Regarding those cases where both the phrasing and the meaning are difficult, and those where both the phrasing and the meaning are easy—this present case is one where the phrasing is difficult but the meaning is easy.
Good son, all sentient beings who have realized and awakened to [the truth] are [still perceived as] "self" and "person."
One understands that what was previously realized constitutes the mark of self (*ātman*), and what was previously awakened to constitutes the mark of person (*pudgala*).
Regarding that which transcends these marks of self and person,
one realizes that what one has perceived is superior to those two marks of self and person.
To maintain that there is something realized is called the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*).
Because the realization of the mind has not yet been forgotten, this mark is so named.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "This is an analogy used for comparative discernment. The meaning is simply that it is the earth..."

Regarding "superior sentient beings": although they have attained the first realization of the mind as being the mark of self (*ātman*), and have further realized the second awakening of the mind as being the mark of person (*pudgala*), yet because they remain mindful of this realization, it constitutes the mark of sentient beings (*sattva*). The Commentary states:
"If one realizes that what is realized is empty, then even 'self' does not apply; if one realizes that what is awakened to is empty, then even 'person' does not apply. Thus, they do not apply.
In this state, there remains a single point of "knowing" the mind; is this not the mark of a sentient being?
This is what is called "the numinous tortoise dragging its tail": as one brushes away the traces, new traces arise.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Good son, what is meant by 'sentient beings' up to the 'mark of sentient beings'? Tiantai said:
"Within the combination of dharmas such as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), one falsely conceives of a self arising;
therefore, it is called the mark of sentient beings. Now I say: at the initial moment of conception, one takes up the discarded remains of the parents, and there are five factors involved.
First, form; second, sensation; third, perception; fourth, formations; fifth, consciousness. These five all gather the four great elements to collectively constitute their substance.

At that time, there is the conjunction of the four great elements and the conjunction of the five aggregates, which is conventionally designated as a "physical body" and established with the characteristic of "mine.
As for "conditions," they arise through the commonality of many factors. As for "sentient beings," it is the conjunction of the five aggregates.

Birth is like five fingers joined together to form a fist; because these five form a fist, it is given the name "fist. Likewise, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) form a body, which is conventionally designated as a "sentient being.
This is also called the "view of sentient beings" (sattva-dṛṣṭi) or the "view of a person" (pudgala-dṛṣṭi). [This occurs] within the mother's womb.
Thus these names arise; they are all false conceptualizations and lack any real substance.

That which is beyond the reach of the mind’s self-realization is due to the views of "self" and "person," characterized by self-exaltation and arrogance, thinking: "I am a sentient being; others are not sentient beings."
This is my own arising of haughtiness; because I am arrogant toward others, it is not for my own sake. Herein there are two types of inferiority:
first, others are inferior to me; second, I am inferior to others. The term "inferior" (下) consists of a single character, as it encompasses both self and other.
Below, an analogy is established: "I am a sentient being. From this, one knows that when that person speaks of a "sentient being," it is neither the self nor the other.

Below, he again explains himself: "Why is it not the self? 'I am a sentient being'—this is not the self. Since this 'self' is neither that [other] nor a sentient being, and that 'other' is likewise neither the self nor a sentient being, then that which is not the self [is the sentient being].
Thus, that which is not the self is the sentient being. Therefore, that which is not the self is [the sentient being].
He is not me. How could he be another? "I am a sentient being": since I am not another, another is also not me.
"I am a sentient being" is a summary statement meaning that because he is neither another nor me, he is neither another nor me.

"This is me and that is not. "As it is with that, so too it is not me. Yet sentient beings, through deluded feelings, cling to existence and distinguish between "that" and "this," claiming there is awakening and realization. Such views are all merely the self and person;

that which this self and person cannot reach, yet they still maintain as something understood, establishing awakening and realization—all these are the false imaginings of the self and person, not departing from these five [aggregates].
The aggregation of the aggregates (skandhas) constitutes the body; this is called the characteristic of a sentient being.
Good son, what is the characteristic of life-span? It refers to the clear illumination of the minds of all sentient beings, which awakens to that which is understood.
Regarding "that which is understood by awakening": when one awakens from the previous grasping at the mark of a sentient being, it is realized that the mind has not yet been extinguished.
Because this awakened mind continues in a subtle, uninterrupted succession, wishing not to be severed or destroyed, it is called the "mark of life-span."
All karmic wisdom cannot see itself, just as the life-faculty [cannot see itself].
All awakened minds are pure karmic wisdom; however, this wisdom is profound and subtle, and thus it cannot see itself.
Therefore, thought-moment after thought-moment is uninterrupted, just as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) cannot be severed.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "As soon as there is a mind of realization, and one does not forget that mind of realization, it is called the mark of self (*ātman*).
As soon as there is a mind of awakening, and one does not forget that mind of awakening, it is called the mark of person (*pudgala*). To fully comprehend this mind of realization..."
To fully realize the awakened mind and to maintain that realization of the mind without forgetting is called the "mark of the sentient being.

If the previous three marks have all been exhausted, and there is only the manifestation of a single-flavored, illuminating awareness, such that one maintains this awakened mind without forgetting, it is called the "mark of life-span. Now, first let us raise the question:
What is the mark of life-span? The answer is: it refers to the great-minded sentient beings at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*).
When one reaches this stage of practice, one employs the illumination of the very mind. This illumination of the very mind is entirely within one’s own radiance;
it is free from the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance of the knowable, without even a trace of defilement.
Consequently, one realizes that all previous notions of a self, a person, and sentient beings have been completely exhausted. One thoroughly illuminates the true source. Part 1.
At all places and at all times, it is entirely this single awakening; there is nothing else.

One then intends to take this wisdom of functioning and cultivate all untainted (*anāsrava*) activities. "Activity" refers to functional application—various practices such as those for one's own benefit or for the benefit of others.
This wisdom that illuminates is precisely the subtle defiled consciousness; it is called...
The subtle within the subtle is like a person who has formed a root that continues incessantly; it cannot be severed by itself, nor can one see it for oneself.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Ānanda, this stillness is not the true reality; it is like a rushing torrent."
It appears tranquil at first glance, yet its current is so swift that it cannot be seen. This is not the absence of flow; in the Chan school, this is called "the life-root remaining unsevered.
When one has not yet reached the secure barrier, it is also said that "wisdom-illumination is manifest before one," yet this is still merely the continuous flow of the eternal and constant.
Furthermore, it is said: "Ten thousand miles, not a single cloud hangs; the void is precisely ready to receive a blow. Why is this so? It is simply because...
Reaching this state is still not in accord with the Way; there is still reliance remaining, and one is still caught in subtle entanglements.

This is called adorning the body with flower garlands and necklaces; it is also called being unable to take a step beyond the top of a hundred-foot pole, or being unable to let go of one's hand atop the ten-thousand-fathom precipice of Hongya.
There is still the Dharma lingering within the breast. Therefore, when a monk asked:
An ancient worthy said: "When Niutou had not yet seen the Fourth Patriarch, why did the hundred birds bring him flowers?

He answered: "It was a time of wealth and honor when one hears. He further asked: "After he saw [the Patriarch], why did they no longer bring flowers? He answered: "It was a time of poverty after one sees.
This present characteristic of life is precisely that period when Niutou had not yet seen the Fourth Patriarch. Furthermore...
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is it like when the bright moon is suspended in the sky? Zhaozhou said, "It is still a man standing on the steps.
The monk said, "I ask the Master to grant me a direct encounter. Zhaozhou said, "Wait until the moon has fallen, then come and see me.
As for the ancients who tamed dragons and subdued tigers, to whom the devas sent offerings and the hundred birds presented flowers—all these were within this very state.
It is a contraction.
Good son, if the mind perceives all cognitions as objects of illumination, they are all defilements.
When the light of the mind shines forth and perceives various cognitions within the pure nature, they are all likewise defilements.
That which perceives the perceived does not depart from objects;
for both the illuminating mind and the perceiving mind are but thoughts of objects.
Master Fuan Hui of Xichu said: "If one uses the wisdom of this dharma-gate to illuminate and perceive what lies before..."
The three marks [of existence] are such that all who possess discernment are defiled by the dust and toil of afflictions.
Why is it that this very wisdom of the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived still relies on the aforementioned non-separation from the delusions of affliction?

It is because there remains a further wisdom of the perceiver that has not yet been forgotten; therefore, it is identical to the previous ailment. This is what Mencius meant when he said, "laughing at others for fifty paces."
Whether it be a hundred paces or even fifty paces, one has not yet ceased running.
Just as when hot water melts ice, there is no separate ice that knows the ice is melting; likewise, the preservation of a self and the awareness of a self are also like this.
The persistence of the self is like water becoming ice; the awakening to the self is like boiling water dissolving the ice. Although ice and boiling water differ, they both return to the same water.
There is nothing else that can know the dissolution of the ice. Therefore, the persistence of the self and the awakening to the self both return to the One Nature.
There is nothing else that can know the awakening to the self.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "It is like hot water melting ice; there is no separate 'ice' that knows the ice is melting.
This is an illustration. It is, for example, like a person in the world pouring boiling water over ice.
As soon as the water reaches it, the ice dissolves and becomes one with the water. Although the ice has been eliminated, there still remains that which can know [the process].
Regarding the person as ice: it is just that when one says "exhausted," it is yet not exhausted. Water is a metaphor for true nature; ice is a metaphor for the four marks [of conditioned existence];
and hot water is a metaphor for wisdom. Thus, Dongpo said: "When the head is severed, there is no longer anyone who can sever;

once the ice has melted, how could one again know 'ice'? To say that "preserving the self and awakening to the self" is likewise so, is because one currently preserves the self that is capable of awakening.

One awakens to the characteristics of that which was previously awakened to by the three preceding characteristics. Although the self of the three preceding characteristics has been eliminated, there remains no such thing as a self;
it is illogical for it to persist further. This "self" that exhausts [the previous notions] is precisely the characteristic of the life-span (*āyuṣka-lakṣaṇa*).
In the analogy, one knows the ice, yet it is illogical to continue knowing that the ice has melted. If one follows the teachings, this is explained in terms of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding these four marks: the first, the mark of self (*ātman*), is that which is transgressed by Bodhisattvas of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The second and third, the marks of person (*pudgala*) and sentient being (*sattva*), are those transgressed by Bodhisattvas from the second through the tenth stages.

The final, the mark of life-span (*āyuṣka*), is that which is transgressed by Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samābodhi*). This mark of life-span is termed the "flesh-adhering impurity."
Only after one has finally shed this last vestige does one enter the stage of Sublime Enlightenment and become a Buddha.
Master Cong of Siming said: Regarding "longevity" (*āyuṣka*), the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* speaks only of "longevity" and does not mention "life-force" (*jīvaka*).
Regarding what is now called "life-span" (*āyus*): "Life" (*āyu*) refers to the false conceptualization that there is length or brevity within the five aggregates (*skandha*) of form and mind.
What is termed "life-span" likewise refers to the calculation of the accomplishment of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) within the dharma-realm of the aggregates of form and mind;

its continuous maintenance without interruption is called "life. This "life" and "span" are essentially one and the same. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* divides this into two conceptualizations: "self" and "life."
The roots are maintained and not severed; because one clings to this, one conceives of a self-body, which is called the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
As for "the mind illuminating purity," the mind is itself life. Life is merely the breath of inhalation and exhalation. This breath is merely the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).
If this wind of the breath is not pure, it becomes obstructed; all of this arises from this mind’s knowing of all phenomena.
"Knowing" is wisdom (*jñāna*). Wisdom is illumination. To illuminate all phenomena is called "that which is realized through awakening.
Regarding "all karmic wisdom": here karma is itself wisdom, and this wisdom is itself karma. By means of this power of the karma of ignorance, one knows all things.
Regarding the Buddha-dharma: this wisdom is not the wisdom of the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience).
When this wisdom arises through superior karma, people call it the "spiritual terrace" (*lingtai*). That which is not seen by this wisdom is like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*);

it is said that those in the world who know the life-faculty are few. If the mind knows that the life-span has length or brevity, and knows it to be an illusion and transformation, this is the Chapter on Emptiness.
It says: "The mind is like an illusion. Therefore it says, "If the mind illuminates and perceives, all are awakened. "Illumination" means knowing.

Knowing that all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely illusory and false is what is meant by "awakened. The single character "one" (*yi*) following "awakened" includes both the awakening itself and the wisdom that awakens;

for that which is capable of awakening is also [part of] the defilements. These defilements consist of the four great elements, the five aggregates (*skandha*), and the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses (*āyatana*).
All are afflictions. That which can perceive and that which is perceived, as well as that which knows and that which is known, are all dust and dross.
That which can perceive is like boiling water; that which is perceived is like ice. Thus it is said, "like boiling water dissolving ice. Who is it that knows the ice has dissolved?

Both the knower and the known are devoid of intrinsic substance; therefore, the word "who" (者) is used. If one persists in the notion of a self that possesses the knowledge of knowing, one perceives only the self.
This refers to the objects perceived by awakening. It is also like hot water and ice: that which melts and that which is melted are both devoid of marks.
Therefore, it is said, "it is likewise so.
Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand these four marks; though they may practice the Way with diligent effort for many kalpas, they [will achieve nothing].
This is called the conditioned; it can ultimately never bring about any of the fruits of sainthood.

One cannot thoroughly comprehend the characteristics of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life span. Even if one practices diligently for many kalpas, one will still be unable to realize the unconditioned fruit of sainthood.
Therefore, it is called the "final age of the True Dharma" (*saddharma-paryavasāna*).

The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* states: "During the period of the True Dharma, those who practice all attain realization. In the final age, people mostly grasp at signs (*nimitta*).
Now, since they grasp at signs, even if it be the True Dharma, it is the same as the final age."
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "From this point on, all [teachings] clarify that clinging to a self is a loss of the Way.

This means that if one cultivates practice with these four marks of existence (the four phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing), then every action will be accompanied by subject and object.

These are all conditioned phenomena of birth and extinction; therefore, they do not result in the fruit of sainthood. This is precisely as the Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'Six perfections practiced for many kalpas...'"
Such a person is not called a bodhisattva. Not only do they fail to achieve the fruits of sainthood, but they are also said to belong to the final age within the true Dharma of the Buddha.
Why is this? Generally, the True Dharma lasts for one thousand years, the Semblance Dharma for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma for ten thousand years.

Furthermore, during the time of the True Dharma (saddharma), people do not grasp at signs; thus, when they practice, all realize the fruit. In the time of the Final Dharma (paścima-dharma), many people grasp at signs.
Now that we have already fallen into the time of grasping at the signs of realization, even though this is the True Dharma, it is no different from the Final Dharma.
If one encounters this sudden teaching and thoroughly understands the source of the illness, then even in the final age, it will be no different from the True Dharma.
Zhuangzi said: "The world has lost the Way; the Way has lost the world."

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "The divine self (*ātman*) is originally the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). This nature does not maintain itself independently; rather, it undergoes conjunction through the influence of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), one falsely discriminates a self and fails to comprehend the four marks [of existence]. Even if one were to practice for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust,"
One will ultimately fail to become a sage because the self has not been eliminated and the nature of fire has not been severed. Eliminating the self is the essential gateway for entering the Path.
Whether in the Mahayana or Hinayana, if one does not eliminate the self, one will never be a sage. Even during the Buddha’s lifetime, there were those like this;
therefore, it is said that in the final age of the True Dharma, during the latter five hundred years, although the teaching is the True Dharma, how can it be propagated?
Those who uphold [the teachings] often mislead people with heterodox dharmas, reviling the Buddhas and cursing the patriarchs; all such things occur during the final age of the True Dharma.
Although the dharma itself remains correct, those who propagate it are labeled heterodox; this is what is meant by the "final age."

Why is this? This single phrase poses a question: "Since those who have practiced in the past have already spent many eons and their practice has been diligent and arduous, for what reason have they not realized the fruit of sainthood?"
To recognize all things as the self for the sake of nirvana, and to claim there is realization and awakening because of this, is called "accomplishment.
Why is it called the final age of the True Dharma? It is because one clings to various signs as the path to quiescence.
This is because there is the notion of "realization" and the designation of "attainment.
Master Fu’an Huì of Xishu said: "This clarifies the recognition of the 'self' as real. He replied:
"It is precisely because one is not in accord that one recognizes the self as *nirvāṇa*, and thus posits realization, awakening, understanding, and awareness. Therefore..."

Though one may exert oneself with hardship for many eons, in the end it will be of no benefit. It is like mistaking the body in a dream for one's own self and laboring diligently at household affairs;
despite all manner of exhaustion, not a single thing will ultimately benefit one’s assets.
Master Cong of Siming said: "In this world, there is a certain kind of person who studies the art of non-arising, desiring not to undergo birth and extinction.
Yet, by giving rise to such a mind, they have already fallen into birth and extinction. Those who seek it in this way move further and further away from the Way.
They think, 'I am an Arhat,' 'I am without mind,' or 'I have reached the destination. This is like leading one blind man with another; their blindness leads to endless blindness."

Regarding *nirvāṇa*: what dharma is called *nirvāṇa*? You do not recognize the True Principle. For the two vehicles within the triple world, the *śrāvaka* vehicle attains *nirvāṇa* by exiting the birth-and-death of the segmented realm;

this is the *nirvāṇa with remainder*. In the Mahāyāna, one shatters ignorance and ascends to the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjue chuzhu*), realizing a portion of the three virtues; this is Mahāyāna *nirvāṇa*. The Buddha is ultimate *nirvāṇa*; how could there be...?
Being entirely ordinary beings whose three poisons are unsevered, with even a hair’s breadth of the nature of lust, anger, and delusion still present, what kind of nirvana could possibly be realized?
Even if one were to attain supernatural powers, that too would be a form of nirvana;

yet even demonic spirits possess the five supernormal faculties as a result of their karma—how could these be considered realization of nirvana? Furthermore, the Great Teachings criticize the Lesser Vehicle śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, also stating:

Such people are deluded. Kāśyapa himself said: "Before hearing the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra, they were already possessed of false views; how much more so for those who mistakenly identify with the perceptions of self and person?

This is like mistaking fish eyes for pearls, taking such recognition as having reached the destination, calling it awakening, and calling it realization, even claiming, "I have already achieved it. As an ancient said: "This is discrimination; this is clarity. If...
If one does not select virtuous friends and excellent companions to distinguish whether their views are deviant or correct, one will not only bring oneself to ruin but will also lead others astray;
how can the magnitude of such transgression be fully described?
It is like a person who mistakes a thief for their own son; the family's wealth and treasures will ultimately never be secured.
This serves as an analogy for how practicing by grasping at signs will never result in Buddhahood.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "This is an illustration used to clarify the preceding text.
The commentary states: 'If a thief is outside, one may still provide defense; but if he has been raised as a son, how can he be detected? Furthermore, even if one knows the thief is a thief...'"
The thief can do nothing; yet if one recognizes him as one's own son, how can ruin be avoided?

This is used as a metaphor for the fact that while the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) grasping their objects may still be restrained, the *ālayavijñāna* and its false self are difficult to discern. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"Ānanda, your present eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these six act as intermediaries for thieves, robbing you of your own family treasures."
Because sentient beings have been bound by entanglements since beginningless time, they are unable to transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
Master Shou said: "To mistake a false thief for one's own true son is to plunder all family treasures;
to collect fish eyes and take them for pearls is to vainly delude the eye of wisdom. Furthermore, Yongjia said: "To diminish the wealth of Dharma and destroy merit—"

It does not arise from this mind, intellect, or consciousness; yet practitioners, failing to understand its function, engage in cultivation and thus deeply commit the error of mistaking a thief for their own son.
As Zhuangzi said: "No thief is greater than having a mind that seeks virtue. Because the mind has eyes, the sages abandoned it.
Master Cong of Siming said: "The 'robbers' are the six robbers of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
Amidst form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena (*dharmas*), they plunder the family treasures from within; how could they ever gather together again?

This refers precisely to the fact that these robbers are the *avidyā-karma-vijñāna* (ignorant karmic consciousness). Since beginningless time, this thief has harmed me greatly. It simply does not... [text continues].
Reflecting inwardly upon this karma-consciousness of ignorance, it is also called the natural affinity between father and son—the originally enlightened Buddha-nature.

After wandering through the cycle of birth and death, father and son have become estranged. Today, by practicing *yuanjue* (perfect enlightenment), one reunites with this natural affinity and establishes the relationship of father and son.
Ignorance and the dharma-nature are of one essence; the father is the son, and the son is the father. The thief is the escort, and the escort is the thief. If...
To mistake it for something else inevitably leads to being harmed by it.
Why is this? Master Furan Hui of Xichu said: "The previous inquiry was: 'Why did you not attain realization for many kalpas? The answer was: 'Because...'"
Because they recognize the self and grasp at realization, it is further questioned: Nirvana is the true nature of all phenomena;
thus, the essence of the self is also Nirvana. Even if one recognizes the self and grasps at realization, for what reason or cause would this obstruct the Path?
Those who possess craving for a self also crave nirvana; they take the subduing of the root of craving for a self as the characteristic of nirvana.
To crave the self is to crave nirvana; thus, ultimately, they have not transcended craving. It is merely that they are able to subdue the mind of craving for a self so that it does not arise.
This state of non-arising resembles the characteristic of nirvana, but in reality, it is not true nirvana.
Furthermore, those who hate me also hate birth and death.
Since they hate my form, they must hate birth and death; as long as this hating mind is not forgotten, one will never attain liberation.
This is because those who do not understand craving mistake it for true birth-and-death.
Originally they love *nirvāṇa* with the intent to eliminate birth-and-death, yet they do not realize that the mind of craving is the very root of true birth-and-death.
To harbor a separate hatred for birth and death is called not being liberated.
Since one has already given rise to a mind that loves nirvana, one is already bound by birth and death;
to further give rise to a thought that specifically hates birth and death is truly what is called not being liberated.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Now, the cycle of birth and death fundamentally arises from aversion and attachment.
If one seeks liberation, one must exhaust these two sources. If one now feels aversion toward birth and death, this too is fundamentally rooted in aversion.

Although there is a difference between abandoning suffering and delighting in pleasure, aversion and attachment are originally innate habits. If one carries these with one while practicing the Way, how could the fruit of Buddhahood ever be realized? To subdue the self..."

Regarding the claim that the root of craving (*tṛṣṇā-mūla*) constitutes the characteristic of nirvāṇa: because it is [merely] subdued, the state where the root of craving does not arise bears a resemblance to the characteristic of nirvāṇa;

thus, taking the semblance for the reality, one fundamentally takes nirvāṇa to be craving. Intending thereby to eliminate birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), yet since the mind of craving still persists, this is precisely the root of birth-and-death.
With the root of craving as the seed and aversion as the sprout, how can this be called liberation? It is said that this very craving is nirvāṇa...
The mind that clings is precisely the mind of birth and death. Furthermore, why then produce yet another mind that loathes birth and death?
This single mind is simply employed in two places: since you employ this mind to loathe birth and death, you likewise employ this same mind to love nirvana.
How should one know that dharmas are not liberated?
It is because these feelings of aversion and attachment, within the dharma of Perfect Enlightenment, are views that do not constitute liberation.
Master Huì of Fù'ān in Western Shū said: "The single word 'dharma' is the cause of nirvāṇa. As for the "attachment" mentioned previously:
"Nirvana" is termed "non-liberation. Therefore, he further raises this inquiry:
"If attachment to birth-and-death is bondage, and one now realizes that Nirvana is the dharma of quiescent single-mindedness, by what characteristic mark can it be known that it is 'non-liberation'?"
Master Cong of Siming said: "The Buddha-dharma cannot be sought with a mind that has [subjective] intent, nor can it be attained by a mind that is devoid of intent.

One must employ the mind that has intent as the functioning of a mind without intent. The current text states: "Those who possess self-love," and "those who seek nirvana without severing the heart of love.
This heart of love is ignorance (*avidyā*). If ignorance is not destroyed, and if one seeks [nirvana] with this heart of love—
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is far removed from the Way. Those who merely suppress the root of craving are like a tree from which the branches and twigs have been stripped;

though they may wither for a time, they will regenerate once more. If one cuts the very root of the tree, then the principle of non-arising is sought. By cutting the root, one realizes true *nirvāṇa*.

To temporarily suppress the root of craving is like pressing down grass with a stone; when conditions arise, it grows back again, and thus it is not ultimate. This is the case for externalists and ordinary worldlings.

I submit this for your consideration. You take what is [actually] a medicine to be the mark of nirvana; though you use the medicine to treat the illness, you cling to the medicine as if it were the illness itself, and thus the root of the disease becomes even deeper.
Therefore, it is called "true birth-and-death," and it is called "not being liberated. This is not because the Dharma is not subtle, nor that one cannot be liberated from birth-and-death;
rather, it is simply because you yourself fail to apply the Dharma. As the Sutra says: "The blind do not see; it is not the fault of the sun."
This fault is like a person entering the midst of battle using weapons. One who uses them skillfully maneuvers with ease and remains unharmed;
one who does not use them skillfully may find that brandishing a spear and thrusting it into a mouth results not only in a wounded hand, but that their very life is difficult to preserve.
Good son, those sentient beings of the final age who practice for bodhi take their own slight realization to be self-purification,
because they have not yet exhausted the root of the mark of self.
When one has attained some slight realization within oneself, one considers this to be the purification of one's own mind; this is because one has not yet been able to forget the self.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xichu said: "To take one’s own minor realization as personal purification is to fail to recognize that the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is immeasurable and infinite.
Those who are able to enter it do so by entering gradually and becoming increasingly deep. Yet now, these sentient beings..."
At this stage, you are merely externally perceiving that the sense organs and their objects are a provisional union, and internally awakening to the fact that the essence of nature is quiescent;
yet, you have not yet reached the gate of great penetration and great enlightenment. Consequently, the fundamental root of the self-conception (*ātman*) will certainly not be completely eliminated.
How is this known? It shall be understood by examining the application of objects in the following text.
Furthermore, if there is someone who praises that Dharma and one immediately feels joy and desires to deliver them,
yet if there is another who slanders what they have attained and one immediately gives rise to anger and resentment, then one knows that the mark of self is firmly grasped and maintained.
That one gives rise to anger upon hearing disparagement or joy upon hearing praise is because the mark of selfhood is firmly grasped,
lying latent within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), playing among the sensory faculties without ever ceasing.
The mind that clings to a self lies latent within the ālayavijñāna and sports among the six sense faculties, for its thoughts are uninterrupted from moment to moment.
The *Zongjing* says: "Consciousness is itself the mind; it does not maintain its own nature but follows conditions of defilement and purity.
Though it does not inherently unite with them, it unites with them, and because it can contain all true and conventional realms, it is called the ālayavijñāna."
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "As for Zhuangzi’s statement that 'as for Song Rong’s practice of the Way, though the whole world praised him, it did not increase his encouragement;

though the whole world reviled him, it did not increase his obstruction,' if sentient beings today have not yet reached such a state, they rejoice when met with praise and become angry when met with slander."

One can verify this: the mark of self (*ātman*) still persists. Why is this? While the conditions of the world—whether favorable or adverse—are coarse and easy to perceive, it is within the Dharma-gates themselves that it is most difficult to detect.
One may simply say, "I am practicing the Dharma," yet feel resentment toward others and attachment to oneself;
one fails to realize that this very mind is fundamentally the mark of self. This mark of self remains temporarily latent, hidden within the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*.

[In the] midst. If one encounters objects that are either adverse or favorable, they nonetheless manifest intensely at the gateway of the six sense faculties, constantly and forever without interruption or cessation.
An ancient master said: "With a mere light flick of the staff, the three thousand and great thousandfold worlds are incinerated.
Now, as for the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), it belongs to the seeds of the eighth consciousness. All...
The "roots" refer to the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and sixth mental consciousnesses, as well as the functioning of the seventh manas-consciousness.
Within these, seeds perfume active manifestations, and active manifestations perfume seeds, occurring constantly without interruption.
If one were to praise or disparage within this context, it would pertain to the eight winds: gain, loss, defamation, fame, censure, praise, suffering, and pleasure.
The Dharma Master Cong of Siming said: "The 'final five hundred years' refers to this degenerate age when strife and contention are firmly entrenched.
To study Bodhi is the Way. Yet those who study the Way today do not eliminate their self-centered views;

even if they possess a slight degree of knowledge and insight, they immediately claim to have attained realization. Such people fail to recognize the true path to Bodhi and thus mistakenly enter a divergent path."

They regard heterodox paths as the true Way; they claim to have realized what they have not realized and to have attained what they have not attained. Thus it is said that they take their own slight realizations to be self-purification.
During the Buddha’s lifetime, the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners were all categorized among those with false views;
even those among them who possessed supernatural powers still belonged to the ranks of false views. How much more so in the present age, when [they] rely solely on the karma of speech?
They deceive and delude sentient beings; there is no distinction between the "blue eye" and the "white eye" in the world as they follow along into the realms of the heterodox.

Like one blind man leading another blind man, they enter together into the fiery pit. The Buddha, out of compassion for such people, uses words of urgent exhortation to uproot their wrong views and cause them to return to right view;
