thus he praises that Dharma so that they may immediately give rise to joy. Yet, those individuals still desire to use heterodoxy to convert and deliver others.

As for those who receive [the teaching], they claim for themselves that they have already attained the true path capable of transcending birth and death. How could they know that birth and death are accumulating ever more heavily?
They are truly people who are doubly deluded within delusion; both disciple and teacher fall together into ruin.

If there were a person with clear eyes who could skillfully distinguish the virtuous from the depraved, and who exposed their faults and pointed out their falsehoods, this person would immediately give rise to anger and resentment. This is the end.
In the world, this constitutes a bond of enmity. Such a person, because they have not eliminated the mark of self (*ātman*) and stubbornly cling to it, is in essence ignorance (*avidyā*).
The eighth consciousness is also called the *ālaya-vijñāna*. This consciousness of self is exhausted only upon reaching the ultimate state of Buddhahood;
even Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) have not yet exhausted this sense of self. Because this consciousness is so subtle, it is said to "cling."
It remains latent within the field of the eight consciousnesses of the inner mind. Once it is thus latent within, it plays among the various faculties;

that is, when the six faculties are in the eye, it is called "seeing," and when in the ear, it is called "hearing. At the gates of the six faculties, one craves sensory objects such as forms and sounds;

if they are favorable, there is joy, and if they are adverse, there is anger. In all cases, the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) is not severed. This is why the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is placed first: for instance, if...
It is so. Good son, that practitioner of the path does not eliminate the mark of self; therefore, they cannot enter pure awakening.
If they cannot sever the mark of self, how could they possibly awaken to and enter pure awakening?
Master Huì of Fù’ān in Western Shu said: "This summarizes what was previously stated;
because one clings to a self at this point, one loses the Way, and thus is unable to attain awakening into pure and perfect *bodhi*. "

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Awakening" refers to Perfect Awakening; this is the principle of the intrinsically pure nature. It is like a white jade disk that cannot tolerate even the slightest flaw.
If there were even a minor blemish, it would not be pure. This blemish is precisely the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*).
If one retains this grasping at a self, the nature is not pure, just as a solitary crane does not enter the flock of chickens.
Good son, if one knows that the self is empty, there is no one who can destroy the self.
If one knows that the essence of the self is fundamentally empty, then one knows that the one who destroys the self likewise has no place to stand.
I preach the Dharma because I have not yet severed [the view of self].
As soon as the view of self arises, one expounds all dharmas; these are all characteristics of self, for they have not yet been extinguished.
The life-span of sentient beings is also like this.

As long as the mark of self has not been eliminated, these faults and afflictions will persist. If one clings to the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, the affliction is identical in each case.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "From this point on, the text describes taking illness as the Dharma.

This is because he fears that upon hearing the Buddha’s previous teachings, one might rejoice when they are praised and become angry when they are disparaged; as long as anger and joy have not been forgotten, this is precisely the mark of the self."
Now, this is intended as patient endurance without anger, employing it as the realization of non-self. One should think:
"This single body of mine is formed from the harmony of various conditions; ultimately there is no self. Since I have already realized its emptiness, whom are you destroying?"
Considering your ignorance, I now explain to you in various ways the Dharma of the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*).

Yet, this very person who sees existence and non-existence as things to be refuted has not yet attained the emptiness of self. This very act of preaching the Dharma for their sake means that the mark of self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*) has not been severed.
It is the same regarding the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. The Commentary states: "The one who refutes..."

"That" refers to the object; "speaker" refers to the self. The scriptural text states that [the fault] does not exist in the one who reviles; this is a case of clarifying the fault through negation (paryudāsa).
It states that it exists in the speaker; this is a case of clarifying the fault through affirmation (vidhi).
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "If one knows the emptiness of self, this emptiness is primordial emptiness;
it is not an emptiness produced by effort. It is also called the emptiness of inherent virtue (*xingde*). This emptiness empties all phenomena while yet embodying all phenomena.

It is the emptiness that is not empty, and the existence that is not existent. This emptiness and existence are spontaneously possessed within the primordial nature. One should neither rejoice in nor be averse to seeing them."
To see anger and yet not be angry—how could there originally have been either anger or joy? What I am now speaking of has not yet reached that stage.
Because of my speaking, even if people revile me, I do not give rise to anger. Although I do not harbor anger toward others, the internal thought does not cease;
it is merely suppressed for a time, such that it does not manifest on one's countenance, yet it still persists within the mind. Therefore it is said: "If one knows..."
The self is empty, and there is no one who destroys it. Yongjia said: "When the body is in accord with emptiness, whether it is cut by a blade or smeared with incense, what suffering is there?
What joy is there? When the mind is in accord with emptiness, whether it is reviled or praised, what anxiety is there? What delight is there?"

Nevertheless, one establishes the notion of "I" as the speaker; for this reason, one does not feel anger. If such a thought arises, then both the subject (the knower) and the object (the known) have not been discarded.
That there is "that" and "me" is entirely because the mark of self (*ātman*) has not yet been severed.

It is like the two people in the Buddha’s time who stole someone’s lotus flowers and plotted together, saying: "If the other person suddenly notices and calls out, 'Who is stealing my flower? we should act accordingly."
The mandarin ducks cried out, causing others not to suspect them. Indeed, one person entered the pond to steal flowers;
when the owner asked, "Who has stolen my flowers? he did not imitate their cry, but instead replied, "I am a mandarin duck," whereupon he was captured by the owner.
In the original text, the single character "I" (我) has ultimately not been eliminated. Who among people is not harmed by this sickness of the self?
For this reason, the view of sentient beings regarding their life-span remains unsevered; thus it is said, "it is likewise so."
Good son, sentient beings in the final age speak of illnesses as being the Dharma; for this reason, they are called those who deserve compassion.
The mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient being, and the mark of life span—these are the four illnesses.
Sentient beings, out of ignorance and delusion, claim these four illnesses to be the true Dharma; this is truly pitiable.
Although they apply themselves with diligent effort, their various ailments increase; therefore, they cannot enter pure awakening.
By practicing while grasping at signs, the more diligently they strive, the more their ailments grow. How, then, can they awaken to and enter pure awakening?
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "From 'Good sons' up to 'to increase all illnesses,' this constitutes the formation [of the fetters].
To maintain a self is to lose the Way; therefore, one cannot awaken to and enter Perfect Enlightenment. 'Illnesses' refers to the four marks."

If the four marks persist, they are collectively termed "illness. Now, these sentient beings all take this illness of the four marks as the dharma-gate of the single-minded, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas of the ten directions;
it is what is called mistaking a chicken for a phoenix or picking up pebbles for jade.
This is truly pitiable. Yet, though they exert themselves with diligent effort, they only increase their illness further. It is, for example, like...
To cast firewood into a flame and use water to assist ice—this is why one cannot enter pure, awakened awareness.
This constitutes a knot that obstructs the Path; it means that for a practitioner cultivating the Way, it is improper to take the aforementioned afflictions as the Dharma.
Consequently, they are unable to realize and enter pure, perfect *bodhi*.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "It is like a person who has an illness and must take various medicines. Once the medicine reaches the ailment and the disease is eliminated, the medicine should also be discarded.
Yet some people, because the medicine can cure the disease, cling to it and do not discard it; consequently, the medicine itself becomes an illness.
How could they know that while the disease is easy to treat, the medicine-induced illness is difficult to cure? This applies to those who preach with diligent practice."
All these are termed the root of illness. It is solely because one fails to recognize that true nature is fundamentally empty that medicine is treated as an illness.
Though one may diligently seek the Way with vigor, if one does not penetrate the emptiness of the self and phenomena, delusions will arise once more.

One studies Buddhism originally to cure illness, yet after a long time, one instead treats the medicine as the illness; such arduous asceticism is merely labor in vain. As there was once a person in the Buddha’s time...
A woman, weary of her body, set herself ablaze. As she was about to enter the fire, she suddenly encountered a spiritual friend who said to her:
"By burning your body and detesting your body, you will still not escape suffering; that suffering will lead to further suffering, for you have not realized the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Even if you were to burn a thousand bodies, you would still not be free from suffering. It is like a broken donkey-cart: the donkey detests the cart and destroys the old one, yet even though the old cart is destroyed..."
The new vehicle returns once more, yet it does not reach the state of no-self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span.
It is like a bird cast into a net; there is no place from which to escape. Though the mind, in every thought-moment, desires to break free, alas, there is no path by which to go forth.
Seeking an exit, the ancients said: "When the mind roams the Dharma-realm, all thoughts are stilled; it is like the sun resting upon the sky, yet not dwelling in the sky."

Good son, sentient beings in the final age do not understand the four marks [of self]. Taking the Tathāgata’s understanding and his sphere of practice as their own cultivation, they will ultimately achieve nothing.
If one cannot thoroughly comprehend the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of sentient beings, and the mark of life span,
then even if one takes the Buddha’s insight and the path practiced by the Buddha as one's own method of cultivation, in the end, one will still be unable to attain Buddhahood.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "The following passage uses ordinary people to blur the distinction from sages, first suppressing the sages to equate them with oneself.

The commentary states: 'The Buddha expounded the definitive teachings, the Dharma-gates that accord with principle, all of which declare that mind and objects are fundamentally empty, and delusions and karma are fundamentally pure;
ordinary and sage are not different, and cause and effect are both perfect. From the perspective of the Buddha, this is the principle."
It is indeed so. Furthermore, sentient beings have been deluded for a long time; their habitual tendencies are deeply rooted.

Even if they gain faith and understanding in the Dharma gates, what they currently employ is fundamentally based on recollection. They merely use their discriminative consciousness to interpret the unimpeded verbal teachings of others.

This means that the Buddha’s intention was likewise exactly this. [Those who misunderstand] then proceed to sigh at the heavens and question the earth, repudiating cause and effect, and lacking faith in cultivation or realization.
If one holds such a view, it is as Yongjia said: "Vast emptiness that repudiates cause and effect;
such reckless wandering invites calamity. It is also like a poor person counting the wealth and treasures of others. Self-...
Without even half a coin’s worth of merit, they will be unable to accomplish Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
There may be sentient beings who have not attained yet claim to have attained, who have not realized yet claim to have realized;
having gained nothing, they say they have already gained; having realized nothing, they say they have already realized. Such are their delusions.
It is said to people that this is likely because they have not yet severed the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Chan Master Fu’an Huī of Xishu said: "The preceding passage suppressed the Sage to be the same as oneself;
this, however, is merely using oneself to equate with the Sage. The word "or" (*huò*) is an indefinite term, meaning there are some who use themselves to equate with the Sage.
Such a person has never attained the principle realized by the Sages, yet claims to have attained it;

they have never realized the wisdom realized by the Sages, yet claims to have realized it. To claim realization when one has not realized it constitutes a grave offense of false speech against the fundamental precepts.
Therefore, at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the Buddha told Ānanda: "I..."
I instruct the bhikṣus that the site of enlightenment is the straightforward mind. Within all activities throughout the four modes of deportment, there is not even the slightest pretense;

how then can one claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior man? It is like a poor man who falsely styles himself an emperor, only to bring about his own execution—how much more so for a Dharma King!
How could he falsely usurp such a title? If the ground is not straight, the fruit will be crooked. —From *Zhuangzi*.
He said: "This is like arriving today at the destination one set out for yesterday.
Upon seeing those who have attained superior progress, one gives rise to envy in the mind. Because such sentient beings have not yet severed self-love, they are unable to enter pure awakening."

When one sees those who surpass oneself in advancing on the Path, one immediately gives rise to a mind of envy; this is because the mind that cherishes the self is uninterrupted from moment to moment.
How can such a person ever awaken to and enter into pure enlightenment?
Master Cishu Fuan Hui said: "Regarding those who give rise to jealousy upon seeing others achieve excellence or progress, the *Shu* (Commentary) states:

'As for the mind of a sage, there is no distinction between self and others. When they see others excel or when the Dharma teachings spread, their every thought is filled with joy, and they will surely accord with it.
One can verify this within one's own mind; or else, one may immediately realize awakening.'"

False. Why is this? The Buddhas of the ten directions constantly emit light from between their eyebrows day and night, watching over all sentient beings so that they may sever evil and cultivate goodness.
If there is even one person who gives rise to the bodhicitta and studies the Buddha-dharma, the Buddhas of the ten directions will experience immeasurable joy.
However, if one perceives oneself as declining while others flourish, then envy arises.
To feel joy when one’s own prosperity increases and another’s declines—even if one has deeply understood the wondrous realm—is merely an object of the mind;
do not mistake this for attaining realization. Because those sentient beings have not severed self-love, they are unable to enter pure awakening;
this constitutes an obstruction to the Path, which is entirely due to the aforementioned suppression.
The Sage is identical to oneself. When one exerts oneself to equal the Sage, these two classes of sentient beings are both those who have never severed self-love (*ātmasneha*).
Because of this self-love, they are unable to awaken to and enter into pure *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti* (perfectly complete enlightenment).
This Bodhisattva of Pure Practice previously asked: "If the nature of this awakened mind is inherently pure, for what reason is it defiled, causing all sentient beings [to remain so]?"
Confused and distressed, he did not enter. Now the answer says: there are three faults. First, it is improper to recognize me as real; thus one cannot enter pure awakening.
Second, it is improper to speak of illness as the Dharma; thus one cannot enter pure awakening.
Third, it is improper to take the ordinary to oversee the sagely; thus one cannot enter pure awakening. Considering this meaning, whose [fault is it]?

Is it not so? Master Cong of Siming said: "Good son, when sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age do not understand the four marks [of the self] up to the entry into pure awakening—this is because these four views originally arise from false conceptualization within the *tathatā* Buddha-nature. For this reason..."
The physical body is already considered to be substantially existent. Furthermore, one reckons that the "I" which can understand the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is my own mind;
that the four samādhis are the gateways for entering the Path; and that "I" am the practitioner. (This is false conceptualization.

One reckons that what I understand is the Dharma of the Superior Person, and that what I practice is the conduct of the Tathāgata. Such understanding and practice are both entirely false conceptualizations.
Those who do not realize there is no self or person will never achieve success in the nature of Perfect Enlightenment, because they maintain the view of a self as a sovereign master.
Furthermore, there is a class of people with overweening pride who claim to have attained what they have not attained and to have realized what they have not realized;
they falsely represent themselves as spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*) and scheme for gain and offerings. As the Sūtra says: "In the past, there was a poor man who fled to another country."
He falsely claimed to be a prince, but the kingdom did not recognize him; they gave him the princess as his wife.
Whenever he encountered food or drink, he would constantly give rise to anger and reproach. Later, a man from that country happened to see the princess and recounted the aforementioned events.
This visitor said, "I shall teach you a verse. Whenever another person gives rise to anger, if you recite this verse, that anger will naturally subside.
The verse says: "Having incurred debt, one flees to another land; Pretending to be a man of noble station, Coarse food is one's constant sustenance— Why trouble oneself by giving rise to anger again?
The man’s angry mind was indeed subdued. Now, those who increase their arrogance falsely claim to have attained realization and invite others [to witness it].
Seeking fame and profit, they harbor envy toward the worthy and capable, thereby creating the causes for rebirth in hell while remaining unaware of their own condition;
thus it is said that because they have not yet severed self-love, they cannot enter pure awakening—is this not deception?
Good son, for sentient beings in the final age who aspire to achieve the Way, do not allow them to seek awakening, lest it only increase their learning and grow their views of self.
For those who hope to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, do not cause them to seek awakening within their own nature, but only have them study extensively and accumulate much learning; then they—
My view of self has only grown stronger and stronger.
Chan Master Fu’an Huì of Xishu said: "This clarifies that one is heading toward the fruit while remaining deluded regarding the cause.
Those who hope to achieve the Way are heading toward the fruit; those who merely increase their learning are deluded regarding the cause. This is generally the principle of the Sudden Teaching."
The essential point is this: one must first realize the nature of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and only thereafter may one engage in extensive learning to broaden one’s wisdom.

This is as unimpeded as a dragon gaining access to water or a tiger relying on its mountain. The Preface states: "Of the myriad medicinal prescriptions, one should select those that act as specific antidotes;
of the thousand treasures of the sea, one first seeks the wish-fulfilling gem. Yet people in this degenerate age are mostly deluded regarding this principle, adhering instead to mere names.
These phrases lead one to follow the literal text exclusively, searching for branches and plucking leaves, without striving to realize the mind.

If the mind is not realized, then even if you were to memorize as many scriptures as the sands of the Ganges and exhaust all the ink and paper of the world, what benefit would this bring to yourself? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"If the outflows of desire are not first eliminated, then the accumulation of learning will become a source of fault. Thus, everything seen and heard will only serve to increase all manner of evils.
The Treatise says: "To have much learning but no wisdom is to not know the true mark (lakṣaṇa). It is like being in the dark with a treasure but having no eyes.
Various teachings state that śrāvakas contemplate only the fruit and do not contemplate the cause;

they are like a dog chasing a clod of earth rather than chasing the person who threw it. Furthermore, as the *Liezi* says: "The Great Way loses its sheep because of many diverging paths. Thus, the student...

Because many lose their lives through various methods. Zhuangzi also said: "The Way does not desire multiplicity. Multiplicity leads to confusion; confusion leads to agitation; agitation leads to anxiety;
and once there is anxiety, there is no salvation. All of this is a critique of those who do not first bring the mind to clarity before engaging in extensive learning.

The "Shuofu" chapter of the *Liezi* says: A neighbor of Yangzi lost a sheep. He led his own followers and also requested Yangzi’s servant to go after it. Yangzi said, "Alas! You have lost a single sheep; why is there such a large group of pursuers? The neighbor replied, "Because there are many diverging paths. When they returned, Yangzi asked, "Was the sheep recovered? He replied, "It is lost. Yangzi asked, "In what way was it lost? The neighbor said, "At first there were five or six paths; now there are one or two. Yangzi sighed and said, "I too am like this. The neighbor then asked, "How are you like this? Yangzi replied, "When I first set out to study, there were five or six paths; now there are only one or two. The neighbor said, "This is not comparable. The sheep that was lost was a sheep of others; the path you have lost is your own Way. Yangzi was ashamed and did not speak again for three months. Thus, when the Way is divided, the mind becomes confused; when the mind is confused, the Way is obscured. Therefore, the sage unifies the Way and does not allow the mind to be divided. This is called the "One Vehicle. It is because the One Vehicle is vast and great that it can encompass all things. Because it is vast and great, it is called the "Great Vehicle. Because it encompasses all things, it is called the "Universal Vehicle. Because it is universal, it is called the "Vehicle of the Dharma. Because it is the Dharma, it is called the "Dharma-body. Because it is the body, it is called the "True Body. Because it is true, it is called the "Eternal Body. Because it is eternal, it is called the "Unchanging Body. Because it is unchanging, it is called the "Body of Non-action. Because it is non-action, it is called the "Body of No-birth. Because it is no-birth, it is called the "Body of No-extinction. Because it is no-extinction, it is called the "Body of Non-arising. Because it is non-arising, it is called the "Body of Emptiness. Because it is empty, it is called the "Body of Non-self. Because it is non-self, it is called the "Body of Purity. Because it is pure, it is called the "Body of Clarity. Because it is clear, it is called the "Body of Stillness. Because it is still, it is called the "Body of Tranquility. Because it is tranquil, it is called the "Body of Non-attachment. Because it is non-attached, it is called the "Body of Non-discrimination. Because it is non-discriminating, it is called the "Body of Non-conceptualization. Because it is non-conceptualizing, it is called the "Body of Non-thought. Because it is without thought, it is called the "Body of Non-mind. Because it is without mind, it is called the "Body of Non-consciousness. Because it is without consciousness, it is called the "Body of Non-perception. Because it is without perception, it is called the "Body of Non-grasping. Because it is without grasping, it is called the "Body of Non-clinging. Because it is without clinging, it is called the "Body of Non-obstruction. Because it is without obstruction, it is called the "Body of Non-hindrance. Because it is without hindrance, it is called the "Body of Non-limitation. Because it is without limitation, it is called the "Body of Non-boundary. Because it is without boundary, it is called the "Body of Non-duality. Because it is non-dual, it is called the "Body of Non-distinction. Because it is non-distinct, it is called the "Body of Non-separation. Because it is non-separated, it is called the "Body of Non-difference. Because it is non-different, it is called the "Body of Non-change. Because it is non-changing, it is called the "Body of Non-decay. Because it is non-decaying, it is called the "Body of Non-extinction. Because it is non-extinguished, it is called the "Body of Non-birth. Because it is non-born, it is called the "Body of Non-death. Because it is non-dying, it is called the "Body of Non-suffering. Because it is non-suffering, it is called the "Body of Non-emptiness. Because it is non-empty, it is called the "Body of Non-form. Because it is non-form, it is called the "Body of Non-characteristics. Because it is non-characteristic, it is called the "Body of Non-desire. Because it is non-desirous, it is called the "Body of Non-anger. Because it is non-angry, it is called the "Body of Non-delusion. Because it is non-deluded, it is called the "Body of Non-ignorance. Because it is non-ignorant, it is called the "Body of Non-obscuration. Because it is non-obscured, it is called the "Body of Non-defilement. Because it is non-defiled, it is called the "Body of Non-purity. Because it is non-pure, it is called the "Body of Non-bondage. Because it is non-bound, it is called the "Body of Non-liberation. Because it is non-liberated, it is called the "Body of Non-attainment. Because it is non-attained, it is called the "Body of Non-loss. Because it is non-lost, it is called the "Body of Non-increase. Because it is non-increasing, it is called the "Body of Non-decrease. Because it is non-decreasing, it is called the "Body of Non-growth. Because it is non-growing, it is called the "Body of Non-diminution. Because it is non-diminishing, it is called the "Body of Non-exhaustion. Because it is non-exhausted, it is called the "Body of Non-finitude. Because it is non-finite, it is called the "Body of Non-beginning. Because it has no beginning, it is called the "Body of Non-end. Because it has no end, it is called the "Body of Non-middle. Because it has no middle, it is called the "Body of Non-extremes. Because it has no extremes, it is called the "Body of Non-birth-and-death. Because it is beyond birth-and-death, it is called the "Body of Nirvana. Because it is Nirvana, it is called the "Body of the Tathagata. Because it is the Tathagata, it is called the "Body of the Buddha. Because it is the Buddha, it is called the "Body of the Dharma. Because it is the Dharma, it is called the "Body of the Sangha. Because it is the Sangha, it is called the "Body of the Jewel. Because it is the Jewel, it is called the "Body of the Three Treasures. Because it is the Three Treasures, it is called the "Body of the Great Vehicle. Because it is the Great Vehicle, it is called the "Body of the Universal Vehicle. Because it is the Universal Vehicle, it is called the "Body of the Dharma. Because it is the Dharma, it is called the "Body of the Truth. Because it is the Truth, it is called the "Body of Reality. Because it is reality, it is called the "Body of Suchness. Because it is suchness, it is called the "Body of Non-falsity. Because it is non-false, it is called the "Body of Non-deviation. Because it is non-deviant, it is called the "Body of Non-errancy. Because it is non-errant, it is called the "Body of Non-confusion. Because it is non-confused, it is called the "Body of Non-delusion. Because it is non-deluded, it is called the "Body of Non-attachment. Because it is non-attached, it is called the "Body of Non-obstruction. Because it is non-obstructed, it is called the "Body of Non-hindrance. Because it is non-hindered, it is called the "Body of Non-limitation. Because it is non-limited, it is called the "Body of Non-boundary. Because it is non-boundary, it is called the "Body of Non-duality. Because it is non-dual, it is called the "Body of Non-distinction. Because it is non-distinct, it is called the "Body of Non-separation. Because it is non-separated, it is called the "Body of Non-difference. Because it is non-different, it is called the "Body of Non-change. Because it is non-changing, it is called the "Body of Non-decay. Because it is non-decaying, it is called the "Body of Non-extinction. Because it is non-extinguished, it is called the "Body of Non-birth. Because it is non-born, it is called the "Body of Non-death. Because it is non-dying, it is called the "Body of Non-suffering. Because it is non-suffering, it is called the "Body of Non-emptiness. Because
Yangzi said, "At the center of a forked road there is yet another fork; I do not know where it leads, so I have returned.
Yangzi’s countenance changed with a look of sorrow. He did not speak for a long time, and he did not smile for the rest of the day.
His disciples marveled at this and asked him, saying, "A sheep is a lowly beast, and moreover, it was not yours. Why do you diminish your speech and withdraw your smiles?"
Yangzi did not answer. His disciples were left without instruction. One of his followers, Mengsun Yang, went out and informed Xindu Zi.
On another day, Xindu Zi entered together with Mengsun Yang and asked:
"In the past, there were three brothers who traveled between Qi and Lu. They studied under the same teacher and returned home having advanced in the Way of benevolence and righteousness."

The father asked, "What is the way of benevolence and righteousness? The eldest son said, "Benevolence and righteousness lead me to cherish my own person before seeking fame. The middle son said, "Benevolence and righteousness lead me to sacrifice my life to establish my name.

The youngest son said, "Benevolence and righteousness lead me to have both my person and my name united. These three methods are mutually opposed, yet they all agree with Confucianism; which is right and which is wrong? Yangzi said: The father asked, "What is the way of benevolence and righteousness? The eldest son said, "Benevolence and righteousness lead me to cherish my own person before seeking fame.

The middle son said, "Benevolence and righteousness lead me to sacrifice my life to establish my name. The youngest son said, "Benevolence and righteousness lead me to have both my person and my name united. These three methods are mutually opposed, yet they all agree with Confucianism; which is right and which is wrong? Yangzi said:
There was a man who lived by a river. He was accustomed to the water and skilled at swimming. He operated a boat to ferry people across for profit, providing for a hundred mouths with his earnings.
Those who carried provisions to study there formed a large company, yet nearly half of them drowned.
They had not learned to swim, nor had they learned how to avoid drowning, and yet the consequences were so severe. If one asks which of these two states is wrong, Xindu Zi departed in silence.
Mengsun Yang remonstrated with him, saying, "Why is it that you, sir, ask such abstruse questions and our master answers so eccentrically?
My confusion has only increased. Xinduzi said, "The Great Way loses its sheep because of many diverging paths; the student loses his resolve because of many methods.
Learning is not fundamentally different, nor is it fundamentally not one—it is only at the end that they diverge. Thus, we must simply return to what is the same and revert to the source."
I. On Grief for Loss and Gain. My son, you were raised in the Master’s gate and studied the Master’s Way, yet you did not fully penetrate the Master’s teachings.
How lamentable! A eulogy on the lotus flower says: Do not laboriously study the Profound Doctrine through hearsay and perception;
such study is but toil spent in vain. How much better it is to remain in non-action, free and expansive; then, vast and open, one is spontaneously and perfectly enlightened.

If you merely wish to be diligent and subdue the afflictions in order to hope for the fruit of Buddhahood, it is not necessary to study extensively or possess great learning; you need only be diligent and restrain delusive thoughts.
Arouse great courage and vigor. That which has not yet been attained, you must cause to be attained; that which has not yet been severed, you must cause to be severed.
You should give rise to a mind of vast resolve: as long as the fruit of Buddhahood has not been attained, it must be attained;
as long as deluded thoughts have not been severed, they must be severed.
Greed, anger, craving, pride, flattery, crookedness, and envy do not arise toward objects; attachment between self and others is entirely extinguished.
The Buddha said that such a person gradually achieves accomplishment.
If one is free from such deluded minds, one will certainly be able to gradually attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
While seeking a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to avoid falling into false views,
one must further draw near to virtuous persons before all false views can be severed.
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "This is an exhortation to sever delusions in order to establish the correct cause.

Its meaning is that the World-Honored One exhorts all sentient beings: those who wish to accomplish the vast and perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas of the ten directions [must do so by severing delusions]."
You should simply subdue the afflictions as I have instructed, giving rise to a mind of great courage and superior resolve.

If you have not yet attained within the true realm of Perfect Enlightenment the meaning of the great wisdom-light and the meaning of its universal illumination of the Dharma-realm, [you must strive accordingly].
The meaning of truly knowing reality; the meaning of purity and immutability; the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
As for all sublime functions, one should cause them to be fully accomplished and attained.

If one has not yet severed the delusions of ordinary beings within the realm of inverted perceptions—namely, greed, anger, attachment, pride, flattery, crookedness, envy, and all obstructive, false phenomena—one should...
One should cause all attachments and endearments to be severed; when all things are entirely empty and quiescent, the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood will be spontaneously accomplished.
Furthermore, one must seek a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) to serve as a witness and a guide, so as not to fall into false views.
Why is this? The commentary states: "Just as merchants entering the sea must rely upon a guide, so too those who study and practice cultivation must depend upon virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra).
Therefore, the Chan school says: prior to King Vairocana (Vaiśvānara), there was awakening without a teacher; from King Vairocana onwards..."
Those who claim to have attained self-awakening without a teacher are entirely celestial māras or non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

Those characterized by greed, hatred, craving, and pride arise from among the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). Craving has no distinct nature of its own and is subsumed under the category of greed (*lobha*).
Deceit, crookedness, and envy are minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*).
If one gives rise to separate feelings of aversion or attachment toward that which is sought, one will be unable to enter the ocean of pure awakening. If,
regarding the Dharma of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) from whom one seeks it, one cannot accept it with faith but instead gives rise to separate feelings of aversion or attachment,
one will be unable to accomplish the vast fruit of perfect awakening (pariniṣpanna-bodhi).
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "The preceding passage is an exegesis in the direct order; this passage is an exegesis in the reverse order.

To clarify in reverse that one does not give rise to hatred or attachment, one then attains entry into Perfect Enlightenment. As for 'hatred and attachment,' one gives rise to attachment toward oneself and hatred toward others.
Therefore it is said: 'Only do not harbor hatred or attachment, and you will be transparently and brilliantly clear.'"

Master Cong of Siming said: "Good son, when sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age reach the pure and perfect *bodhi* (*yuanjue*), even the seeker’s mental application and longing constitute the failure to extinguish *māna* (pride).
If one applies the mind to seek awakening, this too is *ātman* (self) and *pudgala* (person).
Even if one should attain a fragmentary understanding, one will again fall back into the realm of the self. The true Way does not reside in extensive learning."
It does not lie in powerful memory. The *Buddhapiṭaka* (or *Uṣṇīṣa-vijaya-dhāraṇī*) states:

"Ānanda, although you may memorize and uphold the twelve divisions of the sutras of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, with their pure and wondrous principles as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is not equal to cultivating untainted karma for even a single thought-moment. It further states:

"Ānanda, even if one possesses powerful memory, one cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts; if the outflows of desire are not first eliminated, the accumulation of learning will only lead to [delusion]."
This is an error. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "It only increases one's learning and causes the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi) to grow.
If you wish to cultivate the True Way, you must employ the tranquil illumination of Perfect Enlightenment (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā). When distracted, bring it to rest; when dull, clarify it.

With courageous and diligent effort, forcefully subdue and eliminate the afflictions (kleśa). You must give rise to the Four Great Vows: the vow to deliver all sentient beings, the vow to sever all delusions, and the vow...

In the Dharma-gate of study, one vows to attain the Buddha-way. As the contemplation of the mind advances further, anger, attachment, and sycophancy will no longer arise when confronted with external objects.
Furthermore, regarding all perceived objects as being entirely Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti’s *Vajrasamādhi*), one illuminates them with awakening;

thus, the objects encountered are like ice melting in hot water. Should there suddenly be a heavy obstruction where the state does not recede, one must seek out a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for a definitive resolution.
Discern clearly; thus you may avoid being deluded by false views. If the teacher you seek gives rise to attachment or aversion, you will be unable to enter the ocean of pure awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Pure Karma, you should know: all sentient beings, due to grasping at a self and craving, have wandered through beginningless delusion.
As long as they have not eliminated the four kinds of marks, they cannot achieve bodhi.
Love and hatred arise in their minds, and flattery and crookedness dwell within their thoughts; for this reason, they are frequently bewildered and distressed.
One cannot enter the City of Enlightenment; If one can take refuge in the realm of awakening, First eliminate greed, hatred, and delusion, and let no attachment to dharmas dwell in the mind;
Gradually, one may achieve accomplishment. My own body is fundamentally non-existent—how could love or hate arise?
Such a person seeks out virtuous friends And shall never fall into false views.
To harbor a divergent mind regarding what is sought is ultimately non-attainment.
Master Xi-chu Fu-an Hui said: "The City of Enlightenment" uses a city as a metaphor for enlightenment; this is an instance where both the phenomenon and its metaphor are presented together.
A city has three meanings: first, it defends against external enemies; second, it sustains the populace; and third, it opens its gates to welcome and guide others in.
This means: first, the mind-nature is fully realized so that no delusions enter it, like defending against external enemies;

second, the myriad practices increase perfectly as one perceives virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, like nurturing a multitude of people; third, there is no path that does not lead to the integration of self and others, like opening a gate to welcome them in.
If one can return to and awaken to this *kṣetra*, *kṣetra* is a Sanskrit term for *kṣaṇa*, which here means "moment" (*śe*).

The realms (*dhātu*). This is like the soil of the entire land, none of which is not the king’s domain. Once the practitioner has realized that all phenomena belong to awakening, it is as the saying goes:

"When a person of heterodox views speaks of the True Dharma, the True Dharma also becomes heterodox; when a person of orthodox views perceives heterodox teachings, the heterodox teachings also become true.
Attachment to the Dharma is itself *nirvāṇa*. As for the phrase "my body was originally non-existent," my body is...

This is the root of hatred and attachment. If one wishes to eliminate hatred and attachment, do not cling to this deluded body. Since that which is relied upon is empty, how can that which relies upon it be established?
The reason is this: if the skin no longer exists, where will the hair attach?
Chan Master Zongmi of Guifeng of the Tang Dynasty composed a verse for the chapter on the Bodhisattva Purifier of Karmic Obstructions, which says:
Purifying karma means severing the grasping of self and others; The four marks are all conditions for the delusive habit of ignorance.
Taking the sovereign as the root of the self, The mind harbors a seeker, and thus "person" is established.
The lifespan, karma, and consciousness continue to exist in latent succession; This is beyond the reach of sentient beings, the self, and persons.
From this, the afflictions of hatred and attachment arise; How can one who tastes this city of awakening enter it?
Chapter Nine on the Bodhisattva Purifying All Karmic Obstructions concludes.
In the *Commentary on the Collected Verses of the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhi-citta-uttaratantra-sūtra*, Lecture on the Chapter of Bodhisattva Pujue, Master Cong of Faming says:
"Zen is fundamentally without sickness; that which is sick is not Zen. Sickness is one's own sickness, not [the fault of] Zen."
"Sickness is Zen. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Zen is the Buddha-mind; its wisdom-mirror is perfectly clear and bright. It is also translated as 'abandoning evil.
The Tathāgata’s purely immaculate wisdom originally possesses no evil, for evil is precisely sickness.
The Sage takes Zen as medicine to treat the sicknesses of sentient beings; how could one use sickness to treat the sickness of others? Now, Pujue speaks of Zen with great eloquence."

Regarding "the sick": it is because meditation (*dhyāna*) can cure illness that it is called "meditation-illness. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "A good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is a great causal condition;
therefore, they transform and guide others so that they may attain Buddhahood. Now, those who seek a good spiritual friend refer to one who serves as a teacher and model for others.
Yet in this final age, their own insight is not clear; like one blind person leading another blind person, they only further ruin the eyes of the sightless.

To mistake the heterodox for the orthodox is to deceive oneself and others. My Buddha, foreseeing the future with his far-reaching vision, urgently proclaimed the strategic methods for saving those afflicted by illness.
He spoke of four illnesses; yet in reality, illnesses are immeasurable. Nevertheless, these four illnesses fundamentally arise from the body, and the body arises from the mind.
Since the root of illness lies in the mind, there is no path other than Chan (meditation). However, the human mind has many facets—how tragic!
Since wisdom is not uniform, four illnesses are consequently formed. If one seeks illness within the mind, which mind is the illness and which mind is not?
It can be known by means of the methods of effort, cessation, naturalness, and extinction.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Pujue rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
The Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "If the practitioner still harbors the notion of a self before them, they must not yet apply their efforts.
Only when they have reached this state and all prior faults have been abandoned, and the four marks [of self, person, being, and life] have been eliminated, are they fit for cultivation.

Within the mental application of cultivation, there is again the presence of right and wrong. Since right and wrong exist, awakening is as yet not universal; therefore, one is instructed to rely on a teacher to avoid these pitfalls."
One is submerged in four maladies. Once these four maladies are eliminated, the nature of awakening is free from flaw; only then is awakening truly universal. It is further said:

one must universally awaken to the beginning and the end, universally awaken to the coarse and the subtle, and universally awaken to the shallow and the deep; therefore, you should inquire about this.
The World-Honored One of Great Compassion has eloquently expounded upon the maladies of dhyāna.

Praising the Buddha in the preceding chapter, he skillfully explained the four characteristics, causing the great assembly to experience what they had never known before; their minds were cleared away, and they attained great peace and stability.
This causes the assembly of practitioners to hear what they have never heard before; their minds become suddenly enlightened, and they obtain great benefit.
Master Huì of Fù’ān in Xīshǔ said: "The 'diseases of Chan' are the four marks previously mentioned;
these are the maladies that afflict practitioners while entering Chan contemplation. 'Vastly open' (tàngrán) means like the vast expanse of water, describing a state of profound depth."
"Great peace and stability" refers to the partial realization, partial abandonment, and partial awakening of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas;
these constitute minor peace and stability. Only the Buddha’s full realization of prajñā constitutes great peace and stability.
World-Honored One, in the final age, sentient beings will become increasingly distant from the Buddha; the worthy and holy ones will remain hidden, while false teachings flourish and blaze.
What kind of person should these sentient beings seek? Upon what dharma should they rely? What practices should they perform? What ailments should they eliminate?
How should they resolve their minds, so that these blind masses do not fall into false views?
The Bodhisattva raised these five questions, entreating the Buddha to reveal the truth for the sake of those who were collectively deluded.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground. Thus he made this request three times, beginning again and again until it was complete.
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "This clarifies the intent of the inquiry. It is like a person who has a son; he is especially anxious when that son is ill.
So it is with the Great Compassion of the Bodhisattvas, which first takes pity on the final age when the worthy sages have vanished and the True Dharma is about to sink."
Yet the heterodox and false teachings of the outsiders were interposing themselves like blazing fire, prevailing widely in the world.

This was precisely a time when the seeds of the Buddha were as precarious as stacked eggs and on the verge of being destroyed; it remains unknown how one might cause all sentient beings [to escape this].

Whom does one seek? As it was previously stated that one seeks a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), this question is now asked. Second, by what Dharma does one rely? Third, what practices does one perform?
Fourth, what ailments must one eliminate? [This is done] so that the blind masses of the末法 (final dharma) age and the sightless sentient beings may [attain liberation].
By relying on these dharmas, one does not fall into the false views of the six teachers. However, those who are "blind in a crowd" are simply people who do not see the Path;
they are all termed "blind in a crowd. They are like the blind who, having lost both eyes, cannot see anything at all;
even if they have discourse, it is not true. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "For example, there was a king who said to his great minister: 'You, lead [this man]...'"
A single elephant was brought to show to the blind men. At that time, the minister, having received the command, assembled the blind men and showed them the elephant;
as they each touched it with their hands, the minister immediately returned and reported to the king:
The minister showed the elephant to the group of blind men. The Great King then summoned the blind men and questioned each of them individually, saying, "Have you seen the elephant?
Each of the blind men replied, "I have seen it. The king asked, "What kind of thing is the elephant?
He who had touched the tusks immediately said, "The shape of the elephant is like a radish root. He who had touched the ears said, "The elephant is like a winnowing basket. He who...
He who touched the head said the elephant was like a rock; he who touched the trunk said the elephant was like a pestle;
he who touched the feet said the elephant was like a wooden mortar; he who touched the back said the elephant was like a bed; he who touched the belly said the elephant was like a jar;
and he who touched the tail said the elephant was like a rope. This is what is meant by "a group of blind men feeling an elephant, each describing it differently."
[The Buddha] said: "Suppose those blind men were to open their eyes and clearly perceive their surroundings, thereby verifying the true form of the elephant;

they would never speak of its tail, tusks, or other parts. The 'blind men' mentioned in this sutra are precisely of this category. Question: What is the difference between the "arousing of the mind" (*cittotpāda*) mentioned previously and this "arousing of the mind"? Answer:
It is said that the former refers to arousing the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta*), whereas this refers to arousing the mind of abiding (*vihāra-citta*); therefore, they are not the same.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "The essence of Chan is stillness; the essence of contemplation (guan) is clarity. In Chan, the mind is stilled so that it does not scatter;

in contemplation, the mind is illuminated so that it does not grow dark. For entering the Way of the Mahayana, one takes cessation (shi) and contemplation as the command tent, and employs meditative concentration (ding) and wisdom (hui) as the vanguard.

That they are able to break through enemy lines and destroy demons is truly due to this. As for the current statement regarding 'skillfully explaining the maladies of Chan,' it is intended to eliminate [them]."
Since the Buddha has long since departed, the sages and worthies have vanished; heterodox teachings flourish, and Māra is powerful while the Dharma is weak.
Gold and brass cannot be distinguished, and the Jing and Wei rivers cannot be separated. Illness is preached as medicine, and the heterodox is taken for the orthodox.

A Zhou jade and a Zheng jade share the same name but differ in substance. Without right view, even arduous asceticism is merely labor in vain. Therefore it is said: "What kind of person must one seek in order to correct [the path]?"
Dharmas are also of many kinds: there are false dharmas and true dharmas, evil dharmas and wholesome dharmas. By means of which dharma is the standard established?
Conduct is also of many kinds: there is the correct and the false. All ninety-six types [of heterodox paths] are causes of false conduct;
for instance, when a *pauṣkarasādi* Brahmin saw a bhikṣu’s body suffering from sores and itching, he would cauterize it with fire, and the non-Buddhists witnessed this.
Because they regard scorching the body with fire as the path, there are those who practice the "five heats" (pañcatapana).
Because monks were unable to end their lives, they threw themselves off cliffs; because non-Buddhists (tīrthika) imitated them, there arose practices such as leaping from cliffs and entering fire.

There are even those who go naked and observe precepts regarding chickens and dogs; all of these are heterodox teachings (mithyādharma). Now, upon what basis are these practiced? Such ailments are also many.

There are various kinds: the disease of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the disease of the sands of dust (*rajas*), the disease of ignorance (*avidyā*), the disease of the body, and the disease of the mind.
Those of the Two Vehicles do not recognize these true diseases; they go to impoverished quarters and dwell in thatched huts—these are all diseases within the Buddha-dharma.

By what method should one eliminate these two types of disease? Furthermore, there are many ways to resolve the mind (*cittotpāda*). Now, for one who seeks Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), how should they resolve their mind?
The Bodhicitta. In this regard, one deeply realizes the inconceivable realm. It is like when Sudhana visited the fifty-three spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), each of whom said:
"I have already previously resolved upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; I do not yet know how you, O worthy one, have resolved your mind.
These five matters all pertain to the final age, when the dragons have perished and the tigers have fled, when the orthodox is abandoned and the heterodox flourishes. Throughout...
Awakening is like the spark struck from flint; the Sugata is like the echo returning from a valley.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Universal Awakening, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
That you are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding such practice is capable of bestowing upon all sentient beings of the final age the fearless eye of the Way."
He can cause sentient beings to purify their Dharma-eye and not fear the afflictions of Māra, enabling those beings to attain the Noble Path. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Pujue (Universal Awakening), receiving these instructions with joy, along with the great assembly, listened in silence.
Master Cong of Siming said: "To resolve the mind and cultivate practice, one must first seek out a person of correct knowledge and vision to provide definitive discernment.

Good son, when sentient beings of the末法 (mofa) age are about to resolve their great mind and seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) with the desire to cultivate practice, they should seek out those who possess all correct knowledge and vision."

Chan Master Fu’an Huì of Xishu said: "Those who wish to cultivate *yuanjue* (perfect enlightenment) must give rise to an immeasurable and vast mind and draw near to great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
To select the right person for this means to choose one who possesses correct knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*).
One who possesses all forms of correct knowledge and vision is one who is entirely free from attachment to any kind of conceptual views."

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "The 'Great Mind' is the bodhicitta. To cultivate Perfect Enlightenment, if one does not take the Great Way as one's mind, who could possibly accomplish such a great resolve?
Those who give rise to the Great Mind are many, but those who attain Buddhahood are few. As the Sutra says:

'Among the three things—the fish eggs, the āmra flowers, and the Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds—these are numerous within the causal stage; yet when the time comes for fruition, they are few.'"
The fruit is few. Although fish produce many offspring, those that become full-grown fish are few; they are damaged by wind, waves, and surges, so that many are lost and few are perfected.
When the *āmra* flower blooms, the blossoms are many, but those that bear fruit are few. It is the same with the Bodhisattva’s generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
One hundred people may resolve their minds toward enlightenment, yet it is not certain that even one among them will attain Buddhahood.

For example, the Buddha and Ānanda both resolved their minds on the Path during the time of the past Buddha Śūnyarāja; however, Ānanda delighted in extensive learning, while Śākyamuni was diligent in energetic exertion.
Thus, when the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood, Ānanda became his attendant. An Shigao practiced together with another person; although this person—
While practicing the path, his mind was prone to much anger. An Shigao said to him, "You are similar to me; you are not beneath me.
If you do not restrain your anger, I fear you will sink into ruin. After death, you will become a great python at Hongting Lake, possessing a majestic presence that extends for a thousand *li*.
You will be able to divide the wind to send forth boats and receive the sacrificial offerings of living beings. Later, you will encounter me as I manifest my body."
Upon meeting, they recounted the aforementioned matters in detail. They took all the gold and silk accumulated within the temple and offered it to Śrīmitra to build a monastery;
subsequently, they were reborn in the celestial realms. Thus, maintaining the precepts in one's heart is something difficult for people to achieve.

Now, having resolved to cultivate the Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa), using the contemplation of stillness and illumination to observe the mind, one must likewise seek out a person of correct knowledge and vision. Next, one must select the proper application of the mind from the very beginning.
If one takes even a single step toward what is deviant, one will remain a member of Māra’s retinue for the rest of one’s life. Those who seek correct knowledge and vision (samyag-jñāna-darśana) say:

"One uses the Buddha-eye to see within the mind; this is called 'knowing. One may only study the Buddha’s knowledge and vision for six periods, and only thereafter employ the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."

To transform and guide sentient beings is not the domain of Buddhas and spiritual friends alone; it extends universally to include both ordinary and sagely beings, as well as teachers of the laity and teachers of men.

During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were those with the four levels of faith; after his passing, there are those of the five grades. One who is fully awakened and skillfully employs knowledge and vision is the one to whom this question is addressed.
People of the present day cannot distinguish between beans and wheat; when encountering others, they first accept whoever enters their path as their master, even while avoiding false teachers.
It is like avoiding snakes and tigers; it is like entering a land of contagious poisons where not even a drop of water may moisten one's lips. As the ancients said:
"It would be better to break the precepts as high as Mount Sumeru than to be tainted by a false teacher. If [the influence] enters the *ālayavijñāna* for even a single thought-moment..."
Even throughout eternal kalpas, it cannot be grasped.
One whose mind does not dwell on signs is a person of right knowledge and vision; such a person’s mind does not cling to signs.
One who possesses correct knowledge and vision does not cling to the realms of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
their mind does not adhere to the realms of the two vehicles. The Essential Dharma of Mind Transmission states:
"Those who awaken by means of vocal teaching are called Śrāvakas; those who awaken by contemplating causes and conditions are called Pratyekabuddhas."
Though they manifest within the afflictions of worldly toil, their minds remain ever pure.
A person of right knowledge and vision, though transforming their body within the midst of worldly toil, has never experienced any defilement or attachment in their mind.
He manifests various faults.

One who possesses correct knowledge and vision, when manifesting these various faults and afflictions, does so desiring to engage in the same activities as sentient beings (*samānārthatā*) in order to gather and transform them.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "He manifests the practice of desire while remaining free from all defiled attachments; he manifests a mind of afflictions..."
This is the one who is eternally pure.
He praises the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and does not allow sentient beings to enter into non-discipline.
Although he manifests various faults and calamities, he also constantly praises the true holy life, ensuring that sentient beings do not fall into them.
Even within rituals that do not rely upon the Vinaya,
one who seeks such a person will immediately attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Those who resolve their minds to practice must seek out individuals possessing this right knowledge and right view to serve as their teachers and friends;
only then can they achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). The *Tripiṭaka* states: *A* means "non-";
*nuttara* means "supreme"; *samyak* means "right"; *saṃ* means "equal"; and *bodhi* means "awakening."
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "This answer is intended for those who have been instructed by a clear master and are ready to serve him;
it is for those about to give rise to the Great Mind, distinguishing them from those of the Two Vehicles who give rise to the Small Mind. This belongs to the Right Cause."
Seeking a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) pertains to the primary condition (pratyaya). However, the internal cause is proximate while the external conditions are remote.

For example, the seed is the cause, whereas soil, water, and so forth are the conditions. The cause resides within, while the conditions exist without; thus, although the seed itself is already present, [it cannot sprout without conditions].
If it does not rely upon soil and water, it will not sprout.
Although soil and water can cause growth, if there is no seed at the time, the soil and water likewise cannot bring it into existence. It is the same for the practitioner learning the Dharma:
although one possesses Buddha-nature within, if one does not rely on the guidance and instruction of a teacher, the Buddha-nature likewise cannot be manifested. As it is said:
Earth, wood, tiles, and rubble have no Buddha-nature by nature; thus, even one who acts as their teacher cannot cause them to possess it.

From this we know that causes are intimate while conditions are remote. Now, when this practitioner has internally generated the Great Mind and externally seeks a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), the causes and conditions are fully assembled.
Once causes and conditions are complete, the Way of the Buddha is finally accomplished. Why is this so?

This is understood. In the *Avataṃsaka*, Mañjuśrī tells Sudhana: "To draw near to and make offerings to spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the primary causal condition for possessing all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
The *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (The Light Praising Prajñā) states:
"Those who wish to study the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) should follow true spiritual friends and always serve those with right knowledge and vision."
This refers to a person. One should seek such a person who possesses all-encompassing right knowledge and vision;
that is, one who well understands the profound Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and of non-arising and non-ceasing;

one who has thoroughly realized that all phenomena, from the very beginning, are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of mental objects, and free from the characteristics of subject and object—ultimately equal, indestructible, and devoid of karma.
There is no retribution; there is neither cause nor effect. Its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*); it abides in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Only then, within ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), does one unfailingly and vigorously establish all phenomena. Such a person is called one who possesses right knowledge and vision.
"The mind not dwelling on signs" means it is free from the realm of afflictions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

"Not clinging to the realm of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas" means it is free from the realm of stagnation in quiescence belonging to the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). As the Sūtra says: "It would be better to be in hell..."
For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they never give rise to the mind of the two vehicles. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"If I were to transform others through the Lesser Vehicle, I would fall into stinginess and greed; such a thing is impossible.

This person of right knowledge and vision, throughout the twelve periods of the day, keeps their mind constantly distant from the realms of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles. Nevertheless, they manifest greed and anger as skillful means.
Regarding delusion (*moha*): although one is amidst the defiled realms of the dust-laden afflictions within the three worlds, the mind is never stained or attached.
This is also as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: the woman Puṣpamitrā was not drowned by the waters of desire; King Anala was not burned by the fire of hatred;
and the Brahmin Jvalanaprabha was not deluded by the perversity of ignorance. It further says: "When a Bodhisattva lives at home..."
Together with his wife and children, he has never abandoned the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). He manifests various faults while praising pure conduct (*brahmacarya*).
This person of right knowledge and vision, through the power of vows made over immeasurable eons, desires to deliver sentient beings who possess faults;
thus, he provisionally employs the method of "commonality of purpose" (*samānārthatā*) to gather them in with affection, ensuring that their minds harbor no mutual suspicion, and so forth.
One must have a mind of intimacy; only when there is mutual intimacy is one capable of receiving instruction, and thus one may teach them. One should tell them:

"If you give rise to lust, anger, ignorance, and so forth, these are transgressions that will cause you to fall into the three miserable realms. If you cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom..."
This is the practice that transcends dreams and illusions, that emerges from saṃsāra, and is truly pure.
Thus, through various praises of the brahmacarya, one constantly causes all sentient beings to enter into the ritual procedures of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Do not allow others to fall away from the Buddha-dharma into the ways of Māra, heterodox paths, or ordinary people who lack discipline and rules.
Generally speaking, that which possesses rules is called the Buddha-dharma; that which lacks rules is the dharma of the heterodox paths. Question:
Regarding the present Buddha-dharma, I do not yet know what its rules are. Answer: There is the dharma of the rules of True Emptiness (śūnyatā). These rules...
This is the method of the Dharma; it can cause the practitioner to sever hindrances and shatter doubts, realize the essence, and give rise to its function.
If those who receive the teaching seek such a person of right knowledge and vision, they will immediately achieve the realization of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "From 'the mind does not dwell on appearances' to 'entering into non-discipline,' one who possesses the mind of the Great Way must certainly not dwell on appearances.
They do not cling to existence or non-existence, nor are they intoxicated by sound or form. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
'They do not cling to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangibles. The mind of such a person is like empty space; like a bird flying through the sky, it does not dwell anywhere."
Emptiness. A mind that dwells upon signs is the mind of ordinary beings, the mind of the two vehicles, or a stubborn, partial, and deluded mind;
these are all minor paths, the tracks upon which swallows and sparrows roam. If it is the mind of the Great Way, that is the realm of the Buddhas.
This is the realm of the Bodhisattva, like the path traversed by a great elephant; therefore it is said:

"The Bodhisattva of the Ten Good Deeds, having resolved upon the Great Mind, forever parts from the ocean of suffering in the three realms. The Śrāvaka merely severs the delusions of views and thought, while the Pratyekabuddha further erodes the residual habits (*vāsanā*).
Yet they lack the mind of compassion and do not deliver sentient beings, like a deer leaping alone without looking back at the herd behind.
Furthermore, one who possesses right knowledge and vision is like a fine jade gem dwelling among mountain rocks;
though mixed within the human world, they may manifest the coarse and evil conditions of worldly toil, yet this is not like a tiger wearing a sheep’s skin.
Just as when fishing, if there is no fragrant bait, the fish will not swallow the hook, so too the wise person employs the fragrant bait as a Buddha-work to cast their net.
The fish of sentient beings within the Dharma-realm are like Master Fu (Fotuo Dashi), who had a wife, children, and kinsmen, and engaged in worldly affairs.
Did Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty not recognize such a man? When Layman Pang’s hundred thousand households of wealth were sunk in the Xiang River, was it because he clung to riches?
At the moment of death, he said: "I only wish to empty all that is seen; be careful not to reify what is non-existent. This...

The two Great Beings [Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti] took hold of wealth, wives, and children, yet they praised the cultivation of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (Perfect Enlightenment), instructing them to sever desire and delusion.

For those remaining in the secular world, they taught that one should not be ensnared by desire; all of this was a skillful means (*upāya*) for entering the discipline (*vinaya*). As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"He manifests the acceptance of the five desires, yet he is also seen practicing dhyāna. It further says: "He manifests having a wife and children, yet he always delights in solitude and detachment."
All of these demonstrate the faults [of other paths]. One who seeks such a person will attain the realization of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Such a person is one whose eyes are upright according to the path of the four reliances (*catur-apāśraya*).

The nine characters beginning with "Anuttara" (無上) are translated as "Unsurpassed Perfectly Equal and Right Enlightenment. A spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) reveals this to people through right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
The precepts of restraint prevent what is non-virtuous; such a person immediately attains the sphere of right-minded conduct, which is the unsurpassed state.
Relying upon this, they give rise to the bodhicitta and all enter the ocean of sarvajñā (omniscience).
Sentient beings of the末代 (final age) who encounter such a person should make offerings to them, not sparing even their own bodies or lives.
Upon seeing one who possesses correct knowledge and correct view, they must make offerings and inquire about the Dharma, never begrudging their body or life.
The ancients who stood in the snow until it reached their waists or severed their arms to seek the Dharma did precisely according to this principle.
Chan Master Fuan Hui of Xishu said: "This passage speaks of the difficulty of relinquishing internal wealth, yet one must still relinquish it.
This means that for a person who has decisively discerned true right view, they should immediately cast off their own body, which is as ephemeral and illusory as a bubble."
With a substance of adamantine and indestructible quality—just as one might exchange an earthenware vessel for a golden jar—it was the Youth of the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat-kumāra*).

As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "I recall that in the past, when I was a brahmin dwelling in the Snowy Mountains practicing the bodhisattva path, there was no Buddha, nor were there any sūtras or Dharma. At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, beheld me."
He tested him by transforming his body into the form of a rākṣasa, which was most terrifying.
Standing before the Bodhisattva, he recited half a verse. Upon hearing the verse, the Bodhisattva felt great joy;

he rose from his seat, lifted up his hair with his hand, and looked in the four directions until he beheld only the Bodhisattva. He then went to him and asked: "Great Being, where did you obtain this?"
This meaning of the half-verse is the true path of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. The rākṣasa said, "You need not ask this.
It has already been many days since I last ate; tormented by hunger and thirst, my mind is distracted and my words are deluded.
This is not something known from my own original intent. The Bodhisattva said, "If you can recite this verse for me in its entirety, I shall [protect you] until the end."
As your disciple, I must speak: your wisdom is excessive; you worry only for yourself and pay no heed to me at all.
Now, driven by hunger, I truly cannot speak. The Bodhisattva asked, "What food do you eat?
He replied, "That which I eat is only the warm flesh and hot blood of humans. The Bodhisattva said, "Simply recite these verses for me in their entirety."
[The discourse] concluded. [The youth] said, "I shall offer my own body as a gift. Kṣānti asked, "Who will believe that you would discard your beloved body for the sake of eight words?
The Bodhisattva said, "Now, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Great Kings shall bear witness for me. Kṣānti immediately granted his permission.
Thereupon, he stripped off his skin-clothing to serve as a Dharma-seat and said, "I pay homage; please sit upon this seat and teach me well."
Kṣānti immediately spoke these words: "When birth and death have ceased, and cessation has occurred, tranquility is bliss. Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisattva reflected deeply;
he then inscribed this verse upon stone walls in various places. He then climbed a tall tree and threw himself down.
Before he had even reached the ground, various sounds issued from the sky. At that time, Kṣānti was [confronted by] Śakra.
He received the bodhisattva with his body, placed him on level ground, and after performing repentance and prostrations, departed.
That spiritual friend constantly manifested purity throughout the four modes of conduct, even manifesting various forms of faults and afflictions.
The mind should be free from arrogance.
Good friend, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—amidst these four modes of deportment—one should always manifest pure conduct.
If, suddenly, all manner of faults and afflictions should appear, the student’s mind must not give rise to arrogance.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "The four modes of deportment are walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
'Constantly manifesting purity' refers to the aforementioned forward movement; 'various faults and evils' refers to the aforementioned reverse movement."
Therefore, Yongjia said: "Whether it be right or wrong, people do not recognize whether it is acting against or with the flow; even Heaven cannot fathom it. The commentary states:
"The expedient path of the Bodhisattva’s manifestations is difficult to fathom. One should simply rely on the Dharma-gate and not doubt his traces."
One does not act out of mere conformity; rather, one manifests sincere devotion. Alternatively, upon seeing someone acting contrary to the teachings, one might give rise to arrogance.

The Chan school also says: "Simply pluck the fruit; do not question its tree. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Regarding all teachers and venerables, one should regard them as the World-Honored One.
If there are those who explain profound meanings and unravel the knots of doubt, they are of benefit to me. Therefore...
One should honor them with all one's heart and not dwell on their other faults. It is like a worn-out bag containing jewels;
one must not fail to take the jewels simply because the bag is bad. Or again, it is like traveling at night along a perilous path where a person carries a torch;
one must not fail to take advantage of the light simply because the person is bad. A bodhisattva is just the same: they obtain the radiance of wisdom from their teacher.
Nor should one take account of their faults. For it is difficult to be a teacher and not easy to be a disciple. Do not, on account of this precept, mistakenly revere a coarse person.
If you wish to verify what is true or false, conduct a discernment as previously described; follow and uphold [the teachings] accordingly. Furthermore, this medicine is for treating disciples;
let the teacher not mistakenly ingest it, for if ingested, it will increase the illness until no medicine can cure it. It is just as the Sūtra says: "Shaving the head..."
Whether one wears the *kāṣāya* while observing the precepts or violating them, gods and humans shall always make offerings to them, ensuring they never lack for anything.
To provide such support is what is called "making offerings. Furthermore, I have said:
"Even a monk who has broken the precepts is superior to diligent non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*). This is a medicine for the laity to take; a disciple of the Buddha must not take it."
