Upon wearing it, one immediately enters hell. It is further said that for a person who has broken the precepts, five hundred great ghosts constantly stand before them, sweeping away their footprints;
such a person may not walk upon the ground of a king, nor may they drink the water of a king.

It would be better to have one's body crushed by an iron mallet until it is like dust, or to have one's body wrapped in hot iron, and to undergo all manner of such sufferings, than for one whose body and speech violate the precepts to receive the clothing, food, drink, and bedding offered out of faith by donors; this is the way of a bhikṣu.
The medicine they take is not for the laity to consume; if the laity were to take it, they too would enter hell.
Therefore, those of the later generations—both monastics and laypeople—should strive to understand the Buddha’s words well.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "In the past, Śākyamuni was a king who abdicated his throne to seek the Dharma from the Rishi Asita for a thousand years.
During that time, he offered his own body as a bed and seat so that the Rishi could rise and sit upon it.

Furthermore, for a thousand years, he gathered firewood and drew water, never allowing his resolve for the Way to regress. Thus, he attained Buddhahood. Is this not indeed an example of not begrudging [one's life]?"
Regarding body and life: Furthermore, in the past, there was a wild fox who, being pursued by a lion, fled for its life and fell into a pit.
Having no means of escape, the fox reflected from the bottom of the deep pit and spoke this verse to itself: "It is a pity that this body is not fed to the lion;
had it been fed to the lion, I too would have gained merit. Now I shall die an unjust death, and this body will perish in vain without benefit."
Regarding this matter, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard from afar the fox reciting the verse. He descended to see him and, standing above the pit, asked the fox:
"You do not spare your own life and possess right knowledge and vision; I now wish to hear your Dharma—may you speak it. The fox replied:
"How could a Dharma Master be below while his disciple is above, and yet the disciple preach the essentials of the Dharma? Śakra...

He brought it forth by means of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). Even after it was brought forth, [the Buddha] was still unwilling to speak. [The Bodhisattva] folded his robe to serve as a seat and requested him to preach;

this was because such matters pertain to the Buddha’s stages of practice (*bhūmi*). Instances such as these are all exemplary models. For sentient beings of the final age who seek perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), how could they allow their own arbitrary whims to sink them into the waves of Saṃsāra?
How could they fail to "strike the bone to extract the marrow" in order to seek Prajñā? Indeed, they must not harbor [such narrow-mindedness].
How much more so regarding the faults of a mind of pride?

Furthermore, for one who seeks the Dharma, even their own body and life should not be cherished, let alone the accumulation of wealth, wives, children, and kinsmen. How much less so the hoarding of treasures, wives, children, and kin?
"Is it something belonging to the body, or something external to the body?
Master Huì of Fù'ān in Xīshū said: "This is the ease with which one relinquishes external wealth. This is the character *tuó*.
Guifeng’s commentary states: This is an error or omission by the translator. Since ancient times in the Western Heavens (India), spoons and chopsticks were not used;
food was eaten by grasping it with the hand, which is called "hand-grasped food" (*piṇḍa-bhakṣa*).

During the Later Tang period, the Tripitaka Master Yijing considered that this term did not fully encompass the methods of eating, as it could not include liquids such as water or broth, nor moist substances which cannot be grasped. Consequently, he changed it [to *piṇḍapāta*].
The character used here is "duàn" (段), meaning a portion or segment, such as a single piece of food in this region.

The *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* also employs this character "duàn. That the present sutra uses "tuó" (摶) instead is an error or an abbreviation; one should further add the character "shí" (食) to read, "furthermore, as for *kavaḍīkāhāra* (segmented food).
In this region, [the term] is not abbreviated; now there is only the character "tuó," which is an abbreviation. Food.
There are four kinds: first, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); second, contact-food (*sparśa-āhāra*); third, volition-food (*manasikāra-āhāra*);

and fourth, consciousness-food (*vijñāna-āhāra*). Now, edible food has transformation as its characteristic; contact-food has the contact with objects as its characteristic; volition and consciousness have aspiration as their characteristic;
and consciousness-food has predominance as its characteristic. These do not depart from the first three types of food. "Wealth" refers to money and riches, as well as bolts of silk.
One's wife and children are one's most intimate kinsmen, as are one's servants and attendants;

the meaning is that if one encounters those aforementioned individuals who know reality and recognize the mind, who understand the disease of ignorance and know the medicine of correct vision, it would be difficult for oneself to relinquish even one's own person.

If one can even give up and offer such things as these, how much more so should one practice giving those things that are easily relinquished—such as food for the body, money, bolts of silk, wives, children, and servants? How could one fail to practice generosity toward them?
If a son of good family does not give rise to evil thoughts toward that spiritual friend, he will be able to ultimately achieve perfect enlightenment.
All states of doubt are termed "evil thoughts. Only when a practitioner does not give rise to such evil thoughts toward a virtuous teacher can they achieve the fruit of Buddhahood.
The mind-flower radiates brilliance, illuminating the lands of the ten directions;
the light of the mind manifests, shining upon all buddha-fields.
Master Fu’an Huì of Xichuan said: "This reveals that drawing near to virtuous friends brings great benefit. That is to say:
Whether one encounters a virtuous friend through adversity or favor, one must not harbor a mind of arrogance.

Should an evil thought arise, it will immediately create obstructions that shroud one's own mind, preventing entry into the Dharma. Since ancient times, those who act as teachers have never been ordinary.
Receiving the Dharma is not an easy matter. The *Dharmapada* states: "Regarding whatever actions a virtuous friend performs, one should not give rise to even a hair’s breadth of doubt.
If one cannot receive the profound verses of the Dharma correctly, it is as stated in the "Fisherman" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*:
"To encounter an elder and fail to show respect is a breach of propriety; to see a worthy person and fail to honor them is a lack of benevolence. Such conduct does not reach the ultimate.
A person who cannot humble themselves toward others, and whose humility is not sincere, fails to attain the truth and thus suffers long-term harm to their person. Alas!

Such lack of benevolence toward others brings about no greater calamity. Once one is free from the obscuration of evil thoughts, they will find joyful companions who will guide and instruct them in the unsurpassed, wondrous Way.
By relying upon their teachings, one will ultimately master the Dharma-gate and achieve attainment.
One achieves the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas of the ten directions. This perfect enlightenment does not depart from the single mind;
it is the awakening of the mind itself. Once the light of wisdom has been manifested, there is no defilement in whatever one encounters.
It is luminously clear and pure, like a hundred flowers in full bloom, illuminating and penetrating everything throughout the worlds of the ten directions. From this point, one returns to the source.
Returning to the source, one transcends the mundane and enters the sacred; once attained, this state endures forever until the limits of the future, its enjoyment inexhaustible.
Thus, we know that drawing near to virtuous friends is by no means a minor benefit.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Furthermore, let alone the accumulation of wealth; it extends even to illuminating the lands of the ten directions.

People of the world know only how to employ phenomena (shi), but do not know how to employ principle (li). Phenomena are precisely lust, anger, and ignorance—dharmas that are by nature unwholesome. Wholesomeness lies in their employment."

Principle (*li*) is precisely lust, anger, and ignorance; it is precisely the gate of great liberation. For ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, the Buddha teaches the departure from lust, anger, and ignorance;
for Bodhisattvas, he teaches that lust, anger, and ignorance are all the Buddha-dharma.

As in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when the monk Susīma used the dharma of lust to guide people, those who responded with a "míng" sound and those who responded with a "cuì" sound all attained samādhi. Aṅgulimāla...
Māra the Wrathful held a sword and sought to kill the Buddha, shouting at him, "Gautama! Stop! Stop! The Buddha said, "It is you who do not stop; it is you who turn me back to stop.
Upon these words, Aṅgulimālya was enlightened to his own nature; he cast down his sword and realized arhatship.
Those who skillfully employ evil dharmas to enter the Way are called "entering Māra. Māra and the Buddha are one and the same.

There is no duality in suchness. When the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada spread gold over the ground to purchase a garden for the construction of a monastery, how could the accumulation of wealth have caused him to cease being a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?
While the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda was still a layman, he loved his wife so much that they would not part.
When the Buddha went out to beg for alms, his brother Nanda brought a bowl of rice to present to the Buddha. His...
His wife took a drop of saliva and smeared it upon her husband’s nose, ensuring that it did not dry. She led him back to the Jeta Grove and forcibly compelled him to shave his head.
The Buddha had him hold the corner of his *kāṣāya* robe as they traveled through the celestial palaces. Nanda saw the beauty of the heavenly maidens.
He asked the goddess, "Why do you have no husband? The goddess replied, "The Buddha’s younger brother Nanda has come here as a man who upholds the precepts.
Subsequently, Nanda maintained the precepts, later attained arhatship, and received a prophecy that he would become a buddha.
How can one who possesses a mind stained by attachment deceive others and fail to achieve the realization of sainthood?
King Śibi killed five hundred Brahmins and was reborn in heaven, while the five hundred fell into hell. As such, the sutras and śāstras take delusion and transgression as the very work of the Buddha;
it may be said that the lotus grows from the mud and does not arise on dry land. If, within this state of delusion...

The true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is like ice being water. Evil possesses all wholesome dharmas; thus, the dharma-gate of the inherently evil nature (*prakṛti-pāpa-dharmamukha*) also functions as a rational poison.
It is like a physician who thoroughly understands all diseases: for a "wholesome" illness, one uses ginseng and *fuling* (poria cocos) to treat it;
yet there are other fevers that must be treated with "Yellow Dragon Decoction," which is cured by yellow dragon dung.
It is pure. Because it cures illness, one does not loathe the impurity of the medicine; this can be understood through reflection.
As soon as the flower of the mind brightens, the Buddha-lands of the ten directions naturally manifest before one—like the moon shining brightly upon a clear pond.
"Good son, the wondrous Dharma realized by that spiritual friend should be free from the four illnesses. What are these four illnesses?

In the cultivation and realization of Perfect Enlightenment, one must not give rise to the minds of effort, cessation, acceptance, or extinction. To possess these four mental states constitutes the four illnesses."
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "From here below, he distinguishes the four illnesses and instructs on how to eliminate them.
First is the illness of effort; second is the illness of cessation; third is the illness of indifference; and fourth is the illness of extinction.
This is first presented as a general outline, stating: 'The wondrous Dharma realized by that Good Knowledge-Holder—this Dharma is the very substance upon which one relies.'"

Above, it was stated that one must be free from the four maladies of effort (*zuò*), cessation (*zhǐ*), spontaneity (*rèn*), and extinction (*miè*). However, although mental maladies are boundless, they are essentially limited to these four;
if even one of them is present, one is unfit to be a teacher. Furthermore, the text raises the question: "What are these four maladies?
The following passage answers this by identifying and demonstrating their characteristics one by one.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: The *Lotus Sūtra* states, "A good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is a great causal condition;

that is to say, they transform and guide others, enabling them to see the Buddha. The *Dhyāna Sūtra* says, "Although all conditions may be complete, the guidance [of enlightenment] depends on a skilled master;
thus, the good spiritual friend is the observer. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states, "Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are good spiritual friends," and [the nature of] the Dharma-realm (*dharmatā*).
The reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) are spiritual friends;
through them, one achieves perfect awakening. The *Avataṃsaka* states: "There are demons of spiritual friends, demons of samādhi, and demons of the bodhicitta.

These demons can cause people to abandon the good and follow evil, and they can also transform people so that they fall into the stages of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). A sutra says: "Except for the reality of all phenomena..."
Characteristics. All else that is external is the work of Māra. How could one not discern such things?

If one does not recognize them, then even a person of right knowledge and vision who is fit to be relied upon will be like a turbid water or a clouded pearl; what leisure will there be to pacify the mind, and what leisure to cultivate contemplation?
Therefore, it is said that this is a great causal condition. Now it is said that one should distance oneself from the four maladies.
These are the four maladies of those who act as teachers themselves; they are not the four maladies of their disciples. Now, those who act as teachers say of themselves:
"What I have attained is profound and subtle; it is not within the realm of you disciples. This is truly what the Māra-king speaks. If one truly knows [this],...
The realm realized by consciousness is like a bird flying through the sky: it does not abide in the sky, yet it traverses the sky of its own accord; there is nothing traversed in that traversal.

Sentient beings sever afflictions where there is nothing to be severed; they study dharma-gates where there is nothing to be studied; they accomplish the Buddha-way where there is nothing to be accomplished.

First is the "disease of fabrication. If there is someone who says, "I shall perform various practices within my original mind, desiring to seek perfect enlightenment," this is called a disease because the nature of perfect enlightenment is not something that can be attained through fabrication.

"Performing various practices" refers to cultivating all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) practices. Because the wondrous nature of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) is not attained through causes or through the conditioned, it is said that "it is not obtained through effort.

The *Commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* also states: "Since this involves contrived activity and the arising of mental states, how could it be consistent with non-action (*asaṃskṛta*) and tranquil illumination?"
Master Cíhuì of Fù’ān in Western Shu said: The *Śūramgama-sūtra* states:

"Whether one engages in contemplation and deliberation, calculation and estimation, initiating mental activity and manifesting conduct, constructing stupas or temples, making offerings to the Buddha or the Sangha, reciting mantras or sutras, delivering monastic or lay lectures, sitting upright in meditation, or performing various other activities, such as dwelling in deep mountains..."
Traversing through worlds, they diligently worry over food and clothing, claiming these are the conditions for the Way; thus they undergo hunger and cold, regarding them as meritorious deeds.

They contemplate emptiness and contemplate existence, loving the body and then loathing it. Among the many gates of practice, they grasp at one and rely upon this single practice, desiring to accord with the awakened mind.
Since this is a conditioned fabrication born of emotional sentiment, how could it possibly accord with the principle of unconditioned, tranquil illumination?

This illness arises from the previous illusory contemplation (*māyā-darśana*). It was said that all Bodhisattvas initiate their practice from this point and, throughout the various stages (*cakra*), they all engage in practice for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Now, having lost the intended meaning of those texts, this has become a pathological obsession.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "When the Master Zhiyi taught *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, he did so precisely to treat these various ailments of sentient beings.
He remarked that 'recently, many have attached themselves to non-Buddhist paths within the Buddha-dharma,' and further stated that 'these individuals give rise to views based upon the Dharma;

such attainments are likewise infinite. If one does not investigate with meticulous detail, it is difficult to distinguish between right and wrong; errors and contradictions will cause the heterodox and the orthodox to become confused.'"
Confused. To err by a hair’s breadth is to miss by billions. The true Dharma cannot be distinguished; jade and stone remain undifferentiated.
Thus one errs both for oneself and for others, and both fall into ruin. How much more so regarding the views of outsiders? They also claim that what is spoken is subtle;
they view the physical marks and likewise fashion them into the form of a Buddha, like the two fruits, the *cintāmaṇi* and the *karkaṭaka*. Their appearance—
Their appearance is generally the same. One can kill a person; the other can revive a person. The *cintāmaṇi* (vintage-ga) is like a persimmon:
the *śubha* (good) variety is beneficial, while the *kalaka* (black/evil) variety is harmful. Those who do not recognize them may mistakenly ingest the latter, which causes great injury.

Even if one follows the instructions of a teacher, there is fear of falling into the two vehicles, external paths, the realm of Māra, or the self-view (*ātman*), all of which are entirely binding dharmas and not states of liberation. We [should] mutually [recognize this].

No. Because they take what is merely a minor realization as *nirvāṇa*, they remain submerged in birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Where there is attachment, they give rise to craving; where there is aversion, they give rise to anger.
Though they possess compassion, it results only in views of attachment. Though they practice self-mortification, it is ultimately nothing but forced endurance.

Though they possess all-encompassing knowledge, it does not transcend mere speculative calculation. Though they have supernormal powers, they are all merely transformations produced by outflows (*āsrava*). As for the four *Vedas* they study...
Regarding the Dharma scriptures: it is not through the power of *dhāraṇī* that one severs the dull afflictions (*dauṣṭhulya-kleśa*). Though these may be severed, they are like a centipede;

once the worldly physician has treated the ailment and the patient recovers, eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*) arise again, gathering into a vast ocean. The net of suffering within the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) is boundless.
How can such things as these be considered the true Dharma? Furthermore, as for the various Buddhas preaching the Dharma of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is for...
Those who cling to existence, or those who cling to emptiness, cannot be transformed by the Buddhas.

To act as if creating something is to create through the body; yet this body is illusory, a mere provisional designation for "body. Even if one could manifest the body of a Buddha, it still cannot be regarded as the true Buddha.
To cherish it is an error, for one will then follow the ranks of the heterodox, such as Kūṭadanta.
The Venerable One transformed a non-Buddhist practitioner; that practitioner was able to manifest the thirty-two marks of a Buddha, indistinguishable from the Buddha himself.

When it came to foxes possessing supernatural powers, a celestial fox was able to manifest the body of a Buddha. If one engages in intentional creation, whether creating as a living being, creating as a Buddha, or creating as a human.
One may become a celestial deity or a Mara king; one must skillfully discern this.

My original mind has performed various kinds of practices, yet this mind is illusory and floating, replete with many clever views—how can it be trusted? One should instead take up *perfect enlightenment* (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) by means of this very illusion.
Moreover, Perfect Enlightenment does not belong to the realm of delusion, nor is it attained through artificial effort; therefore, it is said that "it is not attained through action.

If one relies upon true perfection, this is the Real Mark (*dharmatā*). The Real Mark is itself wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*). It is collectively termed "Dharma" and is also called the "Dharmakāya.
If one practices in reliance upon the Dharmakāya and the Real Mark, then even during the time of practice, there is the vision of the Real Mark Dharma.
The body likewise lacks a self that can cultivate *pariṇirvāṇa-bodhi* (perfect enlightenment), nor is there another who can cultivate it; do not give rise to the notion of "mine.
One must also know that the nature of the mind capable of cultivation is fundamentally empty and quiescent. When one's own mind is naturally empty, neither sin nor merit has a master.

Although one does not seek to produce *pariṇirvāṇa-bodhi*, *pariṇirvāṇa-bodhi* arrives of its own accord, like a reflection in a mirror: it is simply a matter of exhausting the defilements upon the mirror. The mirror—
What need is there for those of middle capacity to worry?
Second is the illness of non-action (*anābhoga*). If there are people who speak thus: "We now neither sever birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor seek nirvāṇa;
we have no thought of arising or ceasing regarding nirvāṇa or saṃsāra, but leave everything as it is, following the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*)."
In seeking perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), that nature of perfect enlightenment is called a "sickness" because it does not exist by mere indulgence.
This means that if one does not sever saṃsāra, does not seek nirvāṇa, neither gives rise to thoughts nor extinguishes them,

and follows conditions and indulges the mind in the hope of realizing perfect enlightenment— without knowing that the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment does not arise from such indulgence of the mind— [it is a sickness].
Because it is capable of awakening, it is said not to be subject to existence. The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué shū*) also states:
"Even if one does not restrict [it] as either good or evil, it is then termed the nature of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)."
Chan Master Fuaan Hui of Xishu said: "The commentary states: Previously, one was driven about in search of the Buddha;
now, one lets the body and mind go free. The intention is that birth and death are empty—what more is there to sever? Nirvana is fundamentally quiescent—why rely on cultivation or seeking?
Without aversion or delight, and without the thought of acting or ceasing, simply accord with reality within all phenomena."
Suchness is spontaneous: heaven is high and earth is deep; fire is hot and water is moist; wind moves and earth is still;
pines are straight and thorns are crooked; cranes are white and crows are black. Each of these distinct categories possesses its own nature as a matter of spontaneity.
Nowadays, there are a certain class of people who say: "Let the false follow its falsity, and let the true remain in its truth; each shall be called according to its own mind—why must it be changed?"
If one acts, one must act with total commitment; if one prefers idleness, one must remain idle. When hungry, one eats; when encountering clothing, one wears it.
One remains ignorant of all matters, whether good or bad, proceeding spontaneously and living in accordance with conditions. When weary, one lies down; when energetic, one moves.
Whether going east, west, south, or north, why fixate on staying or leaving? To say that idleness alone accords with the Way is utterly mistaken.
Knowing this to be an illness, Master Teng-teng said: "There is no need for extensive learning or vast erudition;
one need not possess eloquence or brilliant wit. One does not concern oneself with whether the month is large or small, nor does one take account of the intercalary days of the year.
When people come to question me, I am unable to engage them in discussion. At dawn, I satisfy my hunger with gruel; at the midday meal, I eat once more."
"Sudden! Today one is spontaneously carefree; tomorrow one is carefree and spontaneous. This is the cause of illness. As stated in the "Chapter on Discerning Sounds":
"Perfect Enlightenment is pure and fundamentally has no cultivation, nor any cultivator. To say otherwise would miss the meaning of that text.
To claim that one has already awakened is necessarily to engage in illusion; thus, it constitutes the sickness of "indulgence" (*nyō*).
The Master Sō of Shiming said: "These four are all called 'sicknesses. Sickness refers to the sickness of views (*ken-byō*).
Loving the Buddha and loving non-Buddhists both belong to the sickness of views. This 'indulgence' is the sickness; this is called the sickness of indulging in views. This is that sickness.
It is difficult to cure. If one says that birth and death are not severed, this is the deluded view and deluded illness of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

If birth and death are not severed, birth and death will arrive of their own accord, leading one to fall into hell and transmigrate through the six realms and the twenty-five states of existence; all of these are birth and death.

To not seek liberation from them means that birth and death will have no end—is this not indeed an illness? *Nirvāṇa* is what is realized by those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
To not seek nirvana and not emerge from the triple world—yet to crave nirvana is likewise a sickness of views.

Perfect Enlightenment does not reside within the nirvana of the Lesser Vehicle. If that which you perceive as birth-and-death and nirvana is not the Buddha-nature, then seeking by clinging to these two extremes is already a sickness;
how much more so is this sickness when one seeks nothing at all through incantations? Thus it is born.
These two states—death and nirvana—fall into the two extremes and will never result in Buddhahood; therefore, they are said to be "sicknesses.
Nowadays, those who study Buddhism and the essential dharma of emptiness fail to realize that seeing one's nature is the primary sickness. This sickness of emptiness is difficult to cure.
They hear only that emptiness can destroy all phenomena, but they do not see that all phenomena can destroy that emptiness.
Fire is destroyed because it encounters emptiness; all water is dispersed because it encounters emptiness; all earth brings forth and nurtures because it encounters emptiness;
and all wind arises because it encounters emptiness. It accomplishes all phenomena and destroys all phenomena—how much more so when the human mind clings to emptiness?
Will this not become a sickness? It is not that emptiness is useless; it is simply that one does not know how to employ it.
The Dharma is like a medicinal eye-salve used to treat an illness;
if the medicine itself becomes the illness, it is simply because sentient beings do not recognize the empty stillness of their own nature and fail to penetrate that emptiness of nature.

To the point where they lose this emptiness of nature—yet original emptiness is not something created through effort—if one neither severs birth and death nor seeks nirvana, one falls into the illness of dualistic views.
If one wishes to depart from the maladies of the two extremes, one must rely upon the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

If one relies upon it and practices accordingly, one cultivates various merits and practices non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). There, the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases;
all inverted minds are shattered, and the mind becomes tranquil. Because one flows spontaneously into the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñā*), it is called "following the mind."
To take this as a disease is the third.
Furthermore, if there is someone who says: "I shall now cause all thoughts in my own mind to cease forever."

One attains all natures, which are tranquil and equal. Yet, if one seeks to grasp that nature of perfect enlightenment, because that nature of perfect enlightenment does not consist in the union of stillness, such an attempt is said to be a sickness.
This means that, for instance, when all thoughts are permanently stilled, one attains a state of various natures that are tranquil, unmoving, equal, and non-dual.

In seeking to realize perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), one must understand that the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment cannot be attained through the cessation of the mind. The *Commentary on Perfect Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué shū*) also states:
"The nature is fundamentally without cessation; even cessation is contrary to the nature."
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "The commentary states: 'In the former case, one gives rise to a mind of apprehension;
in the latter, one follows emotional deliberation and falls into error. Now, simply bring [the mind] to rest. When these delusions are exhausted, there is spontaneous equality.
Equality is the truth; why seek another illumination? Because thoughts are stilled, one is free from signs; because one is free from signs, one attains the nature. This nature is..."
The nature of all phenomena being devoid of intrinsic nature is not identical to the nature of awakening. This ailment arises from prior meditative stillness;
one was deluded by taking that stillness as the practice and following the instruction to clarify all thoughts, thereby resulting in this disease of cessation.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Regarding 'stopping the illness': if the deluded mind is scattered, one should stop it by means of stopping;

that very scattering is itself the stopping. This is an excellent medicine—whom would they not take it? The Tathāgatas of the ten directions all rely on *śamatha* (calm abiding) to bring about this stopping.
That it is now described as an 'illness' is because you do not skillfully employ stopping; therefore, it is called an illness. This applies to ordinary beings."

Although the scattering [of the mind] has ceased through the practice of *śamatha*, it cannot be utilized for the sake of the gods of the fourth dhyāna heaven, the Māra kings, the followers of the two vehicles, or the partial bodhisattvas;
rather, it becomes a pit or a trap. As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the Māra king led his various celestial maidens...
Then Māra came to delude the Bodhisattva Lokadhara. Māra said to the Bodhisattva, "O Noble One (Satpuruṣa), accept these twelve thousand celestial maidens to serve as your attendants.
The Bodhisattva did not recognize him as Māra and said, "Kauśika (Lord Śakra), do not offer such unrighteous things to me, a śramaṇa and son of the Śākyas; this is not appropriate for me."
Before he had finished speaking, Vimalakīrti appeared before him and said, "This is not Śakra; it is Māra who has come to surround and besiege you.
At that moment, Māra Pāpīyān thought, "Vimalakīrti is not to be disturbed by me," yet he wished to vanish and depart, but was unable to do so.
Exhausting all his supernatural powers, he still could not depart. He heard a voice from the air saying, "Give these women to him, and only then may you go.
Out of fear, Māra reluctantly gave them up. Vimalakīrti said, "Sisters, since Māra has given you to me, you should all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, for their sake...
The Licchavi Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma of renouncing all desires. The women attained what they had never experienced before.
Māra came again and said to Vimalakīrti, "Householder, one who renounces everything is a bodhisattva. I wish to take these women back with me to the celestial palace.
Vimalakīrti replied, "I have already renounced them; you may take them away as you please. The women said, "Regarding us, we [belong] to the householder..."
"Abiding therein, he delights in the joy of the Dharma and no longer takes pleasure in the joys of the five desires. I am now returning to my palace with Māra;
what Dharma will you teach me so that I may dwell within Māra’s palace? The householder replied, "There is the Dharma of the Inexhaustible Lamp."

"You all should train yourselves in this. As for the 'Inexhaustible Lamp,' it is to delight in always revering the Buddha, to delight in making offerings to the Saṃgha, to delight in firmly upholding the precepts, and to delight in extensively practicing giving.

A single Bodhisattva may inspire hundreds of thousands of sentient beings to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is like one lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps—the light never comes to an end."
One should abide in the palace of Māra by means of this Dharma; thus will the Buddha-way be accomplished in the future.
If one uses the lamp of inexhaustibility as the place of abiding, the lamp can destroy darkness: if one abides in darkness, it becomes light; if one abides in distraction, it becomes concentration;
if one abides in stinginess, one practices relinquishment; if one abides among ordinary beings, one becomes a sage. It is simply a matter of skillful application; it does not constitute a disease.

The practice of *śamatha* cannot subdue the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). To subdue them, one must transform the ninety-five types [of heterodox views]; these are all false *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.

The practice of *śamatha* alone results in the *nirvāṇa* with remainder, which is the exclusive use of it by biased *bodhisattvas*. Like the moon beyond the clouds or a flower emerging from the water, these are all illnesses of *śamatha*.
Now, in cultivating *Perfect Enlightenment*, one employs the Middle Way of the Buddha-nature and the reality of all phenomena.
The marks [of reality]—the principle of suchness—are taken as the object of contemplation, the objective realm, and the basis of reliance.
Whether walking or sitting, speaking or remaining silent, one brings to rest the two extremes: saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; ordinary beings and sages; sound and form; cause and effect;
the primary and secondary realms; fame, profit, wealth, and honor. All such various dharmas are the two extremes. One does not cling to the two extremes, nor does one cling to the middle.
The Dharma of the Path is like traveling across the great ocean: without relying on a boat or oars, and without applying poles or paddles, one naturally reaches the shore.
To study in a manner other than this is called a sickness. It is the wondrous *śamatha* of the Middle Way that empties all marks.
To shatter all delusions is called "stopping that realizes the true essence. This stopping is itself contemplation; object and contemplation are in suchness (*tathatā*).
Continuing thus until the final moment of the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), one will not fall into affliction.
Fourth is the extinction of illness. Suppose there is another person who speaks thus: "I have now forever severed all afflictions;
my body and mind are ultimately empty and non-existent. How much more so, then, are the sense organs, objects, and illusory realms—all are eternally quiescent."
If one seeks to attain perfect enlightenment, that nature of perfect enlightenment is not characterized by quiescence; therefore, it is called a "sickness.
This means that when all illusions are forever severed, body and mind are fundamentally empty, and the six sense faculties and six sense objects are entirely extinguished.

One eternally realizes perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Yet, one does not realize that the wondrous nature of perfect enlightenment cannot be realized through the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).
The *Commentary on Perfect Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué shū*) also states: "How can a mind dwelling in quiescence be in accord with [perfect enlightenment]?"
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: The commentary states that previously one merely ceased the activity of the mind to bring it to stillness;

here, however, one calculates that the body, mind, sense faculties, and objects are fundamentally empty and quiescent. Furthermore, in the former case, it was not that sense faculties and objects were seen as existing, but rather that one did not follow after thoughts of attachment;
hence it was called "ceasing. In this [latter] case, even the sense faculties and objects do not exist, and one maintains this with firm resolve.
The characteristic of emptiness and stillness: because one perceives emptiness and non-existence, it is said that [afflictions] are eliminated and extinguished.

It concludes by stating: "The root of afflictions is precisely the body and mind. If one clings to the body and mind, how can afflictions be severed? Therefore, it designates the severing of afflictions and explains it through the emptiness of the body.

Furthermore, by severing afflictions, the body and mind are emptied. If even the body and mind are empty, what existence could there be for the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*)? The body and so forth...
It is fundamentally empty; therefore, it is called "eternal quiescence. Since all marks have dissolved, the mark of quiescence manifests before one.

If you intend to seek realization of Perfect Enlightenment (Pūrṇabodhi) by means of this mind, consider that the essence of enlightenment is numinous and luminous; it is not merely quiescent extinction. If you dwell in quiescence while remaining attached to the emptiness of delusion, how could you possibly be in accord with it?
Furthermore, the essence of Perfect Enlightenment is neither moving nor still; it integrates both movement and stillness, such that its ocean-like, wondrous functions are unimpeded.
It is inconceivable. How can a mind abiding in quiescence be in accord with this? Though the words seem close, the principle is entirely contrary.
Because it contradicts the principle, it constitutes the disease of extinction. This disease arises from the previous state of quiescent contemplation; among those various wheels—
All claim that it is "quiescent extinction" and the severance of afflictions; yet these four maladies arise from being deluded by that [state] and forming this [view].
All are caused by not taking the holy teachings as a measuring line, nor taking teachers and friends as a guide, but merely elevating one's own mind and forming such an intention.
Therefore, the beginning of every sutra states: "If there be another person who speaks thus," and so forth.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "Regarding those who regard cessation as a disease, it is entirely because they fail to penetrate the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and instead grasp at the mere appearance of emptiness while performing good and evil deeds.
As for those who abide in the principle of emptiness, there are four types of such persons, each grasping it differently."
The Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna contemplate the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), regarding its exhaustion and extinction as the goal.

The Pratyekabuddhas contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, taking the cessation of ignorance and the subsequent links as the ultimate principle through which they attain the realization of a Pratyekabuddha. Bodhisattvas employ the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), regarding the state of ultimate quiescence as cessation.
The cessation of the Hīnayāna does not reach Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). Those of the Universal Teaching regard illusion as cessation; those of the Distinct Teaching...
Ordinary people consider the cessation of phenomena according to conditions to be extinction; such is the view of these three types of persons.
All of them fail to accord with the principle, for they all remain within a state of quiescence while regarding it as extinction. Therefore, I now speak of this:

because they are ill and do not penetrate the nature of extinction—the Tathāgatagarbha, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)—they still dwell outside the gate, lodging in a thatched hut. What is clarified here as "extinction" is extinction without [abiding].

Extinction. Birth and death and nirvana do not extinguish. Sentient beings do not extinguish. Buddhas do not extinguish. The six classes of ordinary beings and the four classes of noble ones do not extinguish.
Form and mind do not extinguish. The two retributions of the environment and the body do not extinguish. Heaven and hell do not extinguish. Afflictions and ignorance do not extinguish.
Views and attachments do not extinguish. The eighty thousand defilements do not extinguish. All dhāraṇīs [do not extinguish].

The gates are not extinguished; water and fire are not extinguished; demons and heterodoxies are not extinguished. All phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds—the teachings of the Buddhas and the teachings of sentient beings—are entirely unextinguished.
This constitutes the permanence of worldly appearances; it constitutes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); it constitutes the myriad phenomena of the universe;
it constitutes the empty *tathāgatagarbha*; it constitutes the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*; and it constitutes the eternally abiding true mind.
The essence of intrinsic purity and luminosity is Vairocana; all manifest perfect enlightenment. All phenomena are the substance of perfect enlightenment;

the roaring of ten thousand apertures is the function of perfect enlightenment. Perfect enlightenment exists within the birth and death of sentient beings, within the *nirvāṇa* of the *śrāvakas*, and likewise within all daily activities.
It is perfect enlightenment throughout the day, yet one has never experienced it as such—just like [the following].
People say that fire cannot burn the mouth. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light;

when you briefly raise your mind, worldly afflictions arise first. This refers to employing birth-and-extinction, where extinction is fundamentally non-extinguishing; one cannot employ it [otherwise].

Arising and ceasing are themselves cessation. This prevents words from reaching true cessation. When the nature abides within arising and ceasing, one points to cessation as "cessation" and regards the pit and the trap as "cessation.
It is like a clod of earth being shattered and falling into an empty valley. Now, taking up the nature of Great Perfect Enlightenment, it is fundamentally without cessation.
What need is there to discuss cessation? That which is primordially ceased is primordially empty; what need is there for further emptiness?

By subsuming cultivation within its nature, one directly points to the twelve links of dependent origination and the Four Noble Truths of suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the path. Since birth-and-death and ignorance are fundamentally unceasing, they are as they are.
The Sūtra says: "Without severing the fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*), one purifies the sense faculties. It also says:
"Without dwelling in the ocean of afflictions, the eyes born of one's parents see the entire trichiliocosm. Layman Pang said: "Difficult, difficult!
A hundred loads of oil spread upon a hemp tree! Laywoman Pang responded: "Easy, easy! The meaning of the Patriarchs is at the tips of the hundred grasses. Lingzhao said: "So it is."
It is neither difficult nor easy. When hunger comes, one eats; when weariness comes, one sleeps. Now it is said: "The difficult is not difficult;

the easy is not easy. When hunger comes, one eats; when weariness comes, one does not sleep. Whether acting, ceasing, following, or extinguishing, throughout the entire world, all ultimately return to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
One who is free from the four ailments knows purity.
When there is no mind of effort, cessation, spontaneity, or extinction, that is the original nature’s purity.
One who contemplates in this way is said to have right contemplation; one who contemplates otherwise is said to have wrong contemplation.
Purity and freedom from defilement is what is called right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). To give rise to a separate understanding is to fall into error.
Master Fu’an Huì of Xīshǔ said: "This summarizes the authenticity or falsity of the four preceding illnesses.
One who is free from these four illnesses knows that which is pure. The Commentary states: "Simply take the preceding four practices and examine your own mind accordingly."
If one enters through a single gate, one knows it to be a sickness; therefore, it is said that by departing [from them], one knows purity.
Yet all four gates are praised and extolled in various sutras, and this is especially true for the first three contemplations, as they possess such textual authority.

That these are now regarded as sicknesses involves two intentions: first, that within the four gates there is no contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*); second, that they are merely followed [mechanically].

The mind dwells exclusively on a single practice; it does not exhaustively investigate the perfect intent of virtuous friends, nor does it thoroughly research the perfect texts of the Buddha’s teachings.

Having merely realized the meaning of one gate, one is unable to remain long under an enlightened teacher; having merely seen the wondrous passages of one sutra, one is unable to extensively fathom the Sage’s intention.
One merely craves what is simple and concise, clinging to a single point as being "perfect. For this reason, the sutra texts collectively censure such attitudes.

These are the four illnesses. One who practices this contemplation is free from the four illnesses; therefore, it is called "right contemplation. If one contemplates otherwise, one grasps the four illnesses;
therefore, it is called "erroneous contemplation. A passage in an external (non-Buddhist) classic states: "That which accords with the Way of Yao and Shun is the Right Way;
that which does not accord with the Way of Yao and Shun is another way. This is of the same intent. Now, regarding these four gates:
It is only the illness that is removed, not the Dharma itself. When one has not yet seen the Way, these four all constitute the illness of attachment;
once the Way is seen, these four can all be relinquished. Entering the Way occurs spontaneously: throughout the day one acts, yet there is never acting;
throughout the day one rests, yet there is never resting; throughout the day one extinguishes, yet there is never extinguishing. This is the Zen school.
It is said: "The person of old remains unchanged; only their conduct has changed.

The fourth question asks: "How does one eliminate [afflictions]? The answer states: "One should eliminate all seeds of hatred and attachment toward oneself and others.

The sequence and provenance of these points can be seen clearly by consulting the text item by item.

Ultimately entering perfect enlightenment, Free from the marks of self, other, and person;

and *nirvāṇa* is a Sanskrit term meaning "extinction and crossing over" (*mie-du*). Thus, it is an instance of citing both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms interchangeably.

Regarding the *Commentary on the Collected Verses of the Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhicitta-parivarta Sūtra*,

The opening of understanding for those of the three capacities—superior, middling, and inferior—is provided by the second [chapter], the *Samantabhadra Sūtra* text.
It serves as the opening for the practice of those of the three capacities—superior, middling, and inferior.

Mañjuśrī represents the wisdom that realizes, while Samantabhadra represents the conduct that arises, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. If there were only understanding without practice, it would be like a well of sand.
Yet there is no moisture. If one has practice but lacks understanding, it is like having clouds in the sky but no rain.
Only when understanding and practice are in harmony can one advance in cultivation and enter the Path; it is like weaving a net, which ultimately serves to catch fish.
One must pack provisions and press forward; thus, there is the "Opening of Practice" by Samantabhadra.

Next is the chapter on the "Universal Eye" from the third [section], which, based upon Mañjuśrī’s exegesis and the practice of Samantabhadra, involves cultivating the contemplation of the two-fold emptiness of self and phenomena, while concurrently emulating the threefold contemplation of the Dharma-realm of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Once one has entered the gate of contemplation, there may arise doubts and lingering attachments.
Therefore, the fourth Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha, gave rise to three doubts and posed questions. His first doubt was as follows:
"If sentient beings have been Buddhas from the very beginning, why is there still all-pervasive ignorance? Could it be that delusion has arisen from the Truth?"
The second doubt says: "Sentient beings possess ignorance fundamentally from the beginning.
For what cause and condition, then, is it further said that they have been Buddha from the very outset? Is this not merely speaking of the false as if it were the true? The third doubt says:

"If ordinary beings throughout the ten directions have fundamentally attained the Way of Buddhahood and subsequently give rise to ignorance, when will all Tathāgatas ever again give rise to all afflictions? Is this not..."

Is it not the case that truth comes first and delusion follows? Therefore, [the text] cites [the opponent's view] and then grants it [a conditional acceptance] in order to assign the fault of infinite regress.

Since Vajragarbha possessed these three doubts, the World-Honored One subsequently used the single analogy of flowers in the sky to answer all three doubts in general, and employed the analogy of gold ore to answer the third doubt specifically.
However, the reason Vajragarbha harbored these doubts was entirely due to [his conditioning] since beginningless time.

Craving. Once craving has been severed, there is immediate entry into realization. Since there is entry into realization, there must necessarily be distinctions and differences;
therefore, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhamati asked a sixth question:

The fruits of the noble ones descend through four stages. At that time, there was a class of individuals with superior faculties within the assembly who, upon hearing the Buddha thus extensively expound various Dharma-gates through skillful means, were able to believe and understand them accordingly.

Practicing in this manner and realizing it in this manner, they simultaneously transcend dreams and illusions and emerge from saṃsāra, proceeding directly toward the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood and bodhi—just as a fine horse proceeds upon seeing the shadow of a whip.

Furthermore, among those seated there, there was another class of people with middling faculties; although they had heard the Buddha provide such an explanation within the preceding six chapters of the sutra, [they remained...]
[It is] understood. However, because their faculties are inferior, they are unable to realize and enter the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness.
Thereupon, the seventh Bodhisattva, Mahātejas, questioned the Buddha: "For example, a great city has four gates; those who come from the various directions do not follow only one path.
Furthermore, as for those of superior faculties who have already realized and entered the two kinds of emptiness and the Dharma-body..."
