One should correctly contemplate that if the Buddha were in the world, he would possess a sixteen-foot golden body, the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and a body of purple-golden diamond; one must not merely stop at such contemplation."
The Buddha’s countenance and marks of excellence are as described in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra*.

When Vaidehī requested the Buddha to instruct her in contemplation, the Buddha taught her to cultivate three types of pure karma: filially supporting one's parents, practicing benevolence and compassion in the world, and receiving and upholding the Three Refuges while being fully endowed with the various precepts.
This was the answer regarding contemplation. Subsequently, he answered regarding meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by means of the sixteen sublime contemplations.
(This is samādhi. Furthermore, one’s current contemplation must involve the purification of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
There are two types of purification of the three karmas: first, the three of the body, four of the mouth, and three of the mind;

second, the body is bathed, the mind severs all攀緣 (*pān-yuan*, objective attachments), and the mouth maintains silence. Moreover, practicing compassion and skillful means, as well as gathering the mind for quiet meditation, are all [part of this].
This is the correct expedient for entering the Way; therefore, it is said that one should practice right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one establishes images and fixes the mind upon them with visualized contemplation, giving rise to right mindfulness, this is equivalent to the days when the Tathāgata was still present.

Regarding the hanging of banners and flowers, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "If you wish to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), you must first maintain the pure prohibitive precepts of a bhikṣu. This is essential.
One should select those who are pure in their observance of the precepts to establish the boundary and construct the *maṇḍala*.

Whether they be monastics or laypeople, they must extinguish poverty and lust in their minds and maintain the Buddha’s pure precepts, conforming to the Buddha’s pure regulations. Outside the four sides, hang banners and flowers everywhere;
within the chamber of the altar, arrange the images of all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions upon the four walls.
Furthermore, facing the image, one should arrange images of Vairocana and the various great transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

During the first seven days, prostrate to the sixteen Tathāgatas and recite mantras and perform the ritual circuit six times each day. During the second seven days, focus the mind single-mindedly on making vows.
During the third seven days, focus single-mindedly on holding the mantra. This continues until the seventh seven-day period, when [the Buddhas of] the ten directions appear...
They appear simultaneously at the place where mirrors reflect one another’s light. This is the ritual procedure for establishing a *maṇḍala* according to the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
Here, it says "suspend various banners and flowers," which carries the same meaning as that text; the only difference is that the ritual of adornment is here somewhat abbreviated.
If one practices according to the method of performing repentance based on its actual application, one should set a period of twenty-one days.

One bows to the names of the Buddhas, as in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* where one prostrates and makes vows during the twenty-one days. Furthermore, it is like people taking medicine who say that within twenty-one days a response will already be felt;
"bowing" here refers specifically to performing the ritual of repentance and paying homage to the Buddhas.

At that time, one should contemplate as follows: "The nature of both the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent; the mutual resonance of cause and response is inconceivable.
My present site of practice is like a jewel of Indra, within which the shadow-forms of Śākyamuni appear.

My own body and shadow appear before the Tathāgata; with head meeting his feet, I take refuge and pay homage. One should likewise contemplate in this manner when paying homage to the Buddha and the Dharma. Thus one should seek.
Mournfully repent. As for those who encounter a virtuous state and attain mental lightness and ease, or those who seek through mournful repentance, it is as stated in the *Caryā-dharma-sūtra*:
"Why is it that I now see only Śākyamuni Buddha, yet do not see the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna, which remains eternally and never perishes?
It is because my eyes are turbid and evil; therefore, I do not see it. Having spoken these words, he further...
Confess. After seven days have passed, the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna will emerge from the earth.
By this, you shall know that your karmic work has not yet been perfected and that there must be obstructions caused by the three hindrances.

You should reveal and confess the evil karma previously committed by yourself. Through the power of your own confession and the further empowering grace of the many Buddhas, [the demonic obstacles...]
One does not give rise [to further afflictions], attains a wholesome state, and achieves mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). The Sanskrit term *kṣamā* is translated here as "repenting of transgressions.

People in the Western Regions say it carries the meaning of "endurance. It is very much like saying to someone who has caused one distress or anger: "Please forgive me; I pray you do not be resentful."
Tiantai said: "To 'repent' (chan) means to acknowledge one's faults; to 'regret' (hui) means to submit. It is like a person who has offended a king and submits their confession to seek clemency.

Furthermore, 'repentance' is named the white dharma (wholesome), while 'regret' is named the black dharma (unwholesome). One regrets the black dharma so as not to commit it again, and one aspires to and honors the white dharma.
Taken together, they involve both rejection and adoption. Moreover, 'repentance' is named the reforming of the past, while 'regret' is named the cultivation of the future. Furthermore, repentance...

Shame (*hrī*) is called "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*); remorse is called "shame before others" (*apatrāpya*). Shame is shame before the heavens; remorse is shame before men. Men see what is manifest; the heavens see what is hidden. Tiantai established three types of repentance:
first, repentance through ritual action (*vidhi-karma-pratikramaṇa*); second, repentance by taking signs (*nimitta-grahaṇa-pratikramaṇa*); third, repentance of non-arising (*anutpāda-pratikramaṇa*).
When repentance through ritual action is accomplished, it extinguishes the offenses of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. This relies on the gate of precepts (*śīla-mukha*). Taking signs...

When the repentance is accomplished, the nature-offense is extinguished; this relies on the gate of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When the repentance of non-arising is accomplished, the offenses of deluded thought are extinguished; this relies on the gate of wisdom (*prajñā*).

The ritual repentance (*vidhi-karma-pratikramaṇa*) is like the construction of a *maṇḍala*: one must practice the ten categories of ritual procedures with diligence, ensuring that not a single detail is omitted.
Although other offenses may be extinguished, the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "For example, if a bhikṣu cuts grass and takes life, two offenses are not extinguished.

Regarding the repentance through signs (*xiang*), as described in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, one may see light or flowers, see the characters for "extinguished offense" in one's own hands, hear a voice from the sky, or experience such visions in dreams.
Regarding the repentance of non-arising (*wusheng*), as described in the *Caryāvidhi Sūtra*: "The entire ocean of karmic obstructions all arise from delusion."

Contemplate their arising; sit upright and contemplate the true mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). "All transgressions are like frost and dew"—through these three types of repentance, the cultivation of even one will extinguish offenses.
Although one may thereby attain a slight degree of tranquility, as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, these are all merely skillful means (*upāya*) that provide temporary relief.

If one does not conceive of them as being the realization of a sage (*ārya*), they are called "wholesome states" (*kuśala-viṣaya*); if one interprets them as the realization of a sage, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
If the repentance for non-arising is accomplished, one immediately ascends to the First Abode (Prathamabhūmi) and manifests as a Buddha throughout a hundred worlds;
how could it be merely a matter of light ease? All three types of repentance are virtuous states that can all reveal Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra).
After the three weeks had passed, he focused his mindfulness exclusively.
Beyond the twenty-first day, he no longer recited the Buddha's name or performed repentance, but instead concentrated solely on gathering and maintaining right mindfulness.
This is to prevent negligence.
Master Fu’an Hui of Xichu said: "This clarifies the application of the mind while remaining free from signs. Regarding 'gathering the thoughts,' the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
'If one practices *śamatha*, one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright with a correct intention, and so forth, even if the mind should wander and scatter.'"
One should immediately collect [the mind] and abide in right mindfulness. Regarding right mindfulness: one should know that there is only mind and no external objects.
Master Cong of the Four Clarifications said: "During the twenty-one days, burning incense, prostrating to the Buddha, seeking compassion, and repenting—all of these..."
This belongs to the realm of conditioned activity; it is in motion and not yet still, like turbid water that becomes even more turbid when stirred.

Now, what is called "gathering the mind" means to clarify the heart and return to oneness—whether by focusing exclusively on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), or focusing exclusively on the provisional (*prajñapti*), or focusing exclusively on the Middle Way (*madhyamā*);

or by focusing exclusively on the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); or by counting the breath as it enters and exits; or by contemplating the realm of the Dharma-dhātu with a single thought as it is in suchness (*tathatā*). Once the mind has been gathered...
After a long time, suddenly one no longer perceives the body nor perceives the mind; it is like clouds or shadows, like a precious moon within a crystal palace.
Ignorant deluded mind naturally vanishes, and the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment naturally manifests.
When the beginning of summer arrives, during the three months of the *varṣā* retreat, one should dwell as a pure Bodhisattva.

Upon encountering the start of summer, one should immediately enter the summer retreat (*varṣā-avasthāna*). Contemplating one’s dwelling for three months without going outside—this is called the contemplation of the pure Bodhisattva’s dwelling.
The mind is detached from the Śrāvakas; it does not rely upon a following of disciples.
The essential teaching for transmitting the Mind is as follows: those who attain awakening by means of vocal instruction are called Śrāvakas.
Since you now dwell in pure contemplation, why wait for vocal instruction? Therefore, it is said that "the mind is detached from the Śrāvakas. Now that the mind is detached from the Śrāvakas, why...
Relying on the assistance of his followers,
when the day of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) arrived, he spoke these words before the Buddha:
"On this day of pure contemplation during the *varṣā*, I make this vow before the Buddha."
Master Xifuxian Hui of Shu said: "Those who dwell as pure bodhisattvas" refers to Mahayana bodhisattvas.
"Sravakas" refers to those of the Hinayana. "Disciples" refers to the assembly of the six harmonies.
As for the assembly of the six harmonies: first, harmony of body; second, harmony of speech; third, harmony of mind; fourth, harmony of precepts; fifth, harmony of benefit; sixth, [harmony of view].

Harmony in vision: dwell together in bodily harmony; do not go where it is not appropriate. When various superior and virtuous people assemble in one place, there is harmony in speech and no contention;
do not listen to what is contrary to propriety. Like-kind energies seek one another; like sounds respond to one another. There is harmony in intention through shared understanding.
Do not covet personal advantage. Be diligent and do not deceive others with a false heart. Maintain harmony through the precepts and practice together. Be cautious and do not harbor greedy desires.
Guard against wrongdoing and cease evil. Do not create enmity or resentment. Share benefits equally; equality is the highest kinship.
If you receive eight *liang* and I receive half a *jin*, let us work together in harmony. Do not give rise to contempt or disdain. Do not rely on your own superior qualities. Great...
The household is at peace and happy. Now, I shall practice according to the Mahāyāna; there is no need for this assembly of followers.
As for me—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—[we shall proceed accordingly].
Regarding the term *bhikṣu*: the *Yuanjue shu* states that he is called (1) "Terrifier of Māras," (2) "Almsman" (*kṣattṛ*), and (3) "One of Pure Precepts.
A *bhikṣuṇī* is a female *bhikṣu*. An *upāsaka* is a male lay practitioner. An *upāsikā* is a female lay practitioner.
I, [Name], am established in the Bodhisattva Vehicle and cultivate the practice of quiescence.
I claim that, according to the Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas,
I have cultivated sublime conduct and entered together into the maintenance of the pure true reality (*dharmatā*).
All have fully awakened to and entered the markless mark. They maintain it without fail.

Taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery—“monastery” (伽藍) meaning a grove for the assembly—I now declare that by taking Perfect Enlightenment as the monastery, I manifest the entirety of my assembly.
One does not rely on any other phenomena.
Body and mind dwell in tranquility within the wisdom of equality.
Body and mind rest peacefully within the Great Perfect Enlightenment, where nature and wisdom merge into a single, indistinguishable state.
The self-nature of nirvāṇa is unconditioned;
its fundamental nature is quiescent and utterly free, for it is neither bound nor subject to any governance.
Now I respectfully request that, rather than following the way of the śrāvakas, I shall enter the three-month summer retreat together with the Tathāgatas and great bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
For the sake of cultivating the supreme cause for the wondrous awakening of a bodhisattva, I shall not be bound by a retinue of disciples.

Do not rely upon the teachings of the Śrāvaka Hīnayāna. With a sincere heart, respectfully invite the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to observe the three-month *varṣā* retreat and cultivate this vast and perfect Dharma-gate of *Awakened Awareness*. Furthermore, what need is there for a large assembly?
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "The Sanskrit term *bhikṣu* contains three meanings:
first, 'one who terrifies Māra'; second, 'a mendicant' (*yācanaka*); and third, 'one of pure precepts. *Bhikṣuṇī* refers to a nun; *nī* means 'woman.
*Upāsaka* is translated here as 'male lay follower,' referring to a practitioner who studies the Dharma. *Upāsikā* is [translated as]..."

"Upāsikā" refers to a woman who studies the Dharma. However, while the Hīnayāna is restricted to the two assemblies [of monks and nuns], the Mahāyāna path is shared by both the laity and the ordained.
"So-and-so" refers to calling out each person's name. "Jù" (踞) means to sit. As for those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle:
"Selecting the sheep and deer carts" distinguishes them from [the other vehicles]. "Practicing the path of quiescent extinction" distinguishes it from the Four Noble Truths.
"Abiding in the true mark" does not mean abiding in phenomenal characteristics. *Gārala* (伽藍) is translated here as "monastic garden" (*zhòngyuán*). A garden is a place where a community resides.

Therefore, Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) is that upon which all virtues rely. According to Guifeng’s Commentary, the meaning of this passage is that the eight consciousnesses are transformed into the four wisdoms.
Question: What are the eight consciousnesses? Answer: The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body constitute the first five consciousnesses;
the sixth is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); the seventh is the manas-consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*); and the eighth is the ālaya-consciousness.

It is the ālaya-vijñāna. However, the first five consciousnesses belong to the external; they are the function (*yòng*). The latter three consciousnesses belong to the internal; they are the essence (*tǐ*).
Furthermore, the first five consciousnesses belong to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), while the latter three consciousnesses belong to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

What are the four wisdoms? Answer: First, the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*); second, the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); third, the wisdom of the equality of nature (*samatā-jñāna*).
The four great elements are the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). As for what is now transformed:

it refers to a Bodhisattva who, upon first ascending to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), transforms the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*) to achieve the Wondrous Observational Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). This wisdom skillfully penetrates all phenomena (*dharmas*).
However, within this sixth consciousness, there exist the natures of goodness, non-goodness, and the indeterminate; these constitute the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), which are thus differentiated.

It is distinct from all other dharmas. Subsequently, upon entering the second stage through to the tenth stage, one then transforms and attains the seventh *manas* consciousness, which becomes the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*). This wisdom is named after its counter-agent;
for because it clings to a self with inequality, it must be overturned. Now, *manas* is here translated as the "defiled root," referring to this consciousness.

Internally, they cling to self-delusion, self-pride, self-love, and self-view; externally, they cling to the existence of ordinary beings and sages, of high and low, and of "that" and "this," and thus cannot attain equanimity.
However, the aforementioned two consciousnesses are those of Bodhisattvas who, during the causal stage, transform them within the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Subsequently, at the resultant stage of the two awakenings—Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimala-saṃbodhi*)—[they are further transformed].
Above, as one transforms and attains the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*, it becomes the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*mahā-ādarśa-jñāna*).

This wisdom receives its name from a metaphor; however, this eighth consciousness previously clung to the internal body and external objects—the mountains, rivers, great earth, the sense organs, the physical body, the vessel-world, and their seeds.
Now, it is like a great perfect mirror, its radiance complete and full. As it is said:
The seventeenth patriarch once encountered a youth holding a mirror in his hand. The patriarch asked, "What does that which you hold in your hand represent?
The youth replied, "It is the Great Perfect Mirror of all Buddhas; without flaw or obscuration within or without, both persons see it together, for the eye of the mind is identical in both.
This refers to the transformation at the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), wherein the eighth consciousness is perfected.

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is [attained], while the first five consciousnesses, as a single path at the stage of fruition, are transformed into the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
This wisdom performs the Buddha-activities. Therefore, the Patriarch said: "The nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is pure;
the Mind of the Equality Wisdom is free from affliction; the Wondrous Observing Wisdom sees without effort; the All-Accomplishing Wisdom..."
Like a circular mirror, the five, eight, six, and seven faculties revolve as effects and causes; they are merely conventional designations and possess no inherent nature.

If one does not linger where these revolutions occur, then amidst the profusion of activity, one dwells eternally in the *nāga-samādhi*. Although it is said that the sixth and seventh consciousnesses revolve within the causal stage, [they are ultimately non-existent].
The five [consciousnesses] and the eight [cognitions] are perfected in their fruition; only their names are transformed, not their essential substance.
Now, "tranquility of body" is the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom), and "tranquility of mind" is the *sudarśana-jñāna* (wonderfully observing wisdom).

These [consciousnesses], associated with the four delusions, falsely conceptualize the *ālaya-vijñāna* as an internal self. Within the principle of equality, they give rise to views of inequality. Now...

Since the nature of the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is quiescent, the seven consciousnesses that take it as their object are themselves suchness (*tathatā*); because their natures are identical, they constitute the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
"The Great Perfect Enlightenment" refers precisely to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Do you not see this?
Puyong addressed the assembly, saying: "When Deshan entered the gate, he immediately struck him with his staff. Is this not the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done?
When Xuansha and Tianlong were wandering the mountains and encountered a tiger, was this not the Wisdom of Equality?
Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "There is a true person of no station who enters and exits through the gates of your faces. You have not yet realized this."
Look, look! Is this not the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*)? Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "Here with me, it is like an ancient mirror:
when a barbarian comes, a barbarian appears; when a Han person comes, a Han person appears. Is this not the wisdom of the great perfect mirror (*ādarśa-jñāna*)?
The meaning is that one employs *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti* (perfectly realized awareness) as one's dwelling place. Since one has already taken *pariniṣpanna-vijñapti*...
When it becomes the place where one dwells, then all natures of consciousness are entirely transformed into the wisdom of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).
This is precisely the fundamental nature of Nirvāṇa—the indestructible essence of the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Because this nature of Nirvāṇa accords with the Principle, its six powers of penetration open up in all four directions; whether great or small, refined or coarse, its movement is nowhere absent, and it has no fixed location whatsoever.
"Can be bound" does not mean being attached to a specific location as in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
"Great Bodhisattvas" refers to Mahāyāna bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (bhūmi). "Great causal conditions" means not being constrained by minor details.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "If one enters the three-month summer retreat at the beginning of the summer, the previous inquiry regarding 'summer retreat' refers to a person cultivating *Awakening of Faith* who separately seeks out a secluded and silent location to establish a site for the Dharma-hall (*dōjō*). Now, when speaking of 'summer retreat' [in this context], it refers to..."
This is the Buddha’s skillful means. For one who cultivates Perfect Enlightenment, it is like the beginning of summer when the monastic community observes the *varṣā* (the retreat).

For ninety days they do not go out or come in; while donors bring offerings, each person cultivates the Real and cultivates Perfect Enlightenment. Alternatively, one may establish a separate altar for the purpose of returning [to the assembly].

When the community enters the summer retreat, there is a fixed period for the commencement; if one does not return, it may hinder the entry into the retreat, yet if one returns, it may again hinder the period of repentance.

When entering meditative contemplation, one may encounter such states; perhaps fearing that these might cause doubt or hinder one's progress in cultivation, the Buddha specifically established this sacred regulation so as not to obstruct correct practice.

Thus it is said: "If, at the beginning of the summer, during the three months of the *an-guo* (rainy-season retreat), one should dwell as a pure Bodhisattva," up to the point where it says, "it need not rely on a multitude.
This clarifies that the Mahāyāna practices the sudden and perfect path (*yuán-dùn xíng*). It does not...
Compared to the Hinayana, the mental orientations of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas differ from those of the Bodhisattvas.

The Bodhisattva takes the *dharmadhātu* as their mind and maintains a contemplation that is free from all relative distinctions. They observe that all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* are their own parents and kinsmen.
As the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "All men are my fathers; all women are my mothers. In every successive birth, there is none from whom I have not derived [birth]."
Receiving birth, all earth and water are my former bodies; all fire and wind are my fundamental substance.
If one regards even earth and water as one's own body, how much more so the grasses, trees, rivers, and the great earth—all are the realm of my own self.
How much more so should sentient beings, the wriggling and the breathing, not be delivered? The Bodhisattva employs [these elements] in this manner.
The mind is fundamentally and immediately distinct from that of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Śrāvakas seek their own regulation and deliverance;

they hasten to realize the fruit, fearing birth and death as if they were ghosts, tigers, or snakes. They desire only their own escape and disregard sentient beings. Compared to the Mahāyāna, the difference is as vast as that between heaven and earth.
Now, when it is said that Bodhisattvas dwell in and cultivate *圆觉* (Perfect Enlightenment), they exclusively employ "quiescent illumination" (*jizhao*), applying profound contemplation.
All things—extending throughout empty space and pervading the Dharma-realm, encompassing the ten directions—not a single sentient being exists outside the mind of Perfect Enlightenment.
Both the primary and secondary retributions are entirely the light of eternal quiescence; whether body or mind, all are Vairocana.
With such a body and mind, how can one restrict them by time? One does not restrict the *saṃghāṭi* (the monastic robe). In a single thought-moment, one delivers all sentient beings;

in a single thought-moment, one seeks to attain perfect enlightenment. How could one be confined to the ninety-day summer retreat (*varṣā*)? The establishment of the summer retreat is a regulation of the Hinayana Vinaya;
it concerns the personal practice of body and mind, and does not exist for those who have forgotten the Great [Vehicle] and whose minds are detached from the Śrāvakas.

Those who merely borrow the name of the elephant are indeed full of intent; you should examine this thoroughly for yourself. On the day of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one should stand before the Buddha and speak these words:

"I, a bhikṣu, am one who has reached the state of being unattached to a following. This intention is distinct from [the practice of] establishing a *maṇḍala* of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) in a secluded place;
it does not enter into the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) tradition of the assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty [monks] at the Jeta Grove.

Regarding the limits of this regulation: when cultivating the mind within *yuanjue* (perfect enlightenment), one may, starting from the beginning of summer, establish a period of retreat (*jie-zhi*) solely within the meditation hall.
For this reason, it is said that one does not bind oneself to a group of followers.

On the day of the retreat for the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna, one still performs the ritual before the Buddha, addressing the assembly by saying: "I, [Name], now rely upon the Saṃgha of the monastery at [Place]..."
Within the boundaries of the monastery, during the first three months of the summer retreat, one repairs dilapidated dwellings.
At present, the Saṃgha and the Buddha, the World-Honored One, observe the summer retreat; their terminology is identical. Now, however, we establish the Bodhisattva Maṇḍala of the Mahāyāna.

Since there is no assembly of followers, we regulate our own bodies and minds before the Buddha and formulate our own expressions, as they do not coincide with the terminology of the Hīnayāna. Thus it continues until...
On the day of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one should speak thus before the Buddha: "The assembly of bhikṣus (male monks) and the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs (female monks).
In Western India, males are called *na* and females are called *ni*.

A *bhikṣu* is translated as "mendicant" (*qǐshì*), for he lives by begging and does not seek improper food, nor does he establish permanent property. An *upāsaka* is a layman of pure faith; he is also called *wōpó*.

*Upāsaka* refers to a lay follower, a woman of pure faith; it is also called *upāsikā*, meaning a man or woman of noble family (*kulaputra/kuladuhitrī*), or a man or woman of true faith (*satyadarśin*).
These are the good men and women who currently receive the three refuges and the five precepts.

These are known as the four assemblies (*catur-parṣad*). Generally, both monastics and laity observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) according to the regulations and cultivate the perfection [of the path].
The Awakened One addressed the Buddha, saying: "I, [Name], am one who dwells upon the Bodhisattva vehicle and cultivates the practice of quiescence.
A Bodhisattva is said to 'accomplish sentient beings through the Great Bodhicitta. Quiescence refers to non-arising and non-ceasing;

it is not the extinction of arising and ceasing as found in the Lesser Vehicle. That which enters together into the mark of pure awakening is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. It is not...
It is the characteristic of birth and death, yet it is not the characteristic of nirvana. It is not birth and death, for it is not the state of ordinary beings;

it is not nirvana, for it is not the state of the two vehicles. Now it is said that this true mark is the Buddha-nature; seeing the eternally abiding true mind is the essence of the nature’s pure luminosity.

This is the empty Tathāgatagarbha; this is what the Buddha knows; this is what the Buddha sees; this is the ocean of the nature of perfect enlightenment; this is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
this is the ground of the principle of true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Abiding in reliance upon this is to abide in the Vairocana-garbha;
it is to abide in the garbha of precepts; it is to abide in the garbha of cause and effect. It is this single thought-moment of deluded mind before us; there is no need for anything else.

Seeking [the truth], one empties the deluded mind; this is precisely the empty Tathāgatagarbha. Whether form or mind, whether the environment or its inhabitants, cause or effect—indeed, all dharmas whatsoever—are the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Abiding by this as one's support, taking the Dharma-realm as the ground of the mind, one dwells peacefully among all sentient beings and thereby attains the Buddha-way. If one does not take the true mark as one's support, it is like...
How many times shall one be born? How can one manifest Perfect Enlightenment (Pariniṣpanna-bodhi)? Therefore, it is said: "I take Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery (*ārāma*).

The two characters "as my" (*wei wo*) refer to one's own body and mind. The "monastery" is the site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*); it is the place where I discipline the mind and cultivate Perfect Enlightenment.

Perfect Enlightenment is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The Dharma-realm has the meaning of being free from all relative distinctions; it encompasses both form and mind, as well as their substratum.
The ten dharma realms are precisely [this]; whether heaven or hell, there is nothing that does not exist within them.
Such is the Bodhisattva. This body and mind are themselves the nature of equality; there is not a single dharma that does not accord with this nature.

This wisdom is the wisdom of Great Perfect Enlightenment, the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā); there is not a single dharma that does not manifest therein. As for the *nirvāṇa* of the Hīnayāna...
That which is bound is limited; however, this Great Vehicle *Nirvāṇa* is without such bonds and is not confined to a single *dharmadhātu*.

Therefore, it is said: "I now respectfully request that, rather than following the *śrāvakas*, you should enter the three-month *varṣā* retreat together with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas.
(The purpose of the *varṣā* retreat for protecting living beings has been explained above. If it is the *varṣā* retreat of a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva...
May all sentient beings dwell in peace and happiness wherever they may be.

Since there is no restriction on either the internal or the external, releasing living beings and providing them with food is a talisman for longevity and an elixir of immortality; therefore, the establishment of the precepts takes non-killing as the foremost principle.
"Good son, this is called the bodhisattva’s manifestation of the summer retreat.
As for the three-month summer retreat mentioned previously, that is merely the appearance of the bodhisattva’s manifestation of the summer retreat."
After the period of three months has passed, one may travel without hindrance.
The long period is one hundred and twenty days; the medium period is one hundred days; and the short period is eighty days.
For those practicing *anāgārika* (the rains retreat), once these periods of three months have elapsed, there is no obstruction to going elsewhere.
Chan Master Fuyan Hui of Xishu said: "Daoming’s three-month period has already concluded, while the summer retreat limit for those of the Small Vehicle has not yet ended.
Since his original intention was not that of a Small Vehicle practitioner observing the *an-guo* (summer retreat), there is no hindrance to his proceeding as he pleases."
The lecturer Mingcong of Siming said: "In the Mahayana tradition, the completion of the summer retreat is called *pravāraṇā* (self-examination).
In the ritual procedure of the Hinayana, two sets of five virtues are established for the face-to-face confession of transgressions, stating: 'Today, the Sangha performs the *pravāraṇā*.'"
I, Bhikṣu [Name], also perform the *pravāraṇā*. Venerable Elders, if you have seen, heard, or suspect any offense in me, please speak to me out of compassion.
If I see the offense, I shall confess it according to the Dharma; for this purpose, I invite you to grant me the *pravāraṇā* that concludes the summer retreat.

From this point forward, there is no hindrance to leaving the boundary to travel through the mountains. Now, in the practice of the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), one also completes the three-month summer retreat (Anju).
When the period is fulfilled, one may go wherever one wishes without obstruction. This is not for the purpose of expiating offenses before a person possessing the five virtues;
rather, it is a formal expression of self-indulgence (Zi-zi) and repentance for transgressions, stating simply that one may go wherever one wishes without hindrance.
"Good son, if sentient beings practicing in that final age who seek the bodhisattva path enter the three periods,
they must never grasp at any of the realms they hear of."
While in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), if a separate thought suddenly arises, one should observe it with wisdom.
Any mental state—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that falls outside the three periods of correct practice previously taught is termed "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
None of these should be grasped or clung to. Hereafter, all cases shall be treated in this same manner.

Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "This serves as a general heading for the realm of preparatory practice (*prayoga*) and the realm of realization, admonishing and exhorting one not to grasp or become attached to erroneous states. Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

'Māra can enter the minds of all sentient beings, causing them to take refuge in his faction with a devotion like lacquer; he would not consider it difficult to have their hands severed or their arms cut off.'"
It is due to the power of spiritual magic that all people believe and submit. Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"Deeply attached to illusory dharmas, they stubbornly accept them and cannot relinquish them. None of these are what is heard or seen within meditative contemplation. As for faith, understanding, practice, and realization:
Although their classes differ, the Dharma that is believed, understood, practiced, and realized remains fundamentally without distinction from beginning to end.
This is not the case unless one possesses the original, fundamental method of the threefold ground for realizing the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*).
One should not grasp at them with attachment. This means that when one understands, one understands that which is believed; when one practices, one practices that which has been understood;
and when one realizes, one realizes that which has been practiced. The three contemplations—quiescence, illusion, and stillness—are enumerated below in the text.

The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "This Sage’s essential regulation is that one wishes, in a single thought-moment, to universally encompass the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time throughout the Dharma-realm, as well as the Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the ten directions within the Dharma-realm; to deliver and liberate sentient beings in a single thought-moment;

to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings in a single thought-moment; and for those who cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle within a single thought-moment, to cause them to achieve it immediately even before they have reached completion."

Accomplishment. Within a single thought-moment, one contemplates that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained perfect enlightenment within my heart, have established all sons within my heart, and abide in the secret treasury within my heart. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"I have placed my children within the secret treasury, and I too shall not long remain outside it; this is what that means.
If one is not in such a state, one must skillfully employ the mind; for if it is not this ground of the mind, it can never be attained."
Good son, if sentient beings practice *śamatha*, they first grasp at ultimate stillness and do not give rise to thoughts.
When stillness reaches its peak, awareness arises;
thus, in the practice of the calm observation of *śamatha*, one first severs discursive thought. Once the power of stillness has reached its limit, it naturally opens.
Awakening.
Thus, in this initial stage of stillness, from a single body to a single world, one first practices the contemplation of stillness;
at the outset, one realizes that within and without the single body there is no stirring of thought, and gradually one perceives that the nature of stillness pervades all.
It fills a single world-system.
Awakening is also like this:

when stillness reaches its ultimate limit and awakening occurs, one first realizes that the characteristics of the body are not empty, and gradually perceives that the Dharma-body pervades everywhere.
[This occurs] within a single world-system.
Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "This is 'quiescent observation. Not perceiving the existence of a body is called 'quiescence';
that which is immediately aware is 'wisdom. Quiescence is the essence and is samādhi; awareness is wisdom and is its function. Thus it is for the practitioner."
When this contemplation is first accomplished, one does not perceive the marks of one's own body; this is called "the stillness of the single body.
Because when the body is still, its very substance is awakening, it is called "the awakening of the single body.
When one no longer perceives the existence of mountains, rivers, the great earth, or the world, this wisdom likewise pervades the entire world; therefore, it is said to be "thus."
"Good son, if one’s awakening pervades a single world-system, one is able to know every single thought that arises in even a single sentient being within that world-system;
it is likewise so for hundreds of thousands of world-systems."
The nature of my awakening is of the same substance as empty space, and all sentient beings are within this nature of my awakening;
therefore, there is no thought that arises which is not known.

Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "As for the thoughts of sentient beings, since the world has already fully become awakening and sentient beings are entirely within awakening, the thoughts they give rise to are all thoroughly understood and realized, like a reflection entering a mirror."
A mirror reflects everything without omission; it is like an image entering a jar—the jar should have no confusion regarding it.

The Four Illuminations Master Cong said: "These three contemplations are clearly explained texts. Before the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng) reached this land, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also presented the three contemplations;
'śamatha' is one of them. Furthermore, they appear in the *Adornment Sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng), which clarifies their sequential order."
The three contemplations—namely, emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—are described as follows in the latter fascicle: "From the Buddha’s crown and hair, all manner of light was emitted.
He then gathered the assembly of bodhisattvas from ten billion buddha-lands throughout the ten directions.
There, in the midst of that assembly, he addressed Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Dharmamati, Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, Vajradhvaja, Vajragarbha, and the youth Sudhana: 'Do you see this...'"

Among the assembly, the Bodhisattva Jingshou (Gaganagañja) asked about the three contemplations of the dharma-realm, the path of the self-nature purity of all Buddhas, and whether these are indeed the dharma-gates of the three contemplations practiced by all bodhisattvas. "Each of you should lead a great multitude of one million followers;
all should study and practice them. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Dharmas produced through causes and conditions—I say they are empty; they are also called..."
It is a provisional designation, and it is also called the meaning of the Middle Way. These are all clear textual proofs arising from the threefold contemplation of the one mind.
Now, what is called *śamatha* is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Emptiness takes ultimate stillness as its meaning. Stillness is like turbid water:
when it is settled, it becomes still; when still, it is pure. When pure, where would there be anything that is not clear? What object would there be that is not...

Purity. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates everywhere; in silent illumination, it encompasses empty space. Returning to observe the world, it is like a dream.
If one grasps this meaning of emptiness, it subverts all phenomena; there is no phenomenon that is not subverted. To "subvert" means to sweep away.
It sweeps away and destroys the afflictions (*kleśa*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the entanglements of craving, and the illusory, provisional, and false constructs of form and mind.
If there were no emptiness to dismantle them, one would cling to them as being existent and undergo the cycle of saṃsāra.
If emptiness treats them, then the four great elements, the five aggregates, and the notions of self, person, sentient beings, and life-span will all be free from attachment to signs.

How much more so for the ignorance, karmic consciousness, and inverted views of sentient beings—if they were not treated by the medicine of emptiness, birth and death would never be brought to an end. First, attain ultimate stillness and do not give rise [to thoughts].
Regarding "recollection": this refers to the "stopping that realizes the truth" (*tattva-sthiti*) among the three types of stopping.

It means: my mind contains all phenomena; it possesses all phenomena; all phenomena are my mind. Now, by means of this space, I further stifle delusion. Stopping is the cessation of攀缘 (*pān-yuan*, objective conditions);
stopping the distracted mind is the attainment of a tranquil mind. When the mind is tranquil, it reaches the ultimate stillness. Stillness...
At the ultimate limit, all phenomena are pure within the single mind, like the bright moon facing ten thousand images.
Thus it is said that from one body to one world, there is nothing that is not Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). This pure mind pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
if a single sentient being within a single world gives rise to a single thought, it is comprehended by means of the mind of Perfect Enlightenment.
One illuminates them with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; thus, one is able to know all sentient beings throughout hundreds of thousands of worlds.
First, employ the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). This contemplation serves as the vanguard, clearing a path through mountains and building bridges over waters;
for destroying all evils, nothing is superior to emptiness. If the mind is distracted, use "stopping by means of the true essence" (*tattva-śamatha*); if it is dull, use emptiness to clarify it.
All phenomena are empty. First employ the contemplation of emptiness, which is *śamatha*.
One must never grasp at any of those perceived objects that have been heard.
Chan Master Furan Hui of Xishu said: "This is a warning against grasping at perverse objects. The Tiantai teachings state:

Whenever one is in a state of meditative concentration, if one perceives auspicious signs, one should verify them by means of three methods. The first is to polish them with meditative concentration."
Second, cultivating and refining based on the fundamental; third, observing with wisdom.
This is like people in the world who wish to know genuine gold and test it by three methods: first, burning; second, striking; and third, rubbing—as explained in the *Lengyan chao*.
Formerly, there was a Chan master sitting in meditation in the mountains who suddenly saw a filial son carrying a corpse.
He came before the Master and, putting on his mourning clothes, wept, saying, "How could you kill my mother?
The Master knew this was a demon and thought to himself, "This is a demonic realm; if I were to take an axe and chop it away, would that not bring liberation?
He then took an axe from a pillar and struck once. The filial son fled. Later, he noticed his thigh was wet, and upon looking at it, he saw—
Blood flowed from his body; it was not intentional, yet he had cut himself. Furthermore, there was a Zen master who, while sitting in meditation, saw a pig come before him.
Thinking it was a demon, the master seized the pig by its snout and cried out, "Bring fire!
When the junior disciples came to look, they saw that the Master was merely holding his own nose and shouting. These instances are all examples of sitting in right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
When practicing dhyāna, if views arise within the mind, external māras will consequently be induced to enter.
This is precisely why the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* speaks of fifty kinds of māras in relation to the five aggregates (skandhas). It is for this reason.
The Lecturer Cong of Siming said: "This refers to those heterodox factions who teach people to speak of 'false emptiness.

They mistakenly direct their biased and small minds toward pure *tathatā*, stubborn emptiness (*wankong*), analytical emptiness (*xikong*), or illusory emptiness (*huanchua kong*). Ordinary people do not recognize these;

they study such heterodox methods, intending to cure the sickness of the mind, yet the sickness becomes even deeper. This is the fault and error of false teachers. Furthermore, there is another kind [of person]..."

For the sake of clothing and food, they endure various sufferings and study heterodox arts; their minds are exhausted and their bodies weary, and even if they achieve mastery in these studies, both body and mind remain in pain.
Furthermore, there is another class of those who affiliate with the Dharma through external learning;

relying on their own deluded interpretations and heterodox views, they attach themselves to what is taught in the Buddha-dharma, falsely citing sutras and treatises to validate their own evil knowledge and perverted realizations.

Lust, anger, and delusion do not obstruct *prajñā*, for afflictions do not hinder bodhi. To practice walking meditation or sitting meditation while failing to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is to mistake mere terminology;

such doubts will surely affect future generations. To force oneself to speak with superficial eloquence at the outset, to plagiarize the Buddha-dharma, and to covet offerings and profit—how could one know that calamity would reach one’s future retribution? Seeing this, how can one not feel a chill in one's heart? All [of you].
The Buddha’s established teachings are not within this realm; they can ultimately never be grasped. My teacher has shown such compassion; how then could one possibly put them into practice?
"Good son, if sentient beings cultivate samāpatti, they should first bring to mind the Tathāgatas of the ten directions."
All Bodhisattvas of the worlds in the ten directions, relying on various gateways, practice gradually through the samādhi of diligent effort.
To cultivate the illusory contemplation of *samāpatti*, they must first bring to mind all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas so that the mind does not become distracted;
only then do they rely upon these various Dharma-gates to gradually cultivate right concentration.
Extensively issue great vows to personally cultivate and form the seeds [of enlightenment].
Extensively issue the most supreme vows, thereby using self-cultivation to establish the seed-nature for attaining Buddhahood.

Master Fu’an Huì of Xichuan said: "This is the contemplation of illusion (*māyā-darśana*). It precedes the contemplation of ultimate stillness (*śānti-darśana*) and does not depend on external [conditions]."
Regarding the conditions: within the present gateway of the contemplation of illusion (*māyā-darśana*), one must rely upon the sacred realm (*ārya-viṣaya*).

While the previous chapter on the contemplation of illusion under "Majestic Virtue" (*vīrya*) concerned the manifestation of beings through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), here, within the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), one first cultivates through self-discipline;

therefore, it concerns the seeking of Buddhahood through great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*). As for "making a vow" (*praṇidhāna*): "exertion" refers to the mobilization of the mind, while "aspiration" refers to the longing and desire for attainment. Thus, [it is said that] the multitude...
Since beginningless time, one has been born with a mind that, in every thought-moment, seeks and desires the objects of bliss, desire, compassion, wisdom, and the six perfections;
these have perfumed the mind and formed habitual tendencies.
Master Cong of Siming said: "This contemplation takes illusory transformation as its characteristic; it establishes the provisional contemplation by taking the meaning of 'contemplation'."

Among all phenomena (*dharmas*), none surpasses the provisional (*prajñapti*). This provisionality arises from the emptiness of original nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), wherein all phenomena are fully present:

the ten realms, the hundred realms, the thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*), the myriad phenomena in their array, and both heavenly and hellish states—all are inherently and originally possessed within this nature.

This is termed "the provisional. These dharmas inherent in nature do not diminish by even a single dharma; every phenomenon remains distinct and complete. That which is called "the provisional" is established upon...

All dharmas are not produced or established through effort; they are inherently complete. Speaking in terms of *śamatha* (calm abiding), all these aforementioned dharmas are themselves the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and the pervasive mark (*vyāpilakṣaṇa*).
Because the mind remains unmoving while following conditions and encountering objects, it is called "convenience-śamatha according to conditions" (*pratyayānuvartana-upāya-śamatha*).
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All meditative concentrations that gather the mind are termed..."
Samāpatti means, in the language of Qin, "the sphere of correct mental activity.

If a bodhisattva, in order to deliver sentient beings, enters the provisional realm to transform them, they encounter the various ailments of sentient beings, as numerous as dust motes or grains of sand. The bodhisattva’s medicinal Dharma cures these dust-and-sand-like illnesses.

Out of compassion, they endure toil; appearing and disappearing in accordance with shifting circumstances, they manifest in various forms, such as Avalokiteśvara as the Horse-herder Maiden, Maitreya, and Master Fu Dashi.
Yet, in their earnest cultivation and realization, they forget their weariness for the sake of the Dharma, dividing their bodies and dispersing their shadows.
Master Benping’s vase-flower bath, Lazy Zhan’s dung-fire yam, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, and Hanshan and Shide—all are emanated beings who manifest for the sake of others.
Therefore, it is said that all Bodhisattvas, relying on various gateways, gradually cultivate and diligently practice the samādhi of austerity.
From the stage of an ordinary person to that of a sage, one can thus transform one's own熏 (xūn, perfuming) into seeds.
If you keep this in mind, you will see that throughout the ten directions, no Tathāgata has ever failed to deliver sentient beings and attain Buddhahood;
having made the Four Great Vows to benefit all sentient beings, they should cultivate the Three Contemplations.
"One must never grasp at any objects perceived by the ears;
this has already been explained above.
Master Fu-an Hui of Xi-chu said: "This is a warning against grasping at deviant objects."
"Good son, if sentient beings cultivate *dhyāna*, they must first employ the method of counting (*gaṇanā*) to practice the tranquil contemplation of *dhyāna*.
First, they must personally know the various categories and the specific counts of their deluded thoughts."

Therefore, it is called the "gate of counting" (*gaṇanā-mukha*). The *Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué shù*) also states: "The mind-objects of arising and ceasing thoughts are precisely the gate of counting.
Within the mind, one clearly knows the specific quantities and divisions of the thoughts of arising, abiding, and ceasing."
Within the wondrously luminous mind, one clearly knows for oneself the four types of mental states: arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. "Arising" refers to the initial emergence of thought;
"abiding" refers to the present state of thought; "changing" refers to the state of differentiation; and "ceasing" refers to the state of quiescent extinction.
As for the absence of the word "changing" in the sutra, it was omitted for the sake of forming a complete phrase. *The Complete Enlightenment Sutra*.
In the *Śāstra*, it is also stated thus:
"In this way, one discerns and counts [the breath] throughout all four postures; there is nothing that is not clearly known.
Within the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, there are various ways of counting the breaths, none of which remain unknown."
Master Cifuan Hui of Xishu said: "This is the contemplation of stillness (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). As for the term 'counting' (*shu*), the character is pronounced in the third tone;
this refers to the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*). It means to harmonize the breath so that it is neither too constricted nor too slippery.
When counting, one proceeds from one to ten, keeping the mind focused on the count to prevent it from wandering or scattering. This is truly because of the practice of counting the breath."

Therefore, as the breath becomes regulated and the mind purified, one ultimately attains thorough penetration and realization. Within the mind, there is nothing unknown regarding the four phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;
the coarse and subtle deluded thoughts; their origins and endings; their boundaries and divisions; and their sequences and quantities. Why is this so?
This is because when the mind is still, one perceives movement. As for the absence of the word "different" (*i*) in the current scripture, it is a case of omission.

According to what is taught in the *Śāstra*, ordinary beings at the stage of the ten faiths perceive the characteristic of extinction; those of the three stages of worthiness perceive the characteristic of difference; those of the ten stages perceive the characteristic of abiding;

and those who have perfected their position perceive the characteristic of arising. As for the characteristic of arising, all stirring thoughts are entirely exhausted, and there remains only the single mind.
The preceding passage refers to being aware during the act of sitting; however, it is not only while sitting that one perceives these as delusions.

Rather, throughout the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—one must recognize the four characteristics of thought, their coarse and subtle aspects, their origins and endings, and their various threads and quantities.
One knows them all at once. Once known, there is no affliction. It is like a malevolent spirit wishing to possess a person;
if one knows its name, it naturally vanishes. This is what is meant by "knowing a thief to be a thief"—the thief can do nothing. These are the several methods.

This is the gateway among the five methods of mental abiding (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-pratipakṣa*). What are the five? First, for sentient beings with excessive greed, the Buddha directs them to enter the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Second, for sentient beings with excessive anger, the Buddha directs them to enter the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*).

Third, for sentient beings with excessive distraction, the Buddha directs them to enter the contemplation of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*). Fourth, for sentient beings with excessive delusion, the Buddha directs them to enter the contemplation of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*). Fifth...
For sentient beings with many obstacles, the Buddha causes them to enter the contemplation of mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti).
As they gradually progress, they eventually come to know even a single drop of rain in hundreds of thousands of worlds as clearly as if they were seeing an object directly before their eyes.
If one maintains mindfulness in every thought throughout walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, then the power of awakening will gradually advance and its essence will become all-pervasive.
Thus, even a single drop of rain within any world-system is perceived as if seen directly before one's eyes.

Chan Master Fuyan Hui of Xishu said: "To say that the pure mind is the self-substance of Perfect Enlightenment, and that the world is fundamentally contained within it—when contemplative practice is perfected, one is entirely in accord with the source.
To know the number of raindrops is certainly appropriate for one's fundamental capacity;
not only raindrops, but all things are likewise so. One example illustrates many; let us take raindrops as our illustration. However..."
Ordinary beings of this sort are deluded regarding this true mind; they follow what their thoughts perceive, and thus lose its function. Even Xunzi said:
"The gentleman nourishes the subtlety of the One and dwells in the precariousness of the One. As for the mechanism of the precarious and the subtle, the gentleman is able to know it.
The *Book of Documents* says: "The human mind is indeed precarious; the Dao-mind is indeed subtle. Only through refinement and unity may one truly uphold it."
Regarding the middle [stage]: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that when the Dragon King sends down rain, even Maheśvara knows the number of drops;
how much more so for a practitioner who contemplates it? If one has reached ultimate realization, one knows this only upon attaining the stage of Buddhahood.
However, in the context of contemplation, because wondrous wisdom is generated, it is permitted that what is seen is identical to that of a Buddha.
None of those objects of perception heard by him can ever be grasped;
this has already been explained above.
This is called the preliminary skillful means for the initial stage of the three contemplations.
The stillness grasped through śamatha, the mindfulness of samāpatti, the methods of counting in dhyāna, and the three contemplations—
these are the practices for the initial commencement.

Master Xifu Huishan of Western Shu said: "Regarding the phrase 'this is called the initial expedient of the three contemplations,' the Bodhisattvas in the preceding *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* asked:

'Which of the three kinds of pure contemplations takes precedence? Therefore, this concluding response states that practicing stillness, illusion, and quiescence alone constitutes the initial expedient."
Master Cong of Siming said: "The statement that 'none of those perceived objects can ultimately be grasped' refers to one who emerges from the provisional to transform sentient beings;

this involves the world and is most difficult. Although one may manifest a hundred billion bodies, the inner mind must remain unmoved, like King Wondrous Adornment (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa*), who, though frequently encountering sounds and forms, was never moved by them. Furthermore, during the Buddha’s lifetime, there was a poor man."
He gave birth to twin sons; one was named Shuangfu (Double Fortune) and the other was named Shuangde (Double Virtue).

When they were about forty or fifty days old, the father went out to plow the fields and the mother went out to gather firewood. While the two children were conversing within their bedchamber, the father suddenly returned home.
Upon seeing and hearing them speak thus—“We were born into a poor and lowly family, and our parents toil with great hardship; how can we bear this feeling?”—he was deeply moved.
The father was struck with wonder and told his wife of it, but she did not believe him. Later, the husband and wife went out again; the wife returned first and secretly observed them.
The two sons acted exactly as had been described before, without any difference. The wife said, "I fear these are spirits or demons," and wished to pile up firewood and burn them alive.
The husband and wife each took one son and went to a place in the fields. From afar, the Buddha’s eye [beheld them].

As for the twelve divisions of the Buddha’s scriptures, they are the pure eyes, precisely because they investigate the root of delusion and illuminate the source of awakening; thus, as for the principle—
It penetrates all the scriptures, leaving no meaning unexhausted. If one understands this, then all the teachings will become as clear as seeing the palm of one's hand.
